en: It is distant;
that is what is called an "obscuration."
The causes by which those who are destined for parinirvāṇa do not yet attain parinirvāṇa are these four.
When they have obtained the appearance of a Buddha, the sublime Dharma, and the instructions and teachings that accord with it, and even those causes have ceased to exist,
at that time their roots of virtue will reach full maturity and they will gradually pass into parinirvāṇa.
It will become so.
Those whose nature is not to pass into parinirvāṇa abide in the group of the fixed;
whether they encounter the necessary conditions or do not encounter them,
they are entirely and in every respect devoid of the fortune to pass into parinirvāṇa.
For those who are subject to parinirvāṇa, what are the conditions for not attaining parinirvāṇa that are incomplete, absent, and have not come to pass?
It was said: "There are two conditions. Which two?"
The primary and the subordinate.
(I)-A-II-4-a What is the primary condition?
It is said:
That is to say:
the voice of others concerning the sublime Dharma, and internal appropriate mental attention.
What is a deficient condition?
It is said:
The inferior conditions are many,
namely:
self-perfection (*ātmasaṃpat*).
The excellence of others, wholesome desire for the Dharma,
and going forth.
Restraint of moral discipline, restraint of the sense faculties,
and moderation in eating.
Devotion to wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night,
and dwelling with clear comprehension.
Seclusion, purification from the hindrances,
and reliance upon meditative concentration.
(Śbh I 10) In that regard, what is my own prosperity?
It is being born as a human being.
Being born in a central land,
having unimpaired faculties,
and possessing serene confidence regarding the [spiritual] sources.
The state of having unerring conduct in one's actions.
In that regard, what is human status?
It is when a certain person here is reborn into the commonality of humans;
and [in the case of] a male, he is endowed with the male faculty, and likewise for a female.
This is called humanity.
What is rebirth in a noble realm?
It is when someone here is reborn in the central regions,
as previously described, up to where there is the movement of virtuous persons.
This is called rebirth in a noble realm.
What is the non-deficiency of the sense faculties?
It is as follows: here, a certain person is not dull-witted and not deaf, and so forth;

or he is not deficient in his major and minor limbs, such that by virtue of this non-deficiency of major and minor limbs—beginning with the non-deficiency of the ears—he is capable of accomplishing the side of wholesome qualities.
This is called the non-deficiency of the faculties.
What is clarity directed toward the [right] sphere?
It is when someone here has acquired faith in the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, resulting in clarity of mind;
this is called clarity directed toward the sphere.
In this context, the "basis" (āyatana) is the Dharma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, for the arising of all mundane and supramundane wholesome qualities (*śukladharma*).
Furthermore, the faith that exists therein, preceded by and dominated by that [basis], is the clarity (*prasāda*) pertaining to the basis,
because it removes the turbidity of the stains of all afflictions (*kleśa*).
(Śbh I 12) What is the state of having non-perverted actions?
It is that by which [one avoids] the five actions of immediate retribution...

For example, from killing one’s mother, killing one’s father, killing an arhat, causing a schism in the Saṅgha, or drawing blood with a malicious mind from a Tathāgata— when any such immediate (ānantarya) karma has not been committed nor practiced in this very life,
this is called "having unturned karma."
These five actions of immediate retribution, when committed and accumulated, cannot—once they have been diverted in this very life—lead to parinirvāṇa or to the arising of the noble path;
therefore, these are called "the turning away from the end of karma."
By this very [person], that personal existence (ātmabhāva) is accomplished through these five factors;
therefore, it is called "perfection of self" (ātmasaṃpad).
What is the excellence of others?
It is as follows: the arising of Buddhas and the teaching of the true Dharma.
The preservation of the teachings that have been taught, the continued practice of those teachings once they have been preserved,
and compassion toward others.
In that regard, what is the arising of the Buddhas?

It is as follows: here, a certain person, having generated a resolute intention for the welfare and benefit of all sentient beings, through many thousands of difficult feats and by means of a great accumulation of merit and wisdom, [over the course of three incalculable eons, in his final body...]
Having attained this body and having sat upon the seat of enlightenment,
he abandoned the five hindrances and established his mind well in the four foundations of mindfulness.
Having cultivated the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, one fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
This is called the arising of the Buddhas.
In exactly this same way, all the Blessed Buddhas arise in suchness throughout the past, future, and present times.
(Śbh I 14) What is the teaching of the true Dharma?

Those very Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, having arisen in the world, and their disciples as well, out of compassion for the world, undertake the teaching of the Dharma concerning the four noble truths— the suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

Namely: the discourses (sūtra), songs (geya), prophecies (vyākaraṇa), verses (gāthā), inspired utterances (udāna), introductory narratives (nidāna), legends (avadāna), historical accounts (itivṛttaka), birth stories (jātaka), extensive teachings (vaipulya), marvelous events (adbhutadharma), and instructions (upadeśa).
This is called the teaching of the true Dharma;
this Dharma has been brought forth, taught, and praised by the virtuous—the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas.
[Therefore, the sublime Dharma— that which explains it— is called "the teaching of the sublime Dharma.
What is the persistence of the dharmas that have been taught?
From the time the true Dharma is taught and the wheel of Dharma is set in motion, as long as the Buddha, the Blessed One, lives and remains,
and even after the Buddha, the Blessed One, has passed into parinirvāṇa, for as long as practice does not decline and the true Dharma does not disappear—
this is called the duration of the true Dharma.
That abiding, moreover, should be understood as being by way of the direct realization of the ultimate dharma.
What is the subsequent engagement with established dharmas?

It is when those very realizers, having recognized that people possess the capacity and fitness for the direct realization of the true dharma, provide them with conformable instruction and admonition exactly as they themselves have realized it.
They continue to function; this is called the continued functioning of established phenomena.
What is sympathetic concern for others?

Others are said to be donors and masters of giving; they show sympathetic concern for one with those life-sustaining requisites that are conducive [to one's practice], namely, robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for use in sickness.
This is called compassion for others.

What is wholesome desire for the Dharma? It is when, for instance, a certain person, having heard the Dharma from the presence of a Tathāgata or a disciple of a Tathāgata, acquires faith; having acquired that [faith],...
He trains himself thus:

"Household life is cramped, an abode of dust; going forth is like the open air. What if I were to renounce my entire circle of kinsmen, wealth, grain, and gold, and go forth from the home to the homeless state, rightly following the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya?"
"And having gone forth, may I accomplish it through practice.
This very desire that has arisen for wholesome qualities is called "wholesome desire for the Dharma."

What is renunciation (*pravrajyā*)? It is that which, having made that very same wholesome desire for the Dharma (*dharmacchanda*) the dominant influence, consists either of full ordination (*upasaṃpad*) through a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*jñapticaturtha-karman*), or the undertaking of the novice’s ethical discipline (*śrāmaṇera-śīla*). This is called renunciation.
What is the restraint of ethical discipline? Having thus gone forth, he dwells possessed of ethical discipline,
restrained by the restraint of the Prātimokṣa.
He is perfected in conduct and sphere of activity,
perceives danger in even the slightest faults,
and trains himself by undertaking the precepts of training.
This is called the restraint of ethical discipline.
What is restraint of the sense faculties?

Relying upon that very restraint of ethical discipline, he becomes one whose mindfulness is guarded, one of constant mindfulness, whose mind is protected by mindfulness, and who dwells in a state of equanimity.
Having seen forms with the eye, he does not seize upon their signs.
He does not grasp at secondary characteristics,
because, on that basis, evil and unwholesome states might flow into his mind;
therefore, he practices restraint over them.
He practices correctly,
guards the faculty of the eye,
and achieves restraint through the faculty of the eye.
He [perceives] sounds with the ear, odors with the nose,
and tastes with the tongue.
Having cognized tangible objects with the body and mental phenomena with the mind, one does not grasp at their signs nor grasp at their secondary characteristics— that is,
those conditions through which evil, unwholesome states might flow into the mind.
He practices for their restraint;
he guards the faculty of mind;
he achieves restraint through the faculty of mind.
This is called restraint of the sense faculties.
What is moderation in eating?
Having thus restrained the sense faculties, he takes food with wise reflection,
not for the sake of intoxication, not for the sake of pride, not for the sake of beautification, and not for the sake of adornment.
"Only for the maintenance of this body, for its preservation, for the allaying of hunger, and for the support of the holy life;
so that I may eliminate old feelings and not give rise to new ones."
There will be for me sustenance, strength, happiness, blamelessness, and a state of ease;
this is called moderation in eating.
What is the application to wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night?
Being thus moderate in eating, he purifies his mind from obstructive states through walking and sitting during the day.
Having purified his mind from obstructive states through walking and sitting during the first watch of the night, he...

Then, having gone out from the monastery and washed his feet outside the monastery, he prepares the lion’s posture on his right side, placing one foot upon the other, perceiving light, mindful and clearly comprehending, and directing his mind specifically toward the perception of rising.

Having awakened very quickly during the final watch of the night, he purifies his mind of obstructive states through walking and sitting. This is called being devoted to wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night.
What is dwelling with clear comprehension?

Being thus devoted to wakefulness, he dwells with clear comprehension in going forth and returning; in looking ahead and looking aside; in bending and stretching [the limbs]; in carrying the outer robe, the inner robe, and the bowl; and in eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting.
Whether dispelling drowsiness and fatigue, walking, standing, sitting, lying down, waking, speaking, or remaining silent, he dwells with clear comprehension.
This is called dwelling with clear comprehension.
What is seclusion?

Having purified the ground for practice by means of these qualities, he dwells in secluded lodgings: in forests, at the foot of trees, in empty dwellings, in mountain clefts, mountain caves, straw huts, open spaces, cemeteries, woods, or wilderness tracts.
Remote lodgings and seats— this is called seclusion.
What is the purification of the hindrances?
Having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, he purifies his mind from the five hindrances:
from sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.
Having purified the mind of these hindrances, he establishes it, free from hindrances, in the serviceability of concentration;
this is called the purification of the hindrances.
(ii) (iii) (iv)
What is the basis of concentration? Having abandoned the five hindrances— which are defilements and afflictions that disturb the mind—

he, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion.

With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, through internal clarity and the unification of the mind, he enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is without applied or sustained thought, born of concentration, and characterized by rapture and bliss.

Through detachment from joy, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending; he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones say, "He who is equanimous and mindful dwells in happiness," and thus he enters and dwells in the third dhyāna.

Through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and through the prior disappearance of mental ease and distress, he enters and dwells in the fourth [dhyāna], which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness.
Having attained meditative absorption, he dwells therein;
this is called the basis of concentration.

In this sequence, he brings together successive conditions— each more distinguished, more distinguished than the last, and most distinguished— which begin with the perfection of one's own being and culminate in the reliance upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
When the mind has thus become completely pure, cleansed, free from blemish, devoid of secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), upright, pliable, stable, and attained to imperturbability,
If, with reference to the four noble truths, one receives from another the voice of instruction and admonition for their full comprehension, abandonment, realization, and cultivation,
then such a person becomes capable and competent to generate the mental attention established by yoga and the right view preceded by it,
through which one directly realizes the four noble truths.
He fulfills liberation and attains final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder.
In this regard, that fulfillment of liberation based on right view and the attainment of nirvana without remainder should be understood as the realization of the lineage (*gotra*).
In this context, from the attainment of self-perfection up to the reliance upon meditative concentration, this should be understood as the inferior condition for realization. Therein,

that voice from another which has the teaching and instruction of the Four Noble Truths as its dominant influence, and that which is wise attention— this should be understood as the primary condition for realization.
This is called the establishment of the spiritual lineages.
(Śbh I 24) (I)-A-III What are the characteristics of a person who abides in the spiritual lineage (*gotrastha*)?
He said:
"The characteristics of a person established in the lineage should be understood as being the opposite of those characteristics of one who lacks the nature for final nirvana."
(I)-A-III’ What, then, are the marks of one whose nature is not to attain parinirvāṇa, by which a person endowed with them is to be known as “one whose nature is not to attain parinirvāṇa”?
He said:
There are many signs of those whose nature is not to attain parinirvāṇa, but I shall explain only a portion of them.

(I)-A-III-a) Here, for a person whose nature is not to attain parinirvāṇa, from the very beginning, the craving for the *ālaya*— residing in the basis (*āśraya*)— is such that it cannot be abandoned by any Buddhas in any way whatsoever;
it is difficult to suppress, deeply rooted, and firmly established.
This is the first sign of a person who does not abide in a spiritual lineage.
Furthermore, another person who abides in the absence of lineage,
having heard through many methods the various and abundant faults of saṃsāra,
Having heard, through many discourses, of the manifold and abundant qualities of nirvāṇa,

he has not produced— even for a mere moment— a vision of the faults, a vision of the dangers, or even a slight sense of spiritual urgency regarding the limited proliferation of saṃsāra, based on the past time, nor will he produce it based on the future time.

With reference to the present time, he did not produce even a slight, inferior degree of vision of qualities, vision of benefits, or mere clarity regarding nirvana, the destruction of craving, dispassion, and cessation; nor, with reference to the past, future, and present times, had he ever produced such [vision].
He will not produce [the thought of awakening], nor does he produce it;
this is the second mark of one who abides in the absence of lineage.
(Śbh I 26) Furthermore, another type of person is one who abides in the absence of lineage (*agotra*).
From the very beginning, he is endowed with an excessive lack of shame and lack of dread;
by means of this, he possesses a heart devoid of compassion, a heart without hesitation, and a joyful heart, whereby he commits every kind of evil,
and never at any time feels remorse on that account.
One perceives that this basis results merely in the ruin of one's very self, including its worldly possessions in this life;
this is the third sign of being established in the absence of lineage.
Furthermore, another person not abiding in a spiritual lineage (*agotrastha*),

when the true Dharma is being taught— whether concerning suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path— in a manner that is complete in all aspects, clear, logical, diverse, and intelligible, does not obtain even a mere turning of the mind.
And let alone merely attaining a state of mental resolve—
such as the bristling of body hair or the welling up of tears.
Based on the past, future, and present time periods,
this is the fourth sign of one who does not abide in a spiritual lineage (agotra).
Furthermore, another person who abides in the absence of lineage (agotra),
if at any time or on any occasion goes forth into homelessness within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya,
Whether he has been condemned by the king,
or accused by thieves, or afflicted by debt, or afflicted by fear, or terrified by the fear of losing his livelihood;
not for the sake of self-taming,
not for the sake of self-pacification, and not for the sake of one's own parinirvāṇa; (Śbh I 28)
It is not for the sake of being a śramaṇa, nor for the sake of being a brāhmaṇa;
likewise, even though he has gone forth, he remains together with householders and those who have gone forth.
Having made a vow, he practices the holy life with the thought, "May I become a god or one of the gods," or else, having renounced the training, he proceeds toward its abandonment.
Or he may be immoral, inwardly rotten, leaking, full of filth, with conduct like the sound of a conch shell;

though not a śramaṇa, he claims to be a śramaṇa, and though not a practitioner of celibacy, he claims to be a practitioner of celibacy. For a person who does not abide in the lineage (agotrastha), such is to be understood as their renunciation throughout the past, future, and present times.

Furthermore, for a person who does not desire training, there is no going forth, no full ordination, and no status as a monk. Therefore, by this method and with this intention, it follows that such a person is designated as "one who has gone forth" only in name, because they merely assume the signs and dress of one who has gone forth, but have not actually gone forth.
This is the fifth mark of a person who does not abide in a spiritual lineage.

Furthermore, another [characteristic] of a person who abides in the absence of lineage (*agotra*) is that whatever wholesome action they perform— whether by body, speech, or mind— [is not directed toward liberation].
All that is performed either with the intention for existence— desiring a distinguished rebirth in the future—
or with the intention for enjoyments— desiring distinguished enjoyments.
This is the sixth characteristic of a person who does not abide in a spiritual lineage (agotra).
Furthermore, many such signs exist for him, endowed with which one who is of a nature not to attain parinirvāṇa is reckoned as "one of a nature not to attain parinirvāṇa."
In that regard, who are the persons established in the lineage (*gotrastha*)?
He replied:
There is a person who abides in the lineage:
one who abides in the lineage alone, having neither entered nor emerged; and one who abides in the lineage and has entered, but has not yet emerged.
One who abides in the lineage, one who has entered, one who has emerged, one with dull faculties, and one with medium faculties.
one of sharp faculties, one whose temperament is dominated by passion, or one whose temperament is dominated by hatred; (Śbh I 30)
one whose conduct is dominated by delusion,
one reborn in an inopportune state, and one reborn in an opportune state.
The negligent,
the non-negligent,
and the one who has entered upon a wrong course.
One who has entered upon a wrong course, one who is obstructed, one who is unobstructed, and one who is far away.
Near and far,
mature and immature,
pure and impure.
(I)-A-IV-a.
In this regard, who is the person established in the lineage (*gotrastha*) who remains merely in the lineage, having neither entered nor emerged?
It is, for example, a certain person here who is endowed with the seeds of supramundane dharmas (*lokottaradharma*).
Furthermore, even now he has not yet obtained, by relying on association with virtuous persons or hearing the true Dharma, faith in the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata;
he does not undertake ethical discipline,
nor does he grasp what he has heard.
He does not increase his renunciation,
nor does he straighten his view;
this one remains merely within the lineage, having neither entered nor emerged.
(I)-A-IV-b.
Who is the one established in the lineage who has entered but not yet emerged?
By the opposite of the previously explained dark side—that is, by way of the white side—one should understand him to be both established in the lineage and having entered.
But this is the distinction: he is not yet an attainer of the noble path, its fruit, and the dissociation from the afflictions.
(I)-A-IV-c.
Who is the one who abides in the lineage (*gotrastha*), has entered [the path] (*avatīrṇa*), and has emerged [from it] (*niṣkrānta*)?
Having stated this very same thing, the distinction is that he becomes a possessor of the noble path (*āryamārga*), its fruit, and the dissociation from the afflictions (*kleśavisaṃyoga*).
(I)-A-IV-d.
What is the person of dull faculties?
It is that person for whom, regarding the object of knowledge (*jñeya-vastu*), [the realization arises slowly].

When the faculties proceed extremely slowly or sluggishly with respect to their object— whether associated with attention consisting of hearing, reflection, or cultivation— and when faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, or wisdom are neither capable nor powerful for the penetration of the Dharma, nor for the swift penetration of its meaning or reality, such a person is called one of dull faculties.
(I)-A-IV-e.

What is one of medium faculties? It is one whose faculties proceed neither too slowly nor too quickly with respect to the object of knowledge as the focal point; all [details] should be stated in full as before.
This is called a person of middling faculties.
(I)-A-IV-f.
Who is the person with sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*)?
It is that person whose faculties proceed without sluggishness and proceed without dullness toward the object of knowledge as their focal point.
Those [mental factors] associated with attention consisting of hearing, reflection, or cultivation—
namely, faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, or wisdom— are capable of penetrating the Dharma or its meaning, and of swiftly penetrating reality;
such a person is called one of sharp faculties.
(I)-A-IV-g. What is a person of passionate temperament (*rāgacarita*)?
It is one who, with respect to an object that incites passion, possesses both intense passion and long-lasting passion.
This is called the person whose temperament is dominated by passion.
(I)-A-IV-h.
What is a person of hateful temperament (*dveṣacarita*)? It is one who, toward an object that is provocative and a basis for aversion, [experiences hatred]. (Śbh I 34)
He possesses intense hatred and enduring hatred;
such a person is called one whose temperament is dominated by hatred.
(I)-A-IV-i.
Who is the person characterized by delusion (*mohacarita*)?
It is one who possesses intense delusion and prolonged delusion regarding the objects of knowledge.
This is called a person whose temperament is dominated by delusion.
(I)-A-IV-j, k, l, m, n, o, p, q Ms.4b5R,
Those who have been reborn in an inopportune state, those who are heedless, those who have entered upon a wrong path, and those who are obscured should be understood as before.
By contrast, those who have been reborn in an opportune state, those who are heedful, those who have not entered upon a wrong path, and those who are unobscured should be understood accordingly.
Who is the person that is distant?
There is the person who is distant from nirvana due to the distance of time, and there is the one who is distant due to the distance of application.

In that regard, what is distant by way of distance in time? It is one who, after many hundreds of births, many thousands of births, or many hundreds of thousands of births, will subsequently become fit— having finally obtained the necessary conditions— to possess the fortune of attaining parinirvāṇa.

Which one is distant by way of distance from application? It is the person who remains in the lineage alone and has not yet entered [the path]; he is capable of quickly attaining the conditions for parinirvāṇa.
Because he has not initiated the application for the sake of nirvāṇa, he is distant due to the distance of his application, not due to the distance of time;
this is called a person who is distant.
What is the person who is near?
There is also the person who is near because they are close in time to passing beyond suffering (*nirvāṇa*).
There is also proximity to nirvāṇa through the proximity of application.
In that regard, what is the proximity of the time for passing beyond suffering?
It is to abide in one's final physical body and dwelling, and to attain parinirvāṇa with that very body;
it is the direct realization of the abandonment of afflictions without interruption at that very moment.
Because the time is near, nirvāṇa is close at hand.
What is proximity through application that leads to proximity to nirvāṇa? It is one who abides in and has entered the lineage;
these, taken together, are called "proximate persons."

(I)-A-IV-t What is the immature person (*aparipakva-pudgala*)? It is that person who has not yet obtained the final body (*antyadeha*), by abiding in which they will attain parinirvāṇa and enter the state of certainty in the rightness (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
This is called an immature person (pudgala).
(I)-A-IV-u. Who is the person who is fully matured (*paripakva*)?
It is one who has obtained their final body, by remaining in which they will attain parinirvāṇa and enter the state of rightness (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Thus, this is called a person who is fully matured.
(I)-A-IV-v What is the impure person? It is a person who has not generated the path of the noble ones.
That which is the fruit of this— the non-realization of freedom from the afflictions— is called an impure person (aviśuddha-pudgala).
(I)-A-IV-w Ms.-,Sh.-,P.11b5:
Who is the person who is purified?
It should be understood as being the opposite of that.
These are to be known as individuals established in the lineage;
that is to say,
those who have not yet entered [the path] are to be caused to enter it.
For the sake of bringing those who are not yet mature to maturity,
and for the sake of purifying those who are not yet purified, the Blessed Buddhas appear in the world and turn the wheels of Dharma.
They are those who establish the foundations of training.
The intermediate summary verse says: "Their nature and their establishment."
The signs and the persons.
All of these, summarized briefly:
The lineage stage is to be understood.
This concludes the lineage stage from the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*.
(Śbh I 40) What is the stage of engagement?

It is said: This nature of entry, this establishment, these signs of those who have entered, and these individuals who have entered— all of that, taken together in brief, is called the "ground of entry."
(I)-B-I What is the nature of that engagement?
In this regard, a person established in the lineage who possesses the dharma of the seed of nirvāṇa—
When a Buddha has appeared and the people of the Middle Country have become— as previously described in detail— neither thieves nor mlecchas,
they will first obtain the opportunity to behold the Buddhas and their disciples, to approach them, and to attend upon them.
Having heard the Dharma from them, they first attain faith, correctly undertake ethical discipline, retain what they have heard, increase their generosity, and purify their views.
Thereafter, through that cause and condition of having correctly adopted the Dharma,
even after the body has disintegrated and that life has completely passed away,
one will obtain superior faculties comprised within the six bases of maturation.
Furthermore, these will also serve as the basis for the arising of the most excellent and supreme forms of faith;

they will also serve as the basis for the undertaking of ethical discipline, the retention of what has been heard, the increase of generosity, and the purification of views— each in their most excellent, supreme, and sublime forms.
Furthermore, those dharmas such as faith that are most excellent, primary, and sublime also become the basis for other maturations;
and those maturations, in turn, become the basis for other virtues that are concordant with supramundane dharmas.
Thus, by generating the power of generosity in which each serves as the cause and support for the other,
one will abide in ever higher stages,
whereby one will enter into parinirvāṇa and the state of absolute certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
That which is the proceeding into a distinguished birth until the attainment of a future mother's body is called "entry."
Why is that?
Because at that time,
he is to attain nirvāṇa.

Because one has entered, correctly entered, and thoroughly entered that which is the path, the track, and the practice for the purpose of proceeding toward nirvāṇa, proceeding gradually, and reaching the ultimate consummation.
Therefore, it is called "having entered," and that is what is meant by the "nature of entering."
(I)-B-II What is the presentation of engagement?
It is the existence of the lineage (*gotra*).
There is engagement,
there is the state of bringing to maturity, and there is maturation.
There is one who has entered [the path] but neither brings others to maturity nor is himself matured;
there is one who has entered and also brings others to maturity but is not himself matured;
and there is one who has entered and is also matured but does not bring others to maturity.
There is also that which has neither entered [the path], nor is it bringing [beings] to maturity, nor is it itself matured.
(I)-B-II-1 What is that lineage?
It is said:
As before.
(I)-B-II-2 What is "entering into that"?
It is when a person established in the lineage, having previously not attained faith in the Dharma and Vinaya spoken by the Tathāgata, [attains it].

That which first occurs as the attainment [of the path], namely, the correct undertaking of ethical discipline, the retention of what has been heard, the cultivation of generosity, and the purification of views, is called "entry."
(I)-B-II-3 What is the state of bringing [beings] to full maturity?
It is when that very person who has thus entered abides in a certain state.
Except for the attainment of the final body that leads to parinirvāṇa and entry into the state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*),

from the point of having entered [the path] onwards, throughout successive births, one perfectly accomplishes faculties that are increasingly superior, preeminent, sublime, and most excellent. (Śbh I 44)
That which performs [this] is called "the state of bringing to full maturity."
(I)-B-II-4 What is that full maturation?
It is that in which he abides.
That which has attained its final body, through which one will enter into parinirvāṇa and the state of correct determination—
this is called "ripened."
What is it that has entered [the path] but neither brings about maturation nor is itself matured?
It is one who, regarding the Dharma and Vinaya spoken by the Tathāgata, has attained everything from initial faith up to the purification of views.
Beyond that, it is when one does not bring about even a single further birth;
this is called "having entered" alone, being neither "bringing to maturity" nor "matured."
What is it that is both entered and brings about maturation, yet is not itself matured?
It is when one has attained everything from initial faith in the Dharma and Vinaya spoken by the Tathāgata up to the purification of one's views.
Prior to that, although they may manifest one, two, or even a great many births,
they have not yet attained their final body— the last body— in which, by remaining, they will pass completely beyond suffering and enter the state of rightness (samyaktva-niyāma).
That is called both "having entered" and "bringing to maturity," yet not "fully matured."
What is it that is both entered [into the path] and matured, yet is not itself that which brings about maturation?
It is as follows:
When that very person who has entered [the path] dwells in such a way,
they obtain and acquire their final body, by means of which they will pass completely beyond suffering and enter into the state of certainty in the rightness of the goal.
That is to say:
it is both entered and fully matured.
It is called "not bringing to full maturity."
In this regard, who is one who has not entered, is not ripening, and is not fully ripened? It is as follows:
a person who possesses the nature for parinirvāṇa and abides solely in their spiritual lineage (*gotra*) is one who has not entered.
This is called a person who has neither entered [the path], nor is ripening, nor is ripened;
however, he is indeed capable of entering and of ripening.
Furthermore, there is a person who is simply incapable of either entering or ripening.

For example, there is the person who lacks the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) and whose nature is such that they do not attain final nirvana; such a person is absolutely incapable of entering [the path] or of maturing, so how much less could they be capable of attaining final nirvana?
(I)-B-II-9. In this regard, all persons whatsoever are included within six categories.
What are these six?

One who is capable, endowed with weak roots of virtue, endowed with middling roots of virtue, endowed with superior roots of virtue, one who has reached the culmination of the preparatory stage, and one who has reached the culmination.

In that regard, who is the person who is only capable? It is one who, though established in the spiritual lineage (*gotrastha*), has not yet, for the first time, obtained faith in the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata,
up to the point of straightening their view.
This is called a person who is indeed capable.
In this regard, who is the person endowed with weak roots of virtue?
It is one who, being established in the lineage, has first attained faith in the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, up to having made their view straight.
This is called the person endowed with weak roots of virtue.
In that regard, who is the person endowed with middling roots of virtue?

It is the person established in the lineage who, having first attained faith in the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, and having straightened their view as far as that point, subsequently brings about one, two, or many births and proceeds toward excellence.
He does not obtain a final body of existence in which, remaining therein, he attains parinirvāṇa and enters the certainty of rightness (*samyaktva-nyāma*).
This is called a person endowed with middling roots of goodness.
In that regard, who is the person endowed with superior roots of virtue?
It is the person who proceeds toward distinction and attains his final existence,
remaining in which he enters parinirvāṇa and enters the certainty of rightness (*samyaktva-nyāma*).
This is called the person endowed with superior roots of virtue.
In this regard, who is the person engaged in the application for finality?

It is the person who, having obtained their final physical existence and having received correct instruction and admonition or the hearing of the True Dharma for the sake of the destruction of the outflows, applies themselves correctly.
Yet, even now, he has not fully and in every way realized the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣaya),
nor has he reached the ultimate goal;
such a person is called one who is practicing for the sake of reaching the ultimate goal (niṣṭhāprayogika).
In that regard, who is the person who has reached the culmination?
It is one who, having been correctly awakened and correctly instructed for the sake of the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava*),
practices accordingly.
One who attains the destruction of all outflows (āsrava) in every way,
has accomplished what was to be done, and has reached the supreme state of coolness—
this is called a person who has reached the ultimate goal (niṣṭhāgata).
In that regard, a person of the capable lineage, relying upon and established in the lineage, acquires weak roots of virtue and becomes one who has entered [the path].
Having entered, relying upon and established in those weak roots of virtue, he acquires middling roots of virtue.
And by means of those [wholesome roots], he brings himself to maturity.
Being thus matured, relying upon and established in the middling wholesome roots, he attains the superior wholesome roots and becomes fully matured.
When, by means of the acquisition of a personal existence brought about through the cause of superior roots of virtue, he accumulates the provisions,
attains one-pointedness of mind,
and enters the state of certainty in rightness,
When one realizes either the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning,
but does not realize the supreme fruit of arhatship,
then one is said to be "one who has reached the culmination of the preparatory stage."

But when one realizes arhatship, which is the abandonment of all afflictions, then one has reached the ultimate goal. Thus, this entire course of practice for śrāvakas— beginning, middle, and end— is demonstrated through the six designations of persons.
In this regard, the beginning of the disciple’s practice is shown by way of the lineage (*gotra*),
and its conclusion is shown by way of its finality (*niṣṭhā*).
The middle was demonstrated by one other than that.
Regarding those individuals who have entered therein, is the time for their parinirvāṇa fixed and equal for all, or is the time for their parinirvāṇa unfixed, immeasurable, and unequal for all?
He replied:

There is no fixed time for their measure, nor is the time for the parinirvāṇa of all of them the same; rather, their parinirvāṇa should be understood as occurring according to what is appropriate and according to the acquisition of conditions—
some after a long time.
For some, parinirvāṇa occurs before long, while for others it occurs very quickly;
nevertheless, every person who abides in the spiritual lineage attains parinirvāṇa swiftly.
He necessarily brings about three births:
in one he enters, and in another he matures.
He becomes fully matured in a single lifetime and attains parinirvāṇa right there;
if he does not attain parinirvāṇa, he necessarily passes away as one still in training (śaikṣa).
Furthermore, it brings about seven existences;
this is called the "establishment of entry."
(I)-B-III-1 What are the marks of a person who has entered [the path]?
Here, a person established in the lineage, at the very moment of having entered, even when undergoing a transition to another birth, does not lose mindfulness.

Even when there is one's own Teacher and his Dharma-Vinaya, or even when a poorly expounded Dharma-Vinaya exists alongside a well-expounded one, having heard the praise, laudation, and benefits of the poorly expounded Dharma-Vinaya through many methods, one does not enter it,
nor does one go forth.
Even though he has gone forth, he very quickly turns back;
by his very nature, a lack of interest in that [renunciant life] persists within him,
like a living creature born in honey that has been cast into vinegar.
Or like those who indulge in sensual pleasures, having been cast into a muddy puddle, it is due to the very same reinforcement of causal power from the past.
Or again, one does not hear the praise, eulogy, or commendation of the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya;
or, having heard only a small amount or a meager amount, or even without having heard it at all. (Śbh I 54)
He descends very quickly indeed, or he goes forth into homelessness;
and having thus gone forth and descended, he does not turn back,
for his inclination toward that state is established by his very nature.
It is like [the attachment] of a honey-bee toward honey,
or of one who indulges in sensual pleasures toward refined modes of sensual conduct; that is,
it occurs precisely through the empowerment of the causal force from the past.
This is the first mark of a person who has newly entered [the path].

Furthermore, another person who has entered [the path] is not yet dissociated from those afflictions that lead to the states of woe and the unfavorable conditions, yet he is no longer reborn in those unfavorable conditions.
And with reference to a person who has entered [the path], the Blessed One said:
"He who possesses even a superior degree of mundane right view does not go to an evil rebirth, even for thousands of births."
Furthermore, when he has entered into the superior roots of goodness that must be brought to maturity through a gradual process, he is then not reborn in the inopportune states (akṣaṇa),
but not in others.
This is the second mark of a person who has entered [the path].
Furthermore, another person who has entered [the path], having heard of the qualities of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha,
or through recollection, attains a vast, wholesome clarity of mind associated with renunciation.
Again and again, through that object of focus, by virtue of his mind being melted with serene faith, he experiences the falling of tears and the bristling of body hair;
this is the third mark of a person who has entered [the path].
Furthermore, another person who has entered [the path] is by their very nature endowed with intense shame and dread of blame regarding the performance of all blameworthy states.
This is the fourth mark of a person who has entered [the path].
Furthermore, another person who has entered [the path] is one who possesses desire; he has intense desire for the formal instruction (uddeśa). (Śbh I 56)
He is one who seeks what is wholesome in private recitation, in inquiry, in yoga, and in mental attention;
this is the fifth mark of a person who has entered [the path].

Furthermore, another person who has entered [the path] is one who, regarding all blameless activities, all undertakings, and applications toward the side of the wholesome, possesses a firm undertaking, a steadfast undertaking, and a resolute undertaking; that is to say, for the sake of attainment.
This is the sixth mark of a person who has entered [the path].

Furthermore, another person who has entered [the path] is of a nature with little passion; they give rise to the outbursts of the afflictions very slowly and do not establish a continuous succession of them.
He is free from deceit and guile, having destroyed pride, conceit, and egoism; he is devoted to virtues and averse to faults.
This is the seventh mark of a person who has entered [the path].

Furthermore, another person who has entered [the path] possesses a mind that is not cowed; regarding sublime states to be realized, they do not disparage themselves, nor do they settle into a state of incapacity.
He becomes abundant in resolute conviction;
this is the eighth mark of a person who has entered [the path].
These and many other similar signs of individuals who have entered [the path] should be understood; of which only this small portion has been described.
Furthermore, these signs are weak for one who abides in weak roots of goodness and has entered [the path]; they are characterized by gaps, are not continuous, and are impure.
For one who abides in middling roots of goodness, they are middling.
For one established in superior roots of virtue, these are superior,
flawless, uninterrupted, and completely pure.
These are called "the marks of a person who has entered [the path]," and endowed with which marks, one who has entered is reckoned as "one who has entered."
Furthermore, these should be understood as the inferential signs of persons who abide in the lineage and those who have entered [the path].
However, only the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the protectors— the Śrāvakas who have attained the supreme perfection— are those who perceive them through direct perception.
They experience it through perfectly pure knowledge and vision;
namely, the spiritual lineage and the entry [into the path].
(I)-B-IV.
Who are the persons who have entered?
There is a person who has entered who has indeed entered, but is neither ripening, nor ripe, nor has departed.
There is one who is ripening but is neither fully ripened nor has departed;
there is one who is fully ripened but has not departed; and there is one who has departed but is not fully ripened.
And the classification of these should be understood as previously described.
Furthermore, those other persons (pudgala) such as those with dull faculties who were described in the stage of the lineage (gotrabhūmi)—
their classification should also be understood here according to their respective application.

In this regard, that which is the nature of the entry, that which is its formal establishment, those which are the signs of those who have entered, and those who are the persons who have entered— all of these taken together are called the "ground of entry."
The summary verse:
Its intrinsic nature, its formal establishment, the signs, and the person themselves—
this entire ground of entry should be understood in brief.
The Stage of Entry in the Śrāvakabhūmi is completed.
(Śbh I 60) What is the stage of renunciation (*naiṣkramyabhūmi*)?
He said:
"Both that which is the attainment of detachment by means of the mundane path, and that which is the attainment of detachment by means of the supramundane path,"
And whatever equipment belongs to those two, having condensed them into a single whole, it is called the stage of renunciation.
(I)-C-I What is the attainment of detachment by means of the mundane path?
It is as follows: here, a certain person perceives the desire realm as coarse.
From the very beginning, he perceives peace in the joy and bliss born of seclusion within both the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the rebirths (*upapatti*) of the dhyānas.
Perceiving thus and dwelling frequently in that state, he attains detachment from sensual desires and enters the first dhyāna.

Thus, from the first dhyāna upwards, he views all the lower stages as coarse and views all the higher stages as peaceful; viewing them in that way and dwelling frequently therein, he attains detachment up to the sphere of nothingness and enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This is called the attainment of detachment by means of the worldly path;
there is nothing higher than this, nor anything more than this.
(I)-C-II What is the attainment of detachment by means of the supramundane path? It is as follows:
here, a certain person is one who has seen true persons.
Skilled in the noble dharmas,
he understands suffering as suffering, exactly as it truly is.
Or [seeing] the origin as origin, or cessation as cessation,
or the path as the path.
He is endowed with the knowledge and vision of one in training (*śaikṣa*).

Then, cultivating the path further, he dissociates himself from the phenomena of the three realms that are to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation, and he truly liberates himself; in this way, he becomes one who has transcended the three realms.
This is called the attainment of detachment by means of the supramundane path.
In this regard, what is the equipment?
Namely: self-perfection, perfection of others,
and a wholesome desire for the Dharma.
Restraint of morality, restraint of the sense faculties,
and moderation in eating.
Dedication to wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night,
dwelling with clear comprehension,
and having virtuous friends.
Hearing and reflecting upon the true Dharma, absence of obstacles,
and renunciation.
And the ornament of a śramaṇa— these factors are called the equipment for proceeding toward worldly and transcendent dispassion.
In this regard, the distinction between the perfection of oneself, the perfection of others, and the desire for wholesome phenomena should be understood as previously explained;
as it was said concerning the inferior condition for the full acquisition of the seed.
(I)-C-III-4. What is the restraint of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*)? It is when, for instance, a certain person here dwells possessed of ethical discipline.
...up to the point where he undertakes and trains himself in the precepts.
How does one dwell possessed of ethical discipline?
It is by being one whose bodily actions and verbal actions are unimpaired with respect to the training rules as they have been undertaken,
and who is of unbroken conduct.
One who acts without flaw is thus possessed of ethical discipline.
How does one become restrained by the Prātimokṣa restraint?
The ethical discipline belonging to the seven classes is called the Prātimokṣa restraint;
these constitute many restraints according to the division of their respective classes.
But regarding this matter, with reference to the restraint of a monk, it is said: "one who is restrained by the Prātimokṣa restraint."

(Śbh I 64) How does one become accomplished in conduct (*ācāra*)? It is when, with respect to deportment (*īryāpatha*), duties (*itikaraṇīya*), or the application to the side of the wholesome (*kuśalapakṣaprayoga*), one conducts oneself in accordance with the world and not transgressing the world, and in accordance with the discipline (*vinaya*) and not transgressing the discipline.
He becomes endowed with it.
In that regard, how is conduct based on the modes of deportment neither transgressive of the world nor transgressive of the discipline?
It is when one walks in whatever place it is proper to walk and in whatever manner it is proper to walk,

such that one does not become censured by the world, nor becomes blameworthy or subject to reproach before the wise, those who have attained the right path, virtuous persons, fellow practitioners of the Dharma, those who uphold the discipline, and those trained in the discipline.
And as it is with walking, so should standing, sitting, and lying down be understood.
In this regard, how is conduct based on what must be done (*itikaraṇīya*) neither transgressive of the world nor transgressive of the discipline?

"What must be done" refers to: covering oneself with robes; the evacuation of feces and urine; water for washing and tooth-sticks; entering the village; the bringing forth and consumption of alms-food; the cleaning and storing of the bowl;
and the washing of the feet, as well as the preparation of bedding and seats.
And the summary of that very [category] consists of the work concerning the bowl and the work concerning the robes;
or whatever else belongs to this class is called "that which is to be done" (*itikaraṇīya*). And that should be applied appropriately wherever it ought to be applied.
And he applies himself to that matter in exactly the way it ought to be applied,
so that he is beyond reproach and unblamed by worldly people;
and he is beyond censure and unblamed by those who uphold the discipline and are trained in the discipline.
For those who have gone rightly, who are fellow practitioners of the Dharma,
such conduct based on what is to be done is neither transgressive of the world nor transgressive of the Vinaya.
In that regard, how is conduct— which is based on the application to the side of the wholesome— neither transgressive of the world nor transgressive of the discipline?
The "side of the wholesome" refers to such things as private recitation, performing respectful services for one's teachers, and attending upon them.
Likewise, there is attendance upon the sick;
giving one's consent after establishing a mind of mutual compassion;
the formal instruction; the practical application; inquiry; and listening to the Dharma from one who is skillful and untiring.
Performing personal service with one's own body for wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life;
encouraging others to undertake the side of wholesome qualities and teaching them the Dharma; and entering into seclusion, sitting cross-legged, and remaining seated.
Thus, whatever other such factors there may be, this is called the application to the side of the wholesome.
This very application to the side of the wholesome, as is appropriate and as has been described, applies itself in that manner wherever it ought to be applied.

By means of which one does not become subject to questioning, nor is one censured by worldly people, by those who uphold the Vinaya, by those trained in the Vinaya, by the virtuous, by those who have attained the right path, by true persons, and by fellow practitioners of the Dharma—
this is called conduct that is the basis for the application of the side of wholesome qualities, which transcends the world and transcends the Vinaya.
Conduct endowed with these characteristics is called the perfection of conduct (*ācārasaṃpad*).
And in this way, he becomes one who is perfected in conduct.
And how does one become accomplished in the range of activity?
There are five improper ranges for a monk.
What are the five?
That is to say: a slaughterhouse, a brothel, a tavern, a royal court, and a caṇḍāla’s tannery as the fifth.
Having avoided these improper resorts forbidden by the Tathāgata, he frequents other resorts that are blameless; in this way, he is one who is perfected in his resort at the proper time.
How does one perceive danger in even the slightest faults?
A "slightest fault" refers to the minor and very minor rules of training (*śikṣāpada*), in which both transgression and recovery are recognized.
Whatever transgression they may commit is a fault that is merely minute;
furthermore, because one emerges from that transgression with little difficulty,
it is called "minute."
In that regard, how does one perceive danger? "Lest, on account of these transgressions, I should become incapable of attaining what has not yet been attained,
or of realizing what has not yet been realized."
For the sake of realizing that which has not yet been realized;
or [thinking], "May I go to a state of woe, or may I be one who goes to a state of woe," or "My own self might reproach me."

"The Teacher, or the deities, or wise fellow-practitioners might censure me according to the Dharma; and a foul report, ill-repute, and bad fame regarding me would arise in all directions and intermediate directions.
Thus, he perceives fear in those undesirable states pertaining to both the present life and future lives, which have that [transgression] as their cause.
By means of which he does not intentionally transgress even those minor and very minor precepts, even for the sake of his life;
and if at any time or on any occasion he should transgress through a lapse of mindfulness, he very quickly makes amends according to the Dharma and emerges from it.
Thus, he perceives danger even in the slightest faults.
How does one undertake and train in the precepts?
It is said:

previously, when he was being ordained through the formal ritual consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapticaturtha-karman*) for the undertaking of the Prātimokṣa restraint, he heard the substance of several of the training rules.

And he has accepted, by his own declaration, that more than two hundred and fifty training rules prescribed in the *Prātimokṣasūtra*— namely, two hundred and fifty plus some more— saying, "I shall train in all of them," having heard this from his preceptors (*upādhyāya*) and teachers (*ācārya*),
as well as from those with whom he converses, those with whom he talks intimately, those who are familiar to him, and those who are dear to him.
And for half a month at a time, he recites the Prātimokṣa Sūtra;
through that, by undertaking all the training rules (*śikṣāpada*), he has obtained the Prātimokṣa restraint (*saṃvara*).
Thereafter, regarding those training rules in which he becomes proficient, he does not transgress them.
And having transgressed, he makes amends in accordance with the Dharma;
furthermore, regarding those training rules in which he is unskilled, [he applies himself].
One whose intellect was previously untrained takes up those [precepts] now through skill in training, having previously undertaken them by means of a formal vow;
from those aforementioned points, as before, he takes them up again from either a teacher or a preceptor through skill in training.
Just as he has been instructed, he trains in those precepts taught by his teacher or those standing in the place of a teacher, neither omitting nor adding anything;
and he grasps both the meaning and the phrasing without error.
In this way, he undertakes and trains in the precepts.
This concludes the detailed analysis of the restraint of ethical discipline.
In that regard, what is the summarized meaning?

Herein, this is the summarized meaning: the aggregate of ethical discipline has been elucidated by the Blessed One as having precisely three characteristics, namely, the characteristic of non-dissipation, [the characteristic of non-decline, and the characteristic of non-defilement].
It has the characteristic of intrinsic nature and the characteristic of the qualities of intrinsic nature.
As for the question "How so?", first, by the statement "he dwells possessed of ethical discipline," the characteristic of non-dissipation of the restraint of ethical discipline is explained.
Furthermore, by the statement "restrained by the Prātimokṣa vow," the characteristic of its intrinsic nature is explained.
Furthermore, as for what was said:
"endowed with proper conduct and range of activity."
By this, the characteristic of the qualities of the Prātimokṣa restraint, undertaken in such a manner by comparison with the supreme [refuge], has been explained.
Nevertheless, others, perceiving that perfection of conduct and range, become confident where they were previously lacking in confidence;
for those who are already confident, there is an increase in their confidence, and being confident, they carry out the duties of the confident.
Nor do they corrupt their minds or utter disparagement;

otherwise, this quality and benefit consisting in the influence of others would not belong to one who is endowed with ethical discipline and endowed with excellence in conduct and sphere of activity. (Śbh I 72)
Conversely, by the opposite of this, there would indeed be a fault for him.
Furthermore, as for what he said:
"Seeing danger even in the slightest faults, one undertakes and trains in the precepts of training"—
by this, the characteristic of the qualities and benefits pertaining to internal mastery is explained.
For what reason?

Even if one who is thus perfected in conduct and sphere of activity should obtain the excellence and benefit of being governed by others, nevertheless, having violated the precepts, for that cause and by that condition, he will be reborn in the states of woe.
Or, for one who has not yet attained it, there is the state of incapacity to attain it, as previously described.
Furthermore, because he perceives danger even in the slightest faults,
let alone in those that are grave, and because he undertakes and trains in the precepts of training, for that reason and by that condition, after the dissolution of the body,
he is reborn in a happy destination; or else, as before, he becomes capable of attaining what has not yet been attained.
For this reason, it is said that this is the quality and benefit of the restraint of ethical discipline, which is governed by internal mastery.
Furthermore, there is another formulation:
in brief, the Blessed One has elucidated both the morality of undertaking vows and the morality that leads to liberation.
And there is the cultivation of ethical discipline (*śīla-bhāvanā*).
In that regard, as for what was first stated,
"he dwells possessed of ethical discipline," by this the state of having undertaken ethical discipline (*samādatta-śīlatā*) is explained.
Furthermore, as for what he said:
"restrained by the restraint of the Prātimokṣa"—by this, the nature of morality that leads to liberation is declared;
for indeed, the morality comprised within the Prātimokṣa restraint is called the training in higher ethics (adhiśīla-śikṣā).
Relying upon the training in higher ethics,
he cultivates the training in higher mind and the training in higher wisdom.
In this way, he sets out for the destruction of all suffering;
that is to say, by relying upon and making the higher training in ethical discipline his precursor. Therefore, the restraint of the Prātimokṣa is called "ethical discipline leading to liberation."
Furthermore, as for what he said:

"Endowed with excellence in conduct and sphere of activity, seeing danger even in the slightest faults, one undertakes and trains in the precepts"—by this, the cultivation of ethical discipline (*śīla*) is declared.
Through these aspects, that morality of the Prātimokṣa restraint is to be cultivated.
And in this way, it becomes cultivated and well-cultivated.
This very restraint of ethical discipline should be understood as being presented through six modes of teaching.
Indeed, this restraint of ethical discipline should be understood as impaired by ten causes;
conversely, it is perfected by those same ten causes.
By which ten causes does one become failed?
From the very beginning, it is wrongly grasped;
it is overly slack.
He becomes one who has transgressed, he becomes one possessed by negligence and indolence,
and he becomes one whose resolve is erroneous.
He is possessed by a failure of conduct, he is possessed by a failure of livelihood,
and he has fallen into the two extremes.
It leads to a lack of deliverance, and one becomes fallen from one's formal undertaking.

In that regard, how is ethical discipline wrongly grasped from the outset? It is when, for example, a certain person has gone forth into homelessness having been pursued by a king, or having been pursued by thieves.
Whether afflicted by debt, or afflicted by fear, or terrified by the fear of lacking a livelihood.
Not for the state of a śramaṇa, not for the state of a brāhmaṇa,
and not for the pacification of the self.
It is not for the sake of self-taming, nor for the sake of one's own parinirvāṇa;
thus, from the very beginning, it is wrongly grasped.
How does one become overly withdrawn?
It is when someone here is shameless, possesses weak remorse, is lax, and acts with negligence regarding the precepts of training.
In this way, one becomes overly withdrawn.

How does one become over-zealous? It is when someone here grasps what has been wrongly grasped and engages in misplaced remorse; that is, feeling remorse regarding matters that ought to cause remorse.
When one gives rise to or expresses a mind of contempt or resentment toward others in an inappropriate place,
it is thus called "excessive."
(Śbh I 76) How is it that [the mind] is seized by negligence and laziness?

For example, suppose here a certain person has committed an offense with reference to past time, and because of a lapse of mindfulness, he has not rectified it according to the Dharma in some instances;
as with reference to past time, so too...
Thus, regarding an offense that he has committed based on the future or the present time,
some of it may not have been remedied according to the Dharma due to his loss of mindfulness;
nor does he, prior to the offense, apply intense effort toward ensuring he does not commit it in the future.
"Suppose that I were to conduct myself and dwell in such a way that, while conducting myself and dwelling in that manner, I would not commit an offense.
Yet, he conducts himself and dwells in such a way that he commits an offense.

Thus, being possessed of this negligence— which is associated with the past, associated with the future, associated with the present, which pertains to what should have been done previously, and which accompanies one— he indulges in the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of reclining, and the pleasure of lying on one's side;
he becomes unskilled and lazy.
One who is deficient in exertion does not perform physical service for wise fellow-practitioners;
thus, one becomes possessed by negligence and indolence.
How is it wrongly directed?
It is when someone here, having made a vow, leads the holy life [thinking]:
"By means of this morality, or vow, or austerity, or practice of the holy life, may I become a god, or one among the gods."
He becomes desirous of gain and honor;
he craves gain and honor from others;
he yearns for gain and honor.
In this way, it becomes wrongly directed.
How is it that one is possessed by a failure of conduct?

It is when someone here, whether regarding their deportment, their duties, or their application to the side of the wholesome, transcends both the world and the discipline (*vinaya*), as previously described.
In this way, one is possessed by a failure of conduct.

How is it that one is possessed by a failure in livelihood? It is when, for example, a certain person here is of great desire, lacks contentment, is difficult to nourish, and is of a nature that is hard to maintain;
and he [seeks] a robe through what is not in accordance with the Dharma.
He seeks not by means of the Dharma, but seeks alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick by means of what is not the Dharma.

And for the sake of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, he adopts an extraordinary and fabricated mode of conduct, motivated by the desire to cultivate an impression of his own virtues.
He demonstrates to others a lack of agitation in the faculties, a lack of restlessness in the faculties, and tranquility of the faculties;
by this, others—recognizing his possession of such qualities—consider that they ought to give and perform services for him, namely:
robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick.

He becomes like a crow—talkative and impudent—a chatterer who proclaims others' names and lineages; though he may be widely learned and a bearer of the Dharma, it is solely for the sake of gain that he speaks of the Dharma to others, whether spoken by the Buddha or by the disciples.
Or else, having exaggerated his own qualities—whether they be real or not—he himself becomes a speaker [of falsehood].
Or he causes others to speak [for him];
or he is a teacher of the unsurpassed [Dharma];
or he is one who desires robes.
Or, being in need of any particular monastic requisite— whether in great quantity or of superior quality— even though he is not lacking,
he displays himself as needing even a plain robe,
thinking: "In this way, faithful brahmins and householders, perceiving his lack of robes, will think that they ought to give and provide him with abundant and excellent robes."
Just as with robes, so it is with any other requisite for the life of a recluse;

when he does not obtain them from faithful brahmins or householders according to his desire, or when wealth is not available and he cannot obtain them, he begs with importunity, having squeezed [them dry].
Having even crushed them, he speaks harshly to them;
or again, having obtained something inferior while such enjoyments are available, he disparages and deprecates that gain.
And in the presence of the donor or the master of the gift, he says this: "O sir!..."
Noble son,
there are certain sons of good family and daughters of good family who are even more low-born and more impoverished than you,
yet they give such excellent gifts and provide such mental satisfaction.
"Why is it that you, being of a much more noble birth and wealthier than they, yet act in such a way as to give them unpleasant things, or to give them inferior and meager gifts?"—
thus, by means of these modes, one resorts to hypocrisy (*kuhanā*), or flattery (*lapanā*), or hinting (*naimittikatā*).

Or, through importunity, or desiring to obtain gain by means of gain, he seeks from others robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick; this is unrighteous. Furthermore, that which is unrighteous constitutes his wrong livelihood.
In this way, that morality is encompassed by a failure of livelihood.
How does it fall into the two extremes?
For example, here a certain person is devoted to and attached to the pursuit of sensual pleasures;
he makes use of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick—whether obtained from others through righteous or unrighteous means.
One who sees the danger but does not discern the escape—this is called one extreme.
Furthermore, in this case, a certain person is devoted to self-mortification; in many ways he torments and afflicts himself, undertaking ascetic vows that are difficult to practice.
For example, he may rely on thorns, or rely on ashes, or rely on a pestle, or rely on wooden planks;
he remains in a squatting posture, devoted to the practice of exertion while squatting;
or he becomes one who tends the sacrificial fire.
As long as he performs the service of the fire three times,
he becomes one who ascends into the water;
as long as he ascends into the water three times, [he becomes one who ascends into the fire].
"Standing on one foot, he turns wherever the sun is"—
whatever else is of this kind, such devotion to self-mortification is called the second extreme.
In this way, it falls into the two extremes.
How is it non-leading to liberation?
It is when someone here clings to a certain moral code or vow with a [wrong] view, thinking:
"By this very moral code or vow alone, purification will come about."
"Liberation will be the departure.
And all the ethical discipline of those outside this [teaching], even if well-guarded and perfectly pure, is said to be "not leading to liberation" because of that kind of purity;
thus, it becomes non-lead-to-liberation.
(Śbh I 82) How does it become fallen away from its undertaking?
It is when someone here becomes entirely shameless and indifferent toward the state of a recluse.
And he becomes one of immoral conduct, of evil nature, internally rotten, leaking, like a heap of filth, whose behavior is like the sound of a conch shell;
though not a *śramaṇa*, he claims to be a *śramaṇa*, and though not a practitioner of celibacy, he claims to be a practitioner of celibacy— in this way, he falls away from his formal undertaking.
The Blessed One has stated that morality ruined by these ten causes constitutes a failure in morality (*śīlavipatti*).
Furthermore, the Blessed One has also spoken of the ruin of morality (*śīlavyasana*),
which should be understood as resulting from two of these causes.
Both that which is non-leading to liberation and the failure to maintain one's commitments,
as well as other such causes, should be understood as nothing other than a failure in ethical discipline.

Furthermore, by the reversal of these very causes established as belonging to the dark side, the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlasaṃpatti*) and the purity of ethical discipline (*śīlaviśuddhi*) are to be understood through the causes belonging to the bright side.
In another instance, however, the Blessed One has spoken of ethical discipline (*śīla*) in the sense of being the "root," as it is said in this verse:
"May one have well-established roots, delighting in the tranquility of the mind;
joined with and yet disjoined from noble and ignoble views, both seen and unseen. Thus is the verse.
In some places it is expressed by the word "ornament" (alaṃkāra),
as it has been said:
"A monk or a nun endowed with the ornament of ethical discipline."
One abandons the unwholesome and cultivates the wholesome;
in some places this is expressed by the term "anointing," as it is said:
"A monk or a nun endowed with the ointment of ethical discipline," as stated previously.
In some places it is expressed by the word "fragrance":
"There exists, Ānanda, a kind of fragrance whose scent wafts even with the wind."
The fragrance blows against the wind, and it also blows with the wind;
in some places, this is expressed by the term "well-conducted conduct" (*sucarita*).
Regarding this, it is said:
"The desirable maturation of good conduct of body occurs both in the present life and in future lives; the same applies to good conduct of speech.
In some places, this is expressed by the term "restraint" (saṃvara).
As it is said: "The giver, the master of generosity, is virtuous;
he abides in restraint, possesses the view of the scriptures, and perceives the fruit."
Moreover, it is said: "He dwells possessed of ethical discipline, restrained by the restraint of the Prātimokṣa," and so forth.

For what reason did the Blessed One describe ethical discipline (*śīla*) by the word "root"? The meaning of "root" is the sense of being a foundation and the sense of being a support. And this very ethical discipline serves as the foundation for all blameless, foremost, excellent, and bliss-bringing mundane and supramundane qualities. (Śbh I 86)
Because it serves as the basis for their arising and acquisition, it is therefore called by the word "root.
Just as the earth is the foundation and support for the arising of grasses, shrubs, herbs, and forest trees,
even so should ethical discipline be described in detail, as previously stated.
For what reason is ethical discipline designated by the term "ornament"?
It is said:
because those other ornaments, such as necklaces and so forth, [do not compare].
Or bracelets, or armlets, or signet rings.
Or garlands of gold and silver:
as long as this person is young, a child with black hair, endowed with fresh youth, so long do these ornaments, when worn, produce mere beauty;
but it is not so for one who is aged.
Of one who is old,
eighty years of age or more, or ninety years of age or more.
With broken teeth and a gray-haired head,
he is known as being like a mockery, even when adorned with those ornaments.
When a calamity regarding health, a calamity regarding wealth, or a calamity regarding kinsmen has arisen, one does not shine.
Furthermore, ethical discipline (śīla) brings beauty to all at all times;
therefore, it is described by the word "ornament" (alaṃkāra).
For what reason is ethical discipline (*śīla*) described by the word "ointment"?
Indeed, that wholesome and blameless undertaking of ethical discipline removes the burning of body and the burning of mind caused by the undertaking of all forms of immoral conduct;
it is like sandalwood ointment or camphor ointment when the time of the supreme summer heat has arrived for one scorched by the sun.
For this reason, ethical discipline is spoken of by the term "ointment."
For what reason is ethical discipline (*śīla*) called a "type of fragrance"?
Indeed, from a person who possesses ethical discipline, a fine sound of praise, fame, renown, and verses of glory issues forth in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Of various kinds... (Śbh I 88)
Whether from root-fragrances, heartwood-fragrances,
or flower-fragrances stirred by the wind, a mind-pleasing scent issues forth in all directions and intermediate directions.
For this reason, ethical discipline (*śīla*) is spoken of by the term "a class of fragrances."
For what reason is ethical discipline called "well-practiced conduct"?
Because this practice leads to happiness, leads to heaven, and leads to a happy rebirth;
therefore, this practice is called "well-practiced conduct."
For what reason is ethical discipline (*śīla*) called "restraint" (*saṃvara*)?
This dharma has cessation as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is characterized by cessation, and it has abstention as its intrinsic nature;
therefore, it is called "restraint."
Furthermore, there are three kinds of reflection for the sake of the purification of this restraint of ethical discipline.
What are the three?
Namely, reflection on bodily action, [reflection on verbal action, and reflection on mental action].
Examination of verbal action, and examination of mental action.
How does one, while examining these actions, purify the restraint of ethical discipline?
One examines in this way whatever action has been intended by the body to be performed:
"Is this bodily action of mine harmful to myself or to others?"

"Is this unwholesome bodily action of mine, which gives rise to suffering and has suffering as its maturation, or is it harmless, wholesome for myself and others, giving rise to happiness and having happiness as its maturation?
If, while reflecting in this way, he understands:
“‘This bodily action of mine is harmful, unwholesome, and leads to the arising of suffering and the ripening of suffering, for myself or for another’—
he withdraws it.”
He does not perform that action, nor does he authorize it.
However, if he knows: "This bodily action of mine is non-afflictive, wholesome," and so forth as before, [he performs it].
He performs that action with his body and does not withdraw it; he carries it through to completion.
Furthermore, whatever bodily action has been performed by him based on the past time, [he likewise does not withdraw].
He also repeatedly examines that:
"Is this bodily action of mine harmful, as before?
If, while examining in this way, he knows: "This bodily action of mine is harmful," [he abandons it], as before.
He confesses it in the presence of his conscious fellow-practitioners and makes amends according to the Dharma.
Furthermore, if, while reflecting in this way, he knows: "This bodily action of mine is harmless," as before;
With that very same joy and gladness, he dwells for the most part training day and night;
