thus his bodily action becomes well-examined and thoroughly purified with respect to the past, future, and present time periods.
Just as it is with bodily action, so should vocal action be understood.
The mind arises in dependence upon past conditioned phenomena;
it arises in dependence upon future and present conditioned phenomena. That mind repeatedly examines them.
“Is this mind of mine harmful? as before;
until he has produced [the thought], he withdraws it.
He does not relinquish that mental action;
rather, by means of the white side, he brings it forth again and does not withdraw it.
He bestows it;
thus, by this, that mental action has been examined and thoroughly purified.
That is to say, in the past, future, and present time periods.
For what reason? Because in the past, in the future, and in the present, whatever [beings] there may be...
Whether they be śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas,
[they perform] bodily action.
Having examined and purified vocal action and mental action, having purified them again and again.
They spoke extensively;
all of them, having thus reflected and purified themselves, [spoke].
As it was said by the Blessed One concerning the Venerable Rāhula:
"O Rāhula, there is bodily action, vocal action, and mental action."
Examine yourself constantly,
remembering the instruction of the Buddhas.
This is the work of a śramaṇa;
train yourself in this, Rāhula.
As you train in this, [you will attain the goal].
Only what is beneficial, not what is evil.
In that regard, he investigates thus: "Is this bodily action, vocal action, or mental action harmful to me? and so on in detail as before.
This is discernment:
that one withdraws some things and confesses them, while granting others;
by means of that very joy and gladness, one dwells frequently practicing the training day and night—this is called purification.
In this regard, ten benefits of such completely pure ethical discipline (śīlasaṃvara) should be understood.
What are these ten?

In this case, a person who possesses ethical discipline, reflecting upon his own purity of virtue, attains freedom from remorse. For one free from remorse, joy arises; for one whose mind is joyful, rapture is born;
and for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil.
With a tranquil body, he experiences happiness;
the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated, and with a concentrated mind, he understands according to reality and sees according to reality.
Knowing and seeing things as they truly are, one becomes weary; being weary, one becomes dispassionate; being dispassionate, one is liberated;
and for one who is liberated, the knowledge and vision arises: "I am liberated."
Until one attains final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder—
when a virtuous person attains freedom from remorse through the predominance of purified ethical discipline,
leading gradually to the attainment of nirvana— this is the first benefit of ethical discipline.
Furthermore, when the time of death has arrived for a virtuous person, [he reflects]:
"Ah, I have indeed performed good deeds with body, speech, and mind."

"Alas, I have not committed evil conduct with my body," as before; "Whatever is the destination of those who have performed merit, who have performed wholesome deeds, and who have provided protection for those terrified by fear—to that destination shall I go after passing away. Thus he attains a second state of freedom from remorse for the sake of proceeding to a happy rebirth.
For a person who is free from remorse, death is auspicious, the time of passing is auspicious, and the future life is auspicious.
This is the second benefit of ethical discipline.
Furthermore, from a virtuous person, a beautiful report of praise, renown, fame, and verse concerning their excellence issues forth in all directions and intermediate directions.
This is the third benefit of ethical discipline.
Furthermore, a virtuous person sleeps in comfort and awakens in comfort,
with body and mind free from distress.
This is the fourth benefit of ethical discipline.
Furthermore, a person who possesses ethical discipline is protected by the gods even while asleep;
this is the fifth benefit of ethical discipline.
Furthermore, a virtuous person does not suspect others of evil, nor is he afraid, nor is his mind terrified. This is the sixth benefit of ethical discipline.
Furthermore, a virtuous person is protected even when caught in the vulnerability of executioners, adversaries, or enemies;
for they always recognize him as "this is a person" and thus treat him with either friendliness or neutrality.
This is the seventh benefit of ethical discipline.
Furthermore, as before, even when an opportunity for harm arises, one is protected from venomous serpents, yakṣas, local spirits, and non-human beings;
that is to say, by making that very ethical discipline the dominant influence.
This is the eighth benefit of ethical discipline.
Furthermore, a virtuous person obtains gains from others with ease and according to the Dharma—
namely, robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick— and because of their excellence in virtue, they are honored.
It is honored by kings, royal ministers, merchants, country folk, wealthy men, guild-leaders, and caravan-merchants.
This is the ninth benefit of ethical discipline.
Furthermore, as before, all his aspirations are fulfilled.

If he should desire: "May I be reborn into the fellowship of the great kṣatriya clans, the great brahmin clans, or the great householder clans in the realm of desire; or among the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, the Nirmāṇarati, or the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods," [it shall be so].
This occurs because of the purity of his ethical discipline (*śīla*).
If he so desires, thinking, "Oh, that I might enter the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and dwell in happiness in this very life," [he is able to do so].
"May I be reborn into the fellowship of the gods who have attained the realm of form," and he dwells and is reborn accordingly;
and that aspiration of one who is virtuous and free from passion succeeds.

If he should desire: "May I transcend those peaceful liberations, attain and dwell in the formless [attainments], and be reborn in the company of the gods who have reached the formless realms," it is as before.
If he desires, "May I attain ultimate, final nirvāṇa," he attains it.
And because of the purity of his moral conduct and because he is free from passion in all respects,
this should be understood as the tenth benefit of ethical discipline.
The aggregate of ethical discipline has been explained in detail;
misfortune and prosperity have been explained;
and the synonymous names have been explained.
The examination of purification has been taught,
and the benefit has been taught.
This very restraint of ethical discipline, complete in all its aspects, supported by the accumulations, has been declared, laid out, disclosed, and revealed;
herein should sons of noble family who desire their own welfare, and who desire the state of a recluse or a brahmin, train themselves.
The summary verse:
The analysis (vibhaṅga) should be known as threefold; accomplishment (saṃpad) is tenfold;
the synonyms (paryāya) are of six aspects; and purification (viśuddhi) is considered to be threefold.
This restraint of ethical discipline has ten kinds of benefits.
What is the restraint of the sense faculties?
For example, here a certain person dwells with the doors of the sense-faculties guarded, with mindfulness protected, with constant mindfulness, and so forth.

In that regard, how does he dwell with the doors of the sense-faculties guarded? He has mindfulness protected, he has constant mindfulness, and so on in detail, up until: he guards the mind-faculty and attains restraint through the mind-faculty.
In this way, he dwells with the doors of his sense faculties guarded.
(I)-C-III-5-a-(1)-ii. In this regard, how does one become one whose mindfulness is guarded?

It is when someone here, having made the guarding of the doors of the sense faculties their primary focus, has mastered what was heard, or has reflected upon it, or has further cultivated it through meditation.
And by that, he has acquired mindfulness dominated by hearing, reflection, and cultivation.

For the sake of not losing, for the sake of attaining, and for the sake of not destroying that very mindfulness which has been acquired, he from time to time applies himself to and practices that very same hearing;
he applies himself to and practices reflection and cultivation.
He does not have a lax application or a discarded application;

thus, from time to time, he maintains the protection of that mindfulness—arisen from hearing, arisen from reflection, and arisen from cultivation—through the practice of yoga consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
In this way, his mindfulness becomes protected.
How does one possess steadfast mindfulness? One is both constant in that very mindfulness and skillful in it. In this context, that which is being constant is called "continuous practice."
In this context, that which is skillful performance is called "respectful performance.
One who thus performs continuously and performs respectfully is said to possess "vigilant mindfulness.
Just as he is one whose mindfulness is guarded, so too he does not lose that mindfulness.
Just as he becomes one of steadfast mindfulness, so too, having attained the acquisition of strength within that very unclouded mindfulness,
he becomes capable and empowered to overcome forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
(Śbh I 102) How does one become one whose mind is guarded by mindfulness?
Dependent upon the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises.
Immediately after visual consciousness, conceptual mental consciousness arises;
by means of that conceptual mental consciousness, one becomes attached to forms of a pleasing nature and feels aversion toward forms of an unpleasing nature.
Making that very [mindfulness] his dominant influence, he guards that mind from such improper conceptualization which gives rise to affliction, so that affliction does not arise.
It is the same for the ear, the nose, the tongue, and the body.
Dependent upon the mind and mental phenomena, mental consciousness arises.
And that mental consciousness is accompanied by improper conceptualization, which gives rise to affliction;
by means of it, one becomes passionately attached to phenomena that have a pleasing form.
He becomes resentful toward phenomena that are unpleasant in form;
however, by making that very mindfulness his dominant influence, he protects his mind from that improper conceptualization which gives rise to affliction, so that affliction does not arise in him.
In this way, his mind becomes guarded by mindfulness.
How does one become one who dwells in an even state?
An "even state" is said to be equanimity, whether it be wholesome or neutral.
Having protected that mind from that improper conceptualization which gives rise to affliction, he directs it toward either wholesome or neutral equanimity.
Therefore, he is called one who dwells in an even state;
in this way, he becomes one who dwells in an even state.
Furthermore, how does one protect the mind from that improper conceptualization which gives rise to affliction?
One does not seize upon the signs (*nimitta*) in those forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects, nor does one seize upon their secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*).
Because, on account of this basis, evil and unwholesome states might flow into his mind; however, if,

due to a lapse of mindfulness or an abundance of afflictions, evil and unwholesome states that flow into the mind should indeed arise— even though he avoids grasping at signs or secondary characteristics— then [he must apply himself].
He practices for their restraint;
by these two modes, that mind is protected from that improper conceptualization which gives rise to affliction.
And how, moreover, having protected that mind by means of these two aspects, does one apply it to wholesome equanimity or to neutral equanimity?
By means of exactly two aspects.
Which two?
As it is said: "He guards the eye-faculty; he attains restraint through the eye-faculty.
As with the eye-faculty, so too with the ear, nose, tongue, and body;
he guards the mind-faculty; he attains restraint through the mind-faculty."
By means of these two aspects, he directs that mind toward either wholesome or neutral equanimity.
How does one not grasp at signs regarding forms cognizable by the eye? "Grasping at signs" is said to be as follows:
Whatever form is the objective range of visual consciousness, one becomes a grasper of that objective range by means of visual consciousness.
In this way, one becomes a grasper of signs, namely, with respect to forms cognizable by visual consciousness.
However, if one avoids that objective range of visual consciousness, one does not become a grasper of signs with respect to forms cognizable by visual consciousness.
Just as it is with forms cognizable by the eye-consciousness, so it is with phenomena cognizable by the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness.

How does one not grasp at secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*) regarding forms cognizable by the eye? "Grasping at secondary characteristics" refers to that which is the objective range (*gocara*) of the conceptual mental consciousness— which arises immediately after and simultaneously with the visual consciousness— regarding those very same forms cognizable by the eye, [and which leads] to passion or to hatred.
Or for the sake of delusion,
he becomes a grasper of it by means of mental consciousness;
thus he becomes a grasper of secondary characteristics with respect to forms cognizable by the eye.

He avoids that range and does not produce that mental consciousness which takes that as its object; thus he does not grasp at secondary characteristics (anuvyañjana) with respect to forms cognizable by the eye,
and likewise with respect to phenomena cognizable by the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
There is another category: the grasping of signs (*nimittagrāha*) and the grasping of secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjanagrāha*).
Among these, the grasping of signs is when one sees forms that have come into the range of vision by bringing into presence the attention (*manaskāra*) born thereof.
Therein, the grasping of secondary characteristics is...
Having brought to presence the mental attention arising from those very forms that have come into the range of the eye, one sees them;
moreover, this is preceded by what has been heard from others.

He hears: "There are such and such forms cognizable by the eye," those names, phrases, and syllables which follow upon them, and having taken them as the dominant influence, relying upon them, and depending upon them, this person discriminates those forms cognizable by the eye exactly as they were heard.
This is called the grasping of secondary marks.
Just as it is with forms cognizable by the eye, so it should be understood regarding phenomena cognizable by the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

Furthermore, there is this grasping at signs (*nimittagrāha*) and grasping at secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjanagrāha*), on account of which, by reason of which, and through the influence of which, evil and unwholesome states (*pāpakā akuśalā dharmāḥ*) flow into the mind.
There is also that which is not on account of which, not by reason of which, and not through the influence of which evil and unwholesome states flow into the mind.

In this regard, that grasping at signs and grasping at secondary characteristics which is an improper grasping (*ayoniśogrāha*)—on account of which, by reason of which, and through the influence of which evil and unwholesome states flow into the mind.
He completely avoids grasping at the sign and grasping at the secondary characteristics of that form.
What are the evil, unwholesome states?
They are: attachment, and the misconduct of body, speech, and mind originated by attachment;
as well as hatred and delusion.
And bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct arising from delusion—these are called "evil, unwholesome states."
How do these leak into the mind?

When the mind, the mental faculty, and mental consciousness arise, proceed, and range toward an object, then those attachments— greed, hatred, and delusion— which have that very object as their focus, which are associated with that mind, mental faculty, and mental consciousness, and which give rise to misconduct of body, speech, and mind, arise, proceed, and range toward it.
Therefore, they are said to "flow along with the mind."

(Śbh I 110) (I)-C-III-5-a-(1)-v-(b)-(Z) Thus, first of all, whatever affliction arises through the grasping of signs (*nimitta*) and the grasping of secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*) with respect to forms cognizable by the eye, up to mental phenomena (*dharma*) cognizable by the mind, [is abandoned].
Thus, for him who avoids grasping at signs and grasping at secondary characteristics, [such perception] does not arise. However, if— due to a lapse of mindfulness or an abundance of afflictions—
even while dwelling alone, he takes as his dominant condition forms previously seen that are cognizable by the eye, [then it may arise].
Taking as a dominant condition those phenomena previously experienced that are cognizable by the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind,
evil and unwholesome states arise;
these, once arisen, he does not tolerate, but abandons, purifies, and brings to an end.
Therefore it is said: "He practices for their restraint."
In whatever forms the eye is to be directed,
and in whatever phenomena cognizable by the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind the mind is to be directed;
He impels them in such a way that he does not become afflicted;
thus, by this means, his mental faculty is protected from that affliction.
Therefore, it is said: "he guards the mental faculty."
Furthermore, regarding those forms cognizable by the eye toward which the eye-faculty should not be directed,
and regarding those phenomena cognizable by the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind toward which the mind-faculty should not be directed—
he does not direct them at all, in any way, or in any manner whatsoever.
Therefore it is said: "One undertakes restraint with the eye-faculty," and so on until, "one undertakes restraint with the mind-faculty.
This, for now, is to be understood as the detailed analysis of the restraint of the faculties.
The summarized meaning: (Śbh I 112) N.30b4, Co.31b1, Ch.407c7. t/ [This concludes] the summarized meaning.
That by which one restrains, that which one restrains, and that from which one restrains.
The manner in which one restrains,
as well as that very restraint itself— all this taken together and condensed into one is called "restraint of the sense faculties" (indriyasaṃvara).
In that regard, by what does one restrain?
One restrains by means of that mindfulness which is guarded and cultivated through constant application of effort toward mindfulness.
What does it restrain?
It restrains the eye faculty;
it restrains the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind faculties.
This conceals.
From what does one restrain?
One restrains from forms that are pleasant and unpleasant, and from sounds, up to and including mental phenomena; therefore, it is said that "one restrains."
How does he restrain himself?
He does not grasp at signs nor grasp at secondary characteristics, because it is on account of these that evil, unwholesome states flow into the mind.
He practices for their restraint;
he guards the faculty and attains restraint through the faculty—
thus he exercises restraint.
What, then, is conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*)? As I have said: "One whose mind is guarded by mindfulness."
That which operates within the state of equilibrium is called conventional reality (saṃvṛti).
Furthermore, there is another summary of the meaning:
that which is the means of restraint, and that which is the object to be restrained.
And that which is conventional restraint— having condensed these two together— they are called "restraint of the faculties."
In that regard, what is the means of restraint?
As it is said:

"He becomes one whose mindfulness is guarded, one whose mindfulness is constant; having seen forms with the eye, he does not grasp at their signs, nor does he grasp at their secondary characteristics."
To the extent that, having cognized mental phenomena with the mind, one does not grasp at their signs nor grasp at their secondary characteristics—
that basis by which evil, unwholesome phenomena flow into the mind—
one practices for their restraint.
Guarding the faculty with the faculty, one attains restraint;
this is called the means of restraint.
What is the object to be restrained?
It is the eye and visible forms, and so on up to the mind and mental phenomena; this is called the object to be restrained.
In that regard, what is conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*)? It is as follows:
"One whose mind is guarded by mindfulness dwells in a state of equanimity"—this is called conventional reality.
This restraint of the faculties is, in brief, of two kinds:
that which is comprised within the power of analytical discernment and that which is comprised within the power of meditative cultivation.
In that regard, that which is comprised by the power of analytical reflection is that by which one perceives the disadvantage in sense objects, yet does not remove or abandon that disadvantage.
In that regard, that which is comprised by the power of cultivation is that by which one perceives the disadvantage in sense objects,
and furthermore, one draws out and abandons that disadvantage.

In that regard, by means of restraint of the sense faculties comprised within the power of analytical reflection (*pratisaṃkhyānabala*), one does not produce nor manifest the outburst of afflictions (*kleśaparyavasthāna*) directed toward objects as its focal point;
however, one does not thereby abandon or eradicate the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) residing in the basis (*āśraya*).
In that regard, by means of the restraint of the sense faculties comprised within the power of cultivation, one does not give rise to nor manifest the outburst of afflictions directed toward objects;
furthermore, one abandons and eradicates the latent tendencies (anuśaya) that are always and at all times embedded within the basis (āśraya).

This is the distinction, this is the intended meaning, and this is the difference between the restraint of the faculties comprised within the power of analytical discernment and that comprised within the power of cultivation.
In this regard, that restraint of the sense faculties which is comprised by the power of analytical discernment is to be understood as being comprised within the path of equipment;
furthermore, that restraint of the sense faculties which is comprised by the power of meditative cultivation is to be understood as having entered the stage of detachment.
(Śbh I 116) (I)-C-III-6 What is moderation in eating?
Just as, for example, a certain person here takes food with discernment,
not for the sake of amusement, nor for the sake of intoxication.
"Not for the sake of adornment, not for the sake of beautification," and so on in detail as before.
How does one consume food with discernment?
Discernment is said to be wisdom;
by means of that wisdom, one perceives the danger in food consisting of mouthfuls, and having become disgusted through the perception of its danger, one consumes it.
Furthermore, what is that vision of the disadvantage? It is as follows:
namely, whatever pertains to the consumption, the transformation, or the pursuit of that very same physical nutriment.
What is the disadvantage resulting from consumption?

It is as follows: when someone here, at a certain time, takes food that is endowed with color, endowed with fragrance, endowed with flavor, and even most excellent—that edible food, as soon as it has been placed in the mouth—
When it has been crushed by the grinding of the teeth, moistened by the flow of saliva, and enveloped by saliva,
at that time it rolls about in the throat;
it completely abandons all its former, ancient, and agreeable qualities.
And it undergoes a further transformation;
while remaining in that state of transformation, it appears like vomited matter.
And if this eating person, this individual, [perceives] him in that condition according to its form...
One should attend to it and keep it in mind;
then, even regarding excellent food that has not yet been digested, no desire for enjoyment whatsoever will arise in him in any way at all.
How much more so, then, in that state?

For when one has made the consumption of food the primary focus through these various modes and this sequence, that beautiful appearance of color vanishes and the disadvantage consisting of impurity manifests.
This is called the disadvantage resulting from enjoyment, namely, with regard to food.
In that regard, what is the disadvantage associated with transformation in food?
When one who has taken and eaten that food undergoes transformation during the middle watch or the last watch of the night, [it becomes a source of suffering].
Then, he increases and produces within this body many various kinds of impure substances, such as blood, flesh, sinews, bones, skin, and so forth;
some of these eventually transform into the nature of excrement and urine.
And it becomes digested and moves toward the lower part;
whatever he must consume during the day, by that his hand, or his foot, or any other major or minor limb is touched.
That becomes loathsome to oneself and to others;
and on that account, many bodily afflictions arise in his body, such as,
for example, an abscess.
scabies, ringworm, and eczema.
Itching, leprosy, and skin eruptions.
leprosy, fever, and cough;
Swelling, emaciation, and epilepsy.
jaundice, anemia, and hemorrhage.
Pittabhagaṇḍara— these and other such bodily ailments arise in the body;
or his food becomes undigested,
whereby choleraic affliction (*viṣūcikā*) settles within his body.
This is called the disadvantage following upon transformation, namely, with respect to food.

In that regard, what is the danger associated with the search for food? The danger associated with the search is of many kinds, consisting of that produced by acquisition and that produced by guarding.
[It is] caused by the loss of unctuousness,
caused by lack of satisfaction,
and caused by lack of autonomy.
And that which is produced by misconduct.

In this regard, what is the disadvantage concerning food caused by its acquisition? It is when someone here, for the sake of food and on account of food, is struck by cold in the cold and struck by heat in the heat.
He exerts himself, strives, and endeavors.

Whether by agriculture, or cattle-herding, or trade, or by various crafts and occupations such as writing, arithmetic, accounting, calculation, and sealing, for the sake of obtaining food not yet obtained;
Or for the sake of accumulation;
just as it is with food, so it is with the cause of food— for one who thus exerts effort and strives.
While he is striving,
if his undertakings fail, he grieves and becomes exhausted on that account.
He laments,
beats his breast,
and cries out.
He falls into delusion,
thinking, "Alas, my exertion has been fruitless!
This is the disadvantage associated with the accumulation [of food], namely, with regard to food.
If he succeeds, then for the sake of guarding that [wealth], he falls into intense anxiety:
"I wonder if my possessions might be seized by the king or by thieves, or burned by fire, or carried away by water?"
Or treasures well-hidden might perish,
or undertakings poorly executed might go to ruin.
"Or perhaps unwelcome heirs might obtain them, or a family ruin might arise within the lineage,
who would bring those possessions to ruin through improper conduct."
This is the disadvantage associated with guarding, namely, in regard to food.
What is the disadvantage caused by the loss of affection?
It is as follows: on account of food, for the sake of food, a mother speaks dispraise of her son, and a son [speaks dispraise] of his mother.
The father [is the witness] for the son, the son for the father,
and the brother for the sister.
A sister [is dear] to her brother,
a companion to a companion,
and how much more so is one person to another!
And they become mutually contentious and fall into dispute;
likewise, noble brahmins, kṣatriyas, householders, and great landowners, for the very sake of food, thus become contentious and fall into dispute,
striking one another with their hands.
They strike with clods of earth, with sticks, and even with weapons.
This is called the disadvantage caused by the loss of affection.
In this regard, what is the disadvantage caused by lack of contentment?

It is as follows: even Kṣatriya kings who have been consecrated upon the crown of their heads, dwelling without satisfaction in their own villages, towns, kingdoms, and capitals, advance against opposing military forces in battle arrays while their conchs are being blown.
With drums being beaten and various arrows being discharged, they encounter there a wandering horse, a wandering elephant,
and a chariot.
They encounter one another with swords;
their bodies mangled by arrows or spears, they meet with death or suffering amounting to death.
This is called the disadvantage caused by lack of contentment, as well as any other similar case.
In that regard, what is the disadvantage caused by lack of autonomy?
It is as follows: when the king’s men assault fortified cities, they are even doused with boiling oil.
With heated fat,
with heated cow-dung mash,
and with molten copper.
With their limbs mangled by heated iron, arrows, and spears, they either meet death or experience suffering equal to death;
this is called the disadvantage caused by lack of autonomy, as well as any other similar case.
In this regard, what is the disadvantage caused by misconduct?
It is as follows: for instance, someone has committed and accumulated much bodily misconduct on account of food;
and just as it was with the body, so too with speech and mind—at the time when that person becomes afflicted by illness—
He is suffering, afflicted and ill;
for him, that former misconduct of body, speech, and mind [becomes manifest].
In the evening, when the shadow of mountains or mountain peaks hangs down, stretches across, and extends far over them,
it occurs to him:
"Alas, I have committed evil; alas, I have not performed merit by way of body, speech, or mind.

Therefore, after death, I shall go to the destination that awaits those who have committed evil. Thus, dying with remorse, he passes away and is reborn in states of woe—namely, in the hells, among animals, or among the hungry ghosts.
This is called the disadvantage resulting from misconduct.
It occurs to him:
"Thus, this food is fraught with danger even while being sought,
and it is fraught with danger even while being consumed."
Even when consumed, transformation is a disadvantage.
Nevertheless, there is still a certain measure of benefit to this food; what, then, is it?
This body subsists on nutriment; it persists by depending on nutriment, not without nutriment. This too is merely a benefit.
Thus, this body, subsisting on nutriment, may remain for a very long time— even for a hundred years or somewhat longer—
if it is properly cared for;
yet there is also its cessation before that.
In this regard, those who are intent merely upon the maintenance of the body have not practiced well; those who are content with the mere maintenance of the body are not truly contented;
nor do they experience the full, blameless benefit resulting from food.

Furthermore, those who are not content with the mere maintenance of the body, nor intent upon the mere maintenance of the body, but rather, relying upon that very maintenance of the body, are intent upon the full realization of the holy life (*brahmacarya*);
They have practiced well,
and they alone, moreover, experience the full, faultless benefit.
“Therefore, it would not be fitting for me to dwell content with merely the inferior benefit of food;
nor would it be fitting for me to fall into the company of fools or to share the same nature as fools.
Having thus understood the faults of food in every respect and in their full extent, he reflects upon this and perceives its danger.
Seeking liberation, he consumes food that is like the flesh of his own son solely for the sake of escaping from hunger;
it occurs to him:
"In this way, these donors and masters of giving have acquired these possessions with great hardship."
Experiencing the great misfortune caused by their search,
they repeatedly press their own skin, flesh, and blood to give it to us;
that is to say, out of compassion and desiring a distinguished fruit, this indeed should be the appropriate and fitting use for us of the alms-food thus obtained.

"If I were to enjoy [these things] while establishing myself in such a state of humility that the services rendered to them would become exceedingly fruitful, of great benefit, great splendor, and great extent,"
And like the moon, I should visit families with body withdrawn and mind withdrawn, modest and not impudent,
without exalting myself.
Not disparaging others:
just as one would be well-disposed and of good cheer through one's own gain, so too should one be well-disposed and of good cheer through the gain of another.
Furthermore, with such a mind, I should approach families; for how could it be possible for one who has gone forth to expect from other families that others should give to me and not fail to give,
or that they should honor me and not fail to honor me?
Abundant, not meager; exquisite, not coarse; prompt, not slow.

While I am thus practicing and approaching families for alms, if others should not give, I would not, on that account, be broken by a mind of malice or a mind of resentment toward them. Nor would I, because of that cause, suffer the ruin of rebirth in a state of misery upon the dissolution of the body—
that is, by making that very mind of malice and mind of resentment predominant— should they treat me with disrespect rather than respect.
If they should give little rather than much, if coarse rather than refined, or if slowly rather than quickly;
“May I not be torn apart by her through a mind of malice or a mind of resentment,” as detailed previously;
“And relying upon this material food, may I practice in such a manner that...”
And I shall perceive that measure by which there will be no cessation of my life-faculty,
nor shall I become exhausted by the alms-food.

"May there be support for my religious life (brahmacarya), and may this enjoyment of alms-food be appropriate, pure, and blameless for me while I am established in the state of a recluse and the state of one who has gone forth. With these considerations,
he takes food after careful reflection.
Furthermore, what is nutriment?
There are four nutriments: edible food, [contact, mental volition, and consciousness].
In this context, however, contact, mental volition, and consciousness are intended as "edible food" (kavaḍīkārāhāra).
What, then, is that?
It is as follows: either churned barley flour or cakes.
Whether it be boiled rice or gruel, clarified butter, or oil.
honey, molasses, and meat.
Fish, dried meat, and salt.
Milk, curd, fresh butter— these and other such requisites which are consumed by being made into mouthfuls.
Therefore, it is called "edible food" (kavaḍaṃkāra). To "take" means to eat, to consume, to partake of, and to ingest.
He eats, he consumes, he tastes.
"Drinks" and "sucks" are synonyms.
"Not for the sake of sport" means that those who enjoy sensual pleasures consume food for that purpose.
"When we, our limbs refreshed and our bodies satiated by food, at the arrival of evening time, when the night has set in,
are sporting together with women who wear their hair tied in topknots, whose arms are hairy like those of bottle-gourds, and whose breasts are like balls,"
"Enjoying ourselves and providing entertainment, we shall manifest levity and frivolity."

Noble lady, these are the corrupt things in this Dharma and Vinaya: namely, those evil and unwholesome states and discursive thoughts associated with sensual desire and associated with sexual intercourse,
by which one is devoured and oppressed, becoming one whose faculties are agitated and whose faculties are haughty.
With a mind that is restless,
with a mind that is agitated,
with a mind that is unsettled, and with a mind that is unpacified.
Furthermore, those who consume food excessively are said to consume it for the sake of intoxication.
However, the learned noble disciple (ārya-śrāvaka), possessing the power of discernment, seeing the danger, and knowing the way of escape, partakes [of food];
he does not consume it in the manner that those who indulge in sensual pleasures do.
Therefore, he said: "not for the sake of intoxication."
"Neither for the sake of intoxication, nor for the sake of beautification, nor for the sake of adornment.
This means that those very same enjoyers of sensual pleasures take food for their own sake, thinking:
"Today we have taken food—namely, abundant and to our satisfaction, according to our power and strength."
It is unctuous, aphrodisiac, and nourishing.
It was endowed with excellent color, endowed with excellent fragrance,
and endowed with excellent flavor; it became fuel.
When the night has passed, we shall be capable and strong enough for physical exercise, namely,
by means of stretching or by striking.
Whether by means of physical exercise, or by jumping up and down, or by digging into the earth;
Whether by the exercise of the arms, or by the pressing of the feet, or by swimming, or by leaping, or by the exercise of the wheel;
Furthermore, by relying on that exertion, we shall become strong and well-proportioned;
we shall be long-lived and free from disease, and our youth will endure for a long time.
"However, old age, which causes disfigurement, will not overcome the body so quickly," [they think].
"And we shall live for a much longer time.
"And we shall be capable of consuming abundant food."
"The food consumed will be properly digested,
and the reduction of the humors (doṣas) will have been accomplished"—
this is for the sake of pride in one's health.
They enjoy [these things] for the sake of the intoxication of youth and for the sake of the intoxication of life;
then, it occurs to them once again:
“Having finished our exercise, we shall prepare for bathing; that is to say, we shall wash our limbs with pure water.
Having washed our limbs, we shall groom our hair and [anoint ourselves] with various ointments.”
“Without smearing our bodies [with unguents], we shall adorn the body with various garments, various garlands, and various ornaments.
In this context, that which consists of bathing, grooming, and anointing is called their *maṇḍana* (adornment);
likewise, for those who have engaged in such adorning, the wearing of garments, garlands, and jewelry is called *vibhūṣaṇa* (decoration).
They enjoy [these things] for the sake of adornment and for the sake of decoration.
Thus, intoxicated by pride, with their bodies adorned through the very nature of such ornamentation,
when the time of midday or the time of evening— the time for a meal— has arrived, they are thirsty and hungry.
With supreme thirst, with supreme delight, and with supreme joy.
Not seeing the danger and not understanding the escape, they take up food as it is obtained,
merely for the sake of play and for the sake of intoxication again and again.
It is for the sake of adornment and for the sake of embellishment.
However, the learned noble disciple, possessing the power of discernment, seeing the danger and knowing the escape, partakes [of it].
But it is not in the manner that those who indulge in sensual pleasures consume;
rather, thinking, "I shall abandon this food by not indulging in it at all, and not while actually consuming it," he consumes it.
"Only for the maintenance of this body"—having eaten, and not without having eaten—is what is called "the maintenance of the body for the sake of life.
Thinking, "Having taken this food, I shall live; I shall not die," he takes it.
Therefore it is said: "merely for the maintenance of this body."
(Śbh I 136) How does one take food for the sake of sustenance?
There are two kinds of progress: there is progress with difficulty, and there is progress without difficulty.
What is sustenance with difficulty? It is when one who consumes food experiences hunger or weakness,
or becomes distressed and severely ill.
Or he seeks alms-food unrighteously, not righteously;
he consumes it with passion, attachment, greed, bondage, infatuation, obsession, and having fallen into a state of intense craving.
The body of the teacher becomes unserviceable and incapable of exertion, whereby his mind enters into concentration slowly.
When inhalations and exhalations proceed with difficulty,
or when sloth and torpor envelop the mind,
this is called a life sustained with difficulty.
What is sustenance without hardship? It is when one takes such food that neither hunger nor weakness arises,
nor does one become excessively distressed or afflicted by illness.
He seeks almsfood in accordance with the Dharma and not contrary to the Dharma;
or, he consumes it without passion, without attachment, without greed, without being fettered, without infatuation, without fixation, and without having fallen into a state of obsession.

Furthermore, his body does not become heavy; it becomes pliant, capable of abandonment, and by means of this, his mind quickly enters meditative concentration. With little difficulty, his inhalations and exhalations proceed smoothly.
Lethargy and drowsiness do not overwhelm the mind;
this is called subsistence with little difficulty.
In that regard, that maintenance of life which occurs through difficult subsistence is for the body blameworthy and afflicted;
whereas that maintenance of life which occurs through little difficulty is [not so].
Furthermore, that sustenance of the body is blameless and unafflicted.
In this regard, the learned noble disciple avoids a way of life that is blameworthy and afflicted,
and pursues a way of life that is blameless and unafflicted.
He practices it;
therefore, he says "for the sake of maintenance."
Furthermore, how does one practice that blameless and unafflicted livelihood which was previously described?
He said:
If [one thinks], "This is for the cessation of hunger and for the support of the holy life:
'I shall abandon old feelings and shall not give rise to new ones,'" [then one eats with proper moderation].
"And there will be for me a journey, strength, happiness, blamelessness, and a state of dwelling in comfort."
Practicing in this way, he maintains a livelihood that is blameless and unafflicted.
And how, moreover, does one take food for the sake of allaying hunger? When the time for a meal has arrived and hunger has arisen, [one takes it].
When he eats, he consumes it in such a measure as to eliminate that very obsession of hunger and the weakness of hunger,
so that once he has eaten, the weakness of hunger does not afflict him again at an improper time,
namely, at the time of evening.
When the night has passed and it is become morning, before the time for the meal has arrived,
he takes food in this way so as to allay hunger.
How does he take food for the sake of supporting the holy life? He consumes it in the proper measure;
he takes such food as this.
By means of which, for one engaged in the side of the wholesome, in this very life immediately after eating, or on that very day, the body becomes unburdensome,
serviceable, and capable of exertion.
By means of which his mind is very quickly concentrated;
inhalations and exhalations proceed with little difficulty;
and sloth and torpor do not envelop the mind.
By means of which he becomes capable and competent to quickly attain what has not yet been attained and to realize what has not yet been realized.
For the sake of realizing that which has not yet been realized;
in this way, he undertakes the holy life for its support.
How does one consume [food] with the thought, "I shall abandon old feelings"?
It is when, with reference to the past, one has consumed food either in immoderate quantity, or what is unwholesome, or what has not been properly digested.
By which various physical ailments arise for him,
such as itching,
leprosy, skin spots, and vitiligo, as described in detail previously.
And on account of that illness, there arise in him bodily sensations that are painful, intense, harsh,
bitter, and disagreeable.

For the sake of pacifying that affliction and for the sake of pacifying those painful sensations caused by it, he partakes of medicine according to the method prescribed by the physician— wholesome, beneficial, favorable, and conformable—
and he consumes suitable food.
By means of which there comes about the abandonment of that arisen affliction and of the painful sensations caused by it;
thus he takes food with the thought, "I shall abandon old sensations."
How does one take food with the thought, "I shall not produce new feeling"?
Taking the present time as a basis, he is happy and free from illness.
Whether he eats excessively, or consumes what is unwholesome, even though he is strong.
Or while it has not yet matured;
by which, with reference to the future time, either tomorrow or the day after tomorrow, [it will occur].
Or cholera might settle in his body,
or some other kind of physical ailment might arise in his body,
such as an itch.
Leprosy,
kiṭibha,
and kilāsa, as detailed previously.
On that account, bodily sensations would arise as before;
and thus, thinking, "I shall not give rise to new sensations," he takes his food.
How does one eat with the thought, "There will be for me sustenance, strength, happiness, blamelessness, and a state of ease"?
First, by eating what one lives, there is thus sustenance;
furthermore, by removing hunger and weakness, there is thus strength for him.
Furthermore, when one abandons old feelings and does not give rise to new ones, in this way there is happiness for him. Moreover,
when he seeks almsfood in accordance with the Dharma and consumes it without attachment or clinging— as described in detail previously— in this way he becomes blameless.
Furthermore,
for one who has eaten, the body does not become heavy and becomes serviceable.
Being capable of abandonment in detail, as previously described, he thus attains a state of dwelling in ease (*sparśavihāratā*).
Therefore it is said: "He takes food with discernment;
not for the sake of sport," and so forth.
"Not for the sake of intoxication,
nor for the sake of adornment"— this is the detailed analysis of moderation in eating, as explained at length previously.
(I)-C-IIl-6-b-(1) Furthermore, what is the summarized meaning?
He said:
What one consumes and how one consumes it—this is the summary meaning.
What does one consume? Namely, edible food (kavaḍīkārāhāra).
Whether it be stirred drinks, cakes,
or boiled rice with sour gruel— as described in detail previously.
How does he consume it?
He consumes it with discernment,
not for the sake of intoxication.
"Not for the sake of intoxication, nor for the sake of adornment," and so on in detail as before.
Furthermore, another summary of the meaning is as follows:

he partakes [of food] embraced by the antidote, avoiding both the extreme of devotion to sensual pleasure and the extreme of self-mortification, for the sake of supporting the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
How is it embraced by the antidote?
As it is said:
"He takes food with discernment."
How is it that he avoids the extreme of devotion to the pleasure of sensual desires?
As it is said:
"Neither for the sake of sport, nor for the sake of intoxication."
"Not for the sake of adornment, nor for the sake of embellishment.
How is it free from the extreme of self-mortification?
As it is said:
"For the cessation of hunger,
and so that I may abandon former sensations."
"I shall not produce new [defilements],
and I shall have sustenance,
strength, and happiness."
How does one enjoy [food] for the sake of supporting the holy life (*brahmacarya*)? As it is said: "for the sake of supporting the holy life."
"Thus, there will be for me blamelessness and a state of dwelling in comfort."
Furthermore, there is another summary meaning:
this food is twofold— food and non-food.
In that regard, non-eating is when one does not consume anything at all, in any way, and in every respect;
and while not eating, one dies.
In that context, eating is of two kinds.
There is balanced eating and unbalanced eating.
Among these, balanced eating is that which is neither too little nor too much.
It is not unwholesome, nor is it undigested, nor is it defiled.
In that regard, irregular eating consists of what is either too little or too much.
He consumes food that is undigested, unwholesome, or defiled.
In that regard, by eating in moderation— not eating too little— one does not produce the weakness of hunger when it has not yet arisen,
and one abandons it when it has arisen. Therein, by eating in moderation rather than eating excessively, the body does not become heavy or unserviceable for action.
He is incapable of abandoning [afflictions], as described in detail previously.

In that regard, by means of food that is digested, wholesome food, and balanced food, he abandons old sensations and will not give rise to new ones; thus his maintenance of life, strength, and happiness are secured.
Through unafflicted eating and moderate eating, there arises both blamelessness and a state of ease.
In this regard, "too little food" is that by which one lives while being overcome by hunger and weakness; "excessive food" is as follows: [the rest of the passage continues].
By this, his body becomes oppressed by a heavy burden, and his food does not digest at the proper time;
therein, due to undigested food, cholera remains within his body.
Or some kind of physical ailment arises in the body;
as it happens with food that has been improperly digested, so it happens with unwholesome food.
In this regard, the distinction concerning unwholesome food is as follows.
The humors increase and one experiences harsh affliction.
In that regard, having sought almsfood through unrighteous means and by consuming tainted food, one partakes of it with attachment.
"Attached, greedy, and fettered," and so on in detail as before;
thus, he who partakes of moderate food and avoids irregular eating.
Therefore, one is said to be "one who acts with moderation regarding food.
And this moderation regarding food has been declared by these aspects; it has been made clear.
It has been disclosed and fully elucidated;
namely, that one partakes of food with discernment.
Not for the sake of intoxication, not for the sake of pride, and not for the sake of adornment.
"Not for the sake of ornamentation," and so on in detail as before.
In that regard, as for what was said:
"He takes food with discernment;
not for the sake of amusement,"
"Neither for the sake of intoxication, nor for the sake of beautification, nor for the sake of adornment," but only to such an extent as—
“For the maintenance of this body,
for its sustenance”— by this, he first rejects total fasting.
Furthermore, as it is said:
"For the cessation of hunger,
for the support of the holy life," and so on in detail, up to "for dwelling in comfort."
By this, he rejects irregular eating.

First, one abandons food that is not moderate—that is, food which is too little.
As it is said:
"For the sake of supporting the holy life (*brahmacarya*)."
By this, he rejects excessive eating.
When he says, "I shall abandon old sensations and shall not give rise to new ones," by this he rejects the state of undigested food and the state of unwholesome food.
As it is said: "There will be for me sustenance and strength.
By this, he demonstrates neither eating too little nor eating too much.
As it is said: "And there will be happiness for me"—by this, he shows that the food is digested and that it is wholesome.
As it is said: "And there will be blamelessness for me, and a state of dwelling in comfort"—by this, he shows that the food is undefiled.
He who, having sought almsfood through unrighteous means, consumes it with attachment and clinging—
as described in detail previously—
consumes it in a state of affliction.
And there is faultfulness for him in that very seclusion and yoga of one who is engaged in the side of the wholesome.
In mental attention, in recitation and study, and in reflection on the meaning, those very same evil and unwholesome discursive thoughts flow into the mind.
Those which are inclined toward that, directed toward that, and leaning toward that.
They cause the continuity of consciousness to proceed in such a way that for him there is no dwelling in contact;
and this lack of dwelling in contact is of two kinds.
And by avoiding excessive food, his body does not become heavy, unwieldy, or unfit for abandonment— as described in detail previously—
and because he does not indulge in the relish of food, he does not experience a state of ill-being caused by the agitation of discursive thoughts.

In detail and in brief.
(Śbh I 150) What is the application to the practice of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night?
In that regard, what is the first watch of the night?
What is the latter part of the night?
What is the application to wakefulness?
What is the state of being devoted to the application to wakefulness?
In this context, "evening" refers to the first part of the night; beginning from the setting of the sun, it is that portion of the night which exceeds one watch (*prahara*).
What is the latter part of the night?
It is the final portion of the night, exceeding one watch (*prahara*).
In that regard, this is the application of the practice of wakefulness (*jāgarikā-yoga*).
As it is said:
"By means of walking and sitting during the day, he purifies the mind of obstructive states;
by means of walking and sitting during the first watch of the night, he purifies the mind of obstructive states."
Having purified himself, washed his feet outside the monastery,
and entered the monastery,
He prepares his bed on his right side, placing one foot upon the other,
perceiving light, mindful and clearly conscious, and keeping in mind the intention to arise; he awakens very quickly during the final watch of the night.
Through walking and sitting, he purifies the mind of obstructive states.
In this regard, this is the application of devotion to the practice of wakefulness:
namely, when a disciple of the Buddha, the Blessed One, hears of the practice of wakefulness and desires to train therein.

For one who has become thus, the desire, vigor, exertion, departure, prowess, steadfastness, undertaking, enthusiasm, perseverance, and the non-reversal of the mind— this is the gathering, the continuity, regarding the practice of wakefulness, thinking: "I shall accomplish the practice of wakefulness authorized by the Buddhas, beginning with the application to the practice of wakefulness."
(I)-C-IIl-7-a-(2)-i-(a)–(d) In this regard, how does one purify the mind from obstructive states through walking and sitting during the day?
"During the day" refers to the period beginning from the time of sunrise until the time of sunset.
“Walking” (caṅkrama) refers to bodily action associated with going back and forth on a long, wide stretch of ground that has been prepared.
“Sitting” (niṣadyā) refers to when someone here sits upon a couch, a stool, or a spread of grass, having assumed the cross-legged posture.
Having set the body erect and established mindfulness before him,
he speaks of the obscurations as the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇāni*).
The obstructive phenomena (*āvaraṇīyā dharmāḥ*) are those factors conducive to the hindrances that provide nourishment for the hindrances.
What, then, are they?
Sensual desire and ill will.
Styāna-middha (sloth and torpor), auddhatya-kaukṛtya (restlessness and remorse), and vicikitsā (doubt).

The sign of resistance consists of attractiveness, darkness, thoughts concerning one's kin, country, and immortality, the recollection of former laughter, play, delight, and socializing, the three times,
and improper reflection on phenomena pertaining to the three times.
How does one purify the mind through the walking meditation (*caṅkrama*) from these?
And from how many things does one purify it?
One purifies it from sloth and torpor (*styāna-middha*), as well as from the obscuration that nourishes sloth and torpor.
By this means, the sign of light has been well-grasped, well-attended to, well-cultivated, well-penetrated, and thoroughly mastered.
With a mind accompanied by light and accompanied by great radiance, whether in a sheltered place or in the open air, he...
While walking back and forth on the walking path, he directs, inspires, and gladdens his mind by means of one or another inspiring object;
that is to say, either by the recollection of the Buddha,
or by the recollection of the Dharma, the Saṃgha, ethical discipline, renunciation, or the deities.
Furthermore, he has heard, mastered, and retained teachings concerning the disadvantages of sloth and torpor (*styāna-middha*) in relation to the body;

namely, the discourses (*sūtra*), mixed prose and verse (*geya*), prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*), verses (*gāthā*), inspired utterances (*udāna*), introductory narratives (*nidāna*), parables (*avadāna*), historical accounts (*itivṛttaka*), birth stories (*jātaka*), extensive treatises (*vaipulya*), marvelous events (*adbhutadharma*), and instructions (*upadeśa*).
In these, sloth and torpor have been censured and reviled in many ways.
Furthermore, the abandonment of sloth and torpor is praised, extolled, and lauded;
he recites it extensively with a melodic voice, or elucidates it for others.
He either reflects upon, weighs, or examines a matter; or he surveys the directions;
or he directs his gaze toward the moon, the lunar mansions, the planets, and the stars.
He moistens his face with water;
thus, this obsession of sloth and torpor does not arise in him if it has not yet arisen, and if it has arisen, it is dispelled.
In this way, his mind has been purified from those obstructive phenomena.
In that regard, by means of sitting, from which obstructive phenomena does one purify the mind?
And how, moreover, does one purify it? He said:
He purifies himself from the four obstructive states:
from sensual desire, ill will, restlessness and remorse, and doubt, as well as from those factors that nourish them.
When the obsession of sensual desire has arisen, for its removal; or when it has not yet arisen, for its prevention— having sat down and assumed the cross-legged posture, he...
Having set the body erect and established mindfulness before him,

he directs his attention to one or another auspicious sign for concentration— whether it be a livid corpse, a festering corpse, a dismembered corpse, a bloated corpse, a devoured corpse, a blood-stained corpse, a skeleton, or a chain of bones.
Furthermore, whatever teachings he has undertaken specifically for the abandonment of sensual desire and for the sake of abandoning longing for sense-pleasures—

teachings that have been retained, mastered verbally, examined by the mind, and thoroughly penetrated through vision; namely, the discourses (*sūtra*), the songs (*geya*), the prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*), and so forth in detail as before.

Those who, by way of many methods, censure, disparage, and loathe sensual desire, sensual longing, attachment to sensual pleasures, addiction to sensual pleasures, and obsession with sensual pleasures;
and who, by way of many methods, praise, extol, and commend the abandonment of sensual desire.
Seated thus, he attends to those phenomena with wise reflection;
in this way, the unarisen obsession of sensual desire does not arise in him,
and the arisen obsession of sensual desire passes away.
— ii In that regard, this is the distinction concerning ill-will (*vyāpāda*):

seated thus, with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness (*maitrī*), free from enmity, free from malice, free from affliction, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, he resolves upon one direction, pervades it, and attains it.
He dwells;
likewise the second, likewise the third, and likewise the fourth, pervading and suffusing the entire infinite world—above, below, and across—and having attained this, he dwells.
The rest is as before.
In this regard, there is a distinction concerning restlessness and remorse:
namely, while seated, he settles the mind internally, settles it thoroughly, brings it to completion, makes it one-pointed, and concentrates it.
The remainder is as before.
In this regard, there is a distinction concerning the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*):
being seated in that manner, he does not attend inappropriately (*ayoniśas*) to the past time.
He does not attend inappropriately to the future or the present time, thinking:
"Did I indeed exist in the past,
or did I not exist in the past?"
Who indeed was I? How indeed was I in the past time?
Who indeed shall I be in the future time?
"How shall I be in the future?
Who am I now, and who shall we become?
From where has this sentient being come?"
Having abandoned such improper mental attention as "having passed away from here, where will he go?", he attends to things properly with respect to the past, the future, and the present.
He sees only phenomena (*dharma-mātra*) and only entities (*vastu-mātra*); he sees what exists as existing and what does not exist as non-existing, and he sees only causes (*hetu-mātra*).
It merely states the result;
it does not superimpose what is non-existent,
nor does it deny or destroy an existing reality.
He knows what is real as it truly is—

namely, as impermanent, or as suffering, or as empty, or as non-self— with respect to those phenomena that are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self. Thus, he attends to them with wise reflection.
He is also free from doubt and free from uncertainty regarding the Buddha;

he is free from doubt and free from uncertainty regarding the Dharma, the Saṅgha, suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; he is free from doubt and free from uncertainty regarding causes and the phenomena arisen from causes. The rest is as before.

"Whatever teachings have been grasped by him with reference to resentment and the signs of resentment, and for the sake of their abandonment," and so forth.
Excitement and remorse are to be discussed;
by means of this [discourse], one begins with excitement and remorse and proceeds toward their abandonment.
"The teachings have been grasped," and so on in detail as before;
this should be stated regarding doubt (*vicikitsā*). Those who, having begun with doubt, [act accordingly]...
And for the sake of abandoning that [hindrance],
teachings have been mastered, as described in detail previously.
In this way, by means of this, the mind becomes purified from the hindrance of sensual desire, and from the hindrances of ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-regret, and doubt.
And from those obstructive phenomena that serve as the basis for such [distraction],
he therefore says:
"By means of walking and sitting, he purifies the mind of obstructive phenomena."
This indeed is declared to be the purification of the mind from those factors that are obstacles governed by the influence of phenomena (dharmādhipateya).

Furthermore, there is the purification of the mind from obstructive phenomena through both self-mastery and mastery over the world. What is that which consists of self-mastery? It is as follows: when any one or another of the hindrances has arisen, [one reflects: "I am not the only one for whom this hindrance has arisen; other beings also have this hindrance. Thus, by means of this reflection, one does not become despondent, but rather generates the thought: "I shall strive with diligence so that this hindrance may be abandoned. This is called purification of the mind through self-mastery. What is purification of the mind through mastery over the world? It is as follows: when any one or another of the hindrances has arisen, [one reflects: "I am not the only one for whom this hindrance has arisen; many other beings also have this hindrance. Thus, by means of this reflection, one does not become despondent, but rather generates the thought: "I shall strive with diligence so that this hindrance may be abandoned. This is called purification of the mind through mastery over the world. Furthermore, there is purification of the mind from obstructive phenomena through self-mastery and mastery over the world. What is that which consists of self-mastery? It is as follows: when any one or another of the hindrances has arisen...

Having recognized the unseemliness [of that hindrance] for oneself, one does not tolerate the arisen hindrance; one abandons it, dispels it, and brings it to an end, feeling shame before oneself because of that hindrance. (Śbh I 160)
By means of that which causes affliction, which weakens wisdom, and which belongs to the side of harm—
in this way, making himself the master, he purifies his mind from obstructive phenomena.
How does one, taking the world as the authority, purify the mind from obstructive states?
Here, when an obstruction has arisen or is present at the very moment of its arising, it occurs to him:
"If I were to give rise to an unarisen obstruction..."
"The Teacher would reproach me; the deities and wise fellow-practitioners would also censure me in accordance with the Dharma.
Thus, making the world itself his authority, he does not give rise to an unarisen hindrance.
And he abandons what has arisen;
thus, taking the world as his authority, he purifies the mind from obstructive states.
Furthermore, for the sake of protecting his bedding and seat, he thinks, "I shall also conform to worldly custom.
During the first watch of the night, he purifies his mind of obstructive states through walking and sitting. Having purified his mind of obstructive states,
Outside the monastery, he washes his feet;
having washed them and entered the monastery,
he prepares his bed for the purpose of nourishing the great elements that are subject to growth through sleep.
This body, having been nourished, will become more workable and more compliant for the continuous application of the side of wholesome qualities by one who is diligent.
For what reason does he lie down on his right side?
It is because of his similarity to the lion, a living being.
What, then, is the similarity in this case?
The lion is the most courageous, energetic, and firm in its prowess among all creatures belonging to the animal realm.
Likewise, a monk who is devoted to the practice of wakefulness dwells having initiated vigor, being courageous, energetic, and firm in his prowess.
Therefore, a lion-like posture for him is truly appropriate.
But this is not the bed of a hungry ghost, nor the bed of a god, nor the bed of one who indulges in sensual pleasures;
for all of them are indeed indolent, lacking in vigor, and deficient in strength and prowess.
Moreover, it is the very nature of things that for one who arranges his bed in the lion’s posture on the right side, there is no such tossing of the limbs;
nor does he lose mindfulness while lying down,
nor does he sleep deeply.
And one does not see evil dreams;
however, for one who prepares the bed otherwise, all faults should be understood to occur by way of the opposite.
Therefore, he said:
Placing one foot upon the other, he prepares his bed on his right side.
How does one who possesses the perception of light arrange his bed?
He has well grasped the sign of light, well attended to it, well cultivated it, and well penetrated it. Attending to that very same sign, he arranges his bed with a mind accompanied by radiance.
And by means of this, even while asleep, his mind does not become shrouded in darkness;
thus, perceiving light, he prepares his bed.
How does one, being mindful, prepare for sleep?
It is by means of those wholesome, meaningful, and beneficial teachings that have been heard, reflected upon, or cultivated by him.
Following that, his mindfulness persists even during the time of sleep; by means of this,
even while asleep, those very same phenomena speak to him as if he were awake,
and his mind frequently dwells upon those very phenomena.
Thus, according to his mindfulness and as he has remembered, whether with a wholesome mind or an indeterminate mind,
he prepares his bed while thus mindful.
How does one lie down with clear comprehension?
When he is asleep yet possesses such mindfulness that at any time his mind becomes afflicted by any one of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*),
he correctly recognizes that very affliction as it arises.
He does not tolerate it; he abandons it;
he penetrates it.
He turns his mind back [from distraction];
therefore it is said that he lies down with clear comprehension.
How does he lie down while attending to the perception of rising? Having made his mind firmly sustained by vigor, he lies down with a very light sleep and very little drowsiness.
Just as a wild deer does not,
in every respect, make its mind inclined toward falling into torpor, nor does it tend toward that state.
It is not inclined toward that;
moreover, this thought occurs to him:
"O, would that I might accomplish in every way and in all respects the vigilance authorized by the Buddha!"
And for the sake of accomplishing that, he dwells with intense application and diligent effort through the practice of profound concentration (*ghanarasa*).
Furthermore, this thought occurs to him:
"Just as I have today dwelt having initiated vigor for the sake of wakefulness..."
He is skillful, untiring, and endowed with initiative for the cultivation of wholesome qualities;
tomorrow at dawn,
when the night has passed.
"Furthermore, I shall dwell with energy aroused and endowed with alertness.
In that regard, by means of one perception of alertness, he does not sleep deeply,
so that he is able to rise very quickly at the time for rising.
He does not wake up past the appointed time. By the second perception of rising, he adopts the lion’s posture as authorized by the Buddha—neither deficient nor excessive.
By the third perception of rising, he does not let his zeal slacken.
When there is a lapse of mindfulness, he applies himself to undertaking [the practice] further and further;
thus, attending to the perception of rising, he prepares his bed.
In the final watch of the night, having awakened very quickly, he purifies his mind of obstructive states through walking and sitting meditation.
This is called the final watch of the night.
The latter part of the night consists of more than one watch.

During that time, perceiving light, mindful and clearly comprehending, and attending only to the perception of rising, he passes the middle watch of the night—more than one watch—without succumbing to torpor;
at whatever time he rises, at that very time his body becomes serviceable.

Having risen, he is not overcome by an excessive obsession of sloth and torpor, such that upon rising he would experience sluggishness, dullness, or the indolence of laziness. Furthermore, in the absence of that sluggishness, dullness, or indolence of laziness, his rising occurs very quickly with mere application of effort.
The purification of the mind from obstructive states through walking and sitting should be understood as previously described.
This, then, is the detailed analysis of being devoted to the practice of vigilance during the first and last watches of the night.
Furthermore, what are the summarized meanings?
Here, for a person who is devoted to the practice of wakefulness, there are four things that ought to be correctly performed.
What are the four?
As long as he is awake, he does not abandon the side of wholesome qualities,
being constant in the cultivation of wholesome dharmas;
and he makes his bed at the proper time, not at an improper time.
And while sleeping, he falls into sleep with an unafflicted mind, not with an afflicted mind.
And he awakens at the proper time; he does not let the time for rising pass by. [The first half of the night and...]
These four are the things that must be correctly practiced by a person who, during the latter part of the night, exerts themselves in the application of wakefulness.
Thus, with reference to these four things that must be correctly practiced, the Blessed One taught his disciples the practice of being devoted to wakefulness.
And how, moreover, has it been taught? To begin with, it says:
"By means of walking and sitting during the day, he purifies the mind of obstructive states."

"Thus, during the first watch of the night, he purifies his mind of obstructive states through walking and sitting. By this, first of all, that which is to be correctly practiced is declared: namely, as long as one is awake, one does not abandon the side of the wholesome, being diligent and constant in the cultivation of wholesome qualities.
Furthermore, because it says:
"Having washed his feet outside the monastery and entered the monastery, he lies down on his right side."
By the phrase "placing foot upon foot," the second thing to be correctly practiced is declared;
namely, that one prepares for sleep at the proper time, and not at an improper time.
Furthermore, as it says:
"Perceiving light, mindful, clearly comprehending, and directing his attention precisely to the perception of rising, he lies down"— by this, the third thing to be correctly practiced is declared:
namely, that one enters into sleep with an unafflicted mind, and not with an afflicted mind.
Furthermore, as it says:
"Having awakened very quickly during the final watch of the night, he purifies his mind from obstructive states through walking and sitting. (Śbh I 170)
By this, the fourth thing to be correctly accomplished has been declared;
namely, that he awakens at the proper time and does not let the time for rising pass by.
Thus, regarding what was stated there:
“Possessing the perception of light, mindful and clearly comprehending, and attending precisely to the perception of rising, he takes up his rest.
Therefore, by these two causes, one enters into sleep with an undefiled mind.
Namely, by means of mindfulness and clear comprehension;
furthermore, by two causes:
He awakens at the proper time and does not let the time pass,
namely by means of the perception of light and the perception of rising.
How, then?
By means of mindfulness, one falls asleep having grasped a wholesome object;
by means of clear comprehension, one very quickly and correctly recognizes the mind as it is falling away from or becoming defiled by that wholesome object.
Thus, by these two causes, his sleep occurs with an unafflicted mind.
Therein, through the perception of light and the perception of rising, he does not sleep deeply,
nor does that obsession of torpor persist long within him.
Thus, by these two causes, he awakens at the proper time and does not let the time for rising pass by.
This is the summary meaning for one devoted to the practice of wakefulness.
That which is the detailed analysis previously mentioned and this which is the summarized meaning—
this is called "application to the practice of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night."
(Śbh I 172) What is dwelling with clear comprehension?
It is when, for example, a certain person here dwells with clear comprehension while advancing and retreating.
In looking forward and looking aside; in drawing back and stretching forth; in carrying the outer robe, the inner robe, and the bowl;
in eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting;
in going, standing, sitting, and lying down.
Whether waking, speaking, remaining silent, or dispelling drowsiness and fatigue, he dwells with clear comprehension.
In that regard, what is advancing?
What is retreating?
And what is dwelling with clear comprehension in advancing and retreating?
In this regard, approaching is as follows:
for instance, here a certain person approaches a village, or another village; a family, or another family; a monastery, or another monastery.
In that regard, retreat is as follows: for instance, a certain person here returns from a village,
or from another village, or from one family, or from another family, or from a monastery, or from another monastery.
In that regard, it is dwelling with clear comprehension:
when stepping forward, one correctly knows, "I am stepping forward";
when stepping back, one correctly knows, "I am stepping back."
He understands correctly: "In this case I should advance; in this case, however, I should not advance.
Or: "This is the time for my advancement..."
"This is the time for walking," he understands correctly;
this is called his clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*). If he is endowed with that clear comprehension, [he acts accordingly].
While stepping forward, he knows, "I am stepping forward";
and he steps forward only where it is necessary to step forward;
and he steps forward at the proper time, not at an improper time.
And in whatever manner it is necessary to approach— with such a mode of conduct, behavior, and deportment that are disciplined— he approaches in that way.
This is called his dwelling in clear comprehension.
That is to say, in advancing and retreating.
In that regard, what is looking forward?
What is looking around? And what is dwelling with clear comprehension regarding looking forward and looking around?
As he moves forward and backward among those objects previously described,
whatever seeing of forms with the eye occurs in the interval that is not preceded by deliberate thought, not preceded by effort, and not preceded by intentional desire—
this is called looking (ālokita).

Furthermore, there is the seeing of forms with the eye by one who has approached and departed from those [places], preceded by intention, preceded by effort, and preceded by desire—such as the dwellings of kings, royal ministers, townsmen, or countryfolk; or those of brahmins, householders, wealthy men, guild-masters, or caravan leaders; or other external lodgings, wind-shelters, inner apartments, palaces, and upper chambers.
Furthermore, whatever else consists of seeing the various wonders of the world,
this is called "looking about" (vyavalokita).
Moreover, that which one correctly understands, according to its own specific characteristics, both as looking ahead (ālokita) and as looking about (vyavalokita), [is called "clear comprehension"].
He also correctly understands that which is to be looked at and that which is to be scrutinized;
he also correctly understands when it is to be looked at and when it is to be scrutinized;
and he also correctly understands how it is to be looked at and how it is to be scrutinized. (Śbh I 176)
This is called his clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*). Endowed with that clear comprehension,
if while looking ahead or looking around he knows, "I am looking ahead" or "I am looking around," [he possesses clear comprehension].

Whatever is to be looked at and whatever is to be observed, that he looks at and observes; whenever there is anything to be looked at and observed, that he looks at and observes; and in whatever manner it is to be looked at and observed, in that manner he looks at and observes.
