This is called his dwelling in clear comprehension, namely, in looking ahead and looking around.
In this regard, what is contraction, what is extension, and what is dwelling with clear comprehension regarding contraction and extension?
As he was thus looking ahead and surveying his surroundings, whether moving forward or returning, whenever he contracted or extended his feet, [he did so with full awareness].
Or he contracts or extends his arms; or he contracts or extends his hands; or he contracts or extends this or that limb or member of the body.
This is called the contraction and extension.
If he correctly understands contraction and extension according to their own specific characteristics,
and correctly understands what is to be contracted and what is to be extended, [then he possesses right mindfulness].
When it is to be contracted and when it is to be extended, he understands that correctly;
how it is to be contracted and how it is to be extended, that too he understands correctly.
This is called his clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*).
Endowed with that clear comprehension,
if while contracting or extending [the limbs] he knows, "I am contracting; I am extending," [he possesses clear comprehension].
Whatever is to be contracted or extended, he contracts or extends it;
when it is to be contracted or extended, then he contracts or extends it;
and in whatever manner it is to be contracted or extended, in that manner he contracts or extends it.
This is said to be his dwelling in full awareness, namely, with regard to the contraction and extension [of the limbs].
In that regard, what is the wearing of the outer robe (saṃghāṭī), what is the wearing of the religious robes (cīvara),
and what is the carrying of the alms-bowl (pātra)?
What is dwelling with clear comprehension regarding the wearing of the outer robe, the inner robe, and the bowl?
It is that his outer robe consists of sixty or ninety patches,
and is sewn with double or single thickness.
This is called the *saṃghāṭī*.
Its wearing, its use, its proper maintenance, and its keeping are what is meant by "wearing.

Furthermore, whatever robe of his there may be—whether it be the middle-sized, the smallest, the basic robe (*adhiṣṭhānika*), an extra robe (*atirekacīvara*), or one that is fit for formal determination (*vikalpanārha*) or has already been determined (*vikalpita*).
That is called "robe";
its wearing, its use, its proper maintenance, and its preservation are called "carrying.
Furthermore, whatever begging bowl he possesses—whether made of iron, clay, or other materials—[is also included].
This is called the bowl;
its use, its proper care, and its maintenance are called "retention.
Furthermore, if he correctly understands that outer robe, the monastic garment, the bowl, or the retention itself according to their own specific characteristics.
He also correctly understands whether the wearing of the outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*), the upper robe (*cīvara*), and the alms bowl (*pātra*) is permissible or impermissible;
he also correctly understands when the wearing of the outer robe, the upper robe, and the alms bowl should be undertaken,
and he also correctly understands how they should be worn.
This is called his clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*).
Endowed with that clear comprehension, if he is wearing his outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*), inner robe (*cīvara*), or alms bowl (*pātra*), he knows: "I am wearing it.
And he wears only that which ought to be worn.
When it is to be worn, he wears it;
and he wears it in the manner in which it should be worn.
This is called his dwelling in clear comprehension regarding the wearing of the outer robe, the upper robe, and the alms bowl.
In this regard, what is the eaten and what is the drunk?
What is chewing?
What is tasting?
What is the state of dwelling with clear comprehension regarding what has been eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted?
Whatever constitutes the enjoyment of alms-food is all called "eaten.
Furthermore, that is divided into two types:
chewed food and tasted food.
In that regard, there is what has been chewed, or stirred porridge,
or cake;
Either boiled rice or gruel,
or whatever other prepared food there may be— altered, edible, and sustaining life—
this is called "chewed food" (khādita).
This is also what is eaten.
What is tasted?
It is as follows: milk, curd, fresh butter, ghee, oil, honey, molasses, meat, fish, dried meat, salt, forest fruits, or various kinds of food.
This is called "tasted," and this is also "eaten";
furthermore, that which is drunk, such as the juice of sugar-candy, is likewise [included].
Or sugar-water, or sour gruel, or the whey of curdled milk.
Either fermented gruel, or buttermilk, or at the very least, even water.
This is called "the drunk.
He correctly understands, according to their specific characteristics, what has been eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted;
and he also correctly understands that which is to be eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted.
When one should eat, drink, chew, or taste, one understands that correctly;
and how one should eat, drink, chew, or taste, one understands that correctly as well.
This is called his *saṃprajanya* (clear comprehension).

Endowed with that clear comprehension, while eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting, if he knows: "I am eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting," then he eats, drinks, chews, and tastes whatever is to be eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted;
and he eats, drinks, chews, and tastes it at the time when it is to be eaten, up to the time when it is to be tasted.
In whatever manner one should eat and taste, so he eats and tastes;
this is called his dwelling in clear comprehension regarding what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted.
In that regard, what is going, what is standing, and what is sitting?
What is sleeping? What is waking? What is speaking?
What is silence? What is the dispelling of drowsiness and fatigue?
What is dwelling with clear comprehension while walking, standing, sitting, lying down, waking, speaking, remaining silent, and dispelling drowsiness and fatigue?
For instance, here someone might be walking back and forth on a path for exercise, or approach fellow practitioners of the Dharma, or set out upon a journey.
This is called his "gone" [state].
For instance, here a certain person stands on the walking-path, or stands before his fellow practitioners, teachers, preceptors, gurus, or those who occupy the position of a guru.
This is called "established.
For example, here a certain person sits down or settles upon a couch, a stool, or a grass mat,
having folded his legs crosswise in the paryanka posture.
Having set the body straight and established mindfulness before oneself—
this is called "seated."
Just as here, a certain person, having washed his feet outside the monastery and entered the monastery, prepares the lion’s posture on his right side—
placing one foot upon the other—
on a couch, or a chair, or a bed of grass.
In the forest, or at the foot of a tree, or in an empty dwelling— this is called "lying down.
Furthermore, just as a certain person here purifies the mind from obstructive states through walking and sitting during the day, so too [does he do so] at night.
Thus, during the first watch of the night and the last watch,
this is called being awake.
For example, here a certain person, being thus devoted to the practice of wakefulness, [studies] those teachings that have not yet been taught.
He recites and masters them, namely: the discourses (*sūtra*), the verses (*geya*), the prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*), and so forth in detail as previously described;
and regarding those teachings he has recited, he cultivates familiarity through speech.
That is to say, by means of extensive recitation,
or by extensively elucidating it to others;
and by speaking with and greeting from time to time wise fellow-celibates or other householders, namely for the purpose of encouragement and providing requisites.
This is called "spoken.

For example, here a certain person, having gone alone to a secluded place, reflects upon, weighs, and examines the meaning of those teachings as they were heard, as they were mastered, and as they have been fully acquired through speech;
or again, being in retreat, he settles the mind within himself.
He establishes, settles, brings near, tames, calms, thoroughly pacifies, makes one-pointed, and concentrates [the mind], or applies himself to the practice of insight (*vipaśyanā*).
This is called "silence.
Just as, for example, here someone, when the summer season has arrived and the time of the most intense summer heat is present, [remains silent].
Whether one is afflicted by heat or becomes exhausted,
when one is weary, there arises at an improper time the fatigue of sleep and a desire to lie down;
this is called the fatigue of sleep.
Furthermore, if he correctly understands, according to their specific characteristics, everything from going up to the dispelling of drowsiness and fatigue;
and if he also correctly understands where one must go up to where drowsiness and fatigue must be dispelled— then [he is practicing rightly].
He also correctly understands when he ought to go, up to and including when he ought to dispel drowsiness and fatigue;
and he understands how he ought to go, up to and including how he ought to dispel drowsiness and fatigue.
He understands that correctly as well;
this is called his clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*). Endowed with that clear comprehension, whether he is walking or even experiencing the fatigue of sleep, [he acts accordingly].

If, while dispelling [drowsiness], he falls asleep, thinking, "I shall go until I have dispelled the fatigue of sleep," then he goes to wherever it is necessary to go and to wherever the fatigue of sleep is to be dispelled.
He goes there and remains there until he has dispelled his drowsiness and fatigue;
and when it is time to go, and when it is time to dispel his drowsiness and fatigue, then he goes, and then he dispels his drowsiness and fatigue.
And just as he ought to go, and just as he ought to dispel drowsiness and fatigue, so he goes; and just as he ought to dispel drowsiness and fatigue, so he dispels it.
This is called his dwelling in clear comprehension, namely, in regard to going, standing, sitting, lying down, waking, speaking, remaining silent, and the dispelling of drowsiness and fatigue.
What is the sequence for dwelling in clear comprehension, and what is the analysis of the objects?
For example, here a certain person dwells depending upon a particular village or town; it occurs to him:
"I must indeed approach this village or town for alms."
Having wandered for alms, one must return once again to the monastery.
Furthermore, there are families here—whether in a village or a city—to which I should not approach;
what, then, are those?
Namely: a tavern, a brothel, a royal palace, a cemetery, or those families that are entirely hostile and unyielding;
yet there are also families whom I ought to visit.

For example, whether they be great kṣatriya families, great brahmin families, great householder families, merchant families, provincial families, wealthy families, guild-leader families, caravan-leader families,
or whatever families I ought to visit, I should not visit them too late in the evening, nor at an improper time.
Nor [should one approach] when donors and masters of giving are preoccupied with their duties, nor when they are engaged in play, pleasure, or adornment,
nor when they have set out for sexual intercourse.
Nor among those who are angry. Furthermore, one should approach them in such a way that, while approaching, I do not encounter a wandering elephant, nor a wandering chariot, nor a fierce horse,
nor a fierce cow, nor a fierce dog.
I shall not trample upon thickets or thorn-hedges; I shall not fall into pits, puddles, or precipices;
nor [shall I fall] into a stream.
Like a ball of dung, like the moon, I should approach families with modesty and without arrogance, having withdrawn my body and withdrawn my mind; not desiring gain, nor desiring honor;

just as I am well-disposed and cheerful in my own gain, so too I am well-disposed and cheerful in the gain of others; not exalting myself, not disparaging others, with a mind of compassion and a mind of pity.
Furthermore, one should approach [other families] in this manner:
"How could it be appropriate for one who has gone forth to have such thoughts regarding the families of others as: 'May others give to me, may they not not give;
may they give quickly, may they not give slowly'? and so on in detail.
Having approached, one should accept [offerings] with moderation;
for the sake of gain, one should not practice hypocrisy, flattery, hinting, or pressuring, nor seek to obtain gain through gain.
Furthermore, that gain should be enjoyed without attachment.
“Without attachment, without greed, without being fettered, without delusion, without fixation, and without having fallen into the state of fixation.”
Furthermore, as for those forms which are to be seen when one is approaching or has already approached that place— some of them are not to be looked at, while others are to be looked at.
Regarding those which are not to be looked at, one should keep the eyes cast down and maintain well-restrained sense faculties.
Furthermore, regarding those things which are to be seen, one should establish well-established mindfulness toward them.
What kind of forms, then, are not to be looked at?
Namely: actors, dancers, jesters, and performers.
Or again, whatever other kind of performance there may be— whether engaged in dance, song, or instrumental music—
and likewise, especially women, or even a young girl of noble appearance who is alluring;
and furthermore, those forms which, when seen, lead to the impairment of celibacy and constitute an obstacle to the holy life.
One should not look at, nor gaze upon, such forms as would lead to the manifestation of evil and unwholesome thoughts.

“What kind of forms, moreover, are to be seen? For example: one who is decrepit, aged, or very old; whose body gasps with a wheezing sound, whose body is bent forward, and who leans upon a staff with a trembling frame; or one who is afflicted, suffering, and severely ill, with swollen feet, swollen hands, a swollen belly, and a swollen face, with a complexion as pale as that of a leper.
One suffering from ringworm, or scabies, or leprosy, with a body afflicted by pain;
one with a putrefied body and impaired faculties;
or one who is dead and deceased—whether dead for one day, two days, or seven days.
Being devoured by crows,
ospreys, vultures, dogs, jackals, or various other creatures belonging to the animal realm;
or being carried out while placed upon a bier, with a canopy spread above it, and a great multitude of people weeping before and behind.
With one weeping, with hair disheveled and smeared with ashes, one should behold the states born of sorrow, born of suffering, born of lamentation, born of dejection, and born of despair;
and other such forms as "this is what must be seen by me"— such forms are to be beheld.
Those which conduce to the support of the holy life and to the manifestation of wholesome thoughts.
One should approach without swaying the body, without swaying the arms, and without swaying the head; one should not laugh loudly, nor clasp hands together, nor approach with a haughty air;
and one should not sit down on a seat without being invited to do so.
One should not sit without having examined the seat,
nor with the whole body collapsed,
nor with one foot placed upon the other.
Not with one leg over the other, nor with the feet drawn together,
nor with the feet spread apart.
Not with one's head covered,
nor with one's upper garment tied up.
Not with the arms akimbo, not with the robe draped over both shoulders, but having put on the robe evenly all around.
One should not wear a robe that is too high or too low, nor one shaped like an elephant’s trunk, a palm-leaf fan, a cobra’s hood, or a lump of boiled beans.
One should not hold out the bowl before solid food has been brought forward.
One should not hold it over hard food or soft food. One should not place the bowl on a patch of ground that is not covered, nor on a precipice, nor on a slope.
One should consume almsfood in its proper order;
one should not cover the curry with rice.
One should not eat rice with curry;
one should not consume food while intent on a state of dissatisfaction.
A morsel should be made neither too large nor too small, but of moderate size and round in shape before it is taken into the mouth.
He does not lick his hands, nor does he lick his bowl;
he does not shake his hands, nor does he shake his bowl;
he does not cut off morsels of food.
The alms-food should be consumed.
“Even when I have returned from those families and am staying in my residence, whether by day or by night, I should walk upon my own personal walking-path,
and not on another’s that is untrustworthy, unauthorized, or unassigned;
nor should I do so with a weary body or an exhausted body.”
When the mind is restrained by non-excitement, engaged in the side of the wholesome, and not followed by unwholesome mental orientations,
with the sense faculties withdrawn inwardly and the mind not turned outward;
Neither too fast nor too hurried, not exclusively engaged in going and returning, but moving at the proper time and staying at the proper time;
likewise, in his own monastery, his own courtyard, or his own individual cell, whether assigned or personal.
Nor should one sit on another's [belonging] that is untrustworthy or where permission has not been granted; likewise, one should not sit on a couch, a stool, a spread of grass,
or in a forest, at the foot of a tree, or in an empty dwelling.
Having crossed his legs in the paryanka posture,
having set the body straight,
and having established mindfulness directed toward the front.
One should sleep during the middle watch of the night;
during the day and the first watch [of the night], one should pass the time in wholesome practices. Furthermore, one should sleep in this manner:
Perceiving light, mindful, clearly comprehending, and attending specifically to the perception of rising, he wakes up very quickly during the final watch of the night.
One should apply oneself to either speaking or the practice of recitation,
or to abandonment and solitary retreat.
In the contemplation of the Dharma,
one should avoid Lokāyata mantras—
those consisting of variegated syllables and diverse words and phrases that are devoid of meaningful purpose.
Those things which do not lead to direct knowledge, nor to full awakening, nor to nirvāṇa; or rather,
those teachings spoken by the Tathāgata which are profound, appearing profound, connected with emptiness,
and in accordance with specific conditionality and dependent origination— these should be respectfully grasped, held firmly and steadfastly.
And having well grasped them, they must not be lost;
this is for the sake of accomplishing practice, not for the sake of gain or honor.
Furthermore, those teachings should be thoroughly mastered through speech;
one should not spend time in social distraction, nor delight in worldly work, nor delight in idle talk.
And from time to time, with mindfulness established, one should converse, chat, and exchange greetings with wise fellow-celibates.
One should be of a nature to inquire,
seeking what is wholesome,
with a mind free from fault-finding.
One who speaks measuredly, one who speaks appropriately, one who speaks with loftiness, and one who speaks with tranquility.
One who wishes to speak a discourse on the Dharma to others should not entertain any evil or unwholesome thoughts by remaining silent.
Nor should one engage in improper reflection on phenomena,
nor become conceited,
nor be satisfied with a mere slight degree of special realization.
One should not become despondent by remaining stuck in mere mediocrity;
one should completely abandon those states that are unfit for cultivation;
and from time to time, one should practice śamatha.
One should apply oneself to insight (vipaśyanā),
delight in abandonment,
and strive for constant application.
One should think, "I shall strive to act with reverence."
(I)-C-III-8-a-(3)-ix Ms., Sh., P.60b2:
Or, being tormented by the heat of the spring season,
or likewise through such exertion;
The cause of exhaustion from evil, exertion, or performing even slight appropriate tasks; and...
If, on account of physical exhaustion, an unseasonable drowsiness should arise,
he should act in such a way that it is quickly and thoroughly dispelled,
so that for a long duration his engagement with the side of virtue is not impaired.
In order that it may not become an obstacle to the side of virtue,
one should clear away sleep for a brief moment; even there, one should ensure one's door is closed.
If there is a monk present, he should be made to enter [the assembly],
and having bound him with the religious robes according to the protection of the Vinaya and the ritual of the Vinaya, [he should be dealt with].
Staying in a secluded place,
he thinks, "I shall dispel my sleepiness," and thereby his drowsiness will be eliminated in every way and in all respects.
(I)-C-IIl-8-a-(4) This refers to that which concerns movement and conduct.
This is the sequence for acting with clear comprehension;
first of all, one engages in such appropriate mental attention.
Whatever mental formation of a mind endowed with wisdom is present, that is called his "clear comprehension."
Thus, the complete accomplishment of all movements and activities by one endowed with clear comprehension is called "acting with clear comprehension.
In this regard, [it includes] going and returning...
Looking slightly, looking around, and contracting [the limbs].
The spreading out [of the bedding],
the outer robe, and the religious robes.
Whatever is held in the alms-bowl,
and whatever is eaten and drunk;
Whatever constitutes being mindful and tasting,
that which is the practice of clear comprehension therein is called "the state of practicing with clear comprehension while wandering in the village."
Having gone there,
he stood and sat.
Sleeping,
waking,
and speaking;

That which is silence and that which is the clearing away of drowsiness and lethargy— whatever constitutes such conduct with clear comprehension is called "possessing clear comprehension while conducting oneself in the monastery."
This, for now, should be understood as the detailed classification of the practice of clear comprehension itself.
(I)-C-IIl-8-b-(1) What is the summary of the meaning?
It consists of the five types of karma associated with movement and—
The five types of actions associated with conduct, those associated with movement,
and the four types of acting with clear comprehension regarding actions associated with conduct— this is called the summary of the meaning.
What are the five types of karma associated with movement?
They are as follows: bodily karma, and... [mental karma].
The activity of the eyes, and the activity of all the limbs and members;
The work of robes and the alms bowl, and the work of alms-gathering.
That is called the fivefold karma associated with movement.
In that regard, first, what was spoken of as "reversing" and "proceeding" teaches bodily action associated with movement.
By what was said— “looking slightly” and “looking around”— the activity of the eye associated with movement is shown.
By the expression "bending and extending," all the activities of the major and minor limbs associated with movement are indicated.
By the statement, "carrying the saṃghāṭī,
the religious robes,
and the alms bowl," it refers to the religious robes associated with wandering.
The ritual procedures for the alms bowl have been taught.
“Eaten, drunk,
chewed,
and tasted.”
By what was said, "having tasted," the activity of alms-gathering associated with movement is taught.
What are the five types of actions associated with conduct? They are as follows: bodily action, and...
The action of speech, the action of mind, and the action of the day.
This is the activity of the night;
it is called the fivefold activity endowed with conduct.
In that regard, first, by what was said— "going," "standing," and "sitting"— the bodily action associated with movement is shown.
By the expression "speaking," the verbal action associated with conduct is indicated.
By what was said— "lying down, remaining silent, and dispelling the drowsiness of sleep"— the mental action associated with conduct is shown.
By the expression "not sleeping," it refers to the daytime activities, the nighttime activities, and the physical activities associated with such conduct.
The verbal action has also been explained.
By the expression "sleeping," it is shown that there are exclusively the activities of the night associated with conduct and mental activity;
one should understand that these constitute the five types of activities associated with conduct.
(I)-C-IIl-8-b-(2) What are the four modes of acting with clear comprehension regarding actions associated with movement and associated with conduct?
At the very outset, when one undertakes a movement or an activity, thinking, "I shall begin such an action as this," one establishes mindfulness upon that very action.
Acting with heedfulness, and being fully possessed by mindfulness of that action and also fully possessed by heedfulness,
in whatever basis and in whatever direction—
At whatever time, to whatever extent, and in whatever manner that basis is to be examined,
at that time, in that place,
to that extent, and in that manner, one examines and thoroughly understands it.
When one reflects and understands in this way, in this very life there is no reproach and no downfall.
One will become free from regret, free from remorse,
and free from subsequent burning anguish.
Furthermore, in future lives, one will be free from fault;
after the body has perished and death has occurred, one will not be reborn in the miserable states, the evil destinies, or the fallen realms among the hell beings,
and one will have established the cause for the accumulation [of merit] to attain what has not yet been attained.
This is a summary of the meaning of acting with clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya-cāritva*). That which was previously explained in detail through its various classifications,
and this summary of its meaning, is called "acting with clear comprehension."
(Śbh I 212) (I)-C-III-9-a-(1) What, then, is a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*)?
One should understand that there are eight reasons why [such a person] is a spiritual friend who is complete in every respect.
What are the eight? They are as follows: here, someone from the very beginning abides in ethical discipline and is one who has heard much.
Being possessed of discernment,
being possessed of subsequent compassion,
and being one whose mind is never weary.
He is endowed with patience, he is endowed with fearlessness,
and he is endowed with the proper use of speech.
How, then, does one abide in ethical discipline? In detail, as previously stated, it is by abiding possessed of ethical discipline.
Restrained by the vows of individual liberation,
desiring the path of the śramaṇa, and desiring the path of the brāhmaṇa.
I have entered this path for the sake of taming myself, for the sake of pacifying myself, and for the sake of attaining my own parinirvāṇa.
In that way, one abides in ethical discipline.
In what way is one "learned" (bahuśruta)? It is by means of that [learning] which pertains to the holy life (brahmacarya), which is virtuous in the beginning, and so forth.
virtuous in the middle, virtuous at the end,
and excellent in meaning;
With excellent phrasing, unadulterated, and complete.
Those things which are completely pure and completely refined, he expresses through verbal articulation;
thus many such dharmas have been mastered by him— retained, mastered verbally, examined mentally, and thoroughly penetrated by insight.
In this way, one becomes one who has heard much.
How does one become an attainer?

One becomes a possessor of the perception of impermanence regarding the impermanent, the perception of suffering regarding suffering, the perception of non-self regarding what is suffering, and the perception of repulsiveness regarding food.

The perception of non-delight in the entire world, the perception of disadvantage, the perception of abandonment, the perception of dispassion, the perception of cessation, the perception of death, the perception of impurity, the perception of a livid corpse, the perception of a festering corpse, the perception of a worm-infested corpse, the perception of a bloated corpse, the perception of a mangled corpse, the perception of a bloody corpse, the perception of a scattered corpse, and the perception of a skeleton.
He becomes a possessor of the perception of the contemplation of emptiness;

he becomes a possessor of the first dhyāna, the second, the third, and the fourth; of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; and of the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, and the fruit of non-returning.

He becomes capable and empowered to instruct others by means of three miracles: the miracle of supernormal power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*), the miracle of mind-reading (*ādeśanāprātihārya*), and the miracle of instruction (*anuśāsanīprātihārya*). [These correspond to] the domain of supernormal powers, recollection of past lives, the divine ear, knowledge of the death and rebirth of beings, knowledge of the mental dispositions of others, the state of an Arhat, and the meditative absorption in the eight liberations.
By means of the miracle of mind-reading and the miracle of instruction,
he thus becomes an attainer.
How does one become compassionate?
One becomes compassionate toward others, endowed with mercy and pity;
one desires their welfare, desires their benefit, desires their happiness, desires their well-being, and desires their security.
In this way, one becomes compassionate.
How does one become untiring in mind?
One becomes a demonstrator, an inspirer, an encourager, and a gladdener;
one is indefatigable in teaching the Dharma to the four assemblies, being skillful, unlazy, endowed with initiative, and of a nature characterized by the arousal of vigor.
In this way, one becomes one whose mind is free from weariness.
How does one become patient?
When reviled, one does not revile in return.
When provoked to anger, he does not respond with anger; when struck, he does not strike back;
when reviled, he does not revile in return.
He is capable of enduring being struck and counter-struck;
even when subjected to severe binding, confinement, beating, reviling, threatening, or mutilation, he considers himself at fault and attributes it to the ripening of his own karma.
He does not become angry toward others,
nor does he harbor resentment;
thus, even when insulted, reviled, or despised, he does not undergo a transformation of mind.
He intends for nothing other than the goal itself;
he is patient with cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping reptiles;
and with harsh, offensive words from others, and with the arising of bodily feelings that are painful, intense, piercing, bitter, disagreeable, and life-threatening.
He is patient and of a nature inclined toward endurance;
thus he becomes one who possesses patience.
How does he become confident?
With an undaunted mind, he teaches the Dharma in the assembly with an unhesitating voice, his mindfulness and eloquence being unconfused;
and because of this confidence, neither fear nor terror caused by timidity overcomes or takes possession of him.
Nor is sweat released from the armpits or from the pores of the skin;
in this way, he becomes confident.
How is he endowed with the faculty of speech?
He is possessed of speech that is clear and articulate.
eloquent,
clear, and intelligible;
worth hearing,
not disagreeable,
and independent;
With such boundless [eloquence],
he is thus endowed with the faculty of speech and possesses excellent speech.
Endowed with these eight qualities, he is one who exhorts, one who reminds, one who instructs, and one who advises.
The teacher of the Dharma.
And how does one become corrupted? Namely, by the failure of morality regarding higher morality,
and by the failure of conduct regarding higher conduct.

He exhorts based on what has been seen, heard, or suspected; with what is true and not false, at the proper time and not the wrong time, with what is meaningful and not meaningless, with gentleness and not harshness, out of friendship and not from within malice.
In this way, he is an exhorter.
How does one act as a reminder?
One reminds [another] of an offense, or of the Dharma, or of the meaning.
How does one remind [another] of an offense?
For instance, when someone has committed an offense but does not remember it, he reminds him: "Venerable sir, in such a place,
regarding such a matter..."
"At such a time,
I fell into such and such an offense"—
in this way, one causes the offense to be remembered.
(Śbh I 220) How does he cause [another] to recollect the Dharma? It is when, for instance, one who is alone does not recollect those teachings that have been heard and mastered.
He wishes to remember; for example, as previously described in detail— such as the *sūtra*, *geya*, and *vyākaraṇa*— he does not remember it, and so one causes him to remember it,
or provides him with a reminder.
Whether by means of inquiry or further questioning,
he thus causes [the other] to remember the Dharma.
How does he cause [them] to remember the meaning?
Just as he might forget that purpose, he reminds him of it;
furthermore, he makes it fresh again and clarifies it.
He teaches and fully elucidates it;
furthermore, he causes others to remember whatever is wholesome, connected with the goal, and connected with the holy life, even if it was performed long ago or spoken long ago.
In this way, one becomes a reminder.
How does one become an instructor?
One provides timely, conformable instruction regarding seclusion, solitary retreat, yoga, mental attention, and calm abiding and insight;
and from time to time, one engages in discourse connected with those topics.

That is to say, he gives a discourse that leads to the removal of mental hindrances—a discourse on ethical discipline, or on concentration, or on wisdom, or on liberation, or on the knowledge and vision of liberation; or a discourse on fewness of desires, or on contentment, or on relinquishment, or on dispassion, or on cessation, or on diminution, or on non-association; or a discourse in accordance with specific conditionality and dependent origination.
In this way, one becomes an instructor.
How is he an instructor?
He is one who instructs in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya within the Teacher’s dispensation;

whether as a teacher (*ācārya*), a preceptor (*upādhyāya*), a fellow practitioner of the Dharma, a guru, or one in the position of a guru, having recognized that someone has not desisted from or has transgressed in any particular matter, [he instructs them].
From time to time he disciplines him, inflicts punishment upon him, and even banishes him;
yet again, in accordance with the Dharma and at the proper time, he accepts his hospitality, his respectful service, and his confession, and acts as one who gathers him back.
Regarding what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, and regarding conduct that has been practiced or not practiced, he instructs and exhorts him.
In this way, he becomes an instructor.

And how does one become a teacher of the Dharma? From time to time, he delivers discourse on matters to be practiced beforehand, namely: discourse on generosity, discourse on ethical discipline, and discourse on heaven.
He extensively elucidates the dharmas belonging to the side of purification— the disadvantages of sensual pleasures and the means of escape from them—
and from time to time he delivers an exalted discourse connected with the four noble truths,
concerning either suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path.
For the sake of maturing sentient beings, or for the purification of sentient beings, or for the long endurance of the true Dharma,
[he teaches] with words and phrases that are appropriate, coherent, conformable, suitable, skillful, fitting, and favorable— the equipment of limbs for one who is prudent. (Śbh I 224)
Furthermore, he delivers that discourse at the proper time,

with respect, in due order, with logical connection and continuity, gladdening, pleasing, satisfying, and encouraging [the listeners], without discouraging them; it is appropriate, coherent, unconfused, righteous, and suited to the assembly, being delivered with a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of benefit, and a mind of compassion.
Not relying on gain, honor, or fame, he does not exalt himself nor disparage others;
thus he becomes a teacher of the Dharma.
And he who is endowed with these eight factors, and who from time to time acts as an exhorter, a reminder, an instructor, an advisor, and a teacher of the Dharma—
for that reason, he is called a "spiritual friend" (kalyāṇamitra).
This, then, is the detailed analysis of the nature of a spiritual friend.
Furthermore, what is the summarized meaning?
If this friend, companion, and compassionate one is from the very beginning desirous of [their] welfare, [then...]
And he desires happiness; furthermore, he understands that welfare and happiness as they truly are,
being undeluded and possessing non-perverted vision.
And he becomes capable and skillful in means for the sake of the attainment and the bringing about of that very benefit and happiness;
he is also dexterous, untiring, endowed with initiative, and of a nature characterized by the exertion of vigor,
namely, with respect to that very bringing about of benefit and happiness.
By these four reasons, a spiritual friend should be understood, in brief, as one who is complete in every aspect. Furthermore,
this is the summary of the meaning of being a spiritual friend.
That which was the previous detailed analysis and this summary meaning— this is called the state of being a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitratā*).
What is the hearing and reflection upon the true Dharma (*saddharma*)?

The true Dharma is that which has been proclaimed, taught, made clear, revealed, and fully elucidated by the Buddhas, the disciples of the Buddhas, the virtuous ones, those who have gone rightly, and the true persons.
Furthermore, what is that?

Namely: the discourses (sūtra), the verses (geya), the prophecies (vyākaraṇa), and so forth in detail as previously described; this twelvefold collection of teachings is called the True Dharma (saddharma).

In this regard, what is the Sūtra? It is that discourse which was given here and there by the Blessed One, concerning various disciples and their various modes of conduct, either connected with the aggregates (skandha) or connected with the elements (dhātu).
Either connected with the analysis of the elements, or connected with the sense-bases,
or connected with dependent origination.
Whether they are connected with food and the truths,
or connected with the disciples, solitary buddhas, and tathāgatas,
or connected with the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, and the limbs of the path;
A discourse connected with the foul, mindfulness of breathing, the trainings, and the clear faiths was delivered.
That discourse was then compiled by the redactors for the long endurance of the teaching, arranged and composed in proper sequence using appropriate sets of names, phrases, and syllables.
That is to say, for the purpose of indicating various matters that are skillful, connected with the goal, and connected with the holy life—
this is called a *sūtra*.
What is *geya*? It is that at the end or conclusion of which verses (*gāthā*) are chanted, as well as those discourses (*sūtra*) whose meaning is yet to be further explained (*neyārtha*).
This is called Geya.
What is *vyākaraṇa*?
It is that in which a disciple who has passed away is prophesied regarding his rebirth,
as well as those sūtras of explicit meaning (*nītārtha*).
This is called exposition.
What is a verse (gāthā)? It is that which is not spoken in prose, but rather composed in metrical feet— consisting of two, three, four, five, or six lines.
This is called a verse.
What is an *udāna*?

It is that which is spoken without mentioning or specifying the name or clan of a person, for the sake of the long endurance of the true Dharma and the long endurance of the teaching in the future; this is called an *udāna*.
What is the *nidāna*?
It is that which is spoken by proclaiming the name and clan of a person and addressing them;
and whatever is connected with the Vinaya, including its origin story (*sotpattika*) and its causal context (*sanidāna*), namely the *Prātimokṣasūtra*.
This is called the introduction.
What is an *avadāna*? It is that which is recounted with an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*),
by means of which illustration there occurs the purification (*vyavadāna*) of the subject matter under discussion.
This is called an avadāna.
What is the category of "past events" (*vṛttaka*)? Whatever is connected with former lives (*pūrvayoga*), this is called "past events."

What is a *jātaka*? It is that which, referring to past times, describes in various instances the conduct of a Bodhisattva during the births and deaths of the Blessed One—what is called the practice of difficult deeds.
This is termed a *jātaka*.
What is the Vaipulya?
It is that wherein the path of the bodhisattvas is taught for the sake of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and for the attainment of the ten powers and unobstructed knowledge.
This is called the Vaipulya.
What are the marvelous phenomena (*adbhutā dharmāḥ*)?
They are those in which [the qualities of] the Buddhas, the disciples of the Buddhas, the monks, the nuns, the female trainees (*śikṣamāṇā*), and the novice monks [are found].

The specific qualities— both common and uncommon, as well as those distinguished from others— which are considered marvelous and wonderful for śrāmaṇerīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, have been explained. These are called the marvelous dharmas (adbhutadharmas).
What are the instructions (upadeśa)?
All the Abhidharma matrices (mātṛkā), the extraction of the essential meaning from the discourses (sūtrānta), and the detailed explanations of the discourses are called "instructions."
And this twelvefold word of the Buddha consists of the Sūtra, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma.
In that regard, as for what was stated—
namely, *sūtra*, *geya*, *vyākaraṇa*, *gāthā*, *udāna*, *avadāna*, *vṛttaka*, *jātaka*, *vaipulya*, and *adbhutadharma*—
this, first of all, is the *sūtra*.
Furthermore, that which is called the "nidāna" is termed the Vinaya.
Furthermore, as for what he says regarding "the instructions," this is called the Abhidharma.

And this very [teaching], contained within the twelve branches of speech and comprised by the three baskets (piṭaka), taught by the virtuous who have attained the right way, is called the "True Dharma" (saddharma).
(Śbh I 234) For him, "hearing" refers to hearing the true Dharma (*saddharma*).
Furthermore, what is that?
For example, there is here someone who is a bearer of the Sūtras,
or a bearer of the Vinaya, or a bearer of the Mātṛkās.
Whether he be one who upholds the Sūtras and the Vinaya, or one who upholds the Sūtras and the Abhidharma, or one who upholds the Vinaya-mātṛkā.
Or one who upholds the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkās;
this is called hearing the true Dharma.
Furthermore, that hearing is of two kinds.
Hearing the phrasing and hearing the meaning.
What is reflection?
It is when someone here, having gone alone into seclusion, reflects upon those very teachings exactly as they were heard,
[avoiding] the six inconceivable points, namely:

Setting aside reflection on the self, reflection on sentient beings, reflection on the world, reflection on the ripening of the karma of sentient beings, the meditative domain of those in meditation, and the Buddha-domain of the Buddhas,
he reflects [on all things] by way of their specific characteristics and general characteristics.
Furthermore, that reflection is twofold:
it has the aspect of counting, which involves the application of counting dharmas;
and it has the aspect of weighing, which consists of examining qualities and defects through reasoning.
If he contemplates a teaching connected with the aggregates,
or if he contemplates any one of the various teachings previously mentioned,
he contemplates by means of these two modes.
Furthermore, as to how [it is so]:
"form" refers to the ten material bases (*āyatana*) and that form which is included within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*); this is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
The three feelings constitute the aggregate of feeling; the six groups of perception constitute the aggregate of perception;
the six groups of volition constitute the aggregate of formations.
The six groups of consciousness constitute the aggregate of consciousness.
In this way, one contemplates the teaching on the aggregates by means of the mode of enumeration and calculation;
furthermore, through successive subdivisions, one should understand that there is an immeasurable method of entry into this contemplation characterized by enumeration and calculation.
How does one contemplate the teaching on the aggregates through reflection that investigates by means of reasoning?
One investigates by means of four reasonings.
What are these four?
Namely: the reasoning of dependence,
the reasoning of causal efficiency, and the reasoning of logical proof.
By means of the reasoning of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā-yukti).
What is the reasoning of dependence?
Dependence is twofold: dependence regarding origination and dependence regarding designation.

In that regard, "dependence regarding arising" means that those causes and those conditions by which the manifestation of the aggregates occurs depend upon those very causes and those very conditions for the arising of those aggregates.
Furthermore, those sets of names, sets of phrases, and sets of phonemes by which the designation of the aggregates occurs, [depend upon them] for that [designation]. (Śbh I 238)
In the designation of the aggregates (*skandha-prajñapti*), those sets of names, phrases, and phonemes (*nāma-kāya*, *pada-kāya*, *vyañjana-kāya*) are required.
This is called the dependence on arising and the dependence on designation regarding the aggregates.

Both that which is dependence on arising and that which is dependence on designation constitute the reasoning, the application, and the means for the arising of the aggregates and for the designation of the aggregates.
Therefore, this is called the principle of dependence.
What is the principle of performing a function (*kāryakaraṇayukti*)?
It is the application of the arisen aggregates (*skandha*), by means of their own causes and their own conditions, to their respective individual functions.
For example: forms are to be seen by the eye.
Sounds are to be heard with the ear,
up to and including mental objects being cognized by the mind;
form should abide within the range of the eye.
By means of sound for the ear,
and so on up to mental phenomena for the mind;
or whatever else is of this same category.
In each respective case, the reasoning, application, or means regarding the mutual performance of functions among phenomena is called the "reasoning of performance" (kāryakaraṇayukti).
What is the reasoning that establishes through proof?
One examines that "the aggregates are impermanent," and that they are "dependently originated, suffering, empty, and non-self" by means of the three types of valid cognition.
That is to say, by means of authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*), direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and inference (*anumāna*)—
by these three instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) which are logically consistent, persuasive to the hearts of the wise, and serve as a formal establishment and proof; namely,
[the demonstration] of the impermanence of the aggregates (*skandha*), or their dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpannatā*), or their nature of suffering (*duḥkhatā*).
Whether it be emptiness or selflessness—
this is called the reasoning that establishes through proof.
What is the reasoning of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-yukti*)?
For what reason are these aggregates (*skandha*) of such a nature, and why is the arrangement of the world (*loka-saṃniveśa*) of such a nature?
For what reason is earth characterized by hardness, water characterized by fluidity, fire characterized by heat, and wind characterized by motion?
For what reason are the aggregates impermanent, and for what reason is nirvana peaceful?
Likewise, for what reason is form characterized by transformation?
Feeling has the characteristic of experiencing; perception has the characteristic of conceptualizing; mental formations have the characteristic of volitional construction.
"Consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing.
This is the nature of these phenomena;
such is their intrinsic being.
This is the very nature of things (*dharmatā*).
And that which is this nature of things is itself here the reasoning, the logical connection, and the means.
It must be exactly so.
Or otherwise,
or it might not exist at all;
in every case, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) alone is the refuge, and the nature of phenomena alone is the reasoning.
For the purpose of settling the mind and for the purpose of making the mind understand,
this is called the reasoning of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-yukti*). Thus, the teaching on the aggregates is examined by means of these four reasonings, as is any other teaching whatsoever.

That correct contemplation which, through these two modes— namely, the mode of counting and enumerating, and the mode of investigating by means of reasoning— is directed toward each respective teaching, that is reflection (*cintā*).
This is called reflection on hearing the true Dharma.
(Śbh I 244) What is the absence of obstacles?
The absence of obstacles is twofold.
With reference to the internal and the external.
In that regard, he will explain the obstacle with reference to both the internal and the external;
the absence of an obstacle should be understood as the opposite of that.
What is the internal obstacle based on internal factors?
It is when someone here has not previously performed meritorious deeds;
because he has not performed meritorious deeds, he does not obtain, from time to time, the appropriate requisites for life.
Namely, regarding the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick;
he possesses intense passion and long-lasting passion, and intense hatred and long-lasting hatred.
He has intense delusion and long-lasting delusion;
or else, he has previously performed actions conducive to affliction,
by reason of which he becomes one who abounds in illness.
In this very life, he becomes one who conducts himself improperly,
by which his wind, bile, or phlegm is frequently provoked,
or choleraic disorder persists in his body.
He becomes heavy with food, having many concerns and many duties, and frequently attends assemblies of the community.
He delights in work, or in talk, or in sleep, or in socializing, or in company, or in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
He is self-aggrandizing, fickle, negligent, or dwells in an unsuitable place.
In this way, such obstacles as these are to be understood as pertaining to the internal.
(Śbh I 246) What are the internal obstacles based on external factors? They are, for example, relying upon an unwholesome person.
Because he does not receive from time to time appropriate instruction and admonition,
or because he dwells in an unsuitable place where,
while making his dwelling, there is much commotion during the day;
At night, there is loud noise, great clamor, and the outcry of a large crowd of people;
there is also the touch of fierce and bitter wind and heat, and fear arising from both humans and non-humans.
Such things as these are to be understood as external obstacles based on external conditions.
This, then, is the detailed analysis.
Furthermore, what is the summarized meaning?
In brief, there are three kinds of obstacles:
the obstacle to application, the obstacle to seclusion, and the obstacle to withdrawal.
In that regard, what is the obstacle to application (*prayogāntarāya*)?
It is that obstacle which, when encountered and present, renders one incapable and powerless to apply oneself to the side of wholesome qualities (*kuśalapakṣa*) in every respect.
Furthermore, what is it?
When he becomes afflicted, suffering, and severely ill;
or when his wind, bile, or phlegm frequently becomes disturbed, or cholera remains in his body;
or furthermore, when a snake, a scorpion, or a centipede bites him, or a human or a non-human being harasses him.
Furthermore, one does not obtain robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, or medicinal requisites for the sick;
this kind of obstacle to application should be understood as such.
What is the obstacle to seclusion? It is when one becomes heavy with food,
has many concerns, many duties, and many tasks to perform, and takes delight in the pleasure of worldly activity.
With his mind distracted by various such duties,
he comes to delight in talk;
though capable and competent for seclusion, abandonment, solitary retreat, and cultivation, he is satisfied with merely receiving and reciting the teachings.
He delights in sleep;
overcome by sloth and torpor, being of a lazy nature, he indulges in the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of reclining, and the pleasure of lying down. He delights in socializing.

Together with householders and renunciants, he engages in talk about kings, or talk about thieves, or talk about food, or talk about drink, or talk about clothing, or talk about courtesans, or talk about streets, or talk about stories of local officials,
or talk about worldly legends, or talk about legends of the ocean.
In this way, he passes his time with talk of such a kind that is connected with what is unbeneficial;
he takes delight therein and frequently becomes one who is occupied with the assembly of crowds;
his mind is distracted and his mind is agitated by various legal disputes.
He delights in social association;
he desires to see householders and renunciants who have not yet attained meditative concentration, and he does not wish to be separated from those with whom he has already met.
One delights in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*),
takes pleasure in conceptual proliferation, is a leader among those things that lead to further involvement, and has cast off the burden regarding those things conducive to seclusion.
Such qualities as these should be understood as obstacles to seclusion.
When these are assembled and present, it is not easy to dwell in remote lodgings in forest retreats, wilderness tracts, or remote areas—
whether in the forest, at the foot of trees, or in empty dwellings.
What is the obstacle to seclusion?
It is as follows: seclusion is said to be calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
Among these, there is an obstacle to calm abiding.
There is an obstacle to insight.
In that regard, what is the obstacle to calm abiding (*śamatha*)?
It is negligence and dwelling in an unsuitable place.
For one who is thus negligent, either lethargy or drowsiness envelops the mind.
Either one relishes mere calm abiding,
or the mind inclines toward lethargy,
or there occurs a state of mental darkness.
Furthermore, by residing in such a location, there may arise external disturbances caused by humans or non-humans,
by which his mind is distracted outwardly;
this should be understood as an obstacle to *śamatha* and an obstacle to solitary retreat (*pratisaṃlayana*).
(Śbh I 252) What is the obstacle to insight?
Namely, self-exaltation and restlessness.
In that regard, self-exaltation is as follows: "I am one who has gone forth from a high family and am not inferior,
whereas other monks are not so"— thus he exalts and elevates himself, and disparages others.
Thus, "one who has gone forth from a wealthy family is not lowly";
thus, "he is handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing";
thus, "he is learned, a repository of what he has heard, and an accumulation of what he has heard."
In this way, thinking, "I am one whose speech is excellent and endowed with eloquence, whereas other monks are not so," he exalts and uplifts himself and disparages others.

While thus grasping at himself, he does not from time to time question or interrogate those monks who are elders, who have known the night [of awakening], and who have practiced the holy life; nor do they, from time to time, reveal to him those points that were unrevealed,
nor clarify those points that have been revealed.
Nor do they thoroughly penetrate and elucidate profound points of meaning with wisdom—both skillfully and perfectly—for the sake of the purification of knowledge and vision.
Thus, this self-aggrandizement of his becomes an obstacle, namely, to insight (*vipaśyanā*).
Furthermore, he becomes a recipient of only a slight, inferior degree of mere knowledge and vision, and of a mere state of dwelling in comfort.
By means of that mere knowledge, mere vision,
and mere pleasant abiding, he exalts himself and holds himself in high esteem.
Holding himself in high esteem, he becomes satisfied with only that much.
He does not exert himself further;
thus, by this self-exaltation, an obstacle is created for him, namely, to insight (vipaśyanā).
Furthermore, he is fickle, with senses that are unpacified, agitated, and haughty;
his mind becomes corrupted, he utters ill-spoken words, and he performs evil deeds;
he does not contemplate the teachings with stability.
He does not contemplate with firmness,
whereby he neither fulfills nor purifies insight (*vipaśyanā*). Thus, this restlessness becomes an obstacle for him, namely, to insight.
There are two factors that are obstacles to *śamatha*:
namely, negligence and dwelling in an unsuitable location.
There are two factors that are obstacles to *vipaśyanā*.
Namely, self-exaltation and restlessness; thus,
that which is an obstacle to calm abiding and that which is an obstacle to insight.
This is called the obstacle to solitary retreat;
furthermore, this is the summary meaning of the obstacle.
This summary meaning and the previous detailed analysis, taken together and condensed into one, are called "obstacles.
It should be understood that the absence of obstacles is the opposite of these obstacles.
The absence, disappearance, non-association, and non-coincidence of these obstacles is called "absence of obstacle."
What is renunciation?
It is that blameless gift which one gives for the sake of adorning the mind, for the sake of equipping the mind, for the sake of the equipment of yoga, and for the attainment of the supreme goal.
In this regard, who is it that gives?
Where does one give? What does one give?
By what means does one give?
How does one give? Why does one give?
By what means does one's giving become irreproachable?
He said: "The giver, the master of giving, gives.
In that regard, who is the giver and who is the master of giving? He who gives with his own hands is the giver."
This one is called a donor;
he whose own property is given, and who desires to give it rather than not desiring to give it—
this one is called a master of generosity (dānapati).
In that regard, where does one give?
It is said: one gives in four ways.
To one who is suffering,
to one who has been helpful,
and to one who is dear.
And for one who is distinguished.
In that context, "to one who is suffering" refers to those who are miserable or beggars.
Whether they be travelers,
or beggars, or the blind, or the deaf;
"Or they are without a protector, or without a refuge, or lacking in necessary provisions."
Furthermore, whoever else belongs to this same category are called those who are suffering.
Who are those who have been benefactors? Namely, one's mother and father, and the one who nourishes and raises one.
It is that which nourishes and that which causes growth; or again, those who rescue one from the midst of a wilderness.
Whether from famine, or from fear of an enemy army, or from imprisonment, or from illness.
They are his instructors in what is beneficial,
teachers of what is conducive to happiness, and providers of welfare and well-being;
and in whatever matters arise, they are his companions, sharing in his joy and sharing in his sorrow.
And they do not abandon him in times of adversity;
furthermore, others who are of this same category are called benefactors.
Who are those who are beloved? Those who are well-acquainted, toward whom one feels either affection or respect.
Those who speak with devotion, those who converse, those who are well-acquainted, and those who are affectionate—
whosoever else are of this same category—
are called "beloved."
Who are the distinguished ones? They are those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who are esteemed as being of virtuous form.
They are unassailable,
delighting in being unassailable,
and free from passion.
Those practicing for the subduing of passion,
those free from hatred,
and those practicing for the subduing of hatred.
Those who are free from delusion and have set out for the removal of delusion,
or whoever else belongs to this same category— these are called "distinguished."
In this regard, what does one give? It is said:
in brief, one gives things categorized as belonging to sentient beings and things categorized as not belonging to sentient beings.
In that context, what is the thing reckoned as a sentient being?
It is, for example: wife and children, female and male slaves, laborers and servants, elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, chickens, women, men, boys, and girls;
or whatever other thing is of this same category.
Furthermore, taking recourse within oneself, one gives away hands, feet, head, flesh, blood, fat, and so forth;
this too is a gift reckoned among sentient beings, wherein the awakenings of a bodhisattva are manifested. However, in this context, this kind of giving is not intended.
However, regarding those beings over whom he possesses sovereignty, mastery, and power, he is worthy of bestowing them upon others.
By thus bestowing [gifts], one makes oneself blameless;
because of that, others do not harbor ill will toward him on account of those causes and conditions;
and those sentient beings who have been bestowed upon others do not come to be harmed.
This is called the irreproachable gift of things reckoned as belonging to sentient beings.
What is a thing reckoned as non-sentient?
It is as follows: the thing consisting of wealth, the thing consisting of grain, and the thing consisting of land.
In that regard, what is the category of wealth?
It is as follows: gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystal, coral, emerald, musāragalva, gold, silver, red pearls, and right-spiraling conch shells.
Or furthermore, whatever else is of this same category— whether it be a jewel, gold, silver, clothing, household utensils, or various kinds of perfumes or garlands—
this is called the category of wealth (*dhanavastu*).
What is grain?
Whatever is edible or drinkable.
That is to say, such as barley, or rice, or wheat.
Either kola fruits, or kulattha beans,
or sesame seeds.
Or black gram, or sugarcane juice, or [radish and...].
"Or grape juice," or whatever else is of this same category.
This is called grain.
(Śbh I 264) What is the object consisting of place (*deśavastu*)?
Namely: land property,
house property, and shop property.
The establishment of a meritorious hall or monastery,
or whatever else is of a similar nature—
this is called the "place-object" (*deśavastu*).
In that regard, whatever object is reckoned as either a sentient being or a non-sentient thing,
this is what one gives.
By what does one give?
It is the volition accompanied by non-greed, which is the mental formation and the action of the mind;
and the bodily and vocal actions produced by that [volition] for the sake of relinquishing the object to be given, whether within one's own continuum or in the continuum of another.
By this, one gives.
In that regard, how does one give?
One gives with faith,
possessing a view based on scripture and seeing the fruit [of giving].
He gives with reverence; with a humble mind, he gives with his own hand and not by casting it away;
he gives at the proper time, so that it may be useful to others.
He gives without harming others; having acquired [the gift] through righteous means, according to agreement, and without violence, he gives what is pure;
he gives what is excellent and appropriate.
By means of which neither others nor oneself become blameworthy,
one gives constantly;
having removed the stain of stinginess and the stain of hoarding, one practices giving.
Before giving, he is well-disposed; while giving, he clarifies his mind; and having given, he is free from regret.
In this manner he gives.
Why does one give?
It is said:
one gives out of compassion, namely, toward those who are suffering.
One gives out of gratitude, namely, to those who have been helpful;
one gives out of affection, respect, and devotion, namely, to those who are dear;
and one gives with the aspiration for mundane and supramundane excellence, namely, to those who are distinguished.
Therefore, it is said that "he gives."

Through these aspects, for the sake of adorning the mind, for the sake of equipping the mind, for the sake of the equipment of yoga, and for the attainment of the supreme goal, the gift of this householder or renunciant becomes irreproachable. This is called relinquishment (*tyāga*).
(Śbh I 268) (I)-C-III-13-a What is the ornament of a śramaṇa?
For example, someone is faithful,
free from deceit,
and has little affliction.
of a nature characterized by initiated vigor,
wise,
and having few desires.
Contented, easy to nourish, and easy to support.
Endowed with the ascetic qualities,
pleasing in appearance,
and moderate in his needs.
Endowed with the qualities of a true person,
endowed with the marks of a wise man,
and patient.
He is gentle and refined.
How does one become faithful? One becomes abundant in serene confidence and abundant in conviction.
Abounding in liberation and possessing zeal for wholesome qualities,
he gains confidence in the Teacher.
He has no doubt and no hesitation;
he honors the Teacher.
He holds them in high esteem, honors them, and reveres them;
having honored, esteemed, honored, and revered them, he dwells in reliance upon them.

Just as toward the Teacher, so too is he faithful toward the Dharma, toward his fellow practitioners, toward the training, toward instruction and admonition, toward hospitality, toward heedfulness, and toward concentration.
Thus he becomes faithful.
How does one become free from deceit?
One becomes upright, of an upright nature.
One reveals oneself as one truly is before the Teacher and toward wise fellow-practitioners;
in this way, one is free from deceit.
How does one become free from illness?
One is of a healthy constitution and is endowed with a digestive system that is balanced and capable of digesting food at the proper time.
Neither too hot, nor too cold,
and free from affliction.
By means of seasonal comfort— that by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted undergoes proper and easy digestion—
one thus becomes free from much affliction.
How does one become naturally endowed with initiated vigor?
One dwells possessed of steadfastness and possessed of vigor.
Zealous,
firm in prowess,
and not casting off the burden regarding wholesome qualities.
He is skillful, untiring, and endowed with diligence.
He becomes one who personally performs services for his learned fellow-celibates;
thus he is of a nature that has initiated vigor.
How does one become wise? One becomes endowed with intelligence, mindfulness, and discernment;
one possesses unimpaired faculties.
One whose faculties are unconfused, who is not deaf,
and who is capable of communicating without hand gestures, is able to understand the meaning of teachings that are well-spoken or ill-spoken.
He is endowed with innate intelligence,
and he is also endowed with acquired intelligence.
In this way, one becomes wise.
How does one become one of few desires?
One does not seek to have it known by others through those qualities, beginning with having few desires, with which one is endowed.
"May others not know of me, thinking, 'He has few desires,' or 'He is endowed with such qualities.'"
In this way, one becomes one who has few desires.
How does one become content?
One is content with whatever robes, alms-food, and lodgings one receives; thus one is content.
Not having obtained a robe—whether coarse or fine—one does not long for it.
He does not become distressed.
Furthermore, having obtained [these things], he uses them without attachment and without clinging, as described in detail previously.
As it is with robes, so it is with alms-food and lodgings.
In this way, he becomes contented.
How is one easy to support?
One has only oneself to support,
and not others— such as children or other people.
Furthermore, there may be others as well,
for whose sake one might undertake a search,
yet other donors and benefactors might perceive him as difficult to support.
In this way, one becomes easy to support.
How does one become easy to support?
One maintains oneself even with very little.
He maintains himself even with coarse food;
thus he is easy to support.
How does one become endowed with the qualities of ascetic purification (*dhutaguṇa*)?
One becomes a recipient of alms-food (*piṇḍapātika*).
He was one who accepts almsfood only from house to house in regular order; he was a one-session eater; he was one who refuses food once he has finished his meal.
One who possesses only three robes; one who wears felt garments; one who wears rag-robes from dust heaps.
A forest-dweller; one who dwells at the foot of a tree;
one who dwells in the open air.
A dweller in cemeteries; one who remains in a sitting posture;
one who accepts whatever seat is offered.
These are the twelve or thirteen ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa) concerning alms-food, robes, and lodgings.
Among them, the practice of eating only alms-food (piṇḍapātika), when divided, becomes twofold:
one who accepts whatever alms-food is obtained (prāptapiṇḍapātika) and one who eats alms-food in regular order (sāvadānapiṇḍapātika).
In this context, what is one who subsists on almsfood obtained by chance?
He partakes of almsfood exactly as it is received and exactly as it is offered, [from houses that have not been previously requested].
What is the one who eats almsfood in regular order?
Having begged and wandered through households from house to house, he consumes the almsfood exactly as it is obtained and exactly as it is received.
But he does not approach families with his trunk raised high, thinking, "From this I shall obtain excellent food and drink as much as I desire.
In that regard, starting from the general category of being a *piṇḍapātika* (alms-food eater), there are twelve [subdivisions]; however, starting from the specific distinctions, there are thirteen.

In that regard, what is the practice of using a single seat? It is when one, seated upon a single seat, consumes as much as is to be consumed, and having risen from that seat, does not consume further.
This is called the practice of eating at a single sitting.
What is the practice of not eating after the proper time?
It is that one does not begin to eat while seated for the purpose of a meal until all the food has been received.
To the extent that he knows, "I will be able to maintain myself," and furthermore,
when he knows, "Beyond this, no further need for food will exist for me," [he partakes].
Then, having taken up everything, he begins to consume it;
in this way, indeed, one becomes a "one who eats after the meal."
How does one become a wearer of the three robes?
One subsists with three robes: the outer cloak (saṃghāṭī),...
With the upper robe and the inner robe,
he does not wear more than three robes as an extra or surplus.
In this way, one becomes a wearer of the three robes.
How is one a wearer of [only] what has been designated?
Whatever robe he wears— whether it be the three robes or an extra robe.
He wears all that made of wool;
nothing else.
In this same way, he wears the nāmatika.
How does one become a wearer of rag-robes?
It is when one takes a robe that has been discarded by others, left over, or cast away on a street or in an alleyway.
at a crossroads, or at a junction, or on a road;
Or on a wrong path,
or mixed with excrement, or mixed with urine,
or smeared with excrement, urine, pus, blood, or phlegm.
Then, having removed what was impure,
taken the essence, cleansed it, sewn it, and dyed it, he wears it.
In this way, one becomes a wearer of rag-robes.
How does one become a forest-dweller?
One dwells in remote lodgings in forests and jungle-thickets.
Those places which are remote from villages and market towns;
in this way, one becomes a forest-dweller.
How does one become a tree-root dweller? One makes one's dwelling at the foot of a tree, relying upon the foot of a tree; in this way, one becomes a tree-root dweller.
How does one become an open-air dweller?
One makes one's dwelling in the open air.
In an uncovered and exposed place;
thus one becomes an "open-air dweller."
How does one become a cemetery-dweller?
One makes one's dwelling in a cemetery.
Wherever a multitude of people who have died is carried forth, there he dwells;
thus he is a dweller in cemeteries.
How does one become a practitioner of the sitting posture?
One passes the time by sitting on a couch, a stool, or a spread of grass;
one does not lean the back or the side against a couch, a stool, a wall, the root of a tree, or a spread of grass.
In this way, one becomes a practitioner of the perpetual sitting posture.
(Śbh I 282) How does one become a person who uses whatever seat is available?
It is when one prepares one's bed upon whatever grass mat or leaf mat is provided.

Whether it be a bed of grass or a bed of leaves, he prepares his bedding exactly as it has been once spread; he does not rearrange it nor alter it. In this way, he is one who accepts whatever seat or bedding is provided.
Why are these called the *dhuta* qualities?
For example, when wool or cotton has been shaken out, cut, and pulverized, at that time it becomes soft, light, and workable— namely,
for the production of thread or for the production of cotton wool.
In the same way, here some person’s mind becomes attached and thoroughly clings to almsfood due to passion for almsfood;
their mind becomes attached and thoroughly clings to robes due to passion for robes; their mind becomes attached and thoroughly clings to lodgings due to passion for lodgings.

By means of these ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa), he purifies, straightens, softens, makes pliable, uprights, clarifies, and renders compliant that which is to say, his mind, for the sake of dwelling in the holy life (brahmacarya).
Therefore, they are called the "qualities of purification" (*dhutaguṇa*).
In that regard, attachment to alms-food constitutes two kinds of obstacles:
attachment to exquisite food and attachment to abundant food.
Among these, one practices as an alms-seeker in order to abandon attachment to exquisite food.
To abandon attachment to abundant food, one becomes a practitioner who eats at a single sitting and a practitioner who refuses food after the proper time.
Attachment to robes is a threefold obstacle:
attachment to an abundance of robes, attachment to the soft texture of robes, and attachment to high-quality robes.

In that regard, one becomes a wearer of the three robes (*traicīvarika*) for the sake of abandoning attachment to many robes; one becomes a wearer of felt robes (*nāmatika*) for the sake of abandoning attachment to the soft texture of robes;
and one becomes a wearer of rag-robes (*pāṃśukūlika*) for the sake of abandoning attachment to fine robes.
Attachment to bedding and seating is a fourfold obstacle; namely,
attachment to social contact and attachment to dwellings.
There is attachment to the pleasure of lying on one's side and attachment to the pleasure of sleeping; there is attachment to bedspreads, counter-spreads, and coverlets.
Among these, one becomes a forest-dweller for the sake of abandoning attachment to social contact.
For the sake of abandoning attachment to shelter, one dwells at the foot of trees, in the open air, and in cemeteries.
Furthermore, dwelling in cemeteries serves to abandon attachment to sexual union.
To abandon attachment to the pleasure of reclining on one's side and the pleasure of lying down, one remains in a sitting posture.
For the sake of abandoning attachment to rugs, counter-rugs, and coverings, he is one who uses whatever matting is available;
thus, he is endowed with the qualities of purification (*dhutaguṇa*).

How does one become pleasing? One becomes endowed with a pleasing manner of approaching and returning, of looking forward and looking aside, of contracting and extending [the limbs], and of carrying the outer robe, the inner robe, and the alms bowl.
In this way, one becomes pleasing to behold.
How does one know the proper measure?
Here, faithful brahmins and householders offer invitations for their own sake,
namely, with the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick.
In that regard, he knows the proper measure in accepting gifts; thus he becomes one who knows the measure.
How does one become endowed with the qualities of a true person (*satpuruṣadharma*)?
Whether having gone forth from a high-born family or from a wealthy family, being handsome, pleasing to behold, and inspiring confidence; or being learned, endowed with eloquence;
or having attained any one of the mere knowledges, the mere visions, or the mere abidings in contact—by means of these, one does not exalt oneself nor disparage others.

[Having understood that one must practice exclusively the Dharma and the qualities in accordance with the Dharma,] he practices in accordance with the Dharma and the qualities in accordance with the Dharma, and not otherwise.
In this way, he becomes one who is endowed with the qualities of a true person.
How does one become endowed with the marks of a wise person?
A fool is characterized by his actions; a wise person is characterized by his actions.
How is this so?
The fool is one who thinks ill-thought thoughts,
speaks ill-spoken words, and performs ill-done deeds;
the wise person, however, is one who thinks well-thought thoughts.
Speaking well-spoken words and performing deeds that are well-done—
one is thus endowed with the marks of a wise person.
How is one patient?
When reviled, one does not revile in return;
when provoked to anger, one does not respond with anger.
When struck, he does not strike back;
when reviled, he does not revile in return.
Furthermore, that venerable one is patient with cold and heat, hunger and thirst, and the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping reptiles.
