He is patient toward ill-spoken words and offensive speech from others; he is patient toward bodily sensations that are painful, intense, harsh, bitter, disagreeable, and life-threatening, being by nature one who endures them.
In this way, he is patient.
How does one become gentle? It is when one is endowed with loving-kindness in bodily action and loving-kindness in verbal action.
Through a mental action of loving-kindness toward the Teacher and toward wise fellow-practitioners,
one becomes a sharer in common enjoyments.
And he is one who does not consume in secret and does not eat in concealment,
[relying] on gains that are righteous, obtained in accordance with the Dharma, placed in his alms-bowl, and contained within his bowl.
He comes to share the same morality and the same view;
endowed with these six qualities that cause affection, which inspire respect and prevent dispute, he acts in a way that is pleasing and honorable.
He is pleasant to dwell with,
being by nature non-harming;
and wise fellow-practitioners rejoice in him as one who is single-minded in his resolve.
In this way, one becomes gentle.
How is one amiable?
One is free from frowning, has a bright facial expression,
and is preceded by a smile.
One who speaks first,
speaks kindly, and is of a nature to gather others.
Having a pure continuum,
he thus becomes graceful.
Endowed with these qualities, he becomes one who desires the Dharma and desires virtuous qualities; he does not desire gain, honor, fame, or praise.
He does not become possessed of a false view that involves superimposition.
Nor does it proceed by way of negation;
it does not superimpose a non-existent phenomenon,
nor does it deny an existent phenomenon.

Having understood that "whatever is poetic, poetical, composed of variegated syllables, marked by specific words and phonemes, and connected with the Lokāyata [materialist] system— that is meaningless"— he avoids it from afar.
One is not led astray by it, nor is one delighted by it.
(Śbh I 292)
He does not carry an excessive number of bowls or robes;
he avoids association with householders, which increases the afflictions,
and cultivates association with the noble ones, which purifies wisdom.

And he does not form friendships with families nor accept their gifts, thinking: "Lest there arise for me, on that account, in many ways, distraction or busywork; or else, through their change or transformation, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair shall arise."
He does not tolerate afflictions and secondary afflictions as they arise one after another;
he abandons them and dispels them.
He eliminates [the fault],
thinking: "May no suffering arise for me on this account, whether pertaining to the present life or to future lives," and he does not squander what has been given out of faith.
Possessing unshakable virtue and unfallen vows,
he partakes of what is given out of faith.
He does not reject what has been given out of faith,
nor does he renounce the training;
rather, he seeks out his own faults and internal transgressions.
He conceals his own virtues and reveals his faults;
he pays no attention to the defects or lapses of others;
and he does not intentionally commit an offense, even for the sake of his life.
And having fallen [into a transgression], he remedies it quickly and in accordance with the Dharma;
furthermore, he is skillful in his duties, diligent, and one who acts for himself.
He does not seek service for his body from others;
rather, he has faith in the inconceivable power of the Buddhas and their disciples, as well as in their profound teaching.
He does not reject [the teaching], having understood: "Only the Tathāgatas are those who know and see; I am not."
Furthermore, he does not abide in the dogmatic adherence to his own views, nor does he grasp at what is improper, nor is he one whose counsel is difficult to relinquish.
Endowed with these qualities, dwelling in this manner and training in this way, he shines, adorned with the ornament of a śramaṇa.
It is just as a certain young man, fond of adornment, a seeker of sensual pleasures, having bathed and anointed himself, dressed in white garments, and decorated with various ornaments, would shine.

Just as one might be adorned with necklaces, armlets, finger-rings, or garlands of gold and silver, even so he, adorned by these various qualities that are the ornaments of a śramaṇa, shines, blazes, and radiates. Therefore, they are called the "ornaments of a śramaṇa."
This is called the ornament of a śramaṇa.
(Śbh I 296) // Summary Verse //

Faithfulness, lack of deceit, little affliction, vigor, wisdom, fewness of desires, contentment, ease of maintenance, easy to support, the ascetic practices, serenity, moderation, being a true person, the marks of a wise man, patience, gentleness, and kindness. [1]
There may be the desire for the attainment of one's own and others' welfare, as well as ethical discipline, the faculties, moderation in food, wakefulness, dwelling in clear comprehension,
a virtuous friend, and hearing and reflecting upon the true Dharma.

The absence of obstacles and renunciation are the final adornment. Worldly detachment as well as supramundane detachment, and the equipment for both of these, constitute the stage known as "Renunciation."
The First Stage of Yoga, contained within the *Śrāvakabhūmi* of the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
In this regard, how many types of persons (*pudgala*) are there who emerge from this stage of renunciation (*naiṣkramyabhūmi*), as it has been taught and as it has been proclaimed?
And how is the classification of persons established?
What is the object of focus? What is the instruction?
What is training?
What are the factors conducive to training?
What is the failure of yoga?
What are the yogas? What is attention? What is that which is to be done by yoga?
How many types of practitioners of yoga are there? What is the cultivation of yoga? What is the fruit of cultivation?
How many are the designations for persons?
How many are the Māras? How many are the deeds of Māra?
How does an undertaking become fruitless?
In that regard, there are twenty-eight types of persons.
Which are the twenty-eight? They are as follows: one of dull faculties.
One with sharp faculties; one with predominant passion;
one with predominant hatred.
One for whom delusion is predominant, one for whom pride is predominant, and one for whom discursive thought is predominant.
One who has attained equanimity;
one of a nature with diminished passion;
one who has entered the path.
One who abides in the fruit;
one who follows through faith;
one who follows through the Dharma.
One liberated through faith,
one who has attained vision,
and a body-witness.
One who has seven births at most,
one who goes from family to family,
and one who has only one interval remaining.
One who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth,
and one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion.
One who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion;
one who flows upwards;
and one who is liberated by occasion.
One of unshakable nature,
one liberated by wisdom,
and one liberated both ways.
In that regard, who is the person of dull faculties?
It is the person whose faculties are dull, slow-moving, and sluggish with respect to the object to be known, as described previously.
Furthermore, he should be understood to be of two kinds.
From the very beginning, he belongs to the lineage of those with dull faculties, yet his faculties have been fully cultivated.
What is a person of sharp faculties?
It is that person whose faculties are sharp, proceeding without slowness and proceeding without dullness regarding the object to be known, as previously described.
Furthermore, he should be understood to be of two kinds.
From the very beginning, he belongs to the lineage of sharp faculties and has cultivated his faculties.
What is a person in whom passion predominates? It is a person by whom passion was practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed in previous births;
by that cause and by that condition, he now possesses both intense passion and long-lasting passion toward objects that provoke passion.
This is called the person for whom lust is predominant.
What is a person in whom hatred predominates? It is a person by whom hatred was previously practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed in other births.
And by that cause and by that condition, one now experiences both intense hatred and prolonged hatred toward an object that provokes aversion;
such a person is called an individual in whom hatred predominates.
What is a person for whom delusion is predominant?
It is a person by whom delusion was previously practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed in other births;
and by that cause and by that condition, there arises now both intense delusion and prolonged delusion regarding an object that provokes delusion.
This is called the person for whom delusion is predominant.
What is a person characterized by an excess of pride? It is a person by whom pride was previously practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed in other births;
and by that cause and by that condition, they now possess both intense pride and enduring pride regarding an object of conceit.
This is called the person for whom conceit is predominant.
What is a person in whom discursive thought (*vitarka*) predominates? It is a person by whom discursive thought was practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed in previous births;
and by that cause and by that very condition, they now possess intense discursive thought and prolonged discursive thought regarding objects conducive to discursive thought.
This is called the person for whom discursive thought is predominant.
(Śbh II 8) Who is the person who has attained equanimity?
It is that person by whom, in previous births, passion, hatred, delusion, pride, and discursive thought were not practiced, cultivated, or frequently pursued.
Furthermore, these phenomena have not been seen by him as defects, nor have they been reviled, scrutinized, or fully understood.

For that reason and by that cause, regarding an object that might provoke passion, aversion, delusion, conceit, or discursive thought, he does not possess intense passion, nor even long-standing passion;
yet it is not the case that passion does not manifest for him with respect to that very object.
Just as it is with attachment, so it is with aversion, delusion, pride, and discursive thought;
such a person is called one who has attained equanimity.
What is a person with little passion?
It is a person by whom passion was not practiced, cultivated, or frequently developed in previous births,
and who has repeatedly seen its disadvantage, reviled it, and thoroughly investigated it.
For that reason and by that condition, when an object capable of arousing passion is now present, manifest, excessive, abundant, and intense, he produces passion slowly;
but toward one that is moderate or slight, he does not produce it at all.
Just as it is with passion, so should it be understood for hatred, delusion, pride, and discursive thought.
This is called the person with little passion.
(Śbh II 10) Who is the person who is a practitioner?
It is said:
There are four persons who have entered the path.
Which four? Namely:
the one who has entered the path toward the fruit of stream-entry, and so forth.
the one practicing for the fruit of once-returning,
the one practicing for the fruit of non-returning, and the one practicing for the fruit of arhatship.
This is called the person who has entered upon the path.
What is the person established in the fruit?
It is said:
the stream-enterer.
The once-returner,
the non-returner, and the arhat—
this is called a person established in the fruit.
What is a person who follows through faith? It is that person who seeks instruction and admonition from others and practices by means of its power, namely, for the sake of attaining the fruit.

However, when the teachings have been taken up, mastered, reflected upon, weighed, and thoroughly examined, he is not himself capable or empowered to pursue those teachings by way of cultivation; rather, he practices through faith that follows another person.
Therefore, he is called a "follower by faith" (śraddhānusārī).

What is a person who follows the Dharma (dharmānusārī pudgala)? It is a person who, regarding the teachings as they have been heard, mastered, reflected upon, weighed, and examined, is himself capable and empowered to follow those teachings by way of cultivation, and does not seek instruction or advice from another.
That is to say, for the sake of attaining the fruit;
this is called a person who follows the Dharma.
(Śbh II 12) Who is the person resolved through faith? It is said:

That very person who follows by faith (śraddhānusārī), at the time when he attains, touches, and realizes the fruit of asceticism (śrāmaṇyaphala) by relying on the instructions and admonitions from another,
at that time is called one resolved through faith (śraddhādhimukta).
Who is the person who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*)?
It is said:

it is that very person who follows the Dharma (*dharmānusārī*) at the time when, having relied upon the instruction and admonition from another, they attain, touch, and realize the fruit of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*).
At that time, he is said to be "one who has attained vision."
What is the person who is a body-witness?
It is that person who enters into and emerges from the eight liberations in forward and reverse order,
and having realized them with the body, dwells frequently therein.
Yet he does not attain the complete destruction of all outflows in every respect;
this is called a person who is a body-witness (kāyasākṣī).
Who is the person who has seven births at most?

It is that person who, through the abandonment of the three fetters—namely, the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), adherence to rites and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*)—becomes a stream-enterer (*srota-āpanna*). Being of a nature not subject to falling into lower realms, destined for enlightenment, and having seven births at most, he, after wandering and transmigrating among gods and humans seven times, makes an end of suffering.
This is called the person for whom seven existences at most remain.
(Śbh II 14) Who is the person who goes from family to family (*kulaṃkula*)? [It is said:]
Birth from family to family is of two kinds: birth from family to family among the gods and birth from family to family among humans.
Among those, birth from family to family among the gods refers to one who links the transition from family to family among the gods and,
having transmigrated, brings an end to suffering.
Regarding birth from family to family among humans:
it is that which links one’s rebirth from one human family to another,
and through wandering in saṃsāra, brings an end to suffering.
Both should be understood as persons who have entered the stream (srotāpanna).
In that regard, who is the person who is a "one-interval" (ekavīcika) practitioner?

It is a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) who is practicing for the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), and for whom the intense and medium-grade afflictions (kleśa) pertaining to the desire realm have been abandoned,
while only a few weak [afflictions] remain.
Having produced a single existence as a god of the desire realm, he attains final nirvana right there;
he does not return again to this world. This is called the person who is a "one-intervaller" (ekavīcika).
Who is the person who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state?
It is said: there are three types of persons who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.

One person who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, immediately upon passing away and at the very moment the intermediate existence is being produced, brings that intermediate existence into being;
as soon as it has been produced, he attains parinirvāṇa.
It is just like a small spark from a splinter of wood which is extinguished as soon as it arises.
The second type of person, one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, brings about the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).
Once the intermediate existence has been brought about, he attains parinirvāṇa after some time while remaining right there.
However, he has not yet been drawn toward that state of rebirth by which he would go.
It is just as when iron balls or iron cauldrons, heated by a blazing fire, are struck with iron hammers and are extinguished by nirvana even as an iron spark flies upward;
likewise, the third type of person, the one who attains nirvana in the intermediate state, having brought forth the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), proceeds toward that state of rebirth.
Furthermore, having arrived [in the intermediate state], one attains parinirvāṇa without even being reborn;
just as a spark of iron flies up and attains extinction before falling to the ground.
These three types of persons who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, when condensed into one, are called "the person who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state."
What is a person who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth?
One who attains parinirvāṇa immediately upon being reborn;
this is called a person who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth.
What is the person who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion?
13) One who, having brought the path into manifestation without exertion, without effort, and without weariness, attains parinirvāṇa after being born there;
this is called the person who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion.
(Śbh II 18) Who is the person who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion?
One who, having brought the path into manifestation through volitional effort, exertion, and toil, attains parinirvāṇa upon being reborn there,
is called a person who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion (sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyī).
What is the person who is one who flows upwards (ūrdhvaṃsrotas)?
It is that person who, being a non-returner (anāgāmin), has been reborn in the first dhyāna and does not attain final nirvāṇa while remaining right there.
Rather, having passed away from there, producing successive higher spheres of rebirth until he reaches the Akaniṣṭha gods or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—
this person is called one who "flows upwards."
Who is the person liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*)?
It is the person belonging to the lineage of dull faculties who falls away from the worldly dwellings in happiness in the present life.
Or he intends toward death,
or he guards his liberation;
he becomes excessively devoted to a practice of heedfulness.
That is to say, having made this very non-retrogression his primary focus,
his side of wholesome qualities remains merely at that level;
he does not proceed toward further distinction as those various nights, days, moments, instants, and hours pass away.
As long as one does not apply intense application,
this person is called one liberated by occasion (samayavimukta).
(Śbh II 20) Who is the person of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*)?
By the opposite of this, the person of immovable nature (akopyadharman) is to be understood.
What is a person liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*)?
It is a person who attains the destruction of all outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) in every respect.
But he does not dwell having personally realized and attained the eight liberations with the body;
this is called a person liberated by wisdom (prajñāvimukta).
What is the person liberated in both ways?
It is the person who attains the complete destruction of all outflows (*āsrava*) in every respect,
and having personally realized the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*) with the body, dwells having attained them.
His mind becomes liberated from both the obscuration of afflictions and the obscuration to liberation;
this is called a person liberated in both ways.
(Śbh II 22) What is the classification of persons? The classification of persons should be understood through eleven distinctions.
By which eleven? Namely:
by the distinction of faculties, and by the distinction of classes.
by the distinction of conduct,
by the distinction of aspiration,
and by the distinction of practice;
By way of the distinction of the paths and fruits, by way of the distinction of the applications,
and by way of the distinction of the meditative attainments.
By way of the classification of rebirth, the classification of decline, and the classification of obstructions.
First, by way of the differentiation of the faculties, there is the establishment of two types of persons: those with dull faculties and those with sharp faculties.
-II-2-a-(2) Based on the distinction of classes, there is a sevenfold establishment of persons:
the monk, the nun, the female trainee, the male novice, the female novice, the layman, and the laywoman.

-II-2-a-(3) Regarding this, the classification of the seven types of persons (*pudgala*) is established by way of the differentiation of their conduct (*carita*). A person in whom passion (*rāga*) is predominant is one whose conduct is characterized by passion (*rāgacarita*).
One in whom hatred predominates is one whose temperament is characterized by hatred; one in whom delusion predominates is one whose temperament is characterized by delusion;
one in whom pride predominates is one whose temperament is characterized by pride.
One for whom discursive thought (*vitarka*) is predominant is one whose temperament is dominated by discursive thought (*vitarkacarita*);
one who has attained equilibrium is one whose temperament is balanced (*samabhāgacarita*).
(Śbh II 24)
One who has little passion should be known as one whose conduct is mild.

In that regard, what are the signs of a person whose temperament is dominated by passion? Here, a person of passionate temperament generates a dense and excessive obsession of passion even toward a small, utterly inferior, and unattractive object; what need is there to mention one that is mediocre or excellent?
Furthermore, that obsession with passion causes it to persist for a long time through the continuity of the stream;
it remains bound for a long duration,
and by means of that obsession, one is overwhelmed by phenomena that provoke passion.
But he is not able to overcome those phenomena that cause passion;
his faculties become moist, his faculties are not harsh, and his faculties are not coarse.
He possesses non-harsh faculties;

he is not by nature excessively inclined to harm others, namely through body or speech; he is difficult to alienate and difficult to cause to feel revulsion; and he is one whose inclinations are inferior.
One whose undertakings are firm, one whose undertakings are stable,
and one who is firm in his vows.
He is firm in his vows and patient regarding the requisites and articles of use; though by nature prone to craving for them, he does not value them highly.
He is abundant in mental joy and abundant in bliss, free from frowning, with a bright facial complexion, and one who is preceded by a smile.
These and other similar characteristics of a person whose temperament is dominated by passion are to be understood.
In that regard, what are the characteristics of a person whose temperament is dominated by hatred?
Here, a person of hateful temperament,
upon encountering even a slight object provocative of hatred, gives rise to a dense and abundant outburst of hostility.
How much more so, then, with a middling or superior degree?
He establishes a continuity of that obsession with hostility for a long time;
it remains bound to him for a long duration.
Due to the obsession of repugnance, he is overwhelmed by hateful phenomena,
yet he is unable to overcome those hateful phenomena;
furthermore, his faculties become harsh.
He possesses harsh faculties, rough faculties, and coarse faculties;
he is by nature excessively inclined to harm others, namely through body and speech;
yet he is easily separated from [unwholesome states] and easily moved to spiritual urgency.
He becomes like a crow: talkative, impudent, and largely lacking in resolute faith.
He is neither one of firm action nor of steady action; he is neither one of firm vows nor of steady vows.
He becomes full of dejection and full of despair;
he is impatient and lacks endurance.
He is of a contrary nature,
one who grasps things in a non-conducive way, difficult to lead back to the right path, and full of malice.

He is cruel in disposition and fierce; he is abusive and speaks with harshness. Even when addressed with only a slight measure of words, he becomes resentful, he becomes angry, he becomes malevolent, he becomes dejected, he remains fixed in his anger, and he gives rise to wrath.
He has a distorted frown;
his facial complexion is not open,
and he hates the prosperity of others.
Abounding in envy—such are the characteristics of a person whose temperament is dominated by hatred; these should be understood as the signs of such an individual.
In this regard, what are the marks of a person of deluded temperament?
Here, a person of deluded temperament gives rise to a dense and abundant outburst of delusion even toward a trifling object that is conducive to delusion.
How much more so in the case of the medium and intense [degrees];
for a long time he establishes the continuity of that obsession by delusion,
and he remains bound by it.
He is overcome by deluding factors,
but he is not able to overcome those deluding factors;
moreover, his faculties become dull.
He becomes dull-witted in his faculties and weak in his faculties, with laxity in his physical actions and laxity in his verbal actions.
one who thinks ill-thought thoughts,
speaks ill-spoken words,
and performs ill-done deeds;
He is indolent, lacking in the energy to exert himself, slow of speech, and dull-witted.
one who has lost mindfulness, one who dwells without clear comprehension, and one who grasps perversely;
Difficult to separate, difficult to cause to feel spiritual urgency, and having inferior inclinations.
He is dull-witted, mute, and communicates only through gestures;
he lacks the capacity to understand the meaning of well-spoken or ill-spoken teachings,
and he is susceptible to external influences, led by others, and guided by others.
These and other similar characteristics of a person whose temperament is dominated by delusion are to be understood.
In that regard, what are the signs of a person whose temperament is dominated by pride?
Here, a person of proud temperament produces a dense and abundant obsession of pride even toward a trivial object conducive to pride;
how much more so, then, toward one that is middling or great!
And he establishes a continuity of that obsession with pride for a long time;
he remains bound by it.

He is overcome by states conducive to pride, but he is unable to overcome those states conducive to pride. His faculties become agitated and his faculties become haughty, and he becomes devoted to the practice of adorning the body.
He speaks words that are excessively haughty and not humble;
he does not, from time to time, perform appropriate honor toward his mother, father, kinsmen, or those who stand in the place of teachers;
he becomes arrogant.
He does not incline his body; he is not habituated to the acts of salutation, prostration, rising to greet, joining the palms, or respectful conduct.
He is self-aggrandizing, exalting himself and disparaging others. He desires gain, desires honor, and desires fame, reputation, and praise.
He becomes like a vessel that is overflowing, difficult to separate from [worldly things], and difficult to cause to feel spiritual urgency;
he possesses exalted resolve,
yet his compassion is dull.
Furthermore, he possesses an excessive abundance of views regarding a self, a sentient being, a living soul, a nourisher, a person, or an individual, and he is full of resentment;
such are the characteristics of a person whose temperament is dominated by pride that should be understood.
In that regard, what are the signs of a person whose temperament is characterized by discursive thought (*vitarkacarita*)?
Here, a person of discursive temperament produces a dense and abundant obsession of discursive thought even toward a trivial object conducive to such thought;
how much more so toward one that is moderate or intense!
And that obsession persists for a long time;
he becomes bound by it and is overcome by those factors conducive to discursive thought.
However, he is unable to overcome those phenomena that are conducive to discursive thought (*vitarka*).
His faculties are unstable; his faculties are fickle, wavering, and distracted.
He is hurried in his bodily activities and hurried in his verbal activities.
He is difficult to separate from [worldly things], difficult to cause to feel spiritual urgency;
he delights in conceptual proliferation, is devoted to conceptual proliferation,
and is full of longing and full of doubt.
He becomes impetuous, one whose vows are unstable and whose vows are uncertain;
one whose activities are unstable and whose activities are uncertain;
full of doubt, and one whose mindfulness is lost.
He delights not in solitude, is full of distraction,
and pursues desire and passion for worldly diversions;
yet he is skillful, untiring, and endowed with diligence.
These and similar qualities are to be understood as the marks of a person whose temperament is characterized by discursive thought (*vitarkacarita*).
This should be understood as the classification of persons according to the distinction of their temperaments.
In this regard, the classification of individuals is established by way of the distinction of their vows:
there is the individual who has made a vow for the Śrāvaka vehicle, and there is the one who has made a vow for the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.
There is [a distinction] in the Mahāyāna:
therein, a person who has made a vow for the Śrāvaka vehicle may belong to the Śrāvaka lineage,
or may belong to the Pratyekabuddha lineage.
There may be one belonging to the Mahāyāna lineage.
In that regard, this person who has made a vow for the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha might belong to the pratyekabuddha lineage,
or he might belong to the śrāvaka lineage.
There may be one who belongs to the Mahāyāna lineage;
in that regard, a person who has made a vow for the Mahāyāna might also belong to the śrāvaka lineage or the pratyekabuddha lineage.
There may be one belonging to the Mahāyāna lineage.
In that regard, a person belonging to the śrāvaka lineage who has made a vow for either the awakening of a pratyekabuddha or for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening—
because of being of the śrāvaka lineage— he will necessarily [revert] at the end.
Having turned back that vow, one remains fixed solely in the vow of the Śrāvaka vehicle.
In this same way, those belonging to the lineage of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle and the lineage of the Mahāyāna should be understood.
In these cases, there occurs for these individuals a shifting of vows and a transgression of vows.
However, there is no shifting of lineage nor any confusion of lineages.
But in this context, these persons should be understood as those who have made the vow for the Śrāvaka vehicle and who possess the Śrāvaka lineage.
Thus, the classification of individuals is established by way of the distinctions among their aspirations.
How is the classification of persons established by way of the distinction of practice?
For these persons as they have been enumerated and described, there is deliverance by means of four practices.
Which are the four?
There is a practice that is painful with sluggish direct knowledge; there is a practice that is painful with swift direct knowledge;
and there is a practice that is pleasant with sluggish direct knowledge.
There is a practice that is pleasant and characterized by swift direct knowledge.

In this context, the practice of a person with dull faculties who has not attained the fundamental dhyānas is called "painful and slow direct knowledge. In this context, the practice of a person with sharp faculties who has not attained the fundamental dhyānas is called "painful and swift direct knowledge."
In that regard, the path of a person with dull faculties who has attained the fundamental dhyānas is called "easy with slow direct knowledge.
In that regard, the path of a person with sharp faculties who has attained the fundamental dhyānas is called "easy with quick direct knowledge.
Thus, the classification of persons should be understood by way of the distinctions in their paths.
In that regard, how is the classification of persons (pudgala) to be understood according to the distinction between the path and its fruits?

For example, there are four types of those who have entered the path (pratipannaka): one who has entered the path toward the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala-pratipannaka), and one who has entered the path toward the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmi-phala-pratipannaka).
of one practicing for the fruit of non-returning, of one practicing for the fruit of arhatship,
and of the four who abide in the fruits. (Śbh II 36)
Of the stream-enterer,
the once-returner, the non-returner, and the arhat.
Those who abide on the path of practice are the "those who have entered" (pratipannaka); their classification is by way of the path of practice.
Those who are established in the fruits of that [path], namely the fruits of the ascetic life (śrāmaṇyaphala), their classification is by way of the fruit of the path.
Thus, the classification of persons occurs through the distinction between paths and fruits.
How is the classification of persons established by way of the distinction of application? For example, there are those who follow through faith and those who follow through the Dharma.
That person who is applied by means of following through faith is one who follows through faith (*śraddhānusārī*).
One who is engaged with the teachings according to the discipline that does not rely on another is a follower of the Dharma (dharmānusārī).
Thus, the classification of individuals (pudgala) occurs through the distinction of their application.
In that regard, how is the classification of persons established by way of the distinctions of meditative attainments?
For example, there is the "body-witness" who, having personally realized the eight liberations with the body and having attained them, dwells therein;
yet he has not fully and completely attained the destruction of the outflows.
Possessing form, one sees forms;
being internally percipient of the formless, one sees forms externally;
[this is] the beautiful liberation.
Having realized it with the body and attained it, he dwells therein:
the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness.
He enters and emerges from the sphere of nothingness, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
and the cessation of perception and feeling, both in direct and reverse order.
And he emerges [from it].
Thus, there is the classification of persons according to the distinctions of meditative attainments.
How is the classification of persons established by way of the distinction of rebirth?
For example, there is the one for whom seven existences are the maximum,
and the one who goes from family to family (*kulaṃkula*).
the one with a single interval,
the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, and the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth;
those who attain parinirvāṇa without exertion,
those who attain parinirvāṇa with exertion,
and those who go upstream.
Thus, the classification of persons is established according to the distinctions of rebirth.
How is the classification of persons established by way of the distinction of falling away?
For example, there is the Arhat who is "liberated by occasion" (*samayavimukta*) and is susceptible to falling away from the states of dwelling in happiness in the present life.
Furthermore, there is the classification by way of the distinction of non-falling away.
The Arhat of immovable nature is one who is incapable of falling away from the pleasant dwellings in this very life;
thus, the classification of individuals is established according to the distinction of non-falling away.
In that regard, how is the classification of persons established by way of the divisions of obscurations?
For example, there is the Arhat who is liberated both ways and the Arhat liberated by wisdom.
Among them, the Arhat liberated by wisdom is one who is liberated from the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
It is not because of an obstruction to meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
However, an Arhat who is liberated in both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*) is liberated from both the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obstruction to meditative attainment;
therefore, he is called "liberated in both ways."
Thus, the classification of individuals is established by way of the different types of obscurations.
By means of these aforementioned classifications, the systematic arrangement of the individuals as they were previously enumerated should be understood according to their respective order.
(Śbh II 42) (II)-A-II-3 What, therein, is the object (*ālambana*)?
He said:
There are four objects of focus.
What are the four?
The pervasive object of focus,
the object of focus for purifying conduct, and the object of focus for skillfulness.
And the object for the purification of afflictions.
In that regard, what is the pervasive object of focus?
It is said: that too is of four kinds.
Namely: non-conceptual reflection, non-discriminative reflection,
and the limit of phenomena.
And the accomplishment of the task.
In that regard, what is the conceptual image?
It is when, for instance, a certain person, relying upon hearing the true Dharma or receiving instruction and admonition, [perceives] what has been seen, or...

Based on what has been heard or what has been conceptually constructed, one contemplates and investigates with the modes of insight belonging to the stage of meditative concentration a reflected image that resembles the object of knowledge.
He investigates, examines thoroughly, and engages in detailed analysis.
In that regard, the object to be known is as follows:
either the foul or loving-kindness.
Whether it be specific conditionality and dependent origination, the analysis of the elements,
or mindfulness of breathing;
skill in the aggregates, skill in the elements, skill in the sense bases, and skill in dependent origination;
Skill in discerning what is possible and what is impossible;
the coarseness of the lower stages and the tranquility of the higher stages.
the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin,
and the truth of cessation;
The truth of the path;
this is called the object to be known. Having relied upon the oral instruction and admonition regarding this very object to be known,
Or, having heard the true Dharma, and by relying upon that, having brought into manifestation a mental attention belonging to the level of meditative concentration,
those very same dharmas—
One is resolved; one is resolved upon that very object of knowledge.
At that time, a resolution occurs regarding the object of knowledge as if it were being directly experienced.
Yet, that object of knowledge has not become perceptible, nor has it been brought together or made manifest before one.
Furthermore, it is not some other substance of that same kind;
rather, it is an experience of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), such an experience of mental attention (*manaskāra*) belonging to the level of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmika*),
by which there arises an appearance resembling that object of knowledge.
That by which it is called a "reflected image resembling the object of knowledge" (jñeyavastusabhāga-pratibimba) is this:
when the yogi, while investigating, determines the qualities and defects regarding that very object of knowledge under consideration.
This is called the conceptualized reflected image (savikalpa-pratibimba).
-II-3-a-(1)-ii What is the non-conceptual image (*nirvikalpa-pratibimba*)?
Here, this practitioner (*yogī*), having grasped the sign of the image (*pratibimba-nimitta*), does not further engage in insight (*vipaśyati*).
He investigates, examines closely, and reflects thoroughly.
He enters into thorough investigation;
rather, while not yet liberated from that very object, he calms that mind by way of tranquility (śamatha).
That is to say, through the ninefold mental abiding, he establishes the mind within itself.
He establishes, settles, and brings near.
It tames, it pacifies,
it completely calms.
He makes it one-pointed and attains concentration;
at that time, his [mind] is free from conceptual construction.
That reflection becomes the object of focus;
that upon which one establishes one-pointed mindfulness in its entirety is the object.
but he does not discern, investigate, or examine it.
He reflects upon it and enters into thorough investigation;
and that reflection is called a "reflection."
The signs of meditative concentration, the objects that are the domain of meditative concentration,
and the methods of meditative concentration.
The gateway of meditative concentration,
the basis of mental engagement,
and the internal body of conceptualization.
It is also called "reflected image" (*pratibimba*); thus, these should be understood as synonyms for that reflected image which shares the same nature as the object of knowledge (*jñeyavastu*).
What is the limit of objects (*vastuparyantatā*)?
It is the extent of existence (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) and the mode of existence (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*) of the objective referent (*ālambana*). Among these, what is the extent of existence?
Because beyond this there is no aggregate of form, nor aggregate of feeling, nor aggregate of perception.
The inclusion of all conditioned things is comprised of five factors: the aggregate of formations or the aggregate of consciousness.
The inclusion of all phenomena is by means of the elements (*dhātu*) and the sense bases (*āyatana*), and the inclusion of all objects of knowledge is by means of the noble truths (*āryasatya*).
This is called the quality of being as extensive as existence (*yāvadbhāvikatā*).
In that regard, what is the quality of being as it is (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*)?
It is the reality and suchness (*tathatā*) of the object of focus.
Being endowed with reasoning consists of four types of reasoning, namely: the reasoning of dependence,
the reasoning of cause and effect, [the reasoning of logical proof, and the reasoning of nature].
By means of the reasoning of logical proof (*upapattisādhanayukti*) and the reasoning of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatāyukti*).
Thus, there is the extent of existence (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) of the object (*ālambana*) and— (Śbh II 48)
The state of being as-it-is and the state of the limit of things, when condensed together into one, are called the "limit of the object."
In that regard, what is the accomplishment of the task?

It is this: through the sequence of cultivation, the sequence of meditative development, and the sequence of frequent practice, that mental attention of this yogin which has the reflected image as its object—pertaining to calm abiding and insight—is brought to fulfillment.
And through its fulfillment, the basis undergoes transformation.
All forms of functional rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*) are calmed;
and through the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*), having transcended the reflected image, there arises in that very object of knowledge a non-conceptual, direct perception and vision.
This occurs for one who has attained and acquired the first dhyāna within the sphere of the first dhyāna.

For one who has attained the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, and for one who has attained the fourth dhyāna, it is within the range of the fourth dhyāna; for one who has attained the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and for one who has attained those, it is within their respective ranges.
This is called the perfection of the task (*kāryapariniṣpatti*).

These are the four universal objects of focus (*ālambanavastu*), which follow along with all objects of focus and have been taught by the Perfectly Awakened Ones (*samyaksambuddha*) of the past, future, and present. Therefore, this is called the "pervasive object of focus" (*vyāpyālambana*).
Moreover, this object of focus belongs to the side of calm abiding (*śamatha*), the side of insight (*vipaśyanā*), and consists of all things, real things,
and the things of cause and fruit;
therefore, it is said to be all-pervasive.
In this regard, that which he calls "the conceptual image" pertains here to the side of insight (*vipaśyanā*);
furthermore, that which he calls "the non-conceptual image" pertains here to the side of tranquility (*śamatha*);
and furthermore, that which he calls "the limit of phenomena" (*vastuparyantatā*) pertains here to both the state of all things and the state of things as they truly are.
When he says, "the accomplishment of the task," this refers here to the relationship between cause and fruit.
As it was said by the Blessed One concerning the Venerable Revata:
"Thus it is heard."
The Venerable Revata asked the Blessed One a question:
"To what extent, Bhadanta, does a monk who is a yogi, a practitioner of yoga, fix his mind upon an object? Upon what kind of object does he fix his mind?"
“But how, again, is the mind well-bound when it is bound to an object?”
-II-3-a-(2)-ii-(a) The Blessed One said:
“Excellent, excellent!
Revata, it is indeed excellent that you ask about this matter, Revata.
Therefore, listen well and attend closely; I shall speak.
Here, Revata, a monk who is a yogin, a practitioner of yoga, may desire to purify his conduct, or he may desire to achieve skillfulness.
Or, desiring to liberate the mind from the outflows (*āsrava*),
he fixes the mind upon a suitable object,
and fixes it properly upon a fitting one.
And therein he becomes one who does not abandon meditative cultivation.
How does he fix the mind upon a suitable object?
If, Revata, [he does so]...
A monk who is a yogi and a practitioner of yoga, being one whose temperament is characterized by passion, fixes his mind upon the object of the foul;
thus he fixes his mind upon a suitable object.
Alternatively, one whose temperament is characterized by hatred fixes it upon loving-kindness.

One whose conduct is dominated by delusion [should practice] regarding specific conditionality and dependent origination; one whose conduct is dominated by pride, regarding the differentiation of the elements.
If, Revata,
That monk, a yogi, a practitioner of yoga, being one whose temperament is characterized by discursive thought (*vitarkacarita*), fixes his mind upon mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
In this way, he fixes his mind upon a suitable object of focus.

If, Revata, that monk, being deluded regarding the specific characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and deluded regarding the entities of self, sentient being, life-force, creature, nourisher, and person, fixes his mind upon skill in the aggregates (*skandha-kauśalya*);
or, being deluded regarding causes, [fixes it] upon skill in the elements (*dhātu-kauśalya*).

One who is deluded regarding the conditions [of dependent origination] is deluded regarding skill in the sense-bases; one who is deluded regarding impermanence, suffering, and non-self is deluded regarding skill in the possible and impossible within dependent origination;
or, one who desires to achieve detachment from the realm of desire.
When sense-desires are gross and forms are peaceful,

or when one desires to achieve detachment from forms, one fixes the mind upon the grossness of forms and the peacefulness of the formless realm; or, in all cases, when one desires to become disillusioned with the view of a self-existent body (satkāya).
Desiring liberation, [one contemplates] the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin, and the truth of cessation.
He fixes the mind upon the truth of the path.
For in this way, Revata,
a monk who is a yogi practicing yoga fixes his mind upon a suitable object of focus.
And how, Revata, does a monk who is a yogi, a practitioner of yoga, fix his mind upon a suitable object?
Here, Revata, whatever knowable thing a monk desires to investigate, [he fixes his mind upon that very thing].
Desiring to investigate, desiring to reflect upon, and desiring to examine it thoroughly,
he has already previously seen, heard, thought, or known that very thing.

Taking that very thing seen as the dominant influence, and taking what is heard, thought, and known as the dominant influence, he attends to it with a mental attention belonging to the level of meditative concentration;
he conceptualizes it and resolves upon it.
He does not see that very object of knowledge present and manifest before him, but rather there arises for him a counterpart of it or a representation of it.
Whether it be mere knowledge, mere vision, or mere recollection, whatever the object may be, this monk— a yogi, a practitioner of yoga— calms his mind from time to time.
From time to time, Revata, he applies himself to the yoga of the insight into phenomena within the domain of higher wisdom.
For it is thus, Revata, that he practices.
A monk who is a yogi, a practitioner of yoga, fixes his mind upon a suitable object of focus.
And how, Revata, does a monk who is a yogi, a practitioner of yoga, correctly bind his mind to the object of focus?
If, Revata, this [monk]...
A monk who is a yogi, a practitioner of yoga, fixes his mind upon an object of focus until that which is to be known has been known by him,
and that in accordance with reality, without error. Thus indeed, Revata, [it is].
The monk who is a yogi, a practitioner of yoga, correctly binds his mind to the object of focus.
And how, Revata, is a monk who is a yogi, a practitioner of yoga, one who does not abandon meditation?
If, Revata, he...
A monk who is a yogi, a practitioner of yoga, thus correctly applying himself to the object of focus, becomes one who practices with continuity and one who practices with reverence.
From time to time, he cultivates the sign of calm, the sign of exertion, and the sign of equanimity;
through the consequence of repeated practice, the consequence of cultivation, and the consequence of frequent application, there occurs the subsiding of all functional rigidity (*dausthulya*).

He attains, touches, and realizes the purification of the basis (*āśrayapariśuddhi*). Through the discernment of the objects of knowledge, he achieves, touches, and realizes the purification of the focal object (*ālambanapariśuddhi*); through the fading away of passion, he achieves, touches, and realizes the purification of the mind (*cittapariśuddhi*); and through the fading away of ignorance, he achieves, touches, and realizes the purification of knowledge (*jñānapariśuddhi*).
It is in this way, Revata, that the monk— (Śbh II 56)
The yogi, the practitioner of yoga, becomes one who does not abandon meditation;
and because, Revata, the monk fixes his mind upon this object of focus,
In this way he binds the mind to the object;
in this way his mind becomes well-bound to the object.
In this regard, there is a verse:
"The yogi who moves among signs, who understands the meaning of all beings,
and who constantly meditates on the image, attains complete purification."

In this regard, by the statement "the yogi practicing amidst signs," constant practice and reverent practice are explained with respect to the sign of calm, the sign of exertion, and the sign of equanimity.
Furthermore, by the statement "one who perceives the welfare of all beings," the limit of phenomena (*vastuparyantatā*) is explained.
Moreover, by the statement "one who constantly meditates on the image," both the conceptual and non-conceptual reflected images are explained.
Furthermore, by the statement "he attains complete purification," the fulfillment of the task is expressed.
Furthermore, it was said by the Blessed One:
"Skilled in the signs of the mind and finding the flavor of seclusion,
the meditator— prudent and mindful— enjoys spiritual joy and happiness free from worldly taints."

In this regard, first, by the statement "skilled in the sign of the mind," both the conceptual and non-conceptual images (*pratibimba*) are designated by the word "sign" (*nimitta*), while the word "skilled" (*kovida*) refers to the limit of phenomena (*vastuparyantatā*).
Furthermore, by the statement "and he experiences the flavor of seclusion," [it is shown that] he is correctly [established] upon the object of focus (*ālambana*). (Śbh II 58)
For one who has applied himself [to practice], delight in abandonment and delight in cultivation have been explained.
Furthermore, by the statement "the meditator is prudent and mindful," the continuous cultivation of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) is explained.
Moreover, by the statement "he enjoys spiritual joy and happiness free from worldly taints," the fulfillment of the task is explained.
This being so, it should be understood that this pervasive object of focus is purified by authoritative scripture and falls within the realm of reasoning.
This is called the pervasive object of focus.
In that regard, what is the object for purifying conduct?
It is as follows: the meditation on the foul (aśubhā) and loving-kindness (maitrī).
These are: dependent origination through specific conditionality, the analysis of the elements,
and mindfulness of breathing.
In that regard, what is the foul?
It is said: the foul is of six kinds.
Namely: impurity by way of decomposition,
impurity by way of suffering,
and inferior impurity.
There is impurity by way of relativity,
impurity by way of afflictions,
and impurity by way of perishability.
In that regard, what is the foulness of the secondary?
It is said:
the foulness of the secondary is to be understood as being based both on the internal and on the external.
Therein, with reference to the internal, they are as follows: the head hairs, the body hairs, and so forth.
Nails, teeth, dust, filth, skin, and flesh.
bone, sinew, vessel, kidney, heart,
the spleen, the lungs, and the intestines;
the small intestines,
the stomach, and the large intestine;
liver, feces, tears,
sweat, saliva, and nasal mucus;
fat, lymph, and marrow.
fat, bile, and phlegm.
pus, blood,
and the skull;
brain matter, and urine.
In that regard, what is the meditation on the foul based on external objects? It is as follows:
a livid corpse, or a festering corpse, and so forth.
Or a corpse that is torn apart, or bloated, or devoured;
Or the blood-stained corpse, or the mangled corpse, or the bones.
Or a chain,
or a skeleton,
or that which is produced from excrement.
Whether caused by urine,
or caused by saliva,
or caused by nasal mucus.
Or smeared with blood, or smeared with pus,
or a mass of excrement;
Or a drain;
in this way, the various types of internal and external impurity based on external objects should be understood.
This includes both the impurity based on the internal and the impurity based on the external.
This is called the impurity of the repulsive.
In this context, what is the impurity of suffering?

That which arises in dependence on a contact to be experienced as painful—namely, the unpleasant feeling, whether physical or mental, that belongs to the category of sensation—is called the impurity of suffering.
(Śbh II 62) In that regard, what is inferior impurity? It is whatever object is most base.
The most inferior realm is the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
because there is no other realm that is more inferior, more base, or more loathsome than it;
this is called the impurity of inferiority (*avarāśubhatā*).
In that regard, what is relative impurity?
It is as follows: a certain object, though being pure, appears as impure when compared to something else that is more pure.
For example, the realm of form (rūpadhātu) appears as impure when compared to the formless realm (ārūpya).
In relation to nirvāṇa, which is the cessation of the view of a real body (satkāyanirodha), everything up to the peak of existence (bhavāgra) is reckoned as impure;
this is the category of impurity based on such relative comparison.
In that regard, what is the impurity of the afflictions?
All fetters, bonds, latent tendencies, secondary afflictions, and outbursts belonging to the three realms are called the impurity of the afflictions.
In that regard, what is the impermanence of the fragile? It is the impermanence and lack of stability of the five aggregates of clinging.
The state of being unreliable and the nature of subject to change—
this is called the foulness of perishability.
Thus, this foulness is the object of focus for the purification of one whose temperament is dominated by passion.
-II-3-b-(1)-ii. In this context, attachment (*rāga*) is as follows: internally, it is the desire for and attachment to sensual pleasures (*kāmacchanda*, *kāmarāga*);
externally, it is the desire for and attachment to sexual intercourse (*maithunacchanda*, *maithunarāga*).
Desire for sense objects is passion for sense objects;
desire for form is passion for form; and desire for the self-identity is passion for the self-identity—this is the fivefold passion.
For the abandonment, the dispelling, and the non-occurrence of those five kinds of attachment, there is the sixfold object of meditation on the foul.
Therein, by means of the internal object of the impurity of the individual, one purifies the mind from sensual desire and sensual passion regarding internal sense-pleasures.

In that regard, by means of the external object of the meditation on impurity, one purifies the mind from desire for sexual intercourse and from lust for sexual intercourse directed toward external objects of desire— specifically, from the fourfold attachment associated with passion: attachment to color, attachment to shape, attachment to touch, and attachment to service.
In that regard, when there is a livid corpse, or a festering corpse,
or a dismembered corpse,
When one brings to mind a bloated corpse or a devoured corpse,
then one purifies the mind from attachment to beauty.
Furthermore, when he brings to mind the livid corpse, he purifies the mind from attachment to shape;
furthermore, when he brings to mind a bone, or a skeleton, or a chain of bones, [he purifies the mind from attachment to color].
Then, when one brings to mind the "scattered" (vikṣiptaka), one purifies the mind from attachment to touch (sparśarāga).
When one brings to mind the "scattered," one purifies the mind from attachment to secondary objects (upacārarāga).
In this way, he purifies his mind of sensual desire for sexual intercourse.
For this very reason, the Blessed One established the external contemplation on impurity with respect to the four charnel grounds (*śivapathikā*). Whichever of these charnel grounds he has seen:
one where corpses that have been dead for one day, or dead for seven days, are being devoured by crows, ospreys, vultures, dogs, and jackals.
In each of those instances, he applies this very body [to the comparison]:
"This body of mine, too, is of such a nature."
"Being thus constituted,
he has not transcended such a nature.
By this, [the stages] beginning with the livid corpse and ending with the devoured corpse have been explained.

Furthermore, when it says, "The path to the cemetery has been seen by means of the vehicle; it is devoid of skin, flesh, blood, and bound together only by sinews," by this the *vilohitaka* (the blood-stained) stage is described.
Furthermore, when it says:
"Those very places on the path of the dead that have been seen," [this indicates the skull, the forearm bone, and the chain of bones].
Furthermore, as it says:
"[The bones of the hands are set apart; the bones of the feet are also set apart."
The bones of the thighs are in one place; the bones of the knees are in another;
and the bones of the ribs, and so forth.
The bones of the upper arms, the bones of the forearms,
and the backbone.
the jaw-circle, the row of teeth,
and the skull of the head;

"Likewise, scattered bones are seen— separated from one another, those of one year, two years, up to seven years old, white like conch shells, pigeon-colored, and mixed with dust and powder"; by this, the "scattered" (vikṣiptaka) stage is described.
Thus, by means of the external object of the meditation on foulness, one purifies the mind from the fourfold passion associated with desire, namely, sexual passion.
Therein, by means of the object of the nature of suffering and impurity, and by means of the inferior object of impurity, he purifies the mind from sensual desire associated with sense objects.
Therein, by means of the object of equanimity and impurity, he purifies the mind from desire for the realm of form.

In that regard, by means of the object of the impurity of the afflictions and the object of the impurity of perishability, one purifies the mind from desire and attachment to the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), starting from the peak of existence (bhavāgra).
This, first of all, is the object for purifying the conduct of one whose temperament is dominated by passion;
this is stated with reference to what is possible.
Everything that has the impurity of the foul (*aśubhatā*) as its object is included [herein];

however, in this context, only the "impurity of the repulsive" (*pratyaśubhatā*) is intended. Other forms of impurity, moreover, serve as objects for the purification of other types of conduct (*carita*).
In that regard, what is loving-kindness?
It is that which [is directed] toward the side of friends or toward the side of enemies.
Or, with regard to the neutral party,

having established an intention for their welfare, there is an adhimokṣa belonging to the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmika*) directed toward the provision of mild, moderate, and intense happiness.
In this context, the friendly party, the hostile party, and the neutral party constitute the object of focus (*ālambana*).

In this context, that which is the resolute intention for benefit and the conviction aimed at bringing about happiness, belonging to the level of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmika*), is the "subject" (*ālambaka*).
That which is the object (*ālambana*) and that which is the subject, taken together as a single unity, are called "loving-kindness" (*maitrī*).

In that regard, as for what was first stated, "with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness," by this, the resolute intention for welfare toward the three categories— the category of friends, the category of enemies, and the category of neutral persons— is explained.
Furthermore, when he says, "without enmity, without rivalry, and without malice," by this the threefold characteristic of that very resolve for welfare is explained.
Therein, the resolve for welfare is characterized by being without enmity;
moreover, that absence of enmity is explained by two phrases.
By way of being without rivals and by way of being free from affliction.
In this context, "being without rivals" has the sense of abiding in a state that is not antagonistic.
Non-affliction is for the purpose of not engaging in harmful actions.
Furthermore, when it says, "vast, exalted, and immeasurable," this explains the bestowal of weak, medium, and intense happiness belonging to the desire realm.
Or belonging to the level of the first or second dhyāna,
or belonging to the level of the third dhyāna; as for what he further said:

By the phrase "having resolved, having pervaded, and having attained, he dwells," it is explained that the resolution for the bringing about of happiness belongs to the level of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmika*). Furthermore, this bringing about of happiness is embraced by the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) for welfare and is accompanied by attention consisting of resolve (*ādhimokṣika-manaskāra*),
directed toward those on the side of friends who are neither suffering nor happy.
It should be understood that this applies to those on the side of enemies and those on the side of neutral persons who desire happiness;
whereas as for those on the side of friends, the side of enemies, or the side of neutral persons, whether they are suffering or not suffering.
In that regard, one who is suffering is the object of compassion;
one who is happy is the object of sympathetic joy—
this is called loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
In that regard, a person whose temperament is dominated by ill will, by cultivating loving-kindness toward sentient beings,
thins out that ill will and purifies the mind of ill will.
-II-3-b-(3) What, then, is dependent origination as conditionality (*idampratyayatā-pratītyasamutpāda*)?

It is that which, throughout the three times, consists merely of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), merely of phenomena (*dharma*), merely of entities (*vastu*), merely of causes (*hetu*), and merely of results (*phala*), and which falls within logical reasoning— namely, by way of the reasoning of dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*), the reasoning of causal efficiency (*kāryakaraṇa-yukti*), and the reasoning of proof through establishment (*upapatti-sādhana-yukti*).

And by the reasoning of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-yukti*), it is established that phenomena themselves are the bringers of phenomena, and that they are devoid of an agent or an experiencer. This is called [the reasoning of the nature of phenomena]. (Śbh II 72)
This is the object of dependent origination through specific conditionality (*idaṃpratyayatā-pratītyasamutpāda*).

When a person with an excess of delusion, one whose behavior is dominated by delusion, attends to this object, they abandon delusion, attenuate it, and purify the mind from the tendency toward delusion.
In that regard, what is the analysis of the elements?
It is as follows: the six elements—the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element.
In that regard, the earth element is twofold:
internal and external.
Therein, the internal is that which, within this body, is internal, individual, solid, of a solid nature, approached, and grasped.
Furthermore, the external earth element is that which is external, hard, characterized by hardness, not approached, and not appropriated.
Now, what is the internal earth element?
It is as follows: hair, and so forth.
body hairs,
nails, teeth,
Dust, impurity, and skin.
flesh, bone,
and sinew.
the vessels, the kidneys, and the heart;
the spleen, the lungs, and the intestines;
the small intestines,
the stomach, and the large intestine;
The liver and excrement—
this is called the internal earth element.
Furthermore, what is the external earth element?
Whether they be pieces of wood, clods of earth, or pebbles.
Whether they be thickets, trees,
or mountain peaks.
Or whatever else is of this same category—
this is called the external earth element.
What is the water element?
The water element is twofold.
It is internal and external.
Therein, what is the internal water element?
That which is internal, individual, viscous, belonging to the viscous, the watery, the aqueous, approached, and grasped— namely,
tears, sweat, and so forth.
phlegm, nasal mucus, and fat;
lymph, marrow, and fat.
bile, phlegm, and pus;
blood,
the brain,
the marrow of the skull, and urine;
This is called the internal water element.
What is the external water element?
That which is external, belonging to the category of water, is the external water element.
Moisture is that which belongs to moisture, is not integrated [with consciousness], and is not appropriated;
furthermore, it consists of springs or lakes.
Whether they be ponds, rivers, or springs.
Or whatever else is of this same category—
this is called the external water element.
What is the fire element?
The fire element is twofold: internal and external.
Therein, what is the internal fire element?
That which is internal, personal, fiery, belonging to the fire-element, consisting of heat, belonging to heat, approached, and appropriated— namely,
that fire which is in this body by which this body is warmed and heated.
It is heated by that [fire] through which what has been eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted undergoes proper and easy digestion;
and because of its intensity, it is reckoned as "burning, burning."
This is called the internal fire element (*tejodhātu*).
What is the external fire element?
It is that which is external, belonging to fire, consisting of heat, belonging to heat, not approached, and not grasped.
Furthermore, that which humans seek from cow-dung powder kept with fire-drills—
once produced, it burns even a village,
or even a portion of a village.
Whether it be a city, or a district of a city, or a country,
or a region of the country, or an island, or a forest thicket;
Whether it be a forest,
or wood, or grass,
Or that which burns cow dung,
or whatever else is of this same category—
this is called the external fire element.
In this regard, what is the wind element?
The wind element is twofold: internal and external.
Therein, the internal wind element is that which is internal, pertaining to the individual, which has become wind or what belongs to wind—lightness and mobility—and which is appropriated.
Furthermore, what is it?
There are winds in this body that move upward;
The downward-moving winds,
the side-lying winds,
and the abdominal winds.
The winds that lie along the spine, the wind-knots,
the razor-like, peppercorn-like, and blade-like winds,
and the piercing colic winds.
The winds of inhalation and exhalation,
and the winds that follow along the limbs and minor parts of the body—
this is called the internal wind element.
What is the external wind element?
It is that which is external, wind, or what has become wind; it is lightness, mobility, and that which is not approached and not grasped.
Furthermore, what is that?
There are external winds from the east, and winds from the south.
northerly winds, westerly winds,
and dusty winds;
The dustless winds, the limited winds, the vast winds, and all-encompassing winds.
The Vairambha winds,
the winds of the wind-circles;
and there occurs a time when a great mass of wind arises, [sweeping away] even the tops of trees.
He causes them to fall; he causes even the tops of walls to fall, and he causes even the peaks of mountains to fall.
Having caused them to fall, he departs, free from any substrate of existence.
Whatever beings seek [air] with the hem of a robe,
or with a palm-leaf fan, or with a bellows—
Or whatever else is of this same category:
this is called the external wind element.
What is the space element?
It is that which is the cavity of the eye, or the cavity of the ear.
Whether it be the cavities of the nose, the cavities of the mouth, or the cavities of the throat.
That by which one consumes, that in which one consumes, or that by which one is consumed;
That which flows downward,
or whatever else is of this same category,
is called the space element (ākāśadhātu).
What is the element of consciousness?
It is eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness;
furthermore, it is the mind (*citta*), the intellect (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
This is called the consciousness element.

In this regard, a person whose temperament is dominated by pride, by attending to this analysis of the elements, eliminates the perception of the body as a single whole and acquires the perception of its impurity; furthermore, he does not become conceited because of it.
He attenuates pride and purifies the mind from that conduct.
This is called the analysis of the elements;
it is the object for purifying the conduct of a person whose temperament is dominated by pride.
In this regard, what is mindfulness of breathing?
Mindfulness that has inhalation and exhalation as its object is called mindfulness of breathing.
In that regard, there are two types of inhalation.
Which two?
Inhalation and intermediate inhalation;
and two exhalations.
Which two?
Exhalation and internal exhalation.
Among these, inhalation is the inward-moving wind that proceeds immediately after exhalation as far as the region of the navel.

In that context, the "intermediate inhalation" (*antarāśvāsa*) is that wind which arises in the interval when this inhalation has ceased but the exhalation has not yet arisen; it is associated with a point of rest, lasts for only a short time, and is similar to that [inhalation].
This is called the intermediate inhalation.
Just as inhalation and intermediate inhalation are to be understood, so too should exhalation and intermediate exhalation be understood.
In this regard, the distinction is that it should be stated that the wind proceeds outward,
starting from the region of the navel.
As far as the tip of the mouth and the tip of the nose, or even further from there to the outside.
There are two causes for inhalation and exhalation.
Which two?
The karma that projects them, and—
The cavity of the navel region, and furthermore,
whatever other cavities of the body there may be beyond that.
(Śbh II 82) There are two bases for inhalation and exhalation.
Which two?
The body and the mind.
For what reason?
Because inhalation and exhalation proceed in dependence upon the body and in dependence upon the mind.
And if those [mental factors] were to proceed solely in dependence upon the body as appropriate,

they would proceed in the case of those who have attained the attainment of non-perception, those who have attained the attainment of cessation, and sentient beings born among the gods of the non-percipient realm.
If they were to proceed based solely on the mind,
then they would proceed for those beings who have attained or been born into the formless realm (*ārūpya*).
If they were to proceed based on both the body and the mind, they would not do so in accordance with what is appropriate.
Therefore, inhalation and exhalation would have to occur for beings who have entered or are born in the fourth dhyāna, as well as for beings in the embryonic stages of *kalala*, *arbuda*, and *peśī*;
yet they do not so occur. Consequently, inhalation and exhalation proceed based upon both the body and the mind, according to the circumstances.
There are two movements of inhalation and exhalation.
Which two?
The downward movement of inhalations.
The upward movement of the two exhalations.
There are two stages of inhalation and exhalation.
Which two? The coarse and the hollow.
And there is subtle porosity.
Among these, gross porosity extends from the region of the navel up to the openings of the mouth and nostrils;
and from the openings of the mouth and nostrils down to the porosity of the region of the navel.
What is subtle porosity?
It consists of all the pores of the body.
There are four synonymous designations for inhalation and exhalation.
What are the four? They are:
winds, inhalations and exhalations, and so forth.
Inhalation and exhalation are bodily formations;
in this regard, they are distinct from other winds.
There is one common synonymous name, namely "wind" (vāyu); the other three names are specific [to each element].
There are two defects for one engaged in the practice of inhalation and exhalation.
Which two?
Excessive laxity in application, and...
And there is the application of excessive tension.
In that regard, for one who has fallen into laziness due to an excessively lax application, either lethargy and sleep envelop the mind,
or it is distracted outwardly.
For one who applies [the practice] with such excessive fixation, either an imbalance of the body or an imbalance of the mind arises.
How does an imbalance of the body arise?
By forcibly suppressing the inhalations and exhalations through intense constraint, uneven winds circulate within the body.
Those winds which first throb within his various major and minor limbs are called "throbbing" (*sphuraka*). Furthermore, as those throbbing winds increase, they become "painful" (*rujaka*).
Those things which produce pain in his various major and minor limbs—
this is called physical imbalance.
How does mental imbalance arise?
Or his mind becomes distracted,
or it is overwhelmed by intense dejection and despair;
in this way, an imbalance of the mind arises.
Indeed, five kinds of cultivation for this mindfulness of breathing should be understood:

namely, cultivation through counting, cultivation through entry into the aggregates, cultivation through entry into dependent origination, cultivation through entry into the truths, and cultivation through the sixteen aspects.
In that regard, what is the cultivation of counting? Briefly stated, the cultivation of counting is fourfold:
namely, counting one by one;
Counting by twos,
counting in forward order, and counting in reverse order.
In that regard, what is counting one by one?
When the inhalation has entered,
one counts "one" with mindfulness bound to the object of the inhalation and exhalation.
When the inhalation has ceased and the exhalation arises and goes out, then one counts the second;
in this manner, one counts up to ten.
Indeed, this counting is neither too brief nor too extensive.
This is called counting one by one.
What is the counting of pairs as one? When the inhalation has entered and ceased and the exhalation has arisen and gone out, then one counts it as "one."
By this method of counting, he counts up to ten;
this is called "counting two as one.
Having condensed these two—the inhalation and the exhalation—into a single unit, he counts them as "one."
Therefore, this is called the counting of pairs as one.
What is counting in the forward order?
By this very method of counting one by one, or by counting two as one, one counts up to ten in the forward order. This is called counting in the forward order.
What is counting in reverse order (*pratilomagaṇanā*)?
It is counting in reverse order starting from ten, then nine, eight, seven, six, five, and so on down to one.
This is called counting in reverse order (pratilomagaṇanā),
when, relying on that single-counting or the dual-single counting during the forward counting (anulomagaṇanā).
He becomes practiced in counting in reverse order,
and his mind does not become distracted in the interim;
with an undistracted mind, he counts.
Then, a specific higher calculation for this is designated.
What is the distinction of counting?
It is either by counting one by one,
or by counting two as one.
Having made two into one, he counts them.
In that process of counting two as one, four inhalations and exhalations constitute one unit; however, by counting each individually, both the inhalation and the exhalation constitute one.
In this way, he counts up to ten;
likewise, by increasing further and further, he even counts up to one hundred by making it a single unit.
Then, by counting that hundred as a single unit, he counts sequentially up to ten.
Thus, for one engaged in counting, having made ten into one and counting up until ten are completed,
by means of that counting of ten as one, his mind is not distracted in the interval.
To this extent, he has cultivated familiarity with counting.
And if, while thus engaged in counting, his mind becomes distracted in the interim,
then he begins counting again from the beginning, either in the direct order or the reverse.

Or in reverse order. And when, through familiarity with counting, that mind— by its own natural impulse— has mounted the path of flow, is bound to the object of the inhalation and exhalation, and proceeds uninterruptedly and continuously,
