it perceives the activity during the inhalation as it occurs.

When inhalation has ceased, there is the apprehension of cessation, which apprehends the state devoid of exhalation; when exhalation has begun, there is the apprehension of activity; and when it has ceased, there is again the apprehension of cessation, which apprehends the state devoid of inhalation—unshakable, immovable, and characterized by non-distraction.
And it proceeds with delight;
by this much, there is a complete transcendence of the stage of counting,
and it becomes necessary to count that [stage] once again.
The mind is not bound to any object other than the inhalation and exhalation;
the inhalations and exhalations, along with the intervals between them and their states of occurrence and cessation, are to be followed and clearly characterized.
This is called the cultivation of counting.
Indeed, this practice of counting is prescribed for those of dull faculties;
for them,
it serves as a basis for non-distraction, leading to the stability of the mind and delight in the mind.
Otherwise, without counting, their mind might be overwhelmed by sloth and torpor,
or the mind might become distracted outwardly;
however, for those engaged in counting, this does not happen.
However, for those who possess sharp faculties and keen intelligence, counting practice becomes a matter of mere fondness;
having been instructed therein, they penetrate the application of counting very quickly indeed,
yet they do not derive delight from it.
Furthermore, having fixed their mindfulness upon the object of inhalation and exhalation, they observe where these proceed, how far they proceed,
in what manner they proceed, and when they proceed.
He follows all that and discerns it with established mindfulness. This is the nature of their preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Through the sequence of practicing, cultivating, and repeatedly performing that application, bodily pliancy (*kāyaprasrabdhi*) arises.
He experiences mental pliancy,
touches one-pointedness, and emerges with delight in the object of focus.
Having thus cultivated familiarity, he enters into the aggregates by means of mental attention toward the objects of the grasped and the grasper.
Furthermore, how does he enter?
By attending to those inhalations and exhalations and to that body which is their basis, he enters into the aggregate of form.
That experience which is associated with the mindfulness that grasps those inhalations and exhalations, he enters into as the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*).

That which is the act of perceiving, he enters into as the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). And that which is this mindfulness and that which is volition (*cetanā*), [he enters into as the aggregate of formations].
Whatever wisdom (*prajñā*) is therein,
he enters into it as the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*);
and whatever mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*) is therein, he enters into it as the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
The frequent dwelling in that state by one who has thus entered into the aggregates is called the cultivation of the entry into the aggregates.

And when he has seen, understood, and fully comprehended that there is merely the aggregates, merely conditioned formations, and merely entities, then he enters into the dependent origination of these very formations.
Furthermore, how does he enter?
He investigates and searches in this way:
“Thus, upon what are these inhalations and exhalations dependent? What is their condition?
To him it occurs: “These inhalations and exhalations are dependent on the body and conditioned by the body; they are also dependent on the mind and conditioned by the mind.”
Furthermore, what is the condition for the body and the mind?
He penetrates this understanding: "The body and the mind have the life-faculty as their condition.
Then he asks: "What, in turn, is the condition for the life-faculty?"
He penetrates the fact that the life-faculty has past formations as its condition.
He penetrates: "What is the condition for those past formations?
and thus he penetrates: "Those past formations have ignorance as their condition."
Thus, conditioned by ignorance is the prior formative force;
conditioned by the prior formative force is the life-faculty;
and conditioned by the life-faculty are both body and mind.
Inhalation and exhalation have the body and mind as their conditions.
In that regard, through the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations;
through the cessation of volitional formations, there is the cessation of the life-faculty.
From the cessation of the life-faculty comes the cessation of body and mind;
from the cessation of body and mind comes the cessation of inhalation and exhalation.
In this way, he enters into dependent origination.
Abiding frequently therein, he is said to have "completed his training in the entry into dependent origination.
This is called the training in the entry into dependent origination.
Having thus cultivated familiarity with dependent origination, he penetrates [the truth]: "These conditioned phenomena that have arisen dependently are impermanent.
Because they are impermanent, having not existed they come to be, and having existed they pass away;
furthermore, these, having not existed, come to be, and having existed, pass away—they are subject to the nature of birth.
They are subject to aging, subject to illness, and subject to death.
Those things subject to birth, aging, sickness, and death are suffering;
those which are suffering are non-self and lack autonomy.
"Devoid of a master.
In this way, he has entered into the truth of suffering by means of the aspects of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
It occurs to him as follows:
"Whatever manifestation of these conditioned phenomena there may be—which is suffering, a disease, and a tumor—all that has craving as its condition.

Furthermore, the complete abandonment of this craving that gives rise to suffering is peace; it is sublime. And for me, who knows thus and dwells frequently in this way, there will be the complete abandonment of craving."

In this way, he has entered into the truth of origin, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path. When, dwelling frequently in that state, he realizes the truths, this is called his cultivation of the entry into the truths.
For one who has thus cultivated familiarity with the truths and has abandoned the afflictions to be abandoned by vision, those remaining [afflictions] to be abandoned by cultivation persist.
-II-3-b-(5)-ii-(e) For the sake of abandoning which [defilements] does one cultivate the sixteen aspects?
Furthermore, what are these sixteen aspects?

(Śbh II 96) That is to say, being mindful while inhaling, he trains himself: "I am inhaling mindfully"; being mindful while exhaling, he trains himself: "I am exhaling mindfully. Inhaling a long breath, he trains himself: "I am inhaling a long breath"; inhaling a short breath, he trains himself: "I am inhaling a short breath"; experiencing the whole body [of breath] while inhaling, he trains himself: "I am inhaling while experiencing the whole body."
Experiencing the whole body while breathing out, he trains himself: "I am breathing out experiencing the whole body.
Calming the bodily formations while breathing in, he trains himself: "I am breathing in calming the bodily formations.
Calming the bodily formations while breathing out, he trains himself: "I am breathing out calming the bodily formations."
Experiencing rapture and experiencing pleasure, he trains himself;
experiencing the mental formations, while calming the mental formations as he breathes in, he trains himself, thinking, "I am breathing in while calming the mental formations";
while calming the mental formations as he breathes out, he trains himself, thinking, "I am breathing out while calming the mental formations."
Experiencing the mind, gladdening the mind, concentrating the mind, and liberating the mind, he trains himself, breathing in while liberating the mind: "I am breathing in while liberating the mind.
Breathing out while liberating the mind, he trains himself: "I am breathing out while liberating the mind."
contemplating impermanence, contemplating abandonment, and contemplating dispassion;
Breathing in while contemplating cessation, he trains himself, thinking, "I am breathing in while contemplating cessation";
breathing out while contemplating cessation, he trains himself, thinking, "I am breathing out while contemplating cessation."
What, then, is the distinction between these aspects?
That learner, having seen the truth and being a possessor of the four foundations of mindfulness,
initiates mental attention focused on inhalation and exhalation for the sake of abandoning the remaining fetters.
Therefore it is said: "Being mindful while inhaling, one trains oneself, thinking, 'I am inhaling mindfully'; being mindful while exhaling, one trains oneself, thinking, 'I am exhaling mindfully.
When one takes either the inhalation or the exhalation as the object, then one trains oneself, thinking, 'I am inhaling long,' or 'I am exhaling long.'"
When one takes the intermediate inhalation or the intermediate exhalation as the object of focus, then one trains oneself, thinking: "I am inhaling and exhaling short.
For in that state, the primary inhalations and exhalations proceed long, while the intermediate inhalations and intermediate exhalations are short.
He observes and knows them exactly as they proceed.

When he resolves upon and takes as his object the inhalations and exhalations that have entered the subtle pores of the body, having entered through the pores of the skin, then he becomes one who experiences the whole body.
Furthermore, at whatever time the inhalation and the intermediate inhalation have ceased,
one takes as an object that state which is empty of inhalation and exhalation and devoid of inhalation and exhalation;
and when the exhalation and the intermediate exhalation have ceased.
When inhalation and the intermediate inhalation have not yet arisen,
he takes as his object that state which is empty of exhalation and inhalation, devoid of them, separated from them, and vacant; at that time,
while breathing in after having calmed the bodily formations, he...
He trains himself: "Experiencing the calming of the bodily formations, I shall breathe in";
experiencing the calming of the bodily formations while breathing out, he trains himself: "Experiencing the calming of the bodily formations, I shall breathe out."
Moreover, indeed, through the consequence of practicing, cultivating, and frequently performing [this],
those inhalations and exhalations which were previously harsh and unpleasant to the touch for one who had not yet become familiar with them proceed;
however, for one who has become familiar with them, others that are gentle and pleasant to the touch proceed.
Therefore it is said: "He trains himself, thinking, 'I shall breathe in while calming the bodily formations.

And when he is thus engaged in the practice of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti) and becomes an attainer of either the first or the second dhyāna, at that time, breathing in while experiencing joy, he trains himself, thinking, "I shall breathe in while experiencing joy."
If, moreover, he is an attainer of the third dhyāna, which is free from rapture, at that time he experiences pleasure.
Beyond the third dhyāna, there is no association with mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti);
by this [fact], everything proclaimed up to the third dhyāna is included.
While he is thus experiencing joy or experiencing happiness, if at any time, on any occasion, through a lapse of mindfulness,
there should arise the thought "I am," or "This I am," or "I shall be," or...
"Or 'I shall not exist,' or 'I shall exist possessing form, or I shall exist without form,' or 'I shall be percipient, or non-percipient.'"

"I shall become neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient"—thus, accompanied by delusion, perception, and volition, there arises a state involving agitation, conceit, conceptual proliferation, and formative activity, which belongs to the sphere of craving.
As soon as it has arisen, he penetrates it quickly with wisdom; he does not tolerate it, but abandons it, dispels it, and brings it to an end.

Thus, experiencing the mental formations, while breathing in with the thought, "I am breathing in calming the mental formations," he trains himself, thinking, "I am breathing in calming the mental formations.
Furthermore, if he is an attainer of the fundamental first, second, and third dhyānas, he is necessarily an attainer of the *anāgamya*, the preliminary stage of the first dhyāna.
Relying upon that, he examines his own mind as it has arisen.

Whether the mind is with lust or free from lust, with hatred or free from hatred, with delusion or free from delusion; whether it is contracted or distracted, sluggish or exerted, agitated or unagitated, tranquil or untranquil, concentrated or unconcentrated, well-cultivated or uncultivated, and whether the mind is liberated or unliberated— [he knows it as it truly is].
He understands and experiences it as it truly is;
therefore, he is called "one who experiences the mind.
When his mind is hindered by the hindrance of sloth and torpor while he is calming it internally, he then demonstrates and inspires him with one or another inspiring object of focus.
He inspires and gladdens [the mind];
therefore it is said that he gladdens the mind.
Furthermore, when he perceives that [the mind] is obstructed by the hindrance of restlessness and the hindrance of remorse while he is exerting himself, [he applies the appropriate remedy].
Then, by means of some suitable object that inspires clarity, he demonstrates it, settles it internally, calms it, and composes it;
therefore, it is said: "composing the mind."

And when that mind, through the sequence of cultivation, the sequence of development, and the sequence of frequent practice, has been distanced from the manifestation of the hindrances and purified of the hindrances, he trains himself while breathing in, releasing the mind, thinking: "I am breathing in, releasing the mind. For one whose mind is thus liberated from the hindrances, there remain latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that obstruct the cultivation of the path and must be abandoned.
He brings the path to manifestation for their abandonment;
that is to say, he correctly, thoroughly, and fundamentally contemplates the very impermanence of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Therefore, it is said that he "contemplates impermanence."
Previously, by relying on the first, second, or third dhyāna, or by relying on the *anāgamya* stage, he practiced the application of calm (*śamatha*).
Now, observing impermanence, he practices the application of insight (*vipaśyanā*).
Thus, his mind, cultivated through both calm and insight, is liberated from the elements, that is, from the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
What are the elements?
They are the element of abandonment, the element of dispassion, and the element of cessation.
Among these, [the first] is due to the abandonment of all conditioned phenomena that are to be abandoned by vision.
The element of abandonment;
the element of dispassion through the abandonment of all conditioned phenomena that are to be abandoned by cultivation;
and the element of cessation through the cessation of all substrates of existence.
Thus, attending to the three realms as peaceful, secure, and healthy, he cultivates calm abiding and insight;
through the sequence of practicing, cultivating, and frequently applying these, his mind is liberated from the remaining afflictions that are to be abandoned by cultivation.
Therefore, it is said that he "contemplates abandonment."
Contemplating dispassion and contemplating cessation, while breathing in, he trains himself, thinking, "I am breathing in contemplating cessation.
In this way, when the afflictions to be abandoned through vision and cultivation have been eliminated, he becomes an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted.
There is nothing further for him to do; he has completed his cultivation. This is called his sixteenfold cultivation.
And this fivefold cultivation is called his mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).

In this regard, a person whose temperament is characterized by discursive thought (*vitarkacarita*) applies himself with a sense of joyful engagement. This object of focus involves effort and mental exertion; it is internal, individual, and extremely proximate.
By means of this, for him who is thus engaged therein, that agitation of discursive thought (*vitarka*) does not occur;
and his mind very swiftly becomes settled upon the object and finds delight in it.
This is the fifth object for purifying the conduct of a person whose temperament is characterized by discursive thought.
-II-3-c. What is the object of skill? It is as follows:

skill in the aggregates (*skandha-kauśalya*), skill in the elements (*dhātu-kauśalya*), skill in the sense-bases (*āyatana-kauśalya*), skill in dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*), and skill in what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*).
In this regard, what are the aggregates,
and what is skillfulness regarding the aggregates?
He said: "There are five aggregates: the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.
Among these, what is the aggregate of form?"
Whatever form there is, all that consists of the four great elements and what is derived from the four great elements.
Furthermore, it is either past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near.
In this context, what is the aggregate of feeling?
Whether it be a contact conducive to pleasant feeling, or one conducive to painful feeling,
or one conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
The six groups of feeling are: feeling born of eye-contact, and feelings born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact.
In that regard, what is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*)?
It is, for example, perception with signs (*sanimitta-saṃjñā*).
the perception of the signless,
the perception of the limited, and the perception of the vast;
The perception of the immeasurable;
the perception of the sphere of nothingness, which is the thought that "there is nothing whatsoever";
and the six groups of perceptions: the perception born of eye-contact, and the perceptions born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact.
What is the aggregate of formations?
It consists of the six classes of volition: volition born of eye-contact, and volition born of contact with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Setting aside feeling and perception, those other mental factors (caitasika-dharma) are [the aggregate of formations].
Among these, what is the aggregate of consciousness?
It is that which is mind (citta), intellect (manas), and consciousness (vijñāna).
Furthermore, those six groups of consciousness are:
eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness.
And this very feeling, perception, and mental formations, as well as this consciousness—whether past, future, or present; internal or external—is to be understood in detail as previously described.
These are called the aggregates (*skandha*).
What is skill in the aggregates? It is [the knowledge] of these aforementioned phenomena as having various distinct natures.
And he knows it by way of its manifold nature,
yet beyond that he neither perceives nor conceptualizes anything;
this, in brief, is called skill in the aggregates (*skandha-kauśalya*).
In that regard, what is the diversity of the aggregates?
The aggregate of form is indeed one thing, the aggregate of feeling is another, and so on up to the aggregate of consciousness;
this is their diversity.
In this context, what is meant by "having many constituent parts"?

It refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), which is of many kinds and various types, distinguished by the difference between the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*), and by the distinction of types such as past, future, present, and so forth.
This is called the manifold nature of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
In the same way, it should be understood for the remaining aggregates as appropriate.
Furthermore, one does not perceive or conceptualize anything beyond that.

One perceives only the aggregates, only the mere entity; however, one does not perceive a self apart from the aggregates as permanent, stable, and subject to no change, nor does one perceive anything belonging to a self.
One does not perceive anything whatsoever here,
nor does one conceptualize it beyond that.
In that regard, what are the elements (dhātu)?
What is skill in the elements?
He replied:
The eighteen elements:
the eye element, the form element, the eye-consciousness element; the ear element, the sound element, the ear-consciousness element;
the nose element, the odor element, the nose-consciousness element; the tongue element, the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element.
The body element, the tangible object element, the body-consciousness element, the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element—
these are called the elements. In that regard, what is skillfulness regarding the elements?

Furthermore, when one knows that these eighteen phenomena arise, are produced, and manifest from their respective elements, from their respective seeds, and from their respective lineages— and when, taking delight in this, one reflects upon it— this is called skill in the elements (*dhātukauśalya*).
When one knows the arising of the eighteen dharmas from their respective domains, this being so, that is skill in causes and conditions; namely, skill in the domains (*dhātu-kauśalya*).
In that regard, what are the sense bases (*āyatana*)?
What is skillfulness regarding the sense bases (*āyatanakauśalya*)?
He said: "The twelve sense bases:
the eye base,"
the sense-sphere of visible form,
the sense-sphere of the ear, and the sense-sphere of sound;
the sense-base of the nose, the sense-base of odors, and the sense-base of the tongue;
the sense-field of taste, the sense-field of the body, and the sense-field of the tangible;
The mind-base (manāyatana) and the phenomena-base (dharmāyatana);
these are called the bases (āyatanas).
What is skillfulness regarding the sense bases (*āyatana-kauśalya*)?

In this regard, the eye is the dominant condition (*adhipati*), visible forms are the objective condition (*ālambana*), and the mind that has just ceased is the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), for the arising of visual consciousness together with its associated mental factors.

In that regard, for the arising of auditory consciousness together with its associated mental factors, the ear is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), sound is the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the mind that has just ceased is the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Likewise, up to the case of the mental consciousness: the mind that has just ceased is the immediate condition, the attention (*manaskāra*) produced from it is the dominant condition, and mental phenomena (*dharma*) are the objective condition for the arising of the mental consciousness together with its associated mental factors.
Thus, the six groups of consciousness arise together with their associated mental factors through three conditions: the immediate condition, the objective condition, and the dominant condition.
Thus,
this skill regarding the conditions within the internal and external sense bases is called skill in the sense bases (*āyatanakauśalya*).
In that regard, what is dependent origination,
and what is skillfulness regarding dependent origination?
He said:
With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises;
with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises.
In detail, up to:
"In this way, there is the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.
This is called dependent origination."
Furthermore, it is phenomena alone that cause phenomena to vibrate; phenomena alone that cause phenomena to quiver;
conditioned factors alone that are the sustainers of phenomena, and these, moreover, because they have arisen from causes.
Because they are dependently originated, they come into being after not having been, and having been, they pass away.
Therefore, these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent.
Furthermore, those things which are impermanent are subject to birth, subject to aging, subject to sickness, subject to death, and subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair.
Because they are subject to aging, and so forth, up to being subject to despair, they are suffering;
furthermore, those which are suffering are devoid of autonomy.
"They are weak and without self"—
this is the knowledge of impermanence and the knowledge of suffering regarding dependently arisen phenomena through these aspects.
The knowledge of selflessness;
this is called skillfulness regarding dependent origination.
Furthermore, skill in the possible and the impossible should be understood as being specifically a particular form of skill in dependent origination.
In this regard, the distinction is as follows:
through skill in knowing what is possible and what is impossible, one understands that there is no uneven causality;
that is, there is the ripening of the fruit of wholesome and unwholesome karmas.
Furthermore, it is accepted that the ripening of the fruit of wholesome [actions] is desirable,
while that of unwholesome [actions] is undesirable;
such knowledge as this is called skill in the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*).
This skill in the five bases, in brief, consists of skill regarding specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-kauśalya*) and skill regarding general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa-kauśalya*).

Among these, skill regarding the aggregates (*skandha-kauśalya*) expresses skill regarding specific characteristics, while by the remaining [bases], skill regarding general characteristics is expressed.
This is called the object of skill (*kauśalyālambana*).
In that regard, what is the object for purifying the afflictions? It is said:
it is the coarseness of the lower stages and the tranquility of the higher stages.
Just as it is for the first dhyāna in the desire realm, so it is up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
In that regard, what is coarseness?
Coarseness is of two kinds.

There is coarseness of intrinsic nature and coarseness of numerical magnitude. In that regard, as for coarseness of intrinsic nature: although the five aggregates exist in both the desire realm and the first dhyāna, those belonging to the desire realm are more fraught with defects and more associated with painful dwelling. (Śbh II 116)
They are also more short-lived, more inferior, and more contemptible;
this is their coarseness of intrinsic nature.
But in the first dhyāna it is not so; therefore, they are said to be calmer and more sublime.
In that regard, what is numerical coarseness?
The aggregate of form belonging to the desire realm is more extensive as something to be fully known and abandoned, and so on up to the aggregate of consciousness.
This is called grossness by way of number.
In this manner, both grossness by way of intrinsic nature and grossness by way of number in the higher stages should be understood according to the appropriate application.
Furthermore, this grossness in the higher stages, up to the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), should be understood as follows:
All the lower stages are more difficult to dwell in and involve shorter lifespans;
however, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is indeed peaceful, as there is no stage superior to it above.
In this context, in brief, the meaning of "grossness" (audārikatā) is the meaning of "disadvantage" (ādīnava).
Whichever stage possesses a greater degree of disadvantage is said to be gross by virtue of that disadvantage.
In whichever stage there is less fault, that is said to be "peaceful" in comparison to the faults.
This is the focal object for the purification of afflictions by means of the mundane path for worldly beings.
Nevertheless, for one who perceives that lower stage as having defects— viewing it as a disease, as lacking security and well-being—
and perceives the higher stage as peaceful;
Those afflictions belonging to the lower stages, extending as far as the stage of the sphere of nothingness— beginning from the desire realm— are abandoned,
yet they are not abandoned absolutely;
for they become once again the causes for rebirth.

Furthermore, by means of the supramundane path, the object for the purification of afflictions is fourfold, namely: the truth of suffering, the truth of origin, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path.
Among these, what is the truth of suffering?

Namely: birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering, association with the unpleasant is suffering, separation from the pleasant is suffering, and the frustration of one's desires is suffering.
In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
Therein, the noble truth of the origin is craving, which leads to renewed existence, is accompanied by delight and lust, and finds delight here and there.
Therein, the noble truth of cessation is the complete abandonment of this very craving;
the noble truth of the path is the noble eightfold path.
Therein, based upon the dark side and the bright side, the establishment of the four truths is made through the arrangement of cause and fruit.
In that context, the truth of suffering is the fruit;
the truth of origination is the cause;
and the truth of cessation is the fruit.
The truth of the path is the cause for attainment and for direct realization.
In this context, the truth of suffering is like a disease; it must first be fully understood. The truth of origination is like the cause of the disease; it must subsequently be abandoned.
The truth of cessation is like a state of health, and it is to be touched and realized;
the truth of the path is like medicine, and it is to be practiced, cultivated, and frequently applied.

-II-3-d-(2)-ii This is indeed real: it is thus, not otherwise, not inverted, and not perverted; suffering is [suffering] in the sense of suffering, up to the path being [the path] in the sense of the path. Therefore, it is called "truth."
Furthermore, its own-characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is not deceptive;
because of seeing that, non-erroneous cognitions arise.
Therefore, it is called "truth" (satya).
Why, then, are these truths exclusively those of the noble ones?
Because the noble ones, regarding these very truths as truths, know and see them as they truly are.
But fools neither know nor see things as they truly are;
therefore, they are called the "Noble Truths."
For the foolish, this is true by way of its intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*), but not through realization;
for the noble ones (*ārya*), however, it is true in both ways.

In that regard, "the suffering of birth" means that as one is being born, painful sensations—both physical and mental—arise; it is not that birth itself is the suffering, but rather that it is the source of suffering. This applies likewise up to "the frustration of desires is suffering," meaning that because of the frustration of desires, physical and mental suffering arises.
But it is not merely the frustration of one's desires that is suffering; rather, it is that [frustration] which is the source of suffering, and so on.
In brief, "the five aggregates of clinging are suffering"—by these synonyms such as birth and so forth, the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhata*) alone is illuminated.

Therein, the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*) and the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*) remain; furthermore, those two are illuminated by way of the suffering inherent in the five aggregates of clinging.
For indeed, the five aggregates of clinging, being permeated by the three types of feeling, are the vessels for that aforementioned suffering-as-suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).

Furthermore, that which was not mentioned—the suffering-of-change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) and the suffering-of-conditioned-phenomena (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*)—is also to be seen as residing in these very same aggregates.
For what reason, then, did the Blessed One proclaim only the suffering-as-suffering by its own specific name?
Furthermore, the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*) and the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*) function by way of a gradual sequence.
For it is in the case of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*) that the cognition of suffering arises equally for both the noble ones (*ārya*) and the foolish.

The suffering of suffering is extremely distressing for those who have not previously cultivated wisdom; thus, when it is taught in this manner, there is an easy entry into the [Four] Truths for those to be trained (*vineya*).
In that regard, how is the threefold nature of suffering established?

First, by the statement "birth is suffering" up to "the frustration of one's desires is suffering," painful feeling together with its basis is described; and that is the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*).

This is the establishment of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*). Furthermore, whatever factors are its opposites, such as youth being the opposite of old age, and health being the opposite of illness.
Life is the condition for death; association with the beloved is the condition for association with the unbeloved;
separation from the unbeloved is the condition for separation from the beloved.
The fulfillment of desires is the remedy for the frustration of desires;
as are the afflictions together with their bases that operate within painful feeling,
and those afflictions that operate within wholesome states such as health and the like, as well as within the feeling produced therefrom.

This is called the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*). In this regard, pleasant feeling (*sukhā vedanā*), together with its basis, undergoes transformation through impermanence; by virtue of becoming otherwise, it produces suffering characterized by that alteration.
Furthermore, the afflictions (kleśa), when active everywhere, become suffering precisely through their manifestation as outbursts (paryavasthāna).
Moreover, there is the transformation of the mind; therefore, it is called the "suffering of change" (vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā), as stated by the Blessed One:
“Taking the hand of a woman with a mind that is agitated and transformed,” and so forth.

And as it has been said: “One who is obsessed by sensual desire experiences the mental pain and dejection born of that obsession with sensual desire, conditioned by that obsession. In this way, one who is obsessed by ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-remorse, or doubt [experiences the same]. Thus, by means of this authoritative and supremely authoritative scripture, the sense of suffering and the sense of transformation are also established for the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Therefore, it is called the suffering of the transformation of afflictions;
this is the formal definition of the suffering of transformation.
Furthermore, the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) is omnipresent within the aggregates of grasping (*upādānaskandha*).

In brief, however, it consists of that which is the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), that which is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) comprised within the afflictions (*kleśa*), and that which is... (Śbh II 124)

Excluding that [feeling] which is comprised of the most excellent pleasant feeling together with its basis, those other aggregates (skandha) which are accompanied by neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, which have arisen from it, which are conditions for its arising, and which belong to that which has already arisen—

this is called the suffering of conditioned formations (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā). Those aggregates which are impermanent, subject to arising and passing away, associated with grasping (sopādāna), followed by the three feelings, possessed of dysfunction (dauṣṭhulya), fallen into a lack of security, and not liberated from the suffering of suffering (duḥkha-duḥkhatā) and the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā)— [this is the suffering of conditioned formations].
And they are not subject to one's own control;
this is called suffering by way of the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
This is the formal definition of the suffering of conditioned formations.

In this context, craving (*tṛṣṇā*), longing (*prārthanā*), desire (*abhilāṣa*), and delight (*abhinandana*) are synonyms. Furthermore, that longing proceeds by way of three aspects, namely: longing for renewed existence (*punarbhava-prārthanā*) and longing for sense objects (*viṣaya-prārthanā*).

In that context, the longing for renewed existence is the craving for rebirth (*paunarbhavikī tṛṣṇā*). Furthermore, the longing for sense objects is of two kinds: that which is accompanied by attachment to mental pleasure regarding sense objects already obtained, and [that which is accompanied by attachment to mental pleasure regarding sense objects not yet obtained].
Regarding objects not yet attained, it is accompanied by a longing for union with them;
therein, that which is accompanied by an attachment to mental pleasure regarding objects already attained is called "accompanied by delight and passion" (*nandīrāgasahagatā*).
Furthermore, that which is accompanied by a longing for union with objects not yet attained is called "rejoicing here and there" (*tatratatrābhinandinī*).
Cessation is also twofold:
the cessation of afflictions and the cessation of secondary afflictions.
The path is also twofold:
that of the learner (śaikṣa) and that of the non-learner (aśaikṣa).
This object of focus, which purifies the afflictions, is to be understood by means of the supramundane path.
Therefore, he said that the object of focus is fourfold:
the pervasive object, the object for purifying conduct, the object for skillfulness, and the object for purifying afflictions.
(Śbh II 126)
In that regard, what is instruction?
Instruction is fourfold:
non-erroneous instruction, [unerring instruction, instruction that leads to the goal, and instruction that is timely].
Instruction on the gradual path,
instruction on the scriptures,
and instruction on realization.
In that regard, what is non-erroneous instruction?

It is when one teaches and causes another to grasp the Dharma and its meaning without error—that which is real and leads to the complete destruction of suffering and the making of an end to suffering.
This is called non-erroneous instruction.
What is gradual instruction? It is when one teaches the Dharma at the appropriate time,
first causing [the student] to grasp and recite the most fundamental points.
Thereafter, he instructs on the profound [truths]; or else, for the sake of the clear realization of the first truth, he instructs on that first of all,
and thereafter on the truths of origin, cessation, and the path.
One first instructs for the attainment of the first dhyāna,
and subsequently for the other dhyāna-attainments;
this should be understood as the type of instruction that follows a gradual sequence.
Therein, instruction based on scripture is that which has been received by him from the presence of his gurus, or from those who stand in the place of gurus— namely, masters of yoga, preceptors,
or the Tathāgata himself.
Or, in the same way, a disciple of the Tathāgata instructs others by means of this [scripture] without making it deficient or excessive;
this is called instruction based on scripture (*āgamāvavāda*).
Therein, instruction based on realization (*adhigamāvavāda*) is that by which those dharmas have been realized by him.
They have been touched and realized by one dwelling alone in seclusion;
likewise, for the sake of others' attainment.
He instructs for the sake of contact and realization;
this is called the instruction on attainment.
Furthermore, there is instruction that is complete in all its aspects. What, then, is that?
It is that which instructs by means of the three miracles.
By the miracle of supernatural power, by the miracle of mind-reading, and by the miracle of instruction.
By means of the miracle of supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*), he displays various kinds of supernormal domains and generates great respect for himself among others; thus,
having developed such respect, they lend an attentive ear.
In yoga, they become attentive with a sense of reverence.

Therein, having examined their mental conduct through the miracle of teaching (*deśanā-prātihārya*), [the teacher] instructs them through the miracle of instruction (*anuśāsti-prātihārya*) according to their faculties and according to their conduct.
He teaches the Dharma instruction according to the actual entry [into the path] and provides guidance regarding practice;
thus, this becomes an instruction complete in all aspects, subsumed within the three miracles.
In that regard, what is training?
It is said:
There are three trainings:
the training in higher ethics,
the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom.
In that regard, what is the training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*)? It is as follows: "He dwells possessed of ethical discipline," and so forth, in detail as previously described.

In that regard, the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*) is [the state] secluded from sensual desires, secluded from evil and unwholesome states, accompanied by applied thought (*savitarka*), and...
Having attained and dwelling in the first dhyāna— characterized by investigation, born of seclusion, and accompanied by joy and bliss— and so on up to the fourth dhyāna,
this is the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*).
Furthermore, all formless attainments (*ārūpya*) and other meditative absorptions (*samādhi-samāpatti*) are also called the training in higher mind.

Rather, by relying upon the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), the initial realization of the truths and the entry into the state of certainty (*nyāmāvakrānti*) occur; it is not possible at all without the meditative absorptions. Therefore, having designated the meditative absorptions as preeminent, they are called the "training in higher mind" (*adhicitta-śikṣā*).
In that context, the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajña-śikṣā*) is the knowledge of the four noble truths as they truly are.
For what reason are there exactly three trainings and not more than that? It is said:
for the purpose of establishing meditative concentration (*samādhi*), for the purpose of providing a basis for knowledge (*jñāna*), and for the purpose of performing what is to be done.
In that context, the training in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*) is for the purpose of establishing meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
for, by relying upon ethical discipline, one attains one-pointedness of mind, which is the concentration of the mind (*cittasamādhi*).
In that context, the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*) is for the purpose of providing a basis for knowledge (*jñāna*).
For thus, when the mind is concentrated, through one-pointed mindfulness, the vision of knowledge (*jñānadarśana*) proceeds toward the object of knowledge exactly as it is.
In that regard, the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*) has the sense of performing what is to be done;
for by means of perfectly pure vision of knowledge, one directly realizes the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
For this indeed is one's own welfare, this is the supreme task—namely, the abandonment of the afflictions; beyond that, there is nothing further to be done.
Therefore, there are only these three trainings.
What, then, is the sequence of these trainings?
For one whose ethical discipline is perfectly pure, there is freedom from remorse;
for one free from remorse, there is joy, gladness, pliancy, and happiness.

For one who is happy, there is concentration of mind; with a concentrated mind, one knows things as they truly are and sees them as they truly are. Knowing and seeing things as they truly are, one becomes disenchanted; being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate; being dispassionate, one is liberated.
Being liberated, one attains final nirvana without grasping.
Thus, these precepts, when cultivated, lead to the highest state— namely,
final nirvana without grasping.
This is the sequential order of these trainings.

In that regard, for what reason is the training in higher ethics called *adhiśīla*, and likewise the training in higher mind (*adhicitta*) and higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*)? It is because of the sense of "predominance" (*adhikāra*) and the sense of "superiority" (*adhika*).
In that regard, how is it by way of the sense of "pertaining to"?
That ethical discipline which pertains to the higher mind (*adhicitta*) is the training in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*);
that concentration of mind which pertains to higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*) is [the training in higher mind].
That is the training in higher mind;
the knowledge and vision directed toward the abandonment of the afflictions is the training in higher wisdom.
Thus it is by way of the sense of "superiority.
How is it by way of the sense of "predominance"?
The training in higher ethics, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom—these trainings exist in this very teaching alone.
They are uncommon [qualities] compared to outsiders;
thus, by way of their superior meaning.
Furthermore, there is training in higher mind that brings about training in higher wisdom, and there is training in higher wisdom that brings about training in higher mind.
For example, a noble disciple who has not yet attained the fundamental meditative absorptions (dhyāna).

The trainee who has seen the goal subsequently applies himself to the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation, and cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness, up to the factor of enlightenment that is equanimity.
This training in higher wisdom (adhiprajñā-śikṣā) brings about the training in higher mind (adhicitta-śikṣā);
furthermore, it has already been stated that the training in higher mind brings about the training in higher wisdom.
In this regard, there exists the training in higher ethical discipline (adhiśīla-śikṣā) which is not the training in higher mind.
It is not with higher wisdom;
there is training in higher ethics and higher mind, but not training in higher wisdom.
However, there is no training in higher wisdom that exists without training in higher ethics and higher mind;
therefore, wherever there is training in higher wisdom, it should be understood that all three trainings are present.
This, then, is the formal establishment of the trainings, in which the practitioner engaged in yoga should train.
In that regard, three types of persons realize the truths.
Which three? They are as follows:
There are those who are not free from passion, those who are largely free from passion,
and those who are entirely free from passion. Among these,
one who is not free from passion in every respect, while realizing the truths, becomes a stream-enterer simultaneously with that realization of the truths.

One who is largely free from passion, while again realizing the truths, becomes a once-returner through that realization of the truths. One who is free from passion, while realizing the truths, becomes a non-returner through that realization of the truths.
There are three faculties:
the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known.
How are these faculties established?
The establishment of the faculty "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) pertains to one who is engaged in the realization of the truths not yet realized.

The establishment of the faculty of knowledge (*ājñendriya*) pertains to the learner (*śaikṣa*) who has already realized them. The establishment of the faculty of one who has known (*ājñātāvīndriya*) pertains to the arhat who is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and has accomplished what was to be done.
There are three gateways to liberation;
namely, emptiness, the wishless, and the signless.
How is the establishment of these three gates of liberation (vimokṣamukha) effected?
It is said: these two are the conditioned (saṃskṛta) and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
In that regard, the conditioned consists of the five aggregates associated with the three realms;
the unconditioned, moreover, is nirvāṇa.
Both of these—namely, that which is conditioned and...
That which is called "unconditioned" exists;
furthermore, that which is called "self" or "sentient being" [also exists].
Whether it be a living soul (jīva) or a sentient being (jantu), this is non-existent.
In that regard, because one perceives defects and perceives the danger in conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta), there arises a lack of aspiration for them.

And because there is no aspiration toward it, the liberation door of wishlessness (apraṇihita) is established. Furthermore, for one who possesses aspiration toward that nirvāṇa, there arises an aspiration characterized by the vision of peace, the vision of excellence, and the vision of renunciation.
Furthermore, the signless door of liberation is established through the vision of escape.
In that regard, when something is non-existent and not found, there is neither aspiration nor non-aspiration.
For one who knows and sees that "just as it is non-existent, so it is non-existent," the door of liberation of emptiness is established.
In this way, there is the formal establishment of the three doors of liberation.
In this regard,
what are the factors conducive to training?
He said:
There are ten factors contrary to training;
as their antidotes, ten factors conducive to training should be understood.
In that regard, what are the ten factors contrary to training?
For example, a young woman of beautiful appearance who is alluring is an extreme obstacle and hindrance for a son of good family engaged in training; likewise,
there is attachment to the conditioned phenomena included within the view of a self-identity,
as well as indolence and laziness.

The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) based on substantial food (*kavaḍaṃkārāhāra*); sensual craving for tastes; and the desire, passion, and attachment toward the various, manifold, and diverse worldly tales and narratives—this is a corruption of the mental application associated with the contemplation of the Dharma.
Furthermore, what is that?
That is to say: doubt, uncertainty, and hesitation regarding the Jewels, or the Truths, or the aggregates, or the fruit of karma;

or, for one engaged in abandonment, the physical rigidity of one who is lax; or the mental attention that is a defilement of calm abiding and insight; or the overwhelming of the mind by sloth and torpor, which is a contraction of the mind.
For one whose vigor is over-exerted, there is physical fatigue and mental distress;
for one whose vigor is overly slack, there is the failure to attain distinction and the exhaustion of the side of wholesome qualities.
Or, through gain, fame, praise, or any mere fragment of pleasure, there arises delight and joy, agitation, lack of tranquility, exultation, and a state of being tossed about.
Terror and trepidation regarding nirvāṇa, which is the cessation of the view of a self-identity;
speaking in excess, and excessive chatter.
Even while speaking on a discourse concerning the Dharma, engaging in contentious debate;
the wandering of the mind and its distraction toward various objects previously seen, heard, or experienced—of many kinds and numerous varieties;
and the dwelling upon inconceivable matters.
These should be understood as the defilements of the mental application consisting in the yoga of reflecting on the Dharma:
namely, relishing the pleasure of meditative attainments (*dhyāna-samāpatti*),
and for one desiring to enter the signless (*ānimitta*), following after the signs of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-nimitta*).

When one is touched by bodily feelings that are painful, even unto those that take away life, there is the loss of control over life and the longing for life; and for one who follows after that longing, there is grieving and exhaustion.
Lamentation;
these are the ten factors that run counter to the training.
Which ten factors that are contrary to the precepts serve as antidotes and thus become conformable to the training? They are as follows:
the perception of foulness.
The perception of impermanence;
the perception of suffering in what is impermanent;
and the perception of non-self in what is suffering.
The perception of repulsiveness in food;
the perception of non-delight in the entire world; and the perception of light.
The perception of dispassion, the perception of cessation, and the perception of death.
Thus, these ten perceptions, when cultivated, developed, and practiced extensively, lead to the abandonment of the ten kinds of obstacles to training and the ten factors contrary to training.
In this regard, there is the light of the Dharma and the light of the meaning.
The light of calm abiding and the light of insight;
taking these lights as the dominant influence, there is the perception of light.
In this context, the intended meaning is that the mental applications of the yoga of reflecting on the Dharma are for the sake of abandoning obstacles.
In that regard, ten further factors conducive to training should be understood.
What are the ten? They are as follows: the prior cause.
Conformable instruction,
proper application,
and constant, respectful practice.
Intense aspiration,
the acquisition of the power of yoga,
and the subsiding of the coarseness of body and mind.
Frequent reflection,
lack of dejection,
and freedom from conceit.
In that regard, what is the prior cause?
It is the prior maturation of the faculties and the full acquisition of the faculties.
In this regard, "conformable instruction" is that instruction which is both non-erroneous and sequential.
In this regard, "appropriate application" is when one applies oneself exactly as one has been instructed.
Applying oneself in such a manner, one generates right view.

In that regard, constant and respectful practice is that mode of application by which one makes time fruitful through the side of wholesome qualities and swiftly accomplishes the side of wholesome qualities. In that regard,
intense aspiration is when one likewise generates a longing for further liberation.
“When shall I dwell having attained that sphere which the noble ones dwell in having attained?
In this regard, the application of the power of yoga is achieved through two causes:
by being naturally of sharp faculties, and...
And through familiarity with long-term practice,
there occurs therein the subsiding of the dysfunctions of body and mind; for just as dysfunctions of body and dysfunctions of mind arise in one whose body is exhausted and weary,
he causes them to subside by adopting a different posture.
Through excessive discursive thought (*vitarka*) and excessive discursive investigation (*vicāra*), there arises coarseness of body and mind;
this one pacifies by means of internal application to mental tranquility (*śamatha*).
Through contraction of the mind, sinking of the mind, and the obsession (*paryavasthāna*) of lethargy and sleep (*styānamiddha*), there arises coarseness of body and mind.
Through the insight into phenomena (*dharmavipaśyanā*) pertaining to higher wisdom and through a mental attention that inspires clarity, one brings about pliancy;
yet, for one whose afflictions have not been abandoned, the corruption of body and mind belonging to the side of the afflictions remains naturally unremoved.
That which is constantly adhering is thoroughly stilled through the cultivation of the correct path.
In that regard, frequent reflection means that one frequently reflects upon what has been ill-done and what has been well-done with respect to the ethical precepts.
He examines both what has not been done and what has been done;
he turns away from what is ill-done and from what was left undone, yet he does not turn back from what is well-done and from what was left undone.
He turns away from evil deeds already committed and does not turn back from good deeds already performed.
Likewise, making the mental attention that investigates whether the afflictions have been abandoned or not yet abandoned his primary focus, he repeatedly examines them.
In that regard, having known that [the afflictions] have been abandoned, one becomes joyful; however,
if one knows they have not been abandoned, one cultivates that very same path again and again,
remaining without despondency therein.
For one who does not know, does not see, and does not attain that which is to be known, seen, and attained after some time, mental distress arises—
a mental exhaustion, a mental affliction.
He does not tolerate that which has arisen but abandons it;
therein lies his lack of conceit.
He is without conceit regarding realization, attainment, and direct experience.
One who grasps without error,
perceiving what is attained as attained,
perceiving what is realized as realized, and perceiving what is directly witnessed as directly witnessed.
Thus, these ten dharmas, from the beginning, middle, and end, accord with the training of the yogin who desires to train; they do not oppose it.
Therefore, they are called "conducive to training."
In this regard, what is the failure of yoga?
It is said:
There are four failures of yoga.
What are the four?
There is a failure of yoga that is absolute.
There is that which is temporary; there is that which results from the loss of attainment;
and there is that which is produced by wrong practice.

In this regard, the ultimate failure in yoga should be understood as pertaining to persons who abide in the absence of lineage (*agotra*). For, because they possess the nature of not attaining final nirvana (*aparinirvāṇadharman*), they are indeed permanently fallen away from yoga.
Within that context, there is also the temporary [failure].
For example, those who abide in the lineage and possess the nature for parinirvāṇa, though lacking the necessary conditions,
will certainly encounter those conditions even after traveling far and wide; and having brought about application and cultivated it, they will attain parinirvāṇa.
Therefore, for them, this lapse from yoga is merely temporary.
In that regard, there is a lapse from yoga consisting in the loss of what has been attained;
as when certain individuals here fall away from the knowledge, vision, touch, and dwelling that they have already reached and realized.
In that regard, there is a failure in yoga caused by wrong practice.
For example, here a certain person, applying himself inappropriately (*ayoniśas*), does not succeed in yoga; he does not accomplish the righteous, wholesome Dharma.

For example, suppose here a certain person has many afflictions and is of a nature characterized by much passion, yet possesses keen consciousness and sharp intelligence, being endowed with innate discernment; he grasps what he has heard and masters what he has heard, whether it be little or much.
Or again, he dwells in the forest,
[welcoming] householders and renunciants who come to him,
who are upright.
He gratifies the minds of those who are upright by means of his teaching of the Dharma and by conduct associated with body and speech that is free from deceitful behavior;
through that causal state and that condition, gain, honor, and fame arise for him.
He becomes renowned and possessed of great merit; he becomes a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick; and he is honored and revered.
He was esteemed as an Arhat by kings, royal ministers, and even by caravan leaders.
His disciples,
both householders and those who have gone forth, follow after him.
When [his disciples] have followed after him, he incites greed in them and turns back for the sake of increasing their numbers.
It occurs to him:
"I have disciples."
If those householders and renunciants who have developed confidence in me, and who regard me as an Arhat, were to approach me and ask questions regarding yoga, mental attention, tranquility,
and insight, and if— when questioned— I were to answer them by saying "I do not know," then that confidence of theirs would be lost.
“May I not be one esteemed as an Arhat;
rather, let me establish the practice myself, having reflected, weighed, and examined it.
Taking this very purpose as his primary motive, being greedy for gain and honor, he goes alone into seclusion and, having himself reflected, weighed, and examined it, establishes the practice.
Furthermore, this practice of his does not descend into the Sūtras, nor is it seen in the Vinaya;
it contradicts the nature of reality (dharmatā).
As for those monks who are upholders of the Sūtras—
The holders of the Vinaya and the holders of the Mātṛkās conceal that basis of yoga from them and do not reveal it,
even to those who are his disciples.
There are householders and renunciants;
he also commands them for the sake of protecting their yoga.
For what reason?
"Lest those who uphold the Sūtras and those who uphold the Vinaya..."
Those who uphold the *mātṛkā*,
having heard this station of yoga, might attempt to reconcile it with the sūtras, yet it would not be found therein.
They might examine it in the Vinaya,
but it would not be found there;
they might investigate it by way of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).

"And that would contradict the nature of reality (dharmatā). On that account, they would become dissatisfied, and with their words of dissatisfaction, they would challenge me and give rise to legal disputes."
“Furthermore, in this way, I would not be honored or revered by kings, royal ministers, and so forth, up to wealthy men, guild-leaders, and caravan-merchants;
nor would I again be a recipient of the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal supplies for the sick.”

Making that very desire for gain and honor his primary motive, he perceives what is non-dharma as dharma; having set aside his true perception and inclination, he illuminates and proclaims non-dharma as dharma.
In this regard, those who follow his approval of views also come to perceive non-dharma as dharma due to their dullness.
Because of their delusion, they perceive what is non-Dharma as Dharma; even though they practice according to the instructions, they should be known as having entered upon a wrong course.
This kind of failure in yoga caused by wrong practice is indeed a semblance of the true Dharma that is actually non-Dharma, leading to the disappearance of the true Dharma.
Thus, these four failures in yoga must be fully understood and avoided by a meditating monk who practices yoga.
In that regard, what is yoga?
It is said:
Yoga is fourfold;
namely, faith, aspiration, vigor, and skillful means.
In this context, faith has two aspects and two bases: it has the aspect of conviction and the aspect of serene clarity;
its bases are the investigation of the reasoning of the Dharma and the resolute confidence in the power of the person.
Zeal (*chanda*) is also fourfold;
namely, for the sake of attainment, as when someone here generates a longing for higher liberations,
in detail as previously described.

For the sake of inquiry, just as someone here might conceive a desire to go to a monastery to hear what has not been heard and to purify what has been heard in the presence of wise fellow-celibates who understand yoga.
Aspiration for the full attainment of the accumulations is as follows: here, a certain person [aspires] for the complete purity of the restraint of ethical discipline,
for the complete purity of the restraint of the sense faculties, and for moderation in eating.
He generates an ever-increasing aspiration for the application of wakefulness and for dwelling in clear comprehension;

he generates zeal, longing, and the desire to act for the sake of such application, just as someone here might generate an aspiration, longing, and the desire to act toward the cultivation of the path through continuous application and respectful application.
Thus, this fourfold zeal consists of:
namely, for the sake of attainment, for the sake of inquiry, for the sake of the accumulation of provisions, and for the sake of application.
In that regard, diligence is also fourfold; namely, for the sake of hearing, and for the sake of reflecting, (Śbh II 154) ... [and so forth].
For the sake of cultivation and for the complete purification of hindrances;
therein, diligence is for the purpose of hearing.
The mental enthusiasm of one who hears what has not been heard before and brings it to complete purification.
It is the state of non-laxity in application;
that is, while one is alone in seclusion, reflecting upon, weighing, and examining the meaning of the teachings exactly as they have been heard.

Thus, for one who has entered into seclusion and cultivates tranquility and insight from time to time; and thus, for one who is devoted day and night to purifying the mind of the hindrances through walking and sitting,
whatever mental enthusiasm there may be—
The state of not relinquishing application.
In that regard, the means are also fourfold:

namely, having made the restraint of ethical discipline and the restraint of the sense faculties the foundation, there is the state of well-established mindfulness; and for one whose mindfulness is thus established, there is heedfulness, which is the guarding of the mind and the cultivation of wholesome qualities.
Likewise, for one who is heedful, there is the application of mental tranquility internally and the insight into phenomena regarding higher wisdom.
And this yoga is fourfold;
it becomes sixteen-fold in its aspects.

Therein, through faith, one has full conviction regarding the goal to be attained. Because of that conviction in attainment, one generates the desire to act toward wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*).
Desiring to act in this way, one dwells devotedly engaged day and night.
He is energetic and possesses firm prowess;

and that vigor, when embraced by skillful means, leads to the attainment of what has not been attained, to the realization of what has not been realized, and to the direct realization of what has not been directly realized.
Therefore, these four factors are called "yoga."
In this regard, what is mental attention?
There are four types of mental attention.
Which four? Namely:
that which operates with effort, and that which operates with interruption.
It is characterized by uninterrupted flow and effortless flow.
In that regard, what is mental attention driven by force (*balavāhana-manaskāra*)?
It is as follows: for a beginner who is merely placing and settling the mind within and discerning phenomena, until such time as he attains [spontaneous] mental attention.
At that time, his mental application is forceful;
having constrained that mind by force, he establishes it in one-pointedness.
Therefore, it is called "forceful application."
In that context, what is the mental application characterized by interrupted flow?

It is the mental application that experiences the characteristics [of the object] belonging to one who, having already attained mental application, proceeds thereafter by means of either the mundane or the supramundane path;
for in that state, meditative concentration is intermingled with discursive thought.
It does not proceed exclusively by way of the mode of cultivation.

In that regard, what is the mental engagement that functions without interruption? It is that which follows after the mental engagement consisting of the discernment of characteristics, up to the mental engagement consisting of the culmination of application.
In that regard, what is the mental engagement that proceeds without effort?
It is the mental engagement that is the fruit of the culmination of application (*prayoganiṣṭhāphala*).
There are four other types of mental attention, namely:
the conformable, the counteractive, and so forth.
It is to be clarified and to be examined;
therein lies the conformable mental attention.
That by which one reviles the object of focus and undertakes correct application,
yet does not abandon the afflictions,
is therein the counteractive [concentration].
That by which one abandons the afflictions is the "inspiring" [sign]. That by which one gladdens, exhilarates, and uplifts the sunken mind through signs that are uplifting is the "uplifting" [sign].
In that regard, there is the mental application of investigation;
namely, the mental application of examination, by taking which as its dominant influence one investigates whether the afflictions have been abandoned or not yet abandoned.
In that regard, for one who attends to the object of focus, how many signs (nimitta) are there to be attended to?
He replied: Four.
Namely: the sign of the object, the sign of the cause, the sign to be avoided, and the sign to be cultivated.
Therein, the sign of the object is that reflected image or appearance which is a counterpart to the knowable thing.
In that regard, the causal sign (*nidānanimitta*) is as follows:
the accumulation of the equipment for meditative concentration (*samādhi-saṃbhāra-upacaya*) and what is concordant with it (*ānulomika*).
Instruction; intense aspiration accompanied by cultivation; a sense of spiritual urgency regarding those phenomena that provoke urgency;
attentiveness consisting in the thorough knowledge of distraction and non-distraction;
and freedom from external interference, whether caused by humans or non-humans, by sounds or by physical exertion.
Likewise, inner concentration of the mind preceded by insight is the causal sign for a subsequent, more intense insight;
likewise, insight preceded by serenity is the causal sign for a subsequent, more intense serenity.
In that regard, there are four kinds of signs to be avoided,
namely: the sign of laxity, the sign of agitation, the sign of attachment, and the sign of distraction.
In that context, the sign of laxity is that sign of the object and sign of the cause by which the mind tends toward laxity. In that context, the sign of agitation is as follows:
That objective sign and causal sign by which the mind becomes agitated is the sign of attachment;
that objective sign and causal sign by which the mind becomes attached to, intensely enamored with, and defiled by the object is [the sign of attachment].
In that regard, the cause of distraction is that sign of the object and that causal sign by which the mind is distracted outwardly;
furthermore, those signs are as described in the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhitā bhūmi*).
For one who resolves upon the object through these mental orientations (*manaskāra*), how many types of resolve (*adhimokṣa*) arise?
He replied:
"There are nine resolves."
Namely: luminous and non-luminous, dull and sharp, limited, extensive, immeasurable, pure, and impure.
Among these, the luminous is resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*).
When the sign of light has been well-grasped, there is a resolve accompanied by light;
therein, it is non-luminous resolve. For example, when the sign of light is not grasped, it is accompanied by darkness.
In that regard, dull resolve is that which falls within the continuum of those with dull faculties; therein,
sharp resolve is [the opposite].
That which falls within the continuum of those with sharp faculties; therein, resolve is limited—
that which is accompanied by limited faith and aspiration, and has a limited object.
Thus, due to the limited nature of mental attention and the limited nature of the object, there is limited resolve (*adhimokṣa*).
In that context, there is extensive resolve (*mahadgata-adhimokṣa*),
such as that which is accompanied by extensive faith and aspiration.
It is that resolve which is resolved upon a vast object;
thus, through the vastness of the mental attention and the vastness of the object, it is a vast resolve. Among these, there is immeasurable resolve.
It is that resolve which, accompanied by immeasurable faith and aspiration,
is directed toward an object that is infinite or boundless;
thus, it is called "immeasurable resolve" both because of the immeasurability of its mental attention and the immeasurability of its object.
In this regard, resolute belief (*adhimokṣa*) is pure when it is well-cultivated,
fully accomplished, and has reached its consummation;
it is impure, however, when it is not well-cultivated, not fully accomplished, and has not reached its consummation.
In that regard, how many are the duties to be performed by one in yoga?
He said:
There are four.
Which four? They are as follows:
the cessation of the basis, and so forth.
The transformation of the basis,
the thorough knowledge of the object, and delight in the object.

In that regard, the cessation of the basis (*āśrayanirodha*) is as follows: for one who is devoted to the cultivation of preparatory mental attention (*prayogamanasikāra*), that basis which is accompanied by functional rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*) is gradually ceased, and the basis accompanied by pliancy (*prasrabdhi*) undergoes transformation.
This is the cessation of the basis; this is the transformation of the basis, which is the task to be accomplished through yoga.
In this regard, there is the thorough knowledge of the object and delight in the object.

There is a thorough knowledge of the object and delight in the object that is preceded by the cessation and transformation of the basis; and it is by taking that thorough knowledge of the object and delight in the object as the dominant condition that the basis ceases and is transformed.

There is the thorough knowledge of the object, delight in the object, and— preceded by the purification of the basis and having the purification of the basis as its dominant influence— the extremely pure knowledge of the object and delight at the time of the accomplishment of the task.
Therefore, it is said that there are four things to be performed for yoga.
In that regard, how many types of practitioners of yoga (yogācāra) are there? He replied:
There are three: namely, the beginner, the one who has practiced, and [the one who has attained mastery].

And there is the one who has transcended mental attention (*atikrāntamanaskāra*). In this regard, the beginner practitioner of yoga (*yogācāra*) is either a beginner in mental attention or a beginner in the purification of afflictions. Among these, the beginner in mental attention is one who is engaged in their first practice; as long as they have not attained mental attention, they do not touch upon one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*).
In that regard, the beginner in the purification of afflictions is as follows:

even when mental attention has been attained, for one who desires to purify the mind of affliction, the undertaking, the grasping, and the repeated practice of the mental attention that experiences characteristics is what constitutes the beginner in the purification of afflictions.
In this context, what is "one who has practiced" (*kṛtaparicaya*)?

Setting aside the attention consisting of the discernment of characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*), one becomes "one who has practiced" with respect to the other six types of attention, ending with that which culminates in application (*prayoganiṣṭha*).
Therein, "one who has transcended attention" (*atikrāntamanaskāra*) should be understood as referring to the attention that is the fruit of the culmination of application (*prayoganiṣṭhāphala*).
He has transcended the mental attention of the cultivation of application and abides in the fruit of cultivation;
therefore, he is said to have "transcended mental attention."

Moreover, one who applies themselves by relying on a wholesome desire for the Dharma is an "beginner" as long as they have not yet produced the roots of goodness conducive to penetration— namely, the levels of heat (*uṣmagata*) and the summits (*mūrdhan*). However, when they produce the roots of goodness conducive to penetration, such as the levels of heat and the summits, [they are no longer a beginner].
The patiences that conform to the truths and the worldly supreme dharmas constitute his stage of practiced familiarity.

When, moreover, he enters the certainty of rightness, realizes the truths, and becomes independent of others and not led by another within the Teacher’s dispensation, [he attains the state of a stream-enterer].
At that time, one has transcended mental attention (*atikrāntamanaskāra*).
Having transcended mental attention that relies on another, one abides in that which does not rely on another;
therefore, it is called "transcending mental attention."
In that regard, what is the cultivation of yoga? It is said:
It is twofold:
namely, the cultivation of perception and the cultivation of the factors conducive to enlightenment.
Among these, what is the cultivation of perception?
For example, one engaged in the mundane path cultivates the perception of disadvantage regarding all lower stages.

Or again, one engaged for the sake of nirvāṇa perceives peace in the element of abandonment, the element of dispassion, and the element of cessation, and cultivates the perception of abandonment, the perception of dispassion, and the perception of cessation.
Or again, one engaged in tranquility cultivates the perception of above and below belonging to the side of tranquility.
One engaged in insight cultivation subsequently cultivates the perception of "before" and "after" belonging to the side of insight cultivation.

Therein, one who perceives above and below contemplates this very body, exactly as it is and exactly as it is disposed—extending from the soles of the feet upward and from the hair of the head downward—filled with various kinds of impurities: "In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs," and so on, as before.
Therein, one who perceives the posterior and the anterior [contemplates]: "In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs," and so on, as before.

For example, suppose a certain person has properly, thoroughly, and well-grasped the sign of contemplation itself; has well-attended to it, well-cultivated it, and well-penetrated it— just as one standing contemplates one sitting,
or one sitting contemplates one lying down.
Or, walking behind, one observes someone walking ahead.

This indeed elucidates the observation through the mode of insight (*vipaśyanā*) regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that have arisen dependently (*pratītyasamutpanna*) throughout the three times.

In that regard, as for what was said, "standing, one observes one who is sitting," this elucidates that by means of present mental attention (*manaskāra*), one observes a knowable object (*jñeya*) belonging to the future.
Even though it is a present state of mental attention (*manaskāra*), when it has arisen, it is called "standing.
