Furthermore, the future state of the object of knowledge (*jñeyāvasthā*) is called "seated" because it has not yet arisen and is oriented toward arising.

Furthermore, as for the statement, “or, seated, he reflects upon what is lying down,” by this is illustrated the reflection upon a past object of knowledge (*jñeya*) by means of a present mental attention (*manaskāra*). For the present state of mental attention, being oriented toward cessation, is called “seated”;
whereas the past state of the object of knowledge, because it has already ceased, is called “lying down.”

Furthermore, as for the statement, "or, walking behind, one examines [the one] walking ahead," by this it is illustrated that there is an examination of the mental attention that has just ceased by means of the present mental attention.
In that context, the mental attention that has arisen and arisen and has just ceased is what "walks ahead."

In this regard, that mental attention which has arisen immediately after [the preceding one], arising anew as each new moment, and which grasps each immediately preceding ceased [moment of attention], is the "follower.
Therein, while cultivating both calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), one cultivates the perception of light belonging to both sides;
this is the cultivation of perception (*saṃjñābhāvanā*).
In that regard, what is the cultivation of the factors conducive to awakening?

It is the repeated practice, familiarity, cultivation, development, and frequent application of the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening; this is called the cultivation of the factors conducive to awakening.
For example, [the cultivation] of the four foundations of mindfulness...
Of the four right endeavors and the four bases of psychic power.
Of the five faculties,
the five powers,
and the seven factors of enlightenment.
Of the noble eightfold path;
of the application of mindfulness to the body, and the applications of mindfulness to feelings, mind, and phenomena;
and of the right exertions, which consist in generating desire, striving, initiating vigor, uplifting the mind, and applying effort for the non-arising of unarisen evil and unwholesome states.
For the abandoning of evil, unwholesome states that have arisen;
for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen;
and for the stability, non-confusion, cultivation, fulfillment, increase, growth, and expansion of wholesome states that have already arisen.
"One generates desire, exerts oneself, arouses energy, uplifts the mind, and strives"— this refers to the right exertions (*samyakprahāṇa*).

[It also refers to] the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) endowed with the formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*) and the concentration of desire, and the bases of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of abandonment and the concentrations of energy, mind, and investigation.
Of the faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom;
of the powers of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom;
and of the factors of enlightenment consisting of mindfulness, the investigation of phenomena, energy, joy, pliancy, concentration, and equanimity.
Of right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
In that regard, what is the body?
What is the contemplation of the body within the body?
What is mindfulness?
What are the applications of mindfulness? He said:
the body is of thirty-five kinds.
Namely: internal and external;
comprised of sense faculties and not comprised of sense faculties;
reckoned as sentient beings and not reckoned as sentient beings.
Accompanied by depravity and accompanied by pliancy;
the primary element body and the derivative element body;
the name-body and the form-body.
Whether belonging to the hells, to the animal realm, to the domain of the ancestors, to the human world, or to the divine realms;
whether possessed of consciousness or devoid of consciousness; whether the internal body or the external body.
The transformed and the untransformed;
the female body, the male body, and the neuter body; and the body of a friend, the body of an enemy, and the body of a neutral person.
The inferior body, the middling body, and the excellent body;
the body of childhood, the body of youth, and the body of old age— this, for now, is the classification of the body.
In this regard, contemplation is threefold: that which, having made the body its primary object, is wisdom consisting of hearing, wisdom consisting of reflection, or wisdom consisting of cultivation;
by means of which wisdom one correctly examines, investigates, penetrates, and realizes the entire body in all its aspects.

In that regard, mindfulness is the non-forgetting of the mind with respect to the syllables, the meaning, and the realization— namely, those phenomena which have been grasped by taking the body as the dominant influence, the meaning of those very phenomena which has been reflected upon, and those which have been directly realized through cultivation—
thinking, "These phenomena have been well-grasped by me."
“No indeed,” or “they have been well-characterized here and there by wisdom,” or “no indeed.”
“Having been well-touched by liberation in each respective case,” the mindfulness [that thinks] “it is not so” becomes present.
This is the application of mindfulness.
Moreover, the application of mindfulness is for the sake of guarding mindfulness, for the sake of non-affliction regarding sense objects, and for the sake of binding [the mind] to the focal object.
Among these, guarding mindfulness is as previously stated: "One becomes one whose mindfulness is guarded, one whose mindfulness is constant.
Regarding that which is for the sake of non-affliction regarding sense objects:

As it has been said: "One whose mind is guarded by mindfulness acts with equanimity; one does not grasp at signs (*nimitta*) nor grasp at secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*)," and so on in detail, until: "one guards the faculty of the mind and achieves restraint through the faculty of the mind.
In that context, it is for the purpose of binding [the mind] to the object of focus (*ālambana*).
As it has been said: for one who binds mindfulness to the fourfold object—
namely, the pervasive object, the object for purifying conduct, the object for skillfulness, or the object for purifying afflictions—
that state of well-established mindfulness which exists through these three modes [is what is meant].
This is called the application of mindfulness.
In that regard, what is feeling?
It is as follows: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Among these, there is pleasant feeling of the body, painful feeling of the body, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling of the body.
Just as it is with the bodily, so it is with the mental;
that is, whether it be pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, it may be accompanied by worldly attachment.
In this way, there are feelings— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— that are either free from worldly attachment, or based on craving, or based on renunciation.
This very sensation is of twenty-one kinds, or else of nine kinds.
Therein, what is mind (*citta*)? It is as follows:
mind with attachment, mind free from attachment; mind with aversion, mind free from aversion; mind with delusion, mind free from delusion; and contracted mind.

The distracted mind, the sluggish mind, the over-exerted mind, the agitated mind, the unagitated mind, the tranquilized mind, the untranquilized mind, the concentrated mind, the unconcentrated mind, the well-cultivated mind, the uncultivated mind, the well-liberated mind, and the ill-liberated mind— summarizing these, there are twenty kinds of mind.
In this context, what are the phenomena?
They are passion and the subduing of passion.
Hatred and the subduing of hatred; delusion and the subduing of delusion; contraction and distraction; laxity and exertion; agitation and non-agitation; tranquility and non-tranquility.
There is well-composedness and not-well-composedness, well-cultivatedness of the path and not-well-cultivatedness of the path, and well-liberatedness and not-well-liberatedness.
Thus, these twenty factors established in the dark and light sides should be understood as belonging to the categories of affliction and purification.
In that regard, pleasant feeling is that which arises in dependence upon a contact to be experienced as pleasant; it is a felt experience, a sensation, belonging to the category of feeling.
Furthermore, that which is associated with the five consciousnesses is bodily, while that which is associated with the mental consciousness is mental.

Just as with that which is to be experienced as pleasant, so too, in dependence upon contact to be experienced as painful or to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, there arises a feeling that is neither agreeable nor disagreeable, which belongs to the category of feeling.
This is called painful and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Furthermore, that which is associated with the five groups of sensory consciousness is bodily.
That which is associated with mental consciousness is mental.

That which is conducive to nirvāṇa, penetrative, and leads to the ultimate goal, the ultimate purity, and the ultimate consummation of the holy life—that is disinterested. Furthermore, that which falls within the realms and falls within existence—that is interested.
Furthermore, that which is associated with the realms of form and formlessness, or which is conducive to dispassion, is based on renunciation;
whereas that which is associated with the realm of desire and is not conducive to dispassion is based on attachment.
In this context, a mind with lust is one that is obsessed by lust toward an object that incites lust;
a mind free from lust is one that is devoid of such obsession by lust.
That which is accompanied by hatred is that which is obsessed with hatred toward an object that incites hatred;
that which is free from hatred is that which is devoid of such obsession with hatred.
Among these, that which is characterized by delusion is that which is obsessed with delusion toward an object that incites delusion.
That which is free from delusion is that which is devoid of the obsession of delusion. These six states of mind should be understood as being associated with the course [of practice].
Among them, three belong to the side of affliction and three are the antidotes to affliction.

In that context, "contracted mind" is that which is bound to an internal object by way of the aspect of calm abiding (*śamatha*). "Distracted mind" is that which has wandered outward among the five strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*).
Therein, "sunk mind" is that which is accompanied by lethargy and drowsiness (*styānamiddha*).
The uplifted mind is that which has been gladdened by a pleasing object of focus. The agitated mind is that which, due to excessive exertion, is possessed by the obsession of agitation.
The non-agitated mind is that which has attained equanimity both at the time of exertion and at the time of withdrawal.

In that context, the "calmed" mind is that which is liberated from the hindrances; the "uncalmed" mind, on the other hand, is that which is not liberated. Therein, the "concentrated" mind is that which, through liberation from the hindrances, has entered the fundamental dhyānas.
That which has not entered [meditative absorption] is "unconcentrated.

In that regard, a well-cultivated mind is one that, through long-term familiarity with that very concentration, becomes capable of attaining it at will, attains it without difficulty, and achieves it swiftly. A poorly cultivated mind should be understood as the opposite of this.
In this context, the "well-liberated mind" is that which is liberated from everything and absolutely;
the "not well-liberated mind" is that which is neither liberated from everything nor absolutely liberated.
Thus, these fourteen states of mind are to be understood as pertaining to the stages of abiding.
Among them, beginning from the stage of purification from the hindrances (*nivaraṇaviśuddhibhūmi*), there are eight states of mind pertaining to abiding:
the contracted, the distracted, and so forth, up to the tranquilized and the untranquilized.

Furthermore, with respect to the purification of the afflictions (*kleśaviśuddhi*), there are six states of mind pertaining to the dwellings (*vihāra*), ranging from "the mind is well-liberated" to "the mind is not well-liberated. Moreover, when an internal hindrance (*nivaraṇa*) exists, one knows: "I have a hindrance."
When an hindrance is absent, he knows, "There is no hindrance in me.
He also understands how the arising of an unarisen hindrance occurs, and he also understands how the disappearance of an arisen hindrance occurs.

In that regard, when there is a fetter of the eye up to a fetter of the mind, he understands: "I have [a fetter] up to a fetter of the mind"; when there is no [fetter] up to a fetter of the mind, he understands: "I do not have [a fetter] up to a fetter of the mind.
Furthermore, he understands how the arising of a [fetter] up to a fetter of the mind occurs when it has not yet arisen.
He also understands how that which has arisen ceases:
when the factor of awakening of mindfulness is present within him, he understands, "The factor of awakening of mindfulness exists in me";
when it is absent, he understands, "It does not exist in me."
He also understands how the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness arises when it has not yet arisen;
and he also understands how, once arisen, it remains stable, is not forgotten, and reaches fulfillment through cultivation, as well as its further increase, growth, and expansion.

Just as it is with the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness, so too should the factors of enlightenment that are the investigation of phenomena, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity be understood.
This thorough knowledge of defiled phenomena by way of their intrinsic nature, cause, disadvantage, and antidote is the body of the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).

Just as the application of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body within the body has been explained, so too should it be understood, as appropriate, for feelings, the mind, and phenomena.
In that regard, how does one dwell contemplating the body within the body?
How [does one dwell] externally?
How is it "internal and external"?
When one dwells contemplating the body in the body internally, that is, within one's own individual body which is reckoned as a sentient being,
in this way one dwells contemplating the body in the body internally.
When one takes as an object external form not reckoned as a sentient being,
in this way one dwells contemplating the body in the external body.
When one takes as an object external form belonging to another that is reckoned as a sentient being, [in this way one dwells contemplating the body in the external body].
In this way, he dwells contemplating the body in the body internally and externally.

Therein, having taken as his object the feelings, mind, and phenomena that have arisen based on internal form— whether pertaining to himself or categorized as belonging to sentient beings— he dwells contemplating feelings, mind, and phenomena within internal feelings, mind, and phenomena.
Taking as an object those feelings, mind, and phenomena that have arisen based on external form not reckoned as a sentient being, one dwells contemplating phenomena in relation to external feeling,

mind, and phenomena. Taking as an object those feelings, mind, and phenomena that have arisen based on external form reckoned as a sentient being, one dwells contemplating phenomena in relation to internal-and-external feeling, mind, and phenomena.
He dwells contemplating phenomena.
There is another formulation:
taking as an object form comprised by the sense faculties, one dwells contemplating the body within the body;
taking as an object form not comprised by the sense faculties—unapproached and unappropriated—one dwells contemplating the body externally with respect to the body.

Taking as an object only that form which is not comprised within the sense faculties—form that has been approached and appropriated—one dwells contemplating the body in the body internally and externally.

In the same way, it should be understood that having first taken the threefold form as a basis, one dwells seeing accordingly by taking as objects the feelings, mind, and phenomena that have arisen, as appropriate.
There is another formulation:

when one takes as an object the form belonging to the stage of meditative concentration that is accompanied by pliancy, in this way one dwells contemplating the body within the body. When one takes as an object one's own internal form belonging to the stage not of meditative concentration that is accompanied by coarseness, in this way one dwells contemplating the body externally in the body.

Taking as an object external form that is accompanied by both coarseness (*dauṣṭhulya*) and pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), one dwells contemplating the body in the internal and external body; in the same way, it should be understood accordingly for the feelings, mind, and phenomena that have arisen based upon that [body].
Another formulation:
taking internal derivative form as his object, he dwells contemplating the body in the body internally;
taking external derivative form as his object, he dwells contemplating the body in the body externally.

And taking as an object that derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) which has arisen depending on that primary matter (*bhūtarūpa*), and which is comprised of the sense faculties and their objects, one dwells contemplating the body in the internal and external body.
In the same way, it should be understood accordingly that whatever feelings, mind, and phenomena have arisen depending on that [body] are also to be treated similarly.
There is another formulation:
when one takes as an object the internal body together with consciousness, one dwells contemplating the body in the body internally;
when one takes as an object the insentient form belonging to the category of sentient beings in states such as the livid-blue and so forth, one dwells contemplating the body in the body externally.

Taking as his object the state of having consciousness in form that was previously without consciousness during the past time, and the state of being without consciousness in form that will be present in the future time— the commonality of dharma, the equality of dharma— he dwells contemplating the body in the internal and external body.
In the same way, one should understand accordingly those feelings, mind, and dharmas that have arisen based upon that [body].
There is another formulation:
taking as an object the internal body of oneself through its forms such as hair, body hair, nails, and so forth, one dwells contemplating the body in the internal body;
taking as an object the internal body of others through its forms such as hair, body hair, nails, and so forth, one dwells contemplating the body in the external body.
Taking as his object the external body of himself— unaltered by such forms as bluish discoloration (*vinīlaka*) and so forth—

and the external body of others, both altered and unaltered by such forms as bluish discoloration and so forth, he dwells contemplating the body in the internal and external body by way of their commonality of nature (*tulyadharmatā*). Based on that, whatever feelings, mind, and phenomena have arisen should also be understood accordingly.
In this manner, many such categories should be understood through the distinctions of body, sensation, mind, and phenomena;
however, only these few categories have been fully elucidated here.

In that regard, as an antidote to the four perversions (*viparyāsa*), the Blessed One established the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). Among these, the foundation of mindfulness of the body was established as the antidote to the perversion of perceiving the impure as pure.
For it is in the cultivation of the foundation of mindfulness of the body that the Blessed One taught the four charnel ground contemplations (*śivapathikā*) associated with the foul (*aśubhā*).
For one who frequently and attentively contemplates this,
the perversion of perceiving the impure as pure is abandoned;
therein, the application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*) is established as the antidote to the perversion of perceiving suffering as pleasure.

Dwelling in the observation of feelings within feelings, one understands as it truly is: "Whatever is felt, that is here [included] in suffering. In this way, the perversion that perceives pleasure in what is suffering is abandoned for him.
Therein, the application of mindfulness of the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*) is established as the antidote to the perversion of perceiving permanence in what is impermanent.

By means of the distinctions of his mind— such as being with passion and so forth— and by perceiving the manifoldness and various diverse modes of that mind throughout the passing of various nights and days, moments, instants, and brief intervals, the perversion that perceives the impermanent as permanent is abandoned.
In that regard, the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is established as the antidote to the perversion of perceiving a self in what is not-self.

Because those afflictions such as the view of self exist in him, and because those wholesome factors such as the view of non-self do not exist in him, there arises the perception of a self in the aggregates;
this does not occur for another who, observing phenomena according to their specific and general characteristics, perceives phenomena as they truly are.
That misconception which consists in taking what is not-self to be self is abandoned.
Another formulation:
for generally the world functions in this way—
failing to understand, as it truly is, that within the aggregates there are merely aggregates and merely phenomena— [thinking] "it is dependent upon the body."
"Since I experience pleasure and pain based upon it,
and am defiled and purified by means of dharma and adharma,
the application of mindfulness to the body (kāyasmṛtyupasthāna) is established in order to remove delusion regarding the objective basis that serves as the support for the self."
The foundation of mindfulness of feeling (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*) was established for the purpose of removing delusion regarding the object of experience of that very self.

Furthermore, the foundation of mindfulness of mind (*citta-smṛtyupasthāna*) was established for the purpose of removing delusion regarding the object of the self, wherein you are deluded by grasping at a self within the mind, the intellect, and consciousness.

And the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*) was established for the purpose of removing delusion regarding the objects of the defilement and purification of that very mind.
Another formulation:
and where one performs an action, (Śbh II 198) [that is the basis].
That for whose sake one acts, that which performs the action, and that by means of which one acts—

Having condensed all that together into one, the four foundations of mindfulness are established; therein, one applies [mindfulness] to the body for the sake of feeling, and to the mind with regard to wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.
There is another formulation:

where one is defiled and purified, from what [cause], who [the agent], and by what means one is defiled and purified— condensing all these into one, the four foundations of mindfulness are established.
In that regard, the body is defiled and purified; by means of feelings, the mind is defiled and purified; and by means of phenomena, [the mind] is defiled and purified.
Regarding this, what is the meaning of "application of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*)?
It is said:
That wherein one establishes mindfulness and that by which one establishes mindfulness is called the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
That wherein one establishes mindfulness is the application of mindfulness as object (*ālambana-smṛtyupasthāna*).
That by which one establishes mindfulness—namely, the wisdom and the mindfulness therein that comprise concentration—is the application of mindfulness as intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-smṛtyupasthāna*).
Other mental states and mental factors associated with that [foundation of mindfulness] are the foundation of mindfulness by association (*saṃsarga-smṛtyupasthāna*).

Furthermore, whatever wholesome path—whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*)—has arisen having the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena as its dominant influence, that is the foundation of mindfulness.
Moreover, it consists of that which is produced from hearing (*śrutamaya*), reflection (*cintāmaya*), and cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*).
Among these, that which consists of hearing and reflection is exclusively with outflows;
that which consists of cultivation may be either with outflows or without outflows.

Having thus cultivated proficiency in the four foundations of mindfulness, having removed the most gross forms of perversion, and having attained direct knowledge of wholesome and unwholesome phenomena,
he immediately thereafter [exerts himself] for the non-arising of unarisen evil and unwholesome phenomena.
"For the abandoning of arisen [unwholesome states],
for the arising of unarisen wholesome states,
and for the stabilization of those that have arisen," and so on in detail as before, up until he exerts and applies his mind.
In that regard, what are the evil, unwholesome dharmas?
They are the defiled bodily, vocal, and mental actions belonging to the desire realm, which are comprised within the misconduct of body, speech, and mind;
and those afflictions that give rise to them, whether they are currently non-associated, not manifest, or have not yet arisen.
Those which are present and have become manifest are "arisen.

In that regard, wholesome factors (*kuśala-dharma*) are those factors which are their opposites—namely, the opposites of misconduct, the opposites of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), or the opposites of the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
These too should be understood as unarisen or arisen in the same manner as the evil, unwholesome factors.

In that regard, when one generates a longing and makes a vow for the non-arising of unarisen evil and unwholesome states, thinking, "I shall not allow them to arise in any way whatsoever," one thus generates desire. Or again, regarding those [states] that have already arisen and are present, one thinks, "I shall not tolerate them in any way whatsoever; I shall abandon them and dispel them."
When, regarding evil and unwholesome states that have not yet arisen, one first generates a longing for their non-arising, makes an aspiration for them, and does not wish to tolerate them—
this is the desire for the non-arising of those [states] that have not yet arisen.
Or, that one does not tolerate arisen [unwholesome states] but abandons them— this is the desire for the abandonment of those that have arisen.

Furthermore, those evil, unwholesome states arise either with a past object as their basis, or with a future object as their basis, or with a present objective field as their basis; they consist of those having a hidden objective field as their basis and those having a manifest objective field as their basis.
Those which have past or future objects as their basis are those having a hidden objective field as their basis.
Those which have present objects as their objective support have perceptible objects as their objective support.
Therein, he exerts himself for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states that have as their object a hidden domain, and for the abandonment of those that have already arisen;
furthermore, he arouses vigor for the non-arising of unarisen [evil, unwholesome states] and for the abandonment of those that have already arisen which have as their object a manifest domain.
For it is through their very firm exertion of vigor that there occurs either non-arising or abandonment.
Moreover, he exerts himself so that weak and middling outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) do not arise when unarisen, and so that they are abandoned when already arisen.
He exerts vigor for the non-arising of unarisen intense outbursts and for the abandonment of those already arisen;
if he courses in relation to a past object, [he does so].
He practices in such a way that no affliction arises in him on account of that object.
However, if it should arise through a lapse of mindfulness, he does not tolerate it, but abandons it, dispels it, and brings it to an end.
Just as it should be understood regarding a past object, so it should be understood regarding a future one as well.
(Śbh II 204) Thus, he is said to "exert himself" for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states, and for the abandoning of those that have arisen.
If he proceeds with respect to a present object,
he proceeds in such a way that no affliction arises by means of that object.
If, however, through a lapse of mindfulness they arise, he does not tolerate what has arisen, but abandons it, dispels it, and brings it to an end;
thus, for the sake of the non-arising of unarisen evil and unwholesome states, and for the abandonment of those that have arisen, it is said that "he exerts vigor."

There are evil, unwholesome states that arise through the power of conceptualization and not by the power of the sense objects; there are those that arise both by the power of conceptualization and by the power of the sense objects.
Among these, those that arise through the power of conceptualization and not by the power of the sense objects—
For example, while one is dwelling [in meditation], those [thoughts] that arise by taking the past or future as their object arise there through the power of volition and the power of the object;
whereas, while one is moving about, they arise with the present as their object.
In that case, improper mental construction necessarily occurs.

In that regard, he exerts himself for the non-arising of those thoughts that arise through the power of conceptualization which have not yet arisen, and for the abandonment of those that have already arisen.
Furthermore, regarding those thoughts that arise through both the power of sensory objects and the power of conceptualization, he exerts himself for their non-arising when they have not yet arisen.
And he exerts energy for the abandoning of those [unwholesome states] that have arisen.

In this regard, "he generates desire for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen" means that he conceives a longing and directs his mind toward the acquisition and manifestation of those wholesome states which have not yet been attained and are not currently present.
An intense desire to acquire and a desire to bring them into manifestation arise within him;
this is "the will for the arising of wholesome states not yet arisen.
And it is said: "He generates the will for the stability, non-confusion, and the fulfillment through cultivation of wholesome states that have already arisen."
"Wholesome states that have arisen" refers to those which have been acquired and are present before one.

In this context, with reference to the non-separation from what has been acquired—that is, the non-decline of what has been acquired—it says "for stability. With reference to the state of not being sluggish due to their manifestation, it says "for non-confusion."

With reference to the perfection and final consummation of those very wholesome states (*kuśala-dharma*) that have been acquired, manifested, and cultivated through repeated practice, it is said: "for the fulfillment of cultivation.

In this regard, he generates longing and directs his mind toward it; and there arises in him an intense desire for stability, a desire for non-forgetfulness, and a desire for the fulfillment of cultivation.
This is called "the will (*chanda*) for the stability, non-forgetfulness, and fulfillment of cultivation of wholesome states that have arisen."
In that context, "exerts oneself" (*vyāyacchate*) means for the sake of bringing into manifestation those [qualities] already attained;
"arouses vigor" (*vīryam ārabhate*) means for the sake of attaining those not yet attained.
Therein, "exerts oneself" means for the stability and non-confusion of those [qualities] already arisen.
“He exerts vigor” for the sake of fulfilling cultivation;

moreover, he strives for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen, and for the stability and non-confusion of those that have already arisen— namely, of wholesome dharmas that are weak or middling.
He exerts vigor for the arising of superior wholesome states that have not yet arisen, and for the cultivation and fulfillment of those already arisen; therein,
he "upholds the mind."
When that mind is applied to one-pointedness in the cultivation of calm (*śamatha*),
for the sake of the non-arising of unarisen evil and unwholesome states—

and so on in detail, up to— for the stability, non-confusion, and fulfillment of the cultivation of arisen wholesome states; yet, when thus withdrawn within, it falls into a state of dullness (*laya*).
And when he perceives that the mind is apprehensive of sinking,
he then takes hold of it and gladdens it by means of one or another uplifting sign that inspires confidence;
in this way, he uplifts the mind.

How does one "exert"? When one perceives that the mind is agitated or suspected of agitation at the time of exertion, one then again withdraws it inwardly and applies oneself to tranquility (*śamatha*).

These are the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*): the desire, exertion, arousal of energy, mental application, and striving for the non-arising of unarisen states belonging to the dark side (*kṛṣṇapakṣya*), and for the abandoning of those that have already arisen— these two are right efforts.
For the arising of wholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen,
the two right efforts should be understood in detail, just as [the two right efforts] were explained for the unwholesome dharmas of the dark side.

In this regard, the first is the abandonment through restraint (*saṃvaraṇaprahāṇa*), which is described in detail as: "one generates the desire for the abandoning of evil, unwholesome states that have already arisen.
The second is the abandonment through abandonment (*prahāṇaprahāṇa*).
Regarding the passage, "He generates the desire for the non-arising of those [states] that have not yet arisen," and so forth:

for an evil thing that has already arisen must be restrained, while that which has not yet arisen is already abandoned by virtue of its non-occurrence; thus, it is to be abandoned by virtue of its non-manifestation.
The abandonment of what has already been abandoned is "abandonment of abandonment.
Among these, cultivation-abandonment is one;
as it is said:
“For the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen,” and so on in detail, up to: “he exerts the mind and strives.
For it is when wholesome states are practiced and cultivated in this way [that they arise].
Those not yet attained are attained, and those already attained are brought into manifestation;
therein, guarding is one [type] of abandonment.
As it is said:
“For the stabilization of wholesome states that have arisen,” and so on in detail, up to “he exerts his mind, he strives.”

For when wholesome qualities have been acquired and brought into manifestation, the avoidance of negligence and the cultivation of heedfulness lead to the stability of those wholesome qualities, to their non-forgetfulness, and to the fulfillment of their development.
In this way, the wholesome states that have arisen are preserved.
This, for now, is the detailed analysis of the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*).
Furthermore, what is the summarized meaning?
It is said:

the perfection of the resolute intention and the perfection of the application regarding the objects to be abandoned and the objects to be adopted within the dark and light sides are fully elucidated.

In this regard, the perfection of higher intention consists in the generation of aspiration, while the perfection of application consists in exertion, the undertaking of vigor, the restraint of the mind, and its intense application.
This much is to be performed by the practitioner.
One must first generate a longing for the abandonment of things that are to be abandoned and for the attainment of things that are to be attained;
one must exert vigor for the abandonment of the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) and for the abandonment of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*);
and from time to time, one should cultivate the signs of tranquility (*śamatha*), exertion (*pragraha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Furthermore, those wholesome factors which serve as antidotes for the abandonment of the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) and the abandonment of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) must be fully cultivated.
All of this is elucidated by means of the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
This is the summary of the meaning.
In that regard, there are four concentrations,
namely: concentration through desire, concentration through energy, [concentration through mind, and concentration through investigation].
There is concentration of will (*cittasamādhi*) and concentration of investigation (*mīmāṃsāsamādhi*).
Among these, the concentration that is obtained by making aspiration (*chanda*) the dominant factor is "concentration of will."
The concentration that is acquired by making vigor, mind, and investigation the predominant factors is this "concentration of investigation."
When he first generates mere desire,
and having generated that desire, he correctly applies his attention to those evil and unwholesome states by way of their intrinsic nature, their cause, their disadvantage, and their antidote,
and he sets forth one-pointed mindfulness; [this is called the stage of "application"].
In this way, he correctly applies his attention to wholesome phenomena by way of their intrinsic nature, their cause, their benefit, and their renunciation;
he establishes one-pointed mindfulness,
and through frequent cultivation of that mode, he touches upon one-pointedness by means of distancing himself from the active manifestation of the outbursts [of the afflictions].
Yet even now, he has not completely eradicated the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of evil and unwholesome states (*akuśala-dharma*).
This is also called that which is dominated by desire (*chanda-adhipateya*).
Furthermore, regarding an object— whether past, future, or present— that is conducive to evil and unwholesome states and conducive to the obsession of weak, medium, or intense afflictions,
he applies himself for the non-arising of what has not yet arisen, or for the abandonment of what has already arisen.
Striving and exerting vigor,
as he dwells upon that object of focus,
he correctly contemplates that object in terms of its intrinsic nature, its cause, its disadvantage, and its remedy.
For one who establishes one-pointed mindfulness and dwells frequently therein, a state of mental one-pointedness arises by means of distancing the active outbursts of the afflictions;
yet, even so, one has not yet eradicated the latent tendencies of evil and unwholesome states.
This is the concentration dominated by energy.
Furthermore, when the mind is sunken, he uplifts it;
when the mind is uplifted, he composes it; and from time to time, he maintains equanimity toward those evil, unwholesome states and the conditions conducive to evil, unwholesome states.

When one correctly contemplates wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, as well as those factors conducive to the wholesome and the unwholesome, by way of their intrinsic nature, their cause, their disadvantage, their benefit, their antidote, and their emergence; and when one establishes one-pointed mindfulness— (Śbh II 216)
The one-pointedness of mind that arises for one who dwells frequently in that state—
detailed at length as far as [the sūtra describes]—
this is called concentration governed by the mind.
In that regard, those factors which are conducive to evil and unwholesome states for one who attends to them inappropriately (*ayoniśomanasikāra*),
become conducive to wholesome states for one who attends to them appropriately (*yoniśomanasikāra*).
When his obsessions (*paryavasthāna*) have been thus distanced, [he attains this].
And when those factors, headed by meditative concentration, which serve as antidotes to the outbursts of the afflictions have arisen,
those evil and unwholesome states do not manifest.
It occurs to him:
“Do I not experience evil, unwholesome states that exist and are present, or rather do I not experience those that do not exist and are not present? Let me investigate this thoroughly.
Making the mental engagement of investigation his primary focus, he investigates whether [those states] have been abandoned or not abandoned;
he contemplates them correctly.
He establishes one-pointed mindfulness;
by dwelling frequently therein, he touches one-pointedness of mind,
through which he becomes free from conceit.
“My mind is liberated from the mere outbursts of affliction, but not from all latent tendencies whatsoever;
yet those wholesome factors, headed by meditative concentration, which serve as their antidotes, have been attained and cultivated by me.”
But he understands as it truly is that [this concentration] is not an antidote to the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*);
this is called his concentration of investigation (*mīmāṃsā-samādhi*).
Having made that fourfold concentration his dominant influence, once the outbursts [of the defilements] have been distanced,
he applies himself to the total and complete eradication of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of all evil, unwholesome states, as well as their antidotes.

Furthermore, for the sake of the full realization of wholesome dharmas, he again generates desire and exerts effort; thus, in detail, he applies himself by means of the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).

For one who has applied themselves in that manner and become such, there are eight formative forces of exertion (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*) which function both for the eradication of their underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and for the fulfillment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). They are as follows:
zeal (*chanda*), [thinking] "When shall I fulfill meditative concentration?"...
"I shall abandon the latent tendencies of evil, unwholesome dharmas.

Effort is the state of not relinquishing application up until the cultivation of the antidotes. Faith is the state of conviction regarding further realization for one who dwells with unremitting application.
It is deep conviction. In this context, pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is that joy and rapture preceded by the clarity of faith,
and for one whose mind is joyful, the gradual subsiding of the heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) belonging to the side of evil and unwholesome states.
In that context, mindfulness is that which is ninefold,
encompassing the nine modes of mental abiding belonging to the side of calm abiding (*śamatha*).
In that context, clear comprehension is the wisdom belonging to the side of insight (*vipaśyanā*).

In this context, volition (*cetanā*) is that mental formation (*cittābhisaṃskāra*) of one who is investigating whether [defilements] have been abandoned or not abandoned; it is that mental formation conducive to calm (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) which gives rise to bodily and vocal action.
Equanimity (*upekṣā*) therein is the non-affliction of the mind and the evenness of the mind for one who moves among past, future, and present bases of evil and unwholesome dharmas.
By these two causes, one discerns and knows the abandonment of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*):
namely, by means of a volition that is not directly present to its object and by means of equanimity that is directly present to its object.
These are the eight formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃskāra*).
And this is the application of the eight formative forces of abandonment for the sake of uprooting the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
In that regard, desire is simply desire; that which is exertion is vigor (*vīrya*).

That which is faith, that which is pliancy, that which is mindfulness, that which is clear comprehension, that which is volition, and that which is equanimity— this is the means. All of this taken together, [constitutes the path].
Those former concentrations of desire and these formative forces of abandonment, when the underlying tendencies have been abandoned and concentration is fully perfected,
are called the "basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of abandonment and the concentration of desire."

The basis of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) is said to be that which is endowed with the formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*) along with the concentrations of energy, mind, and investigation.
For what reason is it called a "basis of psychic power"?
He said:
"Just as one who possesses feet is capable of advancing, retreating, and exerting effort,
even so, for one in whom these qualities exist,"
And this concentration exists in its full perfection;
when his mind is thus purified and cleansed, he—
Free from blemish, devoid of secondary defilements,
and made straight.
When the body is steady and has attained imperturbability, one becomes capable of advancing, retreating, and exerting effort.
For the sake of attaining and realizing supramundane dharmas—
this indeed is the supreme supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), the supreme success (*samṛddhi*), namely, the supramundane dharmas.
Therefore, it is called a "basis of psychic power."

Thus established in concentration, relying upon that concentration, he applies himself to the training in higher mind and the training in higher wisdom. As he applies himself therein, there arises in him—based on the realization of others, namely the Teacher and his disciples—a firm conviction, clarity, and trust; by virtue of its predominance, this is called the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
But where does its sovereignty lie?
He replied:
Its sovereignty lies in the arising of energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, headed by the arising of supramundane dharmas.
Those [faculties] such as vigor and the rest also exercise sovereignty over the arising of supramundane dharmas; they exercise sovereignty up to [the point of] practice;
and wisdom exercises sovereignty over the arising of supramundane dharmas.
Therefore, these five faculties, beginning with faith, come into being.

Furthermore, it is the conviction, clarity, and state of faith that arises from one who perceives a successive attainment of distinction between what preceded and what followed, and which, in accordance with that, leads to the attainment of subsequent supramundane dharmas.
That is called the power of faith in the sense of being uncrushable.
By what, moreover, can it not be crushed? That faith cannot be carried away by either a god, or...
Neither by Māra, nor by Brahmā, nor by anyone else in the world, even with [their] dharma, [can this be overturned].
Or, because it cannot be crushed by the obsession of the afflictions (*kleśaparyavasthāna*),
it is called "unshakeable.
Those qualities such as vigor (*vīrya*) and so forth, which have that [unshakeability] as their chief and are preceded by it, are also called "powers" (*bala*).
Possessing those powers, he, being powerful, having conquered the entire host of Māra, applies himself to the destruction of the outflows;
therefore, they are called "powers."
In this regard, that which is the faculty of faith and that which is the power of faith should be seen as being contained within these four verified confidences (*avetyaprasāda*).
For what reason?
Because the verified confidence of one who has entered the path of rightness (*samyaktvanyāma*) has that as its cause, that as its condition, and that as its basis.

Therefore, because that [body] is its sovereign fruit (adhipatiphala) through the relationship of cause and effect, the Blessed One stated that it should be viewed as such; however, it is not identical with it in essence nor does it possess its characteristics.
In this regard, the faculty of vigor (vīryendriya) is to be seen within the four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa).
For what reason?
What are those right efforts?
They are the right efforts belonging to the stage of application for the sake of abandoning the afflictions that are to be abandoned by vision.
The right efforts (samyakprahāṇa) are intended here;
for they lead to the ultimate abandonment of evil, unwholesome states.
In that regard, the faculty of mindfulness (smṛtīndriya) is to be seen in the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).
Thus, these four foundations of mindfulness lead to the abandonment of all perversions without exception.
In this context, the faculty of concentration is to be understood as being present within the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
Regarding those meditative absorptions that are preparatory for the state of a non-returner (*anāgāmitā*),
therein the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) is to be understood as the knowledge of the four noble truths;
it is that knowledge of the four noble truths which conduces to clear realization (*abhisamaya*) and to the attainment of the fruits of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*).
The powers (balas) are to be understood in the same way as the faculties (indriyas).

Through the sequence of cultivation, development, and frequent practice of these faculties and these powers, he produces the roots of merit conducive to penetration—namely, the weak, medium, and intense levels: the stages of heat (*uṣmagata*), the summits (*mūrdhan*), the patiences conforming to the truths (*satyānulomā kṣāntayaḥ*), and the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).

It is just as if a certain man, desiring to perform a fire-rite with fire and seeking fire, were to set the lower fire-drill upon the upper fire-drill and, exerting himself, striving, and laboring, were to rub them together.
As he exerts himself, strives, and endeavors, heat first arises in the lower fire-drill;
and that very heat, increasing further, rises upward.
(Śbh II 228)
Increasing further in measure, it causes a flameless fire to fall; immediately upon the falling of the fire, a flame arises.
By means of that flame which has arisen, been produced, and come into being, it performs the function of fire.
Just as the exertion of rubbing [the fire-drills] is to be seen, so should the cultivation of the five faculties be regarded.
Just as heat first arises from the lower fire-drill, so should the stages of "heat" (ūṣmagata) be regarded.
These are the precursors and signs for the arising of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) dharmas, which are like fire and burn away the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Just as the heat of that very fire rises upward, so should the "summits" (*mūrdhan*) be viewed;
just as the appearance of smoke [signals fire], so should the "patiences" (*kṣānti*) conforming to the truths be viewed.
Just as the falling of fire without flames should be seen as the worldly supreme dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*),
so should the supramundane, untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas be seen as arising immediately thereafter, like the emergence of flames;
these arise immediately after the five faculties (*indriya*) comprised within the worldly supreme dharmas.
What, then, are they?
He said: the seven factors of enlightenment.
These are the factors of that person who has entered the path of correctness (*samyaktvanyāma*) and possesses such realization of reality as it is (*yathābhūtāvabodha*).
For that realization of reality as it is is comprised of seven factors: three belonging to the side of tranquility (*śamatha*), [and four belonging to the side of insight].
Three belong to the side of insight (*vipaśyanā*), and one belongs to both sides;
therefore, they are called the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
In that regard, that which is the investigation of phenomena, that which is vigor,
and that which is joy— these three belong to the side of insight (vipaśyanā).
In that regard, there is pliancy,
there is concentration, and there is equanimity.
Thus, these three belong to the side of calm abiding (*śamatha*).
Mindfulness belongs to both sides and is said to be omnipresent (*sarvatraga*).
At that time, because he has for the first time attained the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), he becomes a learner (*śaikṣa*) who has seen the goal (*dṛṣṭapada*).
His afflictions to be abandoned by seeing have been abandoned,
while those to be abandoned by cultivation remain;
for their abandonment, he cultivates the noble eightfold path consisting of three aggregates.
In that regard, there is right view, right intention, and right effort;
This is the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*). Among those, right speech, right action, and right livelihood constitute the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*).
In that regard, whatever is right mindfulness and whatever is right concentration,
this is the aggregate of concentration.
For what reason is it called the noble eightfold path?
It is said:
this is the path, this is the practice, of the noble one in training who has seen the truth, and it is comprised of eight factors.
It is without remainder for the sake of abandoning all afflictions and for the realization of liberation;
therefore, it is called the Noble Eightfold Path.
In this regard, that awakening to reality which was attained at the time of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*),

and having attained it, the subsequent establishment of that very [reality] through wisdom according to how it was realized— that both taken together, when condensed into one, are called right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
Taking that right view as the dominant influence, whatever intention of renunciation one forms— an intention free from ill-will and an intention free from harmfulness—
this is called right intention. Even if, for the time being, the mind wanders toward discursive thoughts, [it remains right intention].
He reflects upon such thoughts as these. If, however, his mind wanders toward talk,
he makes right view his dominant influence and, from that very same wholesome intention, engages in talk concerning the Dharma.
This constitutes his right speech (*samyagvāk*).
If he requires robes, almsfood, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the treatment of illness,
he either seeks them out himself or causes others to seek them for him.

He dwells with clear comprehension in going forth and returning; in looking ahead and looking aside; in bending and stretching his limbs; in carrying his outer robe, inner robe, and bowl; in eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting.
Furthermore, having gone to his dwelling, he dwells with clear comprehension in seeking robes and other requisites, and in walking, standing, sitting, and even in dispelling drowsiness and fatigue.

This is called his right action (*samyakkarmānta*). He seeks those requisites, from robes down to medicinal supplies, in accordance with the Dharma, avoiding all things that constitute wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
This constitutes his right livelihood.
Furthermore, as for those right speech, right action, and right livelihood that are comprised within renunciation,
these have already been acquired by him, together with the factors of enlightenment, even prior to the attainment of mental attention.
As for what are called the "virtues dear to the Noble Ones" (āryakānta-śīla), for what reason?

Because this has long been desired, cherished, beloved, and pleasing to the Noble Ones—those who are virtuous and have attained the right path—who think: "May I indeed [practice] the non-doing of verbal misconduct, bodily misconduct, and wrong livelihood."
"May I obtain restraint.
Whatever has been desired, cherished, dear, and pleasing to his mind for a long time, that is obtained by him at that moment;
therefore, it is called "noble-loved" (āryakānta).
For thus, having attained the ethical precepts beloved by the noble ones,
he does not knowingly speak false speech,
nor does he intentionally deprive a living being of life.
He does not take what is not given, he does not engage in sexual misconduct, and he does not seek robes and other requisites through unrighteous means.
Thus, taking those virtues beloved by the Noble Ones as the dominant influence, whatever speech proceeds at the time of cultivating the path, whatever bodily action, and whatever livelihood—
these too are called right speech, right action, and right livelihood.

For one who is engaged in cultivation by relying upon right view, right intention, right speech, right action, and right livelihood, there arises a desire, vigor, exertion, departure, prowess, strength, and the undertaking of mental effort.
Sustained exertion is continuity. This is called right effort:
that mindfulness which, having made the four foundations of mindfulness its sovereign, is comprised of non-perversion and encompasses the nine modes and the stabilization of the mind in nine modes.
This is called right mindfulness and right concentration.
All of this, taken together, is established as the Noble Eightfold Path in terms of what is to be done while moving about and what is to be done while dwelling.
Among these, right speech, right action, and right livelihood pertain to what is to be done while moving about;
furthermore, what is to be done while dwelling is twofold.
They are calm abiding and insight. In that regard, there is right view and right intention.
That which is right effort is insight (*vipaśyanā*);
therein, that which is right mindfulness and right concentration is tranquility (*śamatha*).

Relying thus upon purified verbal conduct, action, and livelihood, one cultivates tranquility and insight from time to time, and realizes the abandonment of all fetters without remainder—the supreme fruit of arhatship.
The prolonged path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) abandons the afflictions through repeated practice over a long period of time;
however, the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), which is dependent solely upon knowledge, abandons the afflictions by the mere arising of that knowledge.
For this reason, right speech, right action, and right livelihood are established on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Thus, this practice and familiarization with these thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣyadharma*) in this sequential order is called the cultivation of the factors conducive to awakening.
(Śbh II 238) In that regard, what is the fruit of cultivation? He said:
There are four fruits of asceticism:
the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the supreme fruit, arhatship.
In this regard, what is asceticism?
What is the fruit? He says:
the path and the abandonment of the afflictions are the fruit.
Moreover, a path that arises later is the fruit of a path that arose earlier—whether it be middling, superior, or equal.
Furthermore, for what reason are four [fruits] established therein?
He said:
By way of being the antidote for the abandonment of the four kinds of afflictions.

For example, the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) is established through the abandonment of those afflictions (*kleśa*) that lack a real objective basis (*nirvastuka*), which lead to rebirth in the miserable states (*apāya*) and serve as the causes for going to those miserable states, and through the arising of their antidotes (*pratipakṣa*).
However, the Blessed One has established it in three categories— namely, among householders— through the abandonment of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Regarding the faction of the poorly proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya and the faction of the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya,
[these fetters are so designated] because they act as obstacles to the arising of the Path for the three fetters.
Among these, within the faction of householders, there is the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is that which causes one to be terrified from the very beginning, such that one does not apply oneself at all; and the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) within a poorly taught Dharma and Vinaya,
by which one sets out wrongly even when having set out, so that the Noble Path does not arise.
There is doubt regarding the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya; although one has set out therein,

one does not practice wrongly, yet because of a lack of cultivation, as long as the vision of things as they truly are does not arise with respect to the object of knowledge, so long do hesitations and perplexities act as obstacles.
For the sake of the arising of the path;
by this reason, first of all, the establishment of the fruit of stream-entry is made.
-II-13-a-(2) For this stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), at most seven more existences remain.
And as for his continuity of birth, it is when he abandons those afflictions (*kleśa*) conducive to the continuity of birth that are comprised within existence as a god and existence as a human.
When, through the abandonment of those [defilements], one brings about at most one more existence as a god and one more existence as a human,
at that time the fruit of the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmiphala) is established.
But when one brings about only rebirth in the divine realms, having abandoned the afflictions pertaining to birth upon returning to this world,
then the fruit of the Non-returner (anāgāmiphala) is established.
The fruit of arhatship is established as the supreme fruit because of the abandonment of those afflictions that lead to rebirth in all states of existence.
Furthermore, that fruit of once-returning was established by the Blessed One through the abandonment of the three fetters and the attenuation of passion, hatred, and delusion;
the fruit of non-returning through the abandonment of the five lower fetters;
and the fruit of arhatship through the complete and total abandonment of all afflictions.
This is called the fruit of cultivation.

In that regard, those persons whose conduct is characterized by passion, hatred, delusion, pride, or discursive thought must first purify their conduct through an object of focus that purifies conduct; only after that do they attain stability of mind.
For them, that object of focus is specifically determined, and they must necessarily apply themselves to it with that very object.
However, for one whose conduct is of equal parts (*samabhāgacarita*), that which is pleasing and agreeable should be employed solely for the sake of stabilizing the mind,
and not for the purification of conduct.
Just as it is with one of equal parts, so should one with little passion (*mandarajaska*) be understood.
However, this is their distinction:
one whose temperament is dominated by passion and so forth becomes an attainer only after a long time when practicing, whereas one whose temperament is balanced attains it before very long.
But one who has little passion attains stability of mind very quickly and with great haste.
In that regard, the characteristics of persons whose conduct is dominated by passion and so forth have been explained previously.
What are the characteristics of a person whose conduct is characterized by equanimity and one who has little defilement?
He said:
In a person whose conduct is characterized by equal proportions of the afflictions, all those signs that belong to those whose conduct is dominated by passion and so forth are indeed present;
however, those passions and so forth are neither excessive nor predominant as they are in those whose conduct is dominated by passion and so forth. Rather, they exist in a state of equilibrium.
When conditions are present, they become manifest.
In that regard, the signs of a person with little passion (mandarajas) are as follows:
he is unobstructed, having accumulated the equipment of primordial purity;
he is full of serene faith, intelligent, meritorious, and endowed with virtuous qualities.
In that regard, there are three obstructions: the obstruction of karma, the obstruction of afflictions, and the obstruction of maturation.
Among these, the obstruction of karma consists of the five actions of immediate retribution.
Furthermore, whatever other intentional karma there may be— weighty karma whose maturation has ripened— that acts as an obstacle to the arising of the Path;
therein, the obscuration of afflictions consists of both intense affliction and prolonged affliction,
which cannot be purified in this present life through the purification of conduct or the purification of the object of focus.
In this context, the obstruction of maturation (*vipākāvaraṇa*) refers to that place of rebirth where the noble path does not arise or function,
or where it brings about its maturation; or it refers to that place where the noble path does arise and function.
Having been reborn there, one becomes dull-witted, mute like a sheep, and communicates only by means of hand gestures;
one lacks the capacity to understand the meaning of well-spoken or ill-spoken teachings.
In that regard, primordial purity consists of very pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) and straight view (*dṛṣṭi*).
Therein, very pure ethical discipline should be understood by way of ten causes;
therein, as for straightness of view:
Through the application of faith, through the application of resolute conviction,
and by being free from deceit and guile.
Because one has well-considered the meaning of the Dharma and possesses an application that is free from longing and free from doubt,
the view that is associated with faith becomes unshakeable within this Dharma and Vinaya.
And it is associated with resolute faith in the inconceivable power of the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas.
He has faith in inconceivable bases of rebirth,
in profound teachings,
and in the indeterminate points.
He does not tremble,
nor does he fall into terror;
and that view which is free from deceit and guile—
By means of which one becomes upright,
of an upright nature, practices according to the instructions received,
and reveals oneself as one truly is.

Or, regarding the phenomena, the meaning of their impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness becomes well-pondered, well-weighed, and well-examined; for this reason, he becomes free from doubt and free from uncertainty,
having departed from the two paths and proceeding toward distinction.
Thus, this fourfold view, as it has been described, is called "straightness of view."
In that regard, as for the accumulation of the provisions (*saṃbhāra*),
the provisions have already been explained in detail;
briefly stated, however, they are of four kinds.
The equipment of merit and the equipment of knowledge are both prior and pertaining to the present life.
Therein, the equipment of merit is that by which one now possesses abundant and favorable requisites and obtains virtuous friends.
And there is no obstacle for one who is thus engaged.
In that regard, the equipment of knowledge is that by which one becomes intelligent and capable of discerning well-spoken and ill-spoken words.
In order to understand the meaning of phenomena,
he becomes a recipient of conformable Dharma teachings and teachings on their meaning.
Regarding instruction and admonition:
therein, the former [cause] is that by which one now obtains matured faculties due to the accumulation of previous roots of virtue;
therein, the pertaining to the present life is, for example, a wholesome desire for the Dharma.
Likewise, for one whose faculties are fully matured, there is the restraint of morality and the restraint of the faculties, as detailed previously.
In that regard, there is an abundance of serene confidence:
one does not waver or doubt regarding the Teacher, but has serene confidence and resolute faith;
and just as toward the Teacher, so too toward the Dharma and the training.
Thus, in detail, as before.
In that regard, *medhā* is that by which one quickly grasps the Dharma, does not forget the Dharma and its meaning even after a long time, and swiftly penetrates both the Dharma and its meaning.

In that regard, "having performed meritorious deeds" means that by virtue of it one becomes handsome, attractive, and pleasing; one becomes long-lived, possesses authoritative speech, is renowned and of great renown, is a great field of merit, and is a recipient of robes and other requisites;
and one is honored and revered by kings and others.
In this context, "endowed with qualities" should be understood as possessing qualities such as fewness of desires and so forth,
as described in the *Śramaṇālaṃkāra*;
he is naturally endowed with these from the very beginning.
Thus, these and similar qualities are to be understood as the marks of a person whose defilements are slight.
In this regard, there are six designations for persons (*pudgala*).
What are the six?
Namely: the śramaṇa, the brāhmaṇa, the brahmacārī, the bhikṣu, the yati, and the pravrajita.
In this regard, there are four types of śramaṇas:
the victor over the path, the teacher of the path, [the one who lives on the path, and the one who deceives with respect to the path].
There are those who live by the path and those who corrupt the path.
Among them, he who is the Sugata is the conqueror of the path.
He who speaks according to the Dharma is the teacher of the path;
he who is well-practiced is one who lives by the path;
he who is wrongly practiced is a defiler of the path.
One is called a Sugata who has attained the complete destruction of attachment, aversion, and delusion;
a speaker of Dharma who teaches the Dharma for the sake of subduing attachment, aversion, and delusion;
and one who is well-practiced who is practicing for the sake of subduing attachment, aversion, and delusion.
One who is immoral, possesses evil qualities, and has entered upon a wrong path;
furthermore, those in training and those beyond training are called "victors over the path" because of their victory over the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation.
Therein, the Tathāgata and the Bodhisattvas who have set out for enlightenment in the future,
as well as the Śrāvakas who are upholders of the Sūtras, upholders of the Vinaya, and upholders of the Mātṛkās—
those who uphold the conventional Dharma and Vinaya— [reside].
They set in motion the eye of the Dharma;
these are called the guides of the path.
Among them are those virtuous ordinary persons who have set out for their own benefit, who possess a sense of shame, who feel remorse for transgressions, and who desire to train.
She is applied to the attainment of what has not been attained, to the realization of what has not been realized, and to the direct manifestation of what has not been directly manifested.
And those who are capable and competent for the realization of that which has not yet been realized—
these are called "those who live by the path."
They possess even a mere warmth by which they are not dead, but are said to be "living" for the sake of the arising of the noble faculty of wisdom;
therefore, they are called "those who live by the path.
In this regard, there is a person who is immoral, of evil character, and so forth, up to one who is unchaste yet claims to be chaste.
This is called a defiler of the path;
by him the path is defiled from its very root and beginning,
whereby he becomes incapable and powerless.
He is unfit as a vessel for the arising of the path,
even when the teaching of the path exists and its realization is present;
therefore, he is called a "corrupter of the path."
And it was with this in mind that the Blessed One said:
"Here is the first ascetic;
here, up to the fourth."
The doctrines of others are empty of true ascetics and brahmins;
where the noble eightfold path is found, there is the first ascetic, and so on up to the fourth.
-II-14-a-(2) In this regard, there are three types of brahmins;
namely, the brahmin by birth, and so forth.
There is the brahmin by designation and the brahmin by practice.
Among these, there is the brahmin by birth.

This one who is born into a brahmin family, born from a womb, produced by a mother, and endowed with [lineage] on the mother’s and father’s side— in this regard, the name "brahmin" exists in the world as a designation, a common appellation, a concept, and a conventional usage.
In this regard, the brahmin by practice is one who has reached the ultimate limit and accomplished his purpose.
By this, evil and unwholesome states are driven away, as it has been said: "There is nothing further to be done by a brahmin; a brahmin is remembered as one who has accomplished his purpose."
In that regard, there are three types of celibate practitioners (*brahmacārin*):
namely, the one who undertakes abstinence, the one who abandons it for a time, and the one who abandons it forever.
Among these, the one who undertakes abstinence...
One who abstains from the practice of sexual intercourse, having undertaken the training,
is a "renouncer of that interval"; this refers to an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has become free from passion for sensual desires by means of the mundane path.
In that regard, one who has abandoned those [defilements] absolutely is,
for example, a non-returner (anāgāmin) or, again, an arhat.
In this regard, there are five kinds of monks:
one who is called a monk because he begs (bhikṣati), and the monk by profession (pratijñā-bhikṣu).
A monk by designation, a monk because his afflictions have been destroyed,
and a monk who has received full ordination through a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations.
In this regard, there are three types of ascetics (*yatayaḥ*):
an ascetic by virtue of restraint from immorality,
who is one that has desisted from unwholesome actions of body and speech.
Through restraint regarding sense objects, one is a *yati*—
one whose doors [of the senses] are guarded by the senses, whose mindfulness is protected, whose mindfulness is prudent, and so on in detail as before.
A *yati* is one who has restrained the afflictions (*kleśa*), whose afflictions to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation have been eliminated,
and who [abandons] every desire and discursive thought (*vitarka*) that arises, as well as discursive thoughts of ill-will and harmfulness.

Covetousness, ill-will, wrong view, anger, enmity, hypocrisy, spite, and so forth—those states leading to the lower realms, to hell, to an evil destiny, and which render one unworthy of being a śramaṇa—as they arise one after another, he does not tolerate them; he abandons them, dispels them, and brings them to an end.
This constitutes his twofold restraint of the afflictions.
Restraint of the outbursts and restraint of the latent tendencies.

In that regard, there are two types of renunciants: those for whom the Dharma and Vinaya are well-expounded, and those for whom the Dharma and Vinaya are poorly-expounded. Among these, the Dharma and Vinaya are well-expounded as follows:
Whether a monk, a nun, a female trainee, a male novice, or a female novice,
one who causes even their own evil and unwholesome states to go forth is,
in the ultimate sense, said to be "one who has gone forth."
In this regard, there is the poorly proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya;
namely, such as the wandering ascetics of the non-Buddhist sects, whether they be Nirgranthas or Pāṇḍuraka wanderers,
or whoever else is of a similar kind.
Therefore, he said that "śramaṇa," "brāhmaṇa," "brahmacārī," "bhikṣu," "yati," and "pravrajita" are synonyms for the person (pudgala).
In this regard, there are eight types of persons and four causes for the establishment of those persons.
Which are the eight types of persons? Namely: the capable and the incapable;
the one who knows the means and the one who does not know the means.
[There are] the constant and the non-constant,
as well as the one who has practiced familiarity and the one who has not practiced familiarity.
In that regard, there are four bases for the classification of persons.

For the establishment of these very eight types of persons, there are four bases of differentiation, namely: the differentiation of faculties—those with matured faculties and those with immature faculties;
and the differentiation of yoga—those who know yoga and those who do not know yoga.
The distinction of application consists of practicing with constancy and respect, and practicing without constancy or respect;
the distinction of time consists of having cultivated the path for a long period and not having cultivated the path for a long period.
How do these four distinctions serve as the bases for the establishment of the eight types of persons?
In that regard, one whose faculties are fully matured is capable;
one whose faculties are not fully matured is incapable.
One who knows yoga is skilled in knowing the means.
"One who knows the application" means one who is skilled in knowing the method.

One who practices with continuity and reverence is called "constant" (*sātatika*) and "careful" (*nipaka*); one who does not practice with continuity and reverence is called "inconstant" (*asātatika*) and "uncareful" (*anipaka*).
One who has cultivated the path for a long time is one who has achieved proficiency;
one who has not cultivated the path for a long time is one who has not achieved proficiency.
Thus, the classification of the eight types of persons is established according to the distinction of their faculties and the distinction of the duration of their application to yoga.

To whatever extent a person’s faculties are immature, to that extent— even if they are skilled in means, constant in practice, and well-trained— they do not become an achiever of the righteous, wholesome Dharma.
In that case, if his faculties are matured but he is not skilled in means, he does not become one who propitiates [the teacher].
(Śbh II 260)
One whose faculties are matured and who knows the skillful means is neither constant nor one who attains swift higher knowledge.
In that regard, one whose faculties are matured and who knows the skillful means is constant but has not yet completed his practice;
he has not yet accomplished his own purpose or fulfilled what was to be done.
And because he has mature faculties, knows the skillful means, is constant, and has practiced cultivation,
he thus becomes one who attains success and is swift in direct knowledge.
And he has accomplished his own purpose and fulfilled what was to be done.
In this regard, a yogin engaged in yoga should understand that there are four Māras and many deeds of Māra;
these, having been fully understood, must be avoided.
In that regard, there are four Māras, namely:
the Māra of the aggregates (skandhamāra), the Māra of the afflictions (kleśamāra), [the Māra of death (mṛtyumāra), and the Māra of the son of gods (devaputramāra)].
The Māra of death and the Māra who is a son of the gods;
the five aggregates of clinging are the Māra of the aggregates.
The afflictions belonging to the three realms are the Māra of the afflictions (*kleśamāra*).
The death and passing away of various beings from their respective classes of beings is the Māra of death (*maraṇamāra*).
