As for the son of a god born in the desire realm who has attained sovereignty, he [acts] against this one who is engaged in the side of virtue in order to transcend the aggregates, the afflictions, and death.
He brings about an obstacle by causing distraction;
this is called the Māra who is a son of the gods.
In that regard, wherever one dies, [that is where he acts].
That by which one dies,
that which is death itself,
and the obstructive thing by which one does not transcend death.
With reference to this, four Māras are established.
Among them, one dies when the five appropriated aggregates (upādānaskandha) have arisen and are present;
another generates [them] from afflictions (kleśa) for the sake of the future.
Once born, one dies.
Death—characterized by passing away, the transformation of beings, the cessation of the life-faculty, and the performance of one's time—is death by its very nature.
Furthermore, the Māra who is a son of the gods brings about obstacles for one who is striving to transcend death.
By which he is either unable to transcend the nature of death,
or transcends it only after a lapse of time;
therein, being subject to Māra, he is an ordinary person who has become free from passion through the worldly path.
Whether remaining here or having been reborn there,
one who is under its influence is one who has not yet abandoned desire. Regarding that person who has not yet abandoned desire:
He alone has fallen into the hands [of Māra] and is subject to being done with as he pleases;
or again, one who is free from passion is bound by the fetters of Māra and not released from the snares of Māra.
Because he will indeed return again to this realm.
In this regard, as for the deeds of Māra:
when a certain wholesome desire for the Dharma has arisen that is associated with renunciation, yet it proceeds by making sensual craving its dominant influence;
It should be understood that this is the work of Māra:
when one dwells with the doors of the senses guarded,

yet the mind still plunges into the grasping of signs and the grasping of secondary characteristics regarding forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena that are provocative of passion.
It should be understood that this is the work of Māra:
when one dwells knowing the proper measure regarding food,
yet the mind— due to attachment and desire for exquisite flavors— falls into partiality toward food through its inclination.
Thus, for one who dwells devoted to the practice of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night,
[there arises] a lack of delight in the pleasure of sleep and the pleasure of reclining.
If the mind inclines toward the pleasure of lying on one's side,
it should be understood that this is the work of Māra;
likewise, for one who dwells practicing clear comprehension.
When walking forward or backward and so forth, having seen a woman of beautiful appearance who is alluring—a child—one’s mind plunges in through improper grasping of signs;
or, having seen the various wonders of the world, the mind plunges in;
or, the mind plunges in toward many concerns and many duties.

For example, when the mind inclines toward delighting in association with householders and renunciants, toward being resolved upon the same activities as evil friends, and toward assenting to [wrong] views,
one should know that this is the work of Māra.
Likewise regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha...
Doubts and perplexities arise regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; regarding this world and the world beyond.
It should be understood that this is the work of Māra,
whether one has gone to the forest, or...
Whether he has gone to the foot of a tree or to an empty dwelling, he sees something great, terrifying, and formidable.
Causing terror and making the hair stand on end,
either in the guise of a brahmin or in the guise of a human being.
Or if someone approaches in the guise of a non-human being and, through improper means, causes one to abandon the side of purity and incites one toward the side of darkness,
it should be known that this is the work of Māra.

When the mind inclines toward gain and honor, or when it inclines toward stinginess, great desire, lack of contentment, anger, resentment, hypocrisy, flattery, and other such qualities that are the opposites of the ornaments of a śramaṇa, one should know that this is the work of Māra.
Thus, these and others of a similar kind should be understood as the works of Māra, pertaining to the four Māras as appropriate.
In that regard, for one who is correctly applied, the undertaking may become fruitless due to three causes;
namely, by way of the non-acquisition of the faculties (*indriya-samudāgama*).
If the faculties have not been fully developed due to instruction that is merely conformable and because of weakness in meditative concentration, [the path is not realized].
If the instruction is conformable and the concentration is complete, yet his undertaking is thus fruitless, [it is because of lack of application].
If the faculties have not yet fully developed, if the instruction is not concordant, and if concentration is weak;
Thus, this undertaking is fruitless;
for even if the faculties have been fully developed,
the instruction is not concordant with them.
If concentration is weak,
such an undertaking is fruitless;
however, if the faculties are fully developed, [it is not so].
If the instruction is conformable [to the truth] yet concentration is weak,
such an undertaking is fruitless.
If the faculties have been fully developed,
the instruction is concordant,
and concentration is powerful, [then one will attain the fruit].
In this way, his undertaking becomes fruitful;
through these three causes it becomes fruitless, and through those same three causes it becomes fruitful.
(Śbh II 272) // Summary Verse //
The persons, their establishment, and then by way of the object;
the instruction, the training, and likewise that which is conducive to the training;
the failure in yoga, yoga itself, and the mental attention of the yogin.
What is to be done, cultivation, the fruit, the synonyms for the person,
Māra, the deeds of Māra, and the futility of exertion.
The Second Yoga Station, contained within the Śrāvaka-bhūmi of the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
(Śbh II 275) Appendix I:
The Stage of Non-Meditative Concentration (Asamāhitā Bhūmiḥ)
(Śbh II 276) What is the stage of non-concentration (*asamāhitā bhūmi*)?
In brief, it should be understood as having twelve aspects.
There is a non-concentrated level that is non-concentrated by its very nature, such as the five groups of sensory consciousness.
There is a non-concentrated level due to a lack of pliancy, such as the mental states and mental factors belonging to the desire realm.
Even when there is one-pointedness of mind, those mental states and mental factors do not proceed embraced by pliancy; therefore, it is called "unconcentrated.
There is a level that is unconcentrated due to a lack of exertion, such as in the case of those who indulge in sensual pleasures and are attached to them while consuming those very desires.

There is a state of non-concentration due to distraction, such as when the minds of beginners engaged in meditative concentration are distracted and dispersed among the five strands of sensual pleasure. There is a state of non-concentration due to contraction, such as when the minds of those same beginners engaged in meditative concentration are withdrawn inwardly and overcome by sloth and torpor.

There is a state of non-concentration due to non-attainment, such as when the minds of those same beginners engaged in meditative concentration are neither afflicted by distraction nor contraction, yet they have not attained mental attention (*manaskāra*).
Regarding those mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*),

there is a state of non-concentration due to incompleteness, such as in the case of those who have attained mental attention (*manaskāra*) but have not attained the mental attention that culminates in application (*prayoga-niṣṭhā-manaskāra*), nor attained its fruit. There is also a state of non-concentration due to affliction (*saṃkleśa*), such as when the mind of those who have attained the mental attention that is the fruit of the culmination of application is defiled by any one of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), beginning with relish (*āsvāda*).

There is a state of non-concentration due to a lack of mastery, as in the case of those who have attained the fruit of the culmination of application (*prayoga-niṣṭhā-phala-manaskāra*) and whose minds are indeed undefiled, yet who have not attained mastery over the signs of entering, remaining in, and emerging from meditative attainments, and thus do not obtain them at will, without difficulty, or without effort. There is a state of non-concentration due to impurity, as in the case of the mental states and mental factors of worldly practitioners who, despite obtaining [attainments] at will, without difficulty, and without effort, have not eradicated the latent tendencies of the afflictions (*kleśānuśaya*).
There is an unconcentrated state due to emergence, namely, that of one who has emerged from a concentration attained but has not fallen away from it;
there is an unconcentrated state due to falling away, namely, that of one who has fallen away from a concentration attained.
The *Asamāhitā Bhūmi* (the Stage of Non-concentration) within the *Yogācārabhūmi* is completed.
(Śbh II 281) Appendix II:
The Stage Consisting of Hearing (Śrutamayī Bhūmiḥ)
(Śbh II 284) A. I-1.
These seven factors lead to the realization of the truths exactly as they truly are and to the perfection of liberation.
There are three aspects of vipaśyanā:
the discernment of phenomena,
diligence, and...
There are three factors on the side of joy and calm abiding:
pliancy, and so forth.
Concentration,
equanimity,
and one is śamatha.
The side of insight (vipaśyanā),
that is to say, mindfulness (smṛti).
It should be understood that the seven types of persons are established on the basis of their faculties, their fruits, and their liberations.
Regarding the path of those who have entered [the stream], there are two types: those with dull faculties and those with sharp faculties,
namely, the follower by faith and the follower by dharma.
Regarding the path of fruition:
those two [types of individuals] are those who have attained through faith and through view.
They are liberated from the hindrances to meditative absorption (*samāpatty-āvaraṇa*), but not liberated from the hindrances of the afflictions (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*);
they are those who realize [the truth] through the body (*kāyasākṣin*).
They are liberated from the obscuration of afflictions but not liberated from the obscuration of meditative absorption;
that is, they are liberated through wisdom.
It is liberated from both the obscuration of meditative attainment and the obscuration of the afflictions; thus,
it is liberated from both parts.
These seven types of three causes lead to the internal settling of the mind and the correct unification of the mind in one-pointedness.
It is that which causes engagement,
abides in accordance [with its object],
and gathers [the mind].
The worldly right view consists of aspects such as [the conviction] that "giving exists," and so forth;
and based on those very [convictions], one perceives the household life as being entirely harmful.
"The household is a fault," and so forth— such aspects constitute right resolve associated with renunciation, which functions as the factor of application.
Once one has entered [the path], correctly adopting right speech,
action, and livelihood is conducive to abiding.

Following that, the cause of engagement and the cause conducive to stability— namely, right effort and mindfulness possessed by one who engages in appropriate mental attention (yoniśo-manasikāra)— should be understood as the cause of withdrawal.
Those who indulge in sensual desires desire wealth and so forth for this reason;
that is to say, it is solely because they desire pleasure.
These seven types of happiness arise from the seven noble riches;
they cannot be attained through any accumulation of ordinary wealth:
the happiness of possessing faith, and...
That which arises from being born in a happy realm;
and that which arises from freedom from regret because one does not engage in any misdeeds, having regard for what is not one's own portion.
Likewise, there is the happiness arising from consideration for the censure of others, from possessing a thorough understanding of the Dharma and its meaning,
and from the absence of lacking material requisites in the future.
This bliss arising from the realization of the ultimate truth—
this manifold, irreproachable bliss—
cannot be attained in any way whatsoever through the accumulation of worldly wealth.
Otherwise, it would merely result in not being destitute of requisites in this very life, and even that would be accompanied by moral fault.
These seven are the powers of the side of Māra and the afflictions (*kleśapakṣa*), which cause harm to the Teaching.
One does not regard the practice of all misdeeds that lead to rebirth in the evil destinies as something that does not pertain to oneself.
They do not regard the practice of obstructive dharmas or the censure of others; they disregard the practice of obstructive dharmas and...
Wholesome, unwholesome,
and accompanied by fault;
Without fault,
whether inferior or superior.
Not understanding the phenomena of dependent origination along with their distinctions between black and white,
and with a mind overwhelmed by the stain of avarice;
They possess many vessels and utensils;
they are dull-witted, of small intelligence, and utterly deluded.

It should be understood that there are precisely these seven powers— such as faith in the Noble Dharma and Vinaya— for the purpose of overwhelming and completely eliminating these forces belonging to the side of Māra and the afflictions.
These seven factors, which are the discordant opposites of the ultimate dharma of nirvāṇa, cause the sublime dharma to diminish and disappear.
These, moreover, are subsumed under three types of failure:
failure regarding utilization,
failure regarding the higher resolve, and [failure regarding the basis].
This is the failure of application.
In that regard, it is the desire for fine robes and so forth,
and the desire for many [robes].
The loss of enjoyment is the failure to utilize the resources derived from those [resources].
The loss of superior intention is the lack of conviction regarding the path and its fruit, nirvāṇa.
Laziness, loss of mindfulness, distractedness of mind, and faulty wisdom constitute failure in application.
Among these, failure in enjoyment belongs to the side of the unwholesome root of greed;
furthermore, failure in intention and application belongs to the side of the unwholesome root of delusion.
The white side should be understood as the opposite of this.
These seven factors belong to the side of ultimate nirvāṇa; they conduce to the non-decline of the true dharma and to its long endurance.
Wisdom consisting of hearing, wisdom consisting of reflection, and wisdom consisting of cultivation.
Avoiding unfavorable circumstances for one's physical basis,
correctly seeking material goods and the Dharma,
and being free from conceit.
The discernment of persons is for the purpose of honoring those worthy of honor and not honoring those unworthy of honor.
In this context, listening is for the sake of understanding meanings that have not yet been understood; reflection is for the sake of investigating meanings that have been well-ascertained.
Cultivation is for the sake of abandoning the afflictions;
the avoidance of unfavorable conditions for the basis is for the sake of achieving the pliancy capable of abandonment;
and the correct pursuit of material goods and the Dharma is for the sake of swift superknowledge.

The investigation of persons is for the sake of not being content with the mere attainment of freedom from conceit; it is for the sake of non-longing for those who possess great merit and so forth once they have been known, and for the sake of longing for those who possess few desires and so forth.

There are these seven bases of rebirth for sentient beings, wherein the consciousnesses of sentient beings manifest as a continuous stream, excluding the miserable realms (*apāya*), the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*), and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

Because they constitute the locus for the state of world-weariness (*nirvit*), the miserable realms (*apāya*) are not stations of consciousness; because consciousness does not manifest there at all, the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*) are not [stations of consciousness] either.

Because it is not uniform—due to the fact that consciousness both manifests and does not manifest—the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is not [a station of consciousness].
In this context, dissimilarity of body refers to diversity of body, and dissimilarity of perception refers to diversity of perception;
by contrast, the opposite constitutes unity of body.
And it should be understood as being characterized by the perception of oneness.
In that regard, from the Brahma-world downward, there is the production of individual existences (*ātmabhāva*) consisting of various physical bodies of a dissimilar nature;
however, among those first produced in the Brahma-world itself, the following thought occurs to them:
“We were created by Brahmā.
And it occurs to Brahmā as well: “These were created by me. This is their similarity of perception.
Above the second dhyāna, all [beings] have bodies that resemble flames, and thus they are "of uniform body.

Furthermore, among the Ābhāsvara host of gods, those who were born earlier and those who were born later have the perceptions of fear and fearlessness because they see the burning flames of the Brahma-world; therefore, their perceptions should be understood as being dissimilar.
It should be understood that all forms of depravity belonging to the side of the afflictions among sentient beings are subsumed within seven types of depravity:
those belonging to the side of passion and aversion pertaining to the inferior realm; [and so forth].
It is the depravity belonging to the side of attachment to the intermediate and superior realms,
as well as that belonging to the side of pride, ignorance, views, and doubt regarding the inferior, intermediate, and superior realms.

A. I-11. By seven aspects, the dharma and vinaya poorly proclaimed by those outside of this [teaching] should be understood as being with fault: through the fault of lack of analytical derivation (*vyutpatti-doṣa*),...
through the fault of conduct,
through the fault of reliance,
and through the fault of intention;
By way of a fault in exertion,
a fault in the higher mind, and a fault in the higher wisdom.
Furthermore, an outsider grasps what he has heard; however,

because that [learning] conforms to the four perversions (*catur-viparyāsa*) and because it establishes discourses on the benefits of debate and release from [worldly] talk, the proficiency produced by it is inherently flawed.

Ethical discipline (*śīla*) is flawed because it is accompanied by failure in conduct and livelihood, or because it is itself not conducive to liberation (*anairyāṇika*). A friend is flawed because they teach a perverted path.
Seclusion (*viveka*) is flawed because the mind is afflicted by false intentions (*mithyā-saṃkalpa*).
The [meditative concentration] regarding the basis of exertion is flawed because it lacks skillful means.
That regarding the higher mind is flawed because one whose mindfulness is lost experiences mental distraction due to craving, pride, ignorance, and doubt.
That regarding the higher wisdom is flawed because it is impaired by the sixty-two types of views.
By contrast, in the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, these same seven points should be understood as being free from fault.
There are seven [procedures] that lead to the pacification of a legal dispute (*adhikaraṇa*) that has arisen among the monks.
The rest is as it appears in the *Vastusaṃgrahaṇī*.
In this regard, there are these seven formal legal procedures (*adhikaraṇa*):
the procedure for the determination of an offense committed in the presence of others, and the procedure for the determination of an offense committed in the past that has been forgotten.

(Śbh II 296) A.
II-1 It should be understood that there are three types of cultivation for a monk, comprised of eight factors, for the sake of abandoning all residual fetters without exception.
The cultivation of ethical discipline,
the cultivation of concentration, and the cultivation of wisdom.
The cultivation of ethical discipline is through right speech, right action, and right livelihood;
the cultivation of concentration is through right mindfulness and right concentration;
and the cultivation of wisdom is through right view, right intention, and right effort.
A. II-2. It should be understood that the establishment of the eight types of persons belonging to the side of purification is based upon correct application together with its fruit:
namely, the four who are entering the paths (*pratipannaka*) and the four who abide in the fruits (*phalastha*).
A. II-3. These two types of giving are to be understood as having eight aspects:
giving that is with fault and giving that is without fault.
In that regard, giving with fault is of seven aspects,
while that which is without fault is of one aspect.
There is giving that is faulty because it is impaired by laziness.
There is that which is faulty due to acting against one's will, belonging to one who fears poverty and desires wealth;
there is that which is faulty due to longing for the past;
and there is that which is faulty due to hankering after the future.
There is that which is faulty due to the fault of contempt;
there is that which is faulty due to the fault of desire for recognition;
and there is that which is faulty due to the desire for enjoyment.
Furthermore, faultless giving is that which is dedicated toward nirvāṇa and constitutes its equipment;
it conduces both to rebirth in a happy destiny for one whose mind is free from worldly desire, as well as to the attainment of great wealth.

One should understand that this person is of a lazy nature and of a nature that does not initiate vigor, because he manifests laziness during eight occasions by relying upon four bases, failing to apply himself with vigor.
(Śbh II 298) [This refers to] the dependence on alms-food, the duties to be performed, the walking and pacing, and the imbalance of the elements.
Having based himself upon these four points, at a time when there is excellent and abundant food and heaviness of the body, [he reflects as follows].

at the time of physical fatigue from meager and coarse food; at the time of wishing to apply oneself to duties while preserving one's strength; and at the time of exhaustion after having performed those duties.
When one desires to set out on a journey during the time of guarding against force;
when one has already set out during the time of fatigue from the road;
or when one is ill during the time of the onset of the suffering of disease.
At a time when one who has recovered from illness fears returning to exertion—
such is the person of a lazy nature,
as long as they do not obtain the basis for indolence.
Only his mere vigor is perceived;
when he encounters the basis for laziness, he very quickly manifests laziness.
Therefore, he is called one of a lazy nature.

By the opposite of this, one should understand that a person who, relying on these very four bases and exerting vigor during these same eight times, overcomes laziness, is one whose nature is characterized by initiated vigor.
Even when obtaining [favorable conditions], he exerts vigor despite the basis of laziness,
let alone when not obtaining them;
therefore, he is said to be "one whose nature is to have initiated vigor."
A. II-6 These eight, embraced by right aspirations, are the causes for a desirable rebirth.
For those who desire the arising of rebirth within the realm of desire, yet do not at all long for seclusion from desires, these lead to rebirth in the eight types of desirable places of rebirth.
The aspiration for the misfortune of humans is limited, consisting of the nature of giving and the nature of ethical discipline.

Likewise, the aspiration for the fortune of humans, or for the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-three, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, the Nirmāṇarati, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin realms, is limited, consisting of the nature of giving and the nature of ethical discipline.

The establishment of the four assemblies of those who have become gods should be understood through three reasons:
because they possess the state of being the foremost in designation,
and because they are universally worthy of offerings.
Because their mode of enjoyment is not dependent on others,
and because they have completely relinquished the pursuit of enjoyment—
it should be understood that for those who have become human beings, the establishment of the four assemblies is due to these four causes.
Because it has as its limit that which is based on the ground, because it has as its limit the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),

desire, exertion, and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding the forms that one sees and the manner in which one sees them— one who is engaged in the first three liberations perceives this as the path of application for the three liberations.

there, one sees forms that are limited or vast, beautiful or ugly, inferior or superior, which are external objects of the unconcentrated state and have come into range of vision;
having mastered them through mental attention directed toward the object of the sphere of concentration so that they no longer appear, [one perceives them].

He knows and sees those objects of meditative concentration through the aspect of calm abiding (*śamatha*); he knows and sees them through the aspect of insight (*vipaśyanā*), [namely, how those objects of meditative concentration are].

B. What is medical treatment?
It should be understood as being of four aspects.
Namely: skill regarding afflictions, skill regarding the origination of afflictions,
and skill regarding the abandonment of afflictions once they have arisen.
It is skill in the non-arising of a disease that has been abandoned once it has arrived.
Furthermore, the detailed analysis of these skills should be understood exactly as it is in the Sūtra.
What is the science of grammar?
It should be understood as having six aspects:
by way of the establishment of the designation of phenomena.
By way of the establishment of the designation of objects;
by way of the establishment of the designation of persons;
and by way of the establishment of the designation of time.
By way of the establishment of the designation of numbers,
and by way of the establishment of the basis for cordiality.
The summary verse (uddāna).

In brief, the basis of the word here consists of: phenomena (dharma), meaning (artha), persons (pudgala), time (kāla), number (saṃkhyā), and the locus (adhikaraṇa), along with their respective qualifiers (sakhila).
In that regard, the formal establishment of the designation of phenomena consists of the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes; and sound is endowed with five qualities:
it is non-vulgar, light, vigorous, coherent, and meaningful.
In this regard, the establishment of the designation of objects should be understood as being of ten aspects:
[the first is] by way of the establishment of the faculties.
By way of the establishment of the great elements, by way of the establishment of karma,
and by way of the establishment of thorough investigation.
By way of the establishment of non-dharma, by way of the establishment of dharma,
and by way of the establishment of prosperity.
By way of the determination of misfortune,
by way of the determination of enjoyment,
and by way of the determination of preservation.

namely, for the purpose of supporting and so forth;
for the purpose of moistening and so forth;

In this regard, it is established by way of seeking;
that is to say, for the purpose of searching and so forth.
In that regard, [it is] by way of the establishment of what is non-dharma (*adharmavyavasthāna*);

for example, the meaning of generosity, restraint, and so forth.
In that regard, from the perspective of the establishment of excellence,

for example, it has the sense of destruction, fear, dejection, and so forth.

A. What is the purity of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviśuddhi*) therein?
It should be understood as being of nine aspects.
For example, a certain person, having gone alone into seclusion, reflects upon the teachings as they were heard and mastered;
avoiding what is inconceivable, he reflects upon what is conceivable,
and he thoroughly understands both the provisional teaching and the definitive teaching.
He reflects by relying on the meaning, not by relying on the letter;
and he gains resolute conviction through some degree of faith.
One examines something with wisdom and reflects upon it firmly; one reflects upon it steadily and reflects upon it subtly.
And he brings that reflection to its conclusion,
not falling into despondency in the interim;
thus, by means of this ninefold purity, it is called "perfectly pure reflection."
B. What is the discernment of the objects of knowledge (*jñeyapravicaya*)?
It is the discernment of the object that is to be examined.
What is the object to be examined? That which is existent is examined as existent, and that which is non-existent is examined as non-existent; this is called the object to be examined.
B.
What is the real entity (*sad-vastu*) that is to be examined?
It should be understood as being of five kinds.
It exists as a specific characteristic, it exists as a general characteristic, it exists as a conventional characteristic, and it exists as a causal characteristic and a resultant characteristic.
(Śbh II 320) B.
I-1 What is that which exists by way of its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇasat*)?
That should be understood as threefold:

existing by way of the characteristic of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-lakṣaṇa-sat*), existing by way of the characteristic of signs (*nimitta-lakṣaṇa-sat*), and existing by way of the characteristic of the present (*vartamāna-lakṣaṇa-sat*).
What is that which exists by way of the characteristic of ultimate reality?
That ineffable reality which, among all phenomena, is the domain of supramundane gnosis and is characterized by non-establishment—
what is the existence of signs (*nimittasat*)?
It should be viewed through four aspects.
Wherever a name is apprehended and a thing is apprehended,
that name does not deviate from that thing, whether by way of deviation through error or by way of deviation due to impermanence.
And that designation functions unimpededly with respect to that object;
it does not follow along in some places nor turn away in others.
What is present existence?
That which has arisen and exists as cause and effect—
all this, when condensed into a single whole, is called "existent by way of its own characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇasat*).
B. I-2 What is existence by way of general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇasat*)?
It should also be understood as being of five kinds.

The general characteristic of birth, the general characteristic of the performance of functions, the general characteristic of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), the general characteristic of all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*), and the general characteristic of all phenomena (*dharma*). What is the general characteristic of birth?
It is the specific nature of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness within their own respective classes.
Having condensed them together, they are called the "general characteristic of birth.
What is the general characteristic of the performance of function?
Wholesome contaminated phenomena (*kuśala-sāsrava-dharma*) are characterized by a commonality through the general characteristic of the performance of function in the production of desirable results.

Just as wholesome factors are characterized by the common characteristic of bringing about a desired result, so too are unwholesome factors characterized by the common characteristic of bringing about an undesired result. Likewise, the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the factors of the path, and the factors conducive to enlightenment are characterized by the common characteristic of performing their respective functions for the attainment of awakening.
What is the general characteristic of all conditioned phenomena?
It is the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena.
What is the general characteristic of all contaminated phenomena?
The state of suffering belongs to all things subject to outflows.
What is the common characteristic of all phenomena?
It is the emptiness and selflessness of all phenomena.
This is what is called the general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).
B. I-3 What is the characteristic of convention (*saṃketalakṣaṇa*)?
That in which the sixfold discourse proceeds is to be understood as the characteristic of convention.
What is the sixfold discourse?
It is discourse connected with ownership and relationship,
and discourse that excludes this or that, or the one or the other.
Discourse based on convention, discourse based on aggregation,
and discourse that is not universal.
And the doctrine is impermanent.
What is discourse associated with ownership?
It is that discourse which is understood through the characteristics [of its objects] by means of their connection to an owner.
Not without a connection to an owner;
for example, when "birth" is mentioned, the statement "Whose is this birth? requires a connection to an owner.

There is the birth of form, the birth of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; yet when "form" is mentioned, discourse does not require a relationship with an owner, such as asking, "To whom does this form belong?
Just as with birth, so too should aging, duration, impermanence, and other such mental non-associated formations be understood according to their respective applications.
This is called discourse associated with a relationship to an owner.
And wherever that [designation] occurs, it should be understood as having the characteristic of convention.
What is discourse that avoids both identity and difference?
It is that discourse which serves neither to explain something by means of itself, nor to explain one thing by means of another.
It is said that "it is devoid of this and that other.

That discourse which uses a thing itself for the purpose of designating that very thing applies both to the characteristic of substance (*dravyalakṣaṇa*) and to the characteristic of convention (*saṃketalakṣaṇa*).
And that discourse which uses one thing for the purpose of designating another thing also applies both to the characteristic of substance and to the characteristic of convention.

Furthermore, this discourse which is neither [the designation] of that by itself nor of one thing by another proceeds entirely as a conventional characteristic (*saṃketalakṣaṇa*) for the purpose of designation.
And what is that discourse which proceeds as a substantial characteristic (*dravyalakṣaṇa*) for the purpose of designating that very same thing?
It is, for example, the discourse: "The solidity of earth."
How does it also operate with respect to conventional characteristics?
It is the statement that "roundness belongs to a stone.

Just as hardness is the characteristic of earth and roundness is the characteristic of a stone, so too is fluidity the characteristic of water, a globule the characteristic of oil, heat the characteristic of fire, a flame the characteristic of fire, motion the characteristic of wind, and velocity the characteristic of air.
How does discourse for the purpose of designating one thing by means of another occur when a substantial entity exists?
For example: "consciousness of the eye," "contact of the body," and so forth.
How does it occur when [the entity] exists only as a designation?
For example, [the speech] regarding the food, drink, vehicle, clothing, ornaments, and so forth of Buddhadatta or Guṇamitra.
How is it that such discourse, which is used for the designation of one thing by another, or of one thing by something else, functions exclusively as a conventional characteristic (*saṃketalakṣaṇa*)?

For instance: "the door of a house," "the wall of a house," "the mouth of a jar," "the side of a jar," "the chariot of an army," "the tree of a forest," "ten of a hundred," or "three of a decade," and so forth.
This is called the discourse that avoids both identity and difference.
(Śbh II 326) B.
I-3-c What is conventional discourse?
The conventional discourse on the designation of intrinsic nature pertains to the characteristics of the sixfold signs.
What are the sixfold characteristics of signs?

They are: the characteristic of the entity, the characteristic of the cognizable, the characteristic of the beautiful and so forth, the characteristic of benefit and so forth, the characteristic of the sign of conventional usage, and the characteristic of the sign of wrong practice and so forth.
What is the characteristic of the object? That which is grasped by consciousness.
What is the characteristic of the cognizable?
That which conduces to the arising of consciousness through mental attention—
what is its characteristic of being beautiful and so forth?
It is that which one grasps by means of contact.
What is the characteristic of favoring and so forth?
It is that which one grasps by means of feeling.
What is the characteristic of the cause for conventional expression?
What is the characteristic of the signs of wrong practice and so forth that one grasps through perception? It is that which one grasps through volition.
What is the discourse concerning the collective? It is the discourse that establishes intrinsic nature with respect to many things that are complete and assembled together.

For example, the discourse concerning a self (*ātman*) and so forth with respect to the internal [aggregates] of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; or the discourse concerning a house, a jar, an army, a forest, and so forth, with respect to external forms, odors, tastes, and tangibles as they are respectively situated.
What is non-pervasive discourse?
Whatever discourse persists in some cases and is excluded in others—
for example, the discourse "house" persists within a house but is excluded from villages, cities, kingdoms, and so forth.
The designation "jar" is excluded from jars, pots, bowls, and so forth;
the designation "army" is excluded from individual women, men, boys, girls, and so forth;
the designation "forest" is excluded from individual trees, roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth.
(Śbh II 328) B.
I-3-f What is the impermanent discourse?
It should be viewed through four aspects:
by way of differentiation, by way of non-differentiation, by way of volitional formation, and by way of transformation.
How is it [viewed] by way of differentiation?
For example, when a jar is broken, that which was called "jar" ceases to exist,
and the term "potsherd" appears.
How is this so by way of non-difference?

For example, when a powder or incense is prepared through the combination of various substances, the designation "various substances" disappears, and the designation "incense" or "powder" appears. How is this due to formative activity (*abhisaṃskāra*)?

For example, when a lump of gold has not yet been fashioned, once it has been transformed through craftsmanship, the designation "lump of gold" ceases and the designation "bracelet," "ring," or "armlet" appears. How does this occur through transformation?

For example, when food and drink have been digested, that which was called "food and drink" disappears, and what is called "excrement and urine" appears; such discourse of this kind should be understood as impermanent.
Thus, that wherein these six kinds of discourse proceed should be understood as the characteristic of convention;
this is called the characteristic of convention.
B. I-4. What is the characteristic of the cause (*hetulakṣaṇa*)?
In brief, it should be understood as being of five kinds.
It is the cause of the desirable, the cause of the undesirable, the cause of nourishment, the cause of engagement, and the cause of withdrawal.
What is the cause of the desirable?
It is wholesome phenomena associated with outflows (*sāsrava*).
What is the cause of the undesirable?
It is unwholesome phenomena.
What is the cause of nourishment?

Wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena that have arisen previously, when practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed, are called the cause for the nourishment of subsequently arisen wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena— those that arise later, later still, and are more nourished and most nourished.
What is the cause of occurrence?
That seed, or that latent impression (*vāsanā*), or that assistant by which the occurrence of various phenomena takes place— that is called their cause of occurrence.
What is the cause of cessation?

The path that brings about the subsiding of all things, leading to complete nirvāṇa and to perfect awakening—possessing its equipment, its application, its origination, and its fulfillment—is called the cause of cessation. This is due to the cessation of formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and the cessation of affliction (*saṃkleśa*).
This entire definition of the cause has been explained in detail; furthermore, its specific classification should be consulted in the investigation of cause and effect.
B. I-5. What is the characteristic of the fruit (*phalalakṣaṇa*)?
That which has arisen, been attained, been established, been perfected, and has proceeded from these five kinds of causes should be understood as the characteristic of the fruit.
B. II. What is the non-existent entity that is to be examined?
That too should be understood as having five characteristics.
It is non-existent as unarisen, non-existent as ceased, non-existent as mutually exclusive, non-existent in the ultimate sense, and absolutely non-existent.
What is non-existence as unarisen? It refers to future conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
What is non-existence through cessation? It is past conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). What is mutual non-existence?

That which is the state of being devoid of, the non-existence of, or the non-occurrence of other phenomena by means of another characteristic— this is what constitutes the ultimate non-existence of those other phenomena.
What, then, is that which does not exist ultimately?
What is that which is absolutely non-existent, established as an intrinsic nature by means of conventional discourse on the designation of intrinsic nature?
It is anything of this kind, such as the son of a barren woman and so forth.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of existence and likewise five kinds of non-existence.
(Śbh II 332) What is the fivefold existence?

There is the existence of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*), the existence of the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*), the existence of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*), the existence of specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), and the existence of inexpressible characteristics (*avaktavya-lakṣaṇa*).
Among these, the first is the ultimate characteristic;
the second is the characteristic of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpanna-lakṣaṇa*).

The third follows the characteristic of convention; the fourth follows the characteristic of the time periods, the characteristic of birth, the characteristic of aging, the characteristic of duration, the characteristic of impermanence,

the characteristic of suffering, the characteristic of emptiness, the characteristic of selflessness, the characteristic of entities, the characteristic of the cognizable, and the characteristic of the graspable.

Characteristics such as those of the auspicious and so forth, characteristics such as those of favoring and so forth, characteristics that serve as the basis for conventional usage, and characteristics that serve as the basis for false practice and so forth—
characteristics of this kind are to be understood as specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*).
Following these, there is the characteristic of the inexpressible, which consists of four modes of inexpressibility.
Because it does not exist, just as, for example, a person (pudgala) is neither different nor non-different from the aggregates (skandhas);
because of its profundity, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is ineffable,
and the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) of the Tathāgatas is inconceivable.

The domain of the Buddha is inconceivable; such as [the questions] "Does the Tathāgata exist after death? and so forth. Because they are associated with what is meaningless, those teachings which are not connected to the Dharma, to the goal, or to the holy life were not even taught by the Blessed One, even though he had fully awakened to them.
Likewise, by way of establishing the characteristics of phenomena, for example, suchness is inexpressible as being either different or non-different from conditioned formations.
(Śbh II 334) B. III-2 What are the five kinds of non-existence?

The non-existence of the characteristic of ultimate reality, the non-existence of the characteristic of independence, the non-existence of all specific characteristics in every respect, the non-existence of the characteristic of lack of distinction, and the non-existence of the characteristic of expressibility.
(Śbh II 337) Appendix IV:
Explanation of the Verses on the Intentional Meaning (*Ābhiprāyikārthagāthānirdeśa*)
(Śbh II 340) A. I-1.
One who has attained perfection in the trainings and has destroyed all doubts.
"Being asked, tell me the training, and what constitutes training within those trainings. Thus [he said].

The Blessed One was questioned by Brahmā with words of praise concerning his own fulfillment of the goal, which is unique in its attainment of the limit of all training precepts (*śikṣāpada*), and concerning his practice for the sake of others, which is unique in its capacity to sever the doubts of all sentient beings as they arise. [Brahmā asked: "What are the trainings, and how many are there?"
And how should one train in them?”

Then the Blessed One, with the intention of encouraging those who are of a lazy nature and intimidated by the many duties [of training], taught all the trainings collectively and in brief through three trainings:
namely, training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla*), training in higher mind (*adhicitta*), and training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*), O worthy one.
"Listen briefly to the three trainings and the training within them. Thus it is said.

In that regard, with reference to ethical discipline (*śīla*), mind (*citta*), and wisdom (*prajñā*), there is training in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*) through instruction in the application of non-distraction for one whose mind is distracted;

training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*) through instruction in the application of concentration for one whose mind is unconcentrated; and training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*) through instruction in the application of liberation for one whose mind is concentrated but not liberated.
Because they bring all the duties of yogins to completion,
these [three trainings] were taught by the Blessed One with the intention that they be included within those very three trainings.
Furthermore, regarding those trainings, the application by which one brings those trainings to completion is as follows: therein—(Śbh II 342)

(3) He should be endowed with the six limbs and possessed of the bliss of the four abidings; he should always be purified by the knowledge of the four aspects in each of the four [abidings]. Thus it is said.
By means of this verse, he demonstrates the application of those three trainings in their proper order.
Regarding the phrase "endowed with the six limbs," this refers to the training in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*); there are six limbs of the trainings.
He dwells possessed of ethical discipline (*śīlavān*).
Restrained by the Prātimokṣa vows,
perfected in conduct,
and perfected in range of activity.
Seeing danger even in the slightest faults, one undertakes and trains in the precepts; by these six factors, the fourfold purity of ethical discipline (*śīlaviśuddhi*) is elucidated.

In that regard, concerning the phrase "he dwells possessed of ethical discipline," the purity of ethical discipline that leads to liberation (*nairyāṇika-śīlatā*) is indicated by the expression "restrained by the Prātimokṣa vows."
For that which pertains to liberation is conducive to deliverance.
By the two phrases "endowed with proper conduct and sphere of activity," the purity of unexcelled ethical discipline is shown.
By the phrase "seeing danger even in the slightest faults," the purity of faultless ethical discipline is shown.
“Having undertaken them, he trains in the precepts” refers to the purity of unerring ethical discipline (*śīla*).

Thus, by means of the accomplishment of the six factors, relying on the application of training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*), the phrase “endowed with the fourfold happiness of stability” demonstrates the application of training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*).
The four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) constitute the fourfold stability of the mind.
And that [state] is called "bliss" because it is a dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
Regarding the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*), it is said: "One should always be pure through the fourfold knowledge regarding the four [truths].

This is because the training in higher wisdom is explained as the purity of the fourfold knowledge—impermanence and so forth—with respect to each of the four truths: suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
A. I-4: His roots shall be well-established, and he shall delight in the tranquility of the mind; joined with or dissociated from views—whether noble or evil views. Thus it is said.
By means of this verse, he demonstrates the sequential arising of the three trainings;
for the first training, that of higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*), is the root.
Because the latter two follow from that [first],
the second [stage] arises from the delight in the concentration of the mind through the sequence beginning with non-regret for one who possesses ethical discipline;
the third arises from the vision of reality as it is by one whose mind is concentrated, through the attainment of noble view and the separation from evil views.

A. I-5: One should be pure from the beginning, delight in meditative concentration, and be skilled in the truths; one should generate [the path], avoid [what is contrary], and cause the truth itself to increase. Thus it is said.
By means of this verse, he demonstrates the specific purity of those very three trainings in their respective order:
therein, "pure from the beginning" refers to the first;
"delighting in meditation" refers to the second.
“Skilled in the truths” refers to the third [truth].
Furthermore, “he should produce skill in the truths” is because of the production of the truth of the path;
“he should avoid” is because of the avoidance of the truths of suffering and its origin.

“*Bṛṃhayet* (one should cause to increase)” means that one increases (*bṛṃhaṇāt*) the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*) by repeatedly abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*) through the stages of weak, medium, and intense [cultivation].
Among the training rules (*śikṣāpada*), there exist four destinies (*gati*) within the three [realms].
Having avoided two destinies, one should fully accomplish two destinies. Thus it is said.
By means of this verse, regarding the bases of training known as ethical discipline (*śīla*), mind (*citta*), and wisdom (*prajñā*), through the accomplishment or failure of these trainings,

there arise— according to their possibility— the four destinies that constitute their results: namely, in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the fortunate rebirth comprised of gods and humans is the fruit of the perfection of higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*).
In the desire realm alone is the miserable destiny, which is the fruit of failure in higher morality subsumed under the other destinies;
in the form and formless realms is the higher destiny, which is the fruit of higher mind subsumed under the celestial destiny;
and the destiny of nirvana, which is not included within the three realms, is the fruit of higher wisdom.

Excluding the first two among these destinies— the good and bad destinies— one should accomplish the latter two, the upward destiny and the destiny of nirvāṇa, by means of both the mundane and supramundane paths; this is what he demonstrates.

A. II Ms. 1 *b5R, MsG.26b3M, P.247a7, D.214b1, N.230b5, Ch.367c7 (7): Two are established as pairs; one leads to nirvāṇa. They are cultivated progressively, as a basis, and either undifferentiated or differentiated. Thus it is said.
In this verse, the training in higher ethics and the training in higher mind appear respectively as the causal basis for the two trainings of higher mind and higher wisdom;
the middle [training] appears as the causal basis for the two trainings of higher wisdom and the training in higher ethics as comprised by the meditative restraint (*dhyāna-saṃvara*);
and the highest [training] appears as the causal basis for the single state of nirvāṇa.
And he demonstrates that [meditation] upon the factors both individually and collectively, as far as possible.
"Because one would be free from remorse at first and happy afterwards,
this is the primary of all trainings in which a wise person should train. Thus it is said.
By means of this verse, it is shown that the training according to the higher morality proceeds by way of being a successive cause for non-regret and so forth, serving as a superior basis.
It demonstrates that.
(9) "Since one who is endowed with the arising of virtue should purify knowledge from that [source],
it is the middle among all trainings wherein the wise person should train. Thus it is said.

It demonstrates that the training in higher mind (*adhicittam-śikṣā*) serves as the proximate cause for the supreme training, through the sequential arising of distinguished roots of virtue consisting of cultivation and so forth.
"From whatever [object] one should liberate the mind and cease conceptual proliferation—that is the supreme of all trainings, wherein the wise person should train. (A. II-3)
He demonstrates the preeminence of the training in higher wisdom because it is the proximate cause for nirvāṇa.
(11) "The practice leading to impurity, as well as that leading to a happy rebirth—
this first practice has been described, and it is considered to be exclusive. Thus it is said.
Just as the training in higher ethical discipline, when failed, is a cause for an unfortunate rebirth, while when accomplished, it is a cause for a fortunate rebirth,
so too it can be accomplished even by itself, without the two subsequent trainings.
He shows that.
(12) "The path leading to purification is not one that leads to the ultimate end; this middle way is said to be neither exclusively [one-sided]. Thus it is said.
Just as the middle way, through the purification consisting in detachment from the desire realm, leads toward purity,
it does not lead to ultimate and complete purification because there is no detachment from the higher realms and because the latent tendency of sensual passion has not been completely eliminated.
This demonstrates how [liberation] cannot be accomplished by a single factor alone, without a superior [path] and without a beginning.
II-4-c) The path leading to purification is that which leads to the ultimate limit of all things.
This supreme path has been taught; it is neither dual nor solitary.

This means that it is the state of being free from passion for the three realms, the permanent eradication of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and how all those supreme qualities are ultimately attained.
This demonstrates that even without the former two, it cannot be accomplished by one alone.
He who trains and he who does not train— both of these are considered wise.
By this half-verse, [the author] demonstrates the characteristic of a wise person through training correctly in these three trainings, rather than training incorrectly:
"He who trains and he who does not train—both of them are considered fools. (14b)
With the second half-verse, he demonstrates the characteristic of a fool regarding both false trainings and the absence of training altogether.

(15) "Through the relinquishing of grasping, through the departure of *dauṣṭhulya*, and likewise through the direct perception of the object of knowledge, the undertaking of training is threefold. Thus it is said.

He demonstrates that through which the three trainings are accomplished in their respective order: by the renunciation of possessions such as home and wife; by the abandonment of that corruption which is the adversary of meditative concentration; and by the direct realization of the reality of the objects of knowledge characterized by the Four Noble Truths.
(16a) "Those with objects and those without objects are conjoined as subtle and gross."

By this half-verse, he demonstrates the distinction between the two supreme [truths] and the first [truth] respectively, by way of their having or not having an object of cognition, and by way of their being subtle or gross.
(16b) Those who have withdrawn through the sound of the vow of renunciation and through focused application. // Thus it is said. //

By the latter half [of the verse], it demonstrates, respectively, that the initial, intermediate, and superior [levels] are accomplished through the fulfillment of one’s vow, accomplished through the seclusion of body and mind, and accomplished through internal wise attention based on the voice of another.
(17) "One training may be alone, another may be accompanied by a second; one may indeed be accompanied by a third—the wise person should transcend these. Thus it is said.
He demonstrates the first as solitary and alone;
the middle, however, does not exist without that [first], and the highest does not exist without those two.
And the transcendence of these [obstacles] should be understood as belonging to the Arhat who is beyond training (aśaikṣa).
(18) One should be unshaken in morality, having undertaken the training vows; one’s conduct should be beyond reproach, avoiding the five points. Thus it is said.

“With unimpaired morality regarding the trainings” shows that he dwells possessed of morality. “He should be one who has undertaken the vows” refers to being restrained by the Prātimokṣa restraint. “With irreproachable conduct” refers to the non-failure of conduct.
“Free from the five places” refers to the non-failure of one’s range of activity (*gocarāvipatti*).
There are five places that are not the proper range for a monk: the royal court, a slaughterhouse, a tavern, a brothel, and a cemetery.
In that context, "slaughterhouse" (ghoṣa) should be understood as a place of killing;
for there, the slaughter of sheep and other animals, which is a habitual evil deed, is carried out by those such as the bell-ringers and butchers.
A. IV-2: There is no offense; then there is emergence; then freedom from remorse; then remorse. Thus it is said.
He demonstrates the perception of danger even in faults as small as an atom.
In this regard, as one who has emerged [from a fault] is so, so is one free from remorse; as one who feels remorse is so, so is one who has not committed an offense.
One should master the training therein and practice it with sincerity.
"He trains by undertaking the precepts"—
this is what he demonstrates.
One should not practice renunciation for the sake of life, nor should one destroy it.
One should always remain established in practice and be one whose discipline is active. Thus it is said.

By this verse, through its four lines, it demonstrates respectively the constancy of ethical discipline, the firmness of ethical discipline, the state of constant practice, and the state of constant engagement.
A. IV-4.
"One should first purify one's thesis; one should also purify one's livelihood.
By this half-verse, he demonstrates the purification of conduct and livelihood.
For conduct (*ācāra*) consists in practicing preceded by a formal commitment (*pratijñā*); thus it is called a "commitment.
As it is said: "Having abandoned the two extremes, one should abandon [even] the vow (*praṇidhāna*). (21b)

By avoiding both the pursuit of sensual pleasure and the pursuit of self-mortification, as well as the dedication toward [rebirth in] heaven and so forth, he demonstrates precisely the purity of ethical discipline.
One should not, under any circumstances, crave those phenomena that create obstacles;
one should not tolerate those phenomena that arise which cause agitation of the mind. Thus it is said.

By means of this verse, he demonstrates the purity of training through two aspects: by showing the lack of attachment to those factors that obstruct the purity of training—such as not guarding the doors of the sense faculties—by viewing them as defects; and by not tolerating unwholesome thoughts such as sensual desire and ill-will that arise and disturb the mind.
Neither too slack nor too strained, with mindfulness always well-established,
one should practice the pure holy life by means of both the fundamental and the proximate [precepts]. Thus it is said.

By avoiding mild regret and regret for what is not a ground for regret, and by avoiding the loss of mindfulness, he illuminates the purity of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) during both the time of completion and the time of application.
"He shall be one who has initiated vigor and is always firm in his prowess; he shall practice heedfulness, being well-established in its five factors. Thus it is said.
Thus he demonstrates the excellence of the purification of training through the vigor that is irreversible in its application and armor, and through the practice of the five kinds of heedfulness.
In this regard, fivefold heedfulness consists of [the factors] accompanied by the past, the future, the present, what was to be done previously, and the accompanying [practice].
One should be one whose virtue is concealed and whose evil is revealed; one should be content with robes and other requisites, whether they be coarse or excellent.
One should maintain one's livelihood with little, and one should subsist even on coarse food;
free from the afflictions, one should adopt the ascetic qualities for the sake of tranquility.

By means of these two verses, he demonstrates the purity of training through the avoidance of the desire for fame— which serves as the cause for great ambition and lack of contentment— and through the avoidance of that great ambition and lack of contentment themselves, which are the causes that obstruct the purity of training.
(27) One may be endowed with proper deportment and observe moderation in receiving [alms];
however, one should never adopt an artificial deportment for that purpose. Thus it is said.

Through the perfection of the modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*), through the absence of hypocrisy toward others, and through knowing the proper measure of receiving [alms], one attains purity of training (*śikṣāviśuddhi*) by taking up the requisites for maintaining life until the end of the holy life (*brahmacaryavāsa*).
(28) One should not boast of one's own actual virtues, nor cause others to do so; furthermore, one should not display those virtues or a desire for gain by means of some pretext.

One should not make a request from others through importunity; one should not accumulate gain here by means of gain, even when that gain has been obtained in accordance with the Dharma. Thus it is said.
By means of these two verses, he demonstrates a specific purity of training through the avoidance of flattery, hinting, belittling, and the desire to acquire gain by means of gain.
One should not be greedy for gain, nor for honor in any way;
and one should not adhere to views that involve superimposition or denial. Thus it is said.
He demonstrates a specific excellence of purity through non-attachment to gain and honor, and through non-adherence to the five kinds of wrong views.
(31) One should not rely upon the Lokāyata mantras, which are devoid of meaning; one should never hold onto what is useless, nor should one possess an excess of bowls or robes. Thus it is said.

By not adhering to the false views of the heterodox treatises external to this [teaching], which are based on the five aggregates of clinging, and by avoiding the wearing of excessive bowls and robes out of greed for gain and honor, he demonstrates the purity of training through the purity of its causes.
(Śbh II 360) A. V-1-g.
One should not associate with householders, for it increases the afflictions.
"But one should associate with the noble ones to purify one's knowledge. Thus it is said.
It demonstrates purification through the avoidance of the cause of the discordant side and the cultivation of the cause of the remedial side.
One should not form a circle of friends that causes grief and distraction;
nor should one tolerate the arisen afflictions that give rise to suffering. Thus it is said.

It demonstrates this: just as association with householders, by causing grief and distraction, increases afflictions and is a cause of suffering; and just as association with noble ones, through the non-endurance of the afflictions that give rise to suffering, is a cause for the antidote.
One whose vows are impaired should never consume what has been given out of faith; nor should one ever reject the true Dharma in any way whatsoever. Thus it is said.
By not being greedy for gain and honor, by not adhering to wrong views, and by not falling away from what has been given in faith through not rejecting the true Dharma,
he demonstrates a distinction of purity by avoiding the causes for the future arising of attachment to sensual desires and wrong views.
(35) One should remain effortless and happy when others stumble or commit a fault;
however, having recognized one's own stumbling fault, one should disclose it again. Thus it is said.

By avoiding the effort of looking for faults in others, by generating a state of mental well-being through non-distraction from one's own side of wholesome qualities, and by revealing one's own faults through the thorough knowledge of them, he demonstrates the purity of his training by means of being free from pride.
(36) And having fallen into an offense, one should settle it according to the Dharma.
Thus, one should be skillful and act for oneself in matters that ought to be done.
He demonstrates purity both by emerging from transgressions and by abandoning the desire to accept service and attendance from others.
(37) One who has faith and perceives faults should never, in any way, deny the power and the teachings of the Buddhas and their disciples.
Purity is elucidated through the perfection of faith and by not seeing faults even when falsely accused.
(38) Regarding dharmas that are profoundly deep and beyond the sphere of ratiocination,
one should not abandon the ancient tradition and cling to one's own personal views. Thus it is said.
The excellence of purification is also elucidated by way of abandoning the persistence in adhering to one's own views.
(39) One should dwell in seclusion in a remote lodging; with firm vigor and exertion, one should cultivate wholesome qualities. Thus it is said.

By means of the seclusion of body and mind, by resorting to lodgings and seats conducive to meditative concentration, by cultivating exclusively pure dharmas while abandoning unwholesome discursive thoughts,

and by being invincible against secondary afflictions such as lethargy and agitation due to well-secured application, he demonstrates the specific method for training in the higher mind (*adhicitta*).

(40) Without desire yet having generated desire, without malice yet possessing the spirit of revulsion; free from torpor yet appearing as if drowsy at the proper time, he is peaceful yet not remaining [in that state].
Free from regret yet possessing regret, free from doubt yet still doubting, he should be at all times and in every way disciplined and possessed of right application. Thus it is said.

By means of these two verses, one pacifies the mind by avoiding the hindrances of sensual desire, ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-remorse, and doubt through the longing for wholesome qualities and the revulsion toward sense pleasures;
and by employing sleep at the proper time as a sign of fitness for application to the side of the wholesome;
and by attending to signs that inspire serene confidence when the mind is sinking or suspected of sinking, so that it remains settled in tranquility.
And for one who has entered the course of training, prior to the commission of an offense, because of the absence of such transgression, because of being accompanied by remorse,
and because of desiring ever-higher distinctions, he demonstrates the purification of the training in higher mind through right application characterized by respect and continuity.
(42) It is indeed impelling and awakening, as well as another that is conjoining;
likewise, it is indicative and gladdening, and another that is sporting.
(43) "The supreme ritual is said to be squeezing and lubricating; it generates sensual passion, so the wise man should avoid it. Thus [it is said].

Here, the specific excellence of the purity of training is elucidated through the abandonment of the eightfold conceptualization—which generates passion for sexual union—beginning from its initial arising and proceeding in sequence until its final consummation.

Among these, "impelling conceptualization" (*nudana-vikalpa*) is that which, associated with improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*), impels the mind toward an object that incites passion. "Awakening conceptualization" (*bodhana*) is that which, associated with the outburst of awakened passion, is directed toward that very same object.
The fetter (*saṃyojana*) is that which seeks out that very object; the sign-grasper (*naimittika*) is that which apprehends various beautiful signs in that very object;
and the affectionate (*snehana*) is that which, once that object has been obtained, is associated with attachment (*adhyavasāna*).
The playful [desire] is that which proceeds through various modes toward the longing for diverse enjoyments regarding that very same object;
the crushing [desire] is that which occurs at the time of the union of the two pairs of organs;
and the supremely adhesive [desire] is that which occurs at the time of the discharge of impurity.
Sensual pleasures cause lack of satisfaction and are likewise shared by many;
they are the causes of unrighteousness and likewise increase craving.
(45) Desires, which are to be avoided by the virtuous, which quickly lead to dissolution, which depend upon conditions, and which are the ground of negligence— [thus it is said].

By means of eight aspects, he demonstrates the method for abandoning sensual desire through the vision of the defects of sensual pleasures, as appropriate, both in the present life and in future lives.
(46) Sensual pleasures are like skeletons, and likewise comparable to lumps of flesh;
they are like torches of straw and likewise comparable to flames of fire.
(47) They are like venomous serpents, and likewise like dreams;
they are similar to ornaments obtained through begging, and like the fruits of trees.
(48a) Having thus fully understood sensual desires, one should not be greedy for them in any way whatsoever.

Here, he demonstrates the nature of the faults (*ādīnava*) in sensual pleasures through comparisons established by all the world, based on the eight previously mentioned faults such as causing lack of satisfaction.
This is for the purpose of showing: "How indeed could a wise person be greedy for those things in which so many faults have been thus revealed?
Among these, they cause lack of satisfaction because they are like a skeleton.
They are common to many because they are like a mass of flesh;
they are causes of unrighteousness because, like a grass torch, they persist in burning without being cast away;
and they increase craving because, like a pit of fire, they possess the common characteristic of generating craving.
They are to be avoided by the virtuous because they are like venomous serpents;
they quickly pass away because they are like dreams;
and they depend on conditions because they are like borrowed ornaments.
The stages of negligence are like fruit at the top of a tree.
One should constantly hear the true Dharma, reflect upon it, and also cultivate it. Having first seen both the peaceful and the sublime, one should become exclusively devoted to cultivation.
Having abandoned the depravity of the afflictions, one should delight in their abandonment.
(50) One should be an investigator regarding the signs; one should be intent upon application;
and one should effect detachment from desire as well as detachment from form.

(51) One should effect the clear realization of the truths and likewise attain complete detachment; one may attain nirvana in this very life through the destruction of the substrata of existence. Thus it is said.

Here, through the seven types of mental attention beginning with that which discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī*), the purification of the training in higher wisdom—which has as its fruit the nirvana with remainder and the nirvana without remainder—is elucidated by means of the purification of the mundane and supramundane paths.
Among these, the mental attention that discerns characteristics is elucidated by the mention of hearing and reflecting upon the true Dharma (*saddharma*);
the mental attention consisting of resolute belief (*adhimokṣika*) is elucidated by the mention of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Through the cultivation of resolute conviction regarding that [object], one first perceives the calm and the gross; this is the stage of seclusion (*prāvivekya*). One should become exclusively devoted to cultivation; this is the stage of gathering joy (*ratisaṃgrāhaka*).
"One should be an investigator" refers to the mental application of investigation (*mīmāṃsā-manaskāra*).
"One should be intent on practice" means being established in practice (*prayoga-niṣṭha*).
And one should effect detachment from the realm of desire (*kāma-vairāgya*) as well as detachment from the realm of form (*rūpa-vairāgya*).
One should effect the clear realization of the truths and indeed all detachment; this is the fruit of the culmination of both mundane and supramundane application.
The exposition of the verses concerning the intended meaning is completed.
